For all who followed the Apostolic doctrines [ὅσοι μὲν γὰρ τοῖς Ἀποστολικοῖς ἕπονθο δόγμασιν] were not promoted to any office, etc. Likewise Sozomen says of the Egyptian monks that, because of their piety, the people judged their doctrine, which was opposed to the heresy of the Arians, to be true, and the Arians' doctrine false: since the truth of our opinion followed from their testimony, which was more sound [ὡς τῆς δόξης ἡμῶν τὸ ἀληθὲς ἔπεστο ἐκ τῆς μαρτυρίας ἀληθεῖς ὑγιέστερον]; the people also followed the opinion of these monks, and thought their testimony (namely about whether that doctrine was false or true) to be true. Sozomen elsewhere says that the peoples in Syria, Cappadocia and the neighbouring regions clung tenaciously to the orthodox doctrine and abominated the heresy of the Arians, just as the Egyptians, following their monks, were set against the Arians [Αἰγύπτιοι τοῖς παρ' αὐτοῖς μοναχοῖς ἑπόμενοι ἐναντίως εἶχον πρὸς τὰς Ἀρείας]. (For in book 4, ch. 9, he himself expresses what here he calls τοῖς μοναχοῖς ἑπόμενοι by saying that the Egyptians, following their monks, opposed themselves to the Arians.) This is what the phrase to follow the true sense of the divine Word means. From this itself it is better understood what the true state of the question is between us and the Arminians. And so it is plain from this chapter too that I have not calumniated the Arminians, nor falsely charged them with those two doctrines, since they themselves confess them. Judge now, best Reader, whether the Arminians rightly close their chapter in Book 1 of the Vindiciae, p. 18, with these words: And this is the first thing by which Vedel's ignorance appears. Is such a shameful slip at the very threshold of the Arcana a bad omen? Or rather, whether I with every right ought to close this chapter with these words: From this, therefore, as also from the preceding chapter, appears the execrable and intolerable impiety of these pretending Antitrinitarians, and a desperate cause. Is such a shameful slip at the very threshold of the Vindiciae a bad omen?

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: Examen Capitis Tertii lib. 1. Vindiciarum.
units.tr: Examination of the Third Chapter of the First Book of the Vindiciae.

units.la: 1. Arminiani fatentur se docere in Apologiâ: Liberum esse debere unicuique interpretari Scripturam interpretatione tali, quam quisquisensui & menti Dei optimè quadrare credit, adeòque etiam Deum colere eo cultus modo quem credit sibi præscriptum esse à Deo. Impostura & fraudulentia Arminianorum circa hoc dogma.
units.tr: 1. The Arminians confess in their Apology that everyone ought to be free to interpret Scripture in whatever way he believes best agrees with the sense and mind of God, and therefore to worship God in whatever mode of worship he believes God has prescribed. The imposture and fraudulence of the Arminians concerning this doctrine.

units.la: 2. Fatentur se docere; Hanc libertatem concedendam esse in omnibus quæ non solùm controversa sunt inter Christianos, sed etiam controverti possunt in futurum. Eam permittendam esse omnibus Christianis, & quidem quousque eam quisque sibi concedi amat. Et sic in omnibus quæ vera esse aliquis sibi persuadet. 3. Arminiani sicco pede transeunt id quod circa fundamentum libertatis istius & tolerantia mutuæ ipsis objectum erat. 4. Fatentur se docere eam libertatem Hæreticis concedendam esse. 5. Fatentur se statuere eam permittendam esse Enthusiastis & fanaticis. 6. Fatentur se docere tales omnes interpretationes non esse peccatum, sed sed cum summâpietate conjunctas. 7. Item : ab ejusmodi libertate Prophetandi nihil periculi imminere.
units.tr: 2. They confess that they teach this liberty must be granted in all matters that are not only controversial among Christians but may also be controverted in future. It is to be allowed to all Christians, indeed as far as each one wishes it to be granted to himself, and so in all things that a person persuades himself are true. 3. The Arminians pass over with dry feet what was objected to them concerning the foundation of this liberty and of mutual toleration. 4. They confess that they teach this liberty must be granted to heretics. 5. They confess that they hold it should be permitted to enthusiasts and fanatics. 6. They confess that they teach all such interpretations are not sin, but are joined with the highest piety. 7. Likewise: no danger threatens from such a liberty of prophesying.

units.la: 1. CApite Tertio conquestus eram de doctrinâ ipsorum circa Libertatem Prophetandi;& quidem objeceram ipsis dogmata quorum ipsos merito pudere debebat ob horrorem quem incutiunt omnibus qui ipsorum labe infecti non sunt. Videamus quid ad singula respondeant. Primum dogma est : Liberum esse debere unicuique interpretari scripturam interpretatione tali quam quis sensui & menti Dei optime quadrare credit: adeoque etiam Deum colere eo cultus modo quem credit sibi praescriptum a Deo esse. Non negant : sed hic mihi vide, Candide Lector, fraudulentiam eorum. Quia enim vident ista verba talia esse quae Libertinismum eorum in doctrinâ nimis manifeste produnt:ideò in statu Quaestionis quem formant, ea plane omittunt, eo fine ut Lectorem,qui non conferet scriptum meum cum responso eorum,decipiant. Itaque transeunt illud, & in transitu calce me feriunt & dicunt: Hoc caput tertium Arcanorum tot concatenatas ineptias habet, ut pœniteat pene eas consectari ac numerare. Ad unam,inquiunt,&praecipuam hanc redeunt omnes:Libertatem Prophetandi extendendam esse ad omnia controversa dogmata, non solum ea quae controversa sunt sed etiam in futurum controverti possunt : eamque omnibus Christianis permittendam esse, quousque eam quisque sibi concedi amat. Vbi unuiquisque videt eos omittere, in statu quaestionis formando, primum dogma sibi à me objectum,quod à secundo & reliquis omninò distinctum est. Nam in primo agitur de formâ quam libertati prophetandi assignant, & indicatur quid per prophetiam, item per libertatem intelligant. At vero secundum,nec non reliqua, agunt de objecto, seu de rebus in quibus illam libertatem concedunt, nec non de subjecto, non solùm generali sed etiam speciali ( quod in statu quaestionis non exprimunt utpote nimis quàm odiosum ) denique de adjuncto & effecto illius.Sed de hac fraude eorum videri possunt etiam Prolegomena Partis Tertiae cap.5. §. 2.
units.tr: 1. In the third chapter I complained of their doctrine concerning the liberty of prophesying, and indeed I had objected to them doctrines of which they ought rightly to be ashamed, because of the horror they strike in all who are not infected with their stain. Let us see how they answer each point. The first doctrine is: Everyone ought to be free to interpret Scripture in whatever interpretation he believes best agrees with the sense and mind of God, and therefore to worship God in whatever mode of worship he believes has been prescribed to him by God. They do not deny it; but look here, kind reader, at their dishonesty. For since they see that these words plainly betray their libertinism in doctrine, they therefore omit them altogether when they frame the state of the question, with the aim of deceiving the reader who does not compare my writing with their answer. So they pass over that point, and in passing they strike me on the heel and say: This third chapter of the Arcana has so many linked absurdities that one is almost sorry to pursue and count them. They all come back, they say, to this one chief point: that the liberty of prophesying must be extended to all controverted doctrines, not only to those that are controverted but also to those that may be controverted in future; and that it must be granted to all Christians, as far as each one wishes it to be granted to himself. Here everyone sees that in framing the state of the question they omit the first doctrine objected to by me, which is entirely distinct from the second and the rest. For the first treats of the form they assign to the liberty of prophesying, and indicates what they understand by prophesying and likewise by liberty. But the second and the remaining ones deal with the object, that is, the matters in which they grant that liberty, and also with the subject, not only general but also particular (which in the state of the question they do not express, since it would be too odious), and finally with its accessory and effect. On this fraud of theirs, see also the Prolegomena of Part Third, chapter 5, section 2.

units.la: 2. Secundum igitur dogma est: Libertatem Prophetandi hanc concedendam esse in omnibus quae non solùm controversa sunt inter Christianos; sed etiam controverti possunt in futurum : Eamque permittendam esse omnibus Christianis: quousque eam quisque sibi concedi amat. Et sic in omnibus interpretationibus quas veras esse sibi aliquis persuadet. Fatentur; sed addunt incrustationem : Ita est, inquiunt, si modo per controversa dogmata intelligantur omnia & sola ista dogmata quae idcirco tantum controversa sunt, quòd nec ἐπιτῶς eorum necessitas decisa cisa sit in Scripturis, nec per evidentem & exceptione omni majorem consequentiam ex Scripturis possit concludi. Verùm hæc incrustatio nulla est. Nam in Apologia sua docent Nulla omninò dogmata quæ inter Christianos controversa sunt, & in futurum controverti possunt esse necessaria ad salutem, ut videbimus infra cap.7. ubi Lectorem monebimus de alia insigni fraude & impostura horum hominum, ex qua apparebit eos contra propriam conscientiam agere. Ex altera parte Libertatem hanc urgent in omnibus illis quæ non necessaria sunt ad salutem. Itaque hoc effugium inane & mera fraus est. Porrò quia Arminiani hoc suum dogma, nimirum Libertatem hanc communem esse debere & eò usque extendi quò eam quisque sibi concedi amat, confirmaverant hoc argumento: quia alioquin vis inferatur conscientiis Apol. c.24. f.277. a. & à me responsum erat: hoc non esse vim inferre conscientiæ Hæreticorum quando iis non permittitur ut Scripturam sacram pro lubitu suo & non secundùm mentem Spiritus S. interpretentur,&c. igitur ut hoc eludant utuntur misero suo coccysmo & retorsione in Vedelium; quod quàm nugax impertinens & sophisticum sit, ostendimus Par. III. prolegem.c.4. §.5.
units.tr: 2. The second doctrine, then, is: This liberty of prophesying is to be granted in all matters that are not only controversial among Christians, but may also be controverted in future; and it is to be permitted to all Christians as far as each one wishes it to be granted to himself. And so in all interpretations that a person persuades himself are true. They confess this, but add a qualification: It is so, they say, provided that by controverted doctrines are understood all matters, and only those doctrines which are controverted for this reason alone, that their necessity has not been decided in Scripture, nor can it be concluded from Scripture by evident consequence greater than every exception. But this qualification is worthless. For in their Apology they teach that no doctrines at all that are controverted among Christians, and may be controverted in future, are necessary to salvation, as we shall see below in chapter 7, where we will warn the reader of another notable fraud and imposture of these men, from which it will appear that they act against their own conscience. On the other hand, they press this liberty in all those matters that are not necessary to salvation. Therefore this evasion is empty and pure fraud. Furthermore, since the Arminians had supported this doctrine of theirs, namely that this liberty ought to be common and extended as far as each one wishes it to be granted to himself, with this argument: because otherwise violence is done to consciences (Apol. c. 24, p. 277 a), and I had answered that this is not doing violence to the conscience of heretics when they are not permitted to interpret Holy Scripture at their own pleasure and not according to the mind of the Holy Spirit, etc., therefore, to evade this, they use their wretched cocksmo and retort it upon Vedelius. How trifling, irrelevant and sophistical this is, we have shown in Part III, Prolegomena, chapter 4, section 5.

units.la: 3. Objeceram ipsis quoque ibidem, eos libertatis prophetandi, tolerantiæ mutuæ, & communionis seu fraternitatis spiritualis fundamentum hoc ponere: quia Hæretici non aliter in conscientiâ suâ deprehendunt: seu studium bonæ conscientiæ atque innoxiæ vitæ. Et refutaram illud ex eo, quia id non sit studium bonæ conscientiæ & innoxiæ vitæ, quod non ad normam boni h. e. veritatem & voluntatem Dei in verbo ejus revelatam revera compositum & institutum est. Ad hoc, quod non exigui momenti est, hi homines ne quidem respondent. Quid autem bona conscientia ipsis sit vidimus Par. III. Arcan. lib.1. c.3. §.4.
units.tr: 3. I had objected to them also in the same place that they lay down, as the foundation of the liberty of prophesying, of mutual toleration, and of spiritual communion or fellowship, this: because heretics do not otherwise find themselves in their conscience; or the zeal for a good conscience and an innocent life. And I refuted it on the ground that this is not zeal for a good conscience and an innocent life, which has not really been composed and established according to the rule of the good, that is, the truth and the will of God revealed in his Word. To this, which is of no small weight, these men do not even reply. But what a good conscience is to them we have seen in Part III, Arcana, book 1, chapter 3, section 4.

units.la: 4. Quartum dogma est: Eam libertatem permittendam Hæreticis sic communiter à totâ Ecclesiâ dictis. Hoc etiam non negant, sed fatentur, ac defendere conantur coccysmo suo de Vedelio cum suis. Et quia dixeram sermonem esse de Hæreticis sic communiter à totâ Ecclesiâ dictis, quales v. g. sunt Antitrinitarii: hinc sophisticantur illi argumento à fallibilitate Ecclesiæ, per quam fieri possit ut erret Ecclesia in judicio de Hæresi & Hæretico & pro Hæresi veritatem condemnet. Sed hoc inane quoque & frivolum est. Nam etsi Ecclesia in hoc mundo errare possit, tamen ista fallibilitas non semper è potentiâ in actum educitur: sed contrà rectè & verè judicat quando illud judicium verbo Dei conforme est; & sic in eo ipso judicio quod verbo Dei revera conforme est, est extra erroris periculum posita. Verùm de hac re copiosè egimus ante hac in Rationali Theologico lib. 3. capp. 6. 7. 9. ubi de judicio intellectus circa res fidei egimus, ac speciatim hanc quaestionem decidimus cap. 9. an'ne judicium infallibile intellectus adeoque etiam Ecclesiae detur? Saltem hoc addam, ne Arminiani conquerendi occasionem se habere putent, quasi à me quicquam praetermissum sit quod ad rem faciat & responsum mereatur. Excipient enim illi, prout quidem faciunt c. 1. Vind. p. 11. Si Ecclesia in eo capite controversia non errat, tum ratio ut detur necesse est. At ratio si detur tum aut illa ratio est extra erroris aleam, aut non; & sic in infinitum. item, hinc inde in Vindiciis suis ogganniunt: Quo judice? an quia tu ineptissimus homo ita censes? Respondeo: Omninò necesse est dari argumentum seu fundamentum quo nitatur istud judicium Ecclesiae; quod argumentum si ex verbo Dei verè desumtum est, extra erroris aleam positum est. h. e. erroneum esse non potest. Nam quod verbo Dei verè conforme est, erroneum non est. Nec tamen sic dabitur progressus in infinitum, nec opus est ut de judice laboretur: si modò verum est, quod ipsi dicunt in dedicatione Vindiciarum suarum, à quolibet salutis suae studioso omnium quae incidere possunt litium ac Controversiarum de fide & vitâ decisionem fieri posse. Vbi autem lis rectè decisa est, certè non datur progressus in infinitum, nec judex deest. Verba Arminianorum ibi sunt haec: Reformationis primum ac praecipuum fundamentum est, Scripturam Sanctam solam esse normam ac regulam fidei ac vitae nostrae, ad quam OMNIVM quae incidere possunt litium ac controversiarum de Religione sive de fide ac vita nostra decisio fieri debet propter ejus divinam perfectionem; & AQVOLIBET salutis suae studioso fieri POTEST, propter ejus clarissimam perspicuitatem in rebus omnibus scitu, creditu, factu ad salutem necessaris. Vbi Arminiani plus dant mihi quàm opus habeo, ad ostendendum eos falsum dicere, cum ajunt, sic dari progressum in infinitum, & inepte quaerere: Quo judice? &c. Dicunt enim primò; ab unoquoque salutis suae studioso. Hoc quippe ut verum est de eo studioso salutis suae, qui verbum Dei tanquam unicam fidei normam rectè sequitur: ita falsum est de iis qui salutis suae studiosi quidem sunt, sed non secundùm scientiam, quales infiniti reperiuntur. Deinde dicunt unumquemque DECIDERE posse illas controversias; quod certè plus est quàm si dixissent unumquemq; judicare posse de earum veritate aut falsitate, judicio scilicet discretionis non autem decisionis, quod Scripturae soli ut normae & Deo in ea loquenti ut judici competit; homini autem aut Ecclesiae tribui non potest nisi improprie & per accidens, respectu nimirum verbi divini, cujus decisionem homo sibi ante oculos ponit, & in judicio discretionis se-quitur. Quo sensu si Arminiani vocem decisionis accipiant, libenter ac-quiesco & habeo quod volo, ex ipsorum propria confessione; quam e-tiam praxi sua quando ipsis libet confirmant. Nam etsi Socinianos non habeant pro Hæreticis, tamen nos Reformatos pro Hæreticis habent. Iam si quis urgeat eos argumento hoc ipsorum proprio à fallibilitate eo-rum, adeoque id in eos retorqueat; tandem eo venient Arminiani ut di-cant, se hoc dicere ex judicio verbi Dei ex quo unusquisque omnes lites adeoque etiam illam decidere possit.
units.tr: 4. The fourth doctrine is: This liberty is to be granted to heretics so called commonly by the whole Church. This too they do not deny, but they confess it, and try to defend it with their cocksmo against Vedelius and his followers. And because I had said that the discussion concerns heretics so called commonly by the whole Church, such as the Antitrinitarians, they quibble with the argument from the fallibility of the Church, by which it may happen that the Church errs in judging about heresy and the heretic and condemns the truth as heresy. But this too is empty and frivolous. For although the Church can err in this world, yet this fallibility is not always brought from power into act; rather, it judges rightly and truly when that judgment conforms to the Word of God, and thus in that very judgment which really conforms to the Word of God, it is placed beyond the danger of error. But we have dealt fully with this matter before, in the Rational Theology, book 3, chapters 6, 7 and 9, where we treated of the judgment of the intellect concerning matters of faith, and specifically settled in chapter 9 this question: whether an infallible judgment of the intellect, and so also of the Church, is given? Let me add this at least, lest the Arminians think they have occasion to complain, as though anything had been passed over by me that bears on the matter and deserves an answer. For they will object, as they do in chapter 1 of the Vindiciae, p. 11: If the Church in that chapter does not err in controversy, then a reason must necessarily be given. But if a reason is given, then either that reason is beyond the hazard of error or it is not; and so on to infinity. Likewise, here and there in their Vindiciae they jeer: By whose judgment? Is it because you, most inept of men, think so? I answer: it is absolutely necessary that there be an argument or foundation on which the judgment of the Church rests; if this argument has been truly drawn from the Word of God, it is placed beyond the hazard of error, that is, it cannot be erroneous. For what truly conforms to the Word of God is not erroneous. Nor, however, will there be a progress to infinity, nor is there need to labour over who the judge is: provided it is true, as they themselves say in the dedication of their Vindiciae, that the decision of all disputes and controversies about faith and life that can arise can be made by anyone who is zealous for his own salvation. Where a dispute has been rightly decided, certainly there is no progress to infinity, nor is a judge lacking. The words of the Arminians there are these: The first and chief foundation of the Reformation is that Holy Scripture alone is the norm and rule of our faith and life, to which the decision of ALL disputes and controversies about religion, or about our faith and life, which can arise, ought to be made, on account of its divine perfection; and it CAN be made by ANYONE zealous for his own salvation, on account of its most clear perspicuity in all matters necessary to know, believe and do for salvation. Here the Arminians give me more than I need, to show that they speak falsely when they say that there is thus a progress to infinity and foolishly ask: By whose judgment? etc. For they say, first: by anyone zealous for his own salvation. This is true of the one zealous for his salvation who rightly follows the Word of God as the sole rule of faith; but it is false of those who are indeed zealous for their salvation, but not according to knowledge, of whom there are countless numbers. Next they say that each one can DECIDE those controversies; which is certainly more than if they had said that each one can judge their truth or falsehood, with the judgment of discernment and not of decision, which belongs to Scripture alone as the norm and to God who speaks in it as judge; but it cannot be attributed to man or to the Church except improperly and by accident, namely with respect to the divine Word, whose decision man sets before his eyes and follows in a judgment of discernment. If the Arminians understand the word decision in this sense, I gladly agree and have what I want, from their own confession; which they also confirm by their practice when it suits them. For although they do not count the Socinians as heretics, yet they count us Reformed as heretics. Now if someone presses them with this argument from their own fallibility, and so turns it back upon them, in the end the Arminians will come to say that they say this from the judgment of the Word of God, by which anyone can decide all disputes, and this one too.

units.la: 5. Dixeram insuper, eos libertatem prophetandi permitti velle etiam iis qui Spiritus S. revelationes in rebus fidei somniant ac venditant h. e. Enthusiastis ac fanaticis Spiritibus. Fatentur & tueri conantur. Nam postquam tergiver-sati essent aliquoties & dixissent, se non ITA (h. e. totidem literis & syllabis) hoc asseruisse; tandem, quia verba eorum quæ in favorem En-thusiastarum & fanaticorum Spirituum in Apologiæ cap. 24. f. 275. b. & 276. a continentur & à me citata sunt manifestissimè mentem eorum aperiunt, hinc ajunt: Sed esto; detur etiam Vedelio Remonstrantes id asseruisse, quid in eo criminis? Iam igitur conceptis verbis rursus dicunt libertatem Prophetandi Enthusiastis & fanaticis hominibus concedendam esse. Horreat Orbis Christianus & obstupescat ob tantam pertinaciam in re turpissimâ! Videamus qua ratione sese tueantur? 1. ajunt: Non enim asseruerunt prophetationes ejusmodi fanaticas licitas esse aut probandas; sed tantùm eos qui eas jaCtant non esse vi opprimendos & carcere aut laqueo suffocandos: Examinentur, refellantur argumentis & rationibus: at ne examinentur flagris aut fustibus nedum tormentis aut carnificina. Respondeo: falsum esse, quod hic ajunt se in Apologiâ tantùm dixisse Enthusiastas & fanaticos homi-nes non esse vi opprimendos. Nam requirunt etiam & postulant ipsis libertatem prophetandi in Ecclesia Dei: Hoc patet primò ex toto con-textu, verbis antecedentibus & consequentibus, quibus contendunt & exponunt quibus libertas Prophetandi in Ecclesiâ Dei libera esse de-beat. Deinde speciatim ex verbis allegatis à me Par. I. lib. 1. c. 3. p. 20. loco Apologiæ modò memorato illud luce clarius meridianâ est: Hujusmodi Spiritum, inquiunt, si extingui non vult, sed uti est 1. Ioh. 4. 1. probari examinari ab omnibus ac singulis fidelibus, profectò omninò LIBERVM ESSE VULT IN ECCLESIA. Hæc est prior ipsorum ratio.
units.tr: 5. I had further said that they wish freedom of prophesying to be permitted even to those who dream up and peddle revelations of the Holy Spirit in matters of faith, that is, to enthusiasts and fanatical spirits. They admit it and try to defend it. For after they had equivocated several times and said that they had not asserted it IN THESE WORDS (that is, in exactly the same letters and syllables), at last, because their words in the Apology, chapter 24, pages 275b and 276a, which I have cited, plainly reveal their meaning, they say: But grant it; suppose the Remonstrants did assert it to Vedel. What crime is there in that? So now, in so many words, they again say that freedom of prophesying must be granted to enthusiasts and fanatical men. Let the Christian world shudder and be astonished at such obstinacy in a most shameful matter! Let us see on what grounds they defend themselves. 1. They say: For they did not assert that such fanatical prophesyings are lawful or to be approved, but only that those who boast of them are not to be oppressed by force and strangled in prison or by the noose. Let them be examined and refuted with arguments and reasons; but let them not be examined with whips or clubs, much less with torments or the executioner. I reply: it is false that they say in the Apology only that enthusiasts and fanatical men are not to be oppressed by force. For they also require and demand for them freedom of prophesying in the Church of God. This is evident first from the whole context, the words before and after, in which they contend for and set out the persons to whom freedom of prophesying in the Church of God ought to be free. Then especially from the words I quoted, Part I, book 1, chapter 3, page 20, from the Apology just mentioned, which is clearer than midday light: Such a spirit, they say, if it is not to be extinguished, but is as it is (1 John 4:1), is to be tested and examined by all and each of the faithful; certainly it WANTS TO BE FREE IN THE CHURCH. This is their first reason.

units.la: Altera ratio in coccysmo ipsorum solito consistit de Vedelio & Reformatis omnibus quos illi Calvinistas vocant. Quemadmodum enim ante dixerunt me & Reformatos omnes haberi pro Hæreticis ab aliis, ita etiam jam dicunt nos haberi ab aliis (h. e. à calumniatoribus Arminianis, & à Socinianis apertis) pro Enthusiastis, ob nostram doctrinam de cooperatione Spiritus S. necessaria ad salutarem intelligentiam Scripturæ sacræ. Hæc calumnia, quæ non solùm nos sed omnes etiam Evangelicos & sic Lutheranos quoque petit, responsionem non meretur. Nos eam cum cæteris injuriis ultori Deo relinquimus, qui cum tempore & forte brevi causam nostram judicabit.
units.tr: The second reason, in their usual clamour, concerns Vedel and all the Reformed whom they call Calvinists. For just as before they said that I and all the Reformed were regarded as heretics by others, so now they say that we are regarded by others (that is, by the Arminian slanderers and by the open Socinians) as enthusiasts, because of our doctrine of the co-operation of the Holy Spirit, which is necessary for the saving understanding of Holy Scripture. This slander, which strikes not only us but all Evangelicals, and so the Lutherans too, does not deserve an answer. We leave it, along with the other injuries, to God the avenger, who will judge our cause in time, and perhaps soon.

units.la: Præterea quia dixeram contra Arminianos, nec Clarissimos DD. Proff. Leydd. nec Scripturam sacram vocem Spiritus sumere pro Spiritualibus verbi Dei interpretationibus, quas quis se habere à Spiritu Dei, id est vel per inspirationem & suggestionem Spiritus, vel anxiliante Spiritu divino sibi persuadet: Respondent illi pro more suo cum convitiis, & quantum ad modò laudatos Theologos attinet dicunt se posse quidem illud probare argumentis quæ evincere, inquiunt, CREDIMVS eos ita sumere vocem Spiritus: Ut verò in gratiam Vedelij argumenta ista afferamus opera precium non est. Benè: quanto bono privor, quòd in mei gratiam argumenta ista afferre nolunt! At debebant saltem in sui & suorum gratiam ista argumenta attulisse. Sed observetur, quod dicunt se argumenta habere quæ CREDVNT evincere illud. Atqui, ut ipsorum propriis verbis utar de se ipsis loquentium in hac ipsâ re pag. 22. An' non fieri potuit, ut hoc ita Remonstrantibus videretur, etsi secus se res haberet? Certum quippe est argumenta ista futilia & inania esse quæcunque tandem illa sint: nam nec vola nec vestigium illius rei in verbis DD. Proff. Leydd. reperitur. Et profectò si hoc probare potuissent Arminiani, ô quàm illi, qui quidvis arripiunt & captant, hanc occasionem quâ me mendacii arguerent nequaquam præteriissent! prout ex eo patet quòd me ibidem mendacii & impudentiæ volunt arguere, quia dixi Apostolos quoque non ita sumsisse vocem Spiritus. In quo tamen frustrà cavillantur. Nam loca quæ afferunt Arminiani, ex 2. Thess. 1. 2. & 1. Ioh. 4. 1. ut & verba D. Bezæ piæ memoriæ mihi contraria non sunt. Etenim Spiritus vox ibi non sumitur pro interpretationibus quas quis se habere à Spiritu Dei id est vel inspiratione & suggestione Spiritus, vel anxiliante Spiritu divino sibi PERSVADET: sed sumitur pro dogmatis quibus PRÆTEXITVR Spiritualis revelationis nomen, item Metonymicè pro eo qui se Spiritus dono praditum DICIT, ad obeundum Propheta munus, ut Dn. Beza recte explicat. In summâ, carpuntur non ii in genere qui persuasi sunt Spiritum Dei sibi revelâsse doctrinam talem: sed ii qui falsas opiniones pro veris proferunt, & praeterea dicunt, jactantur, venditât eas à Spiritu Dei sibi revelatas esse. Quae duo profecto plurimum differunt. Et res est manifestissima. Nam cùm Apostolus 1. Thess. 1. 2. dicit: Ne cito à mente dimoveamini neque terreamini, neque per spiritum neque per sermonem: certè sensus hic non est: ne citò dimoveamini à mente neque per Sermonem, neque per eos qui persuasi sunt Spiritum S. sibi revelâsse doctrinam suam. Nam & Apostoli persuasi, imò persuasissimi erant Spiritum S. sibi revelâsse doctrinam suam. Eadem ratio est 1. Ioh. 4. 1. Et hanc distinctionem veram & solidam esse Arminiani ipsi nôrunt; qui distinguunt inter persuasum esse sibi revelatam interpretationem à Deo esse, & inter jactare ac venditare eam revelationem fanatici in morem. Ita enim in hoc ipso loco Vindic. pag. 21. Vix credo, inquiunt, quenquam pium esse qui non aliquando id sibi PERSVADEAT, si serius precibus diu multumque contenderit interpretationem aliquam à Deo aut Spiritu ejus consequi, etiamsi fanatici instar eam non jactet aut venditet.
units.tr: Moreover, because I had said against the Arminians that neither the most distinguished doctors, the professors of Leiden, nor Holy Scripture use the word Spirit to mean the spiritual interpretations of the Word of God which a man persuades himself that he has from the Spirit of God, that is, either through the inspiration and suggestion of the Spirit or with the help of the divine Spirit, they answer with their usual insults. As far as the Theologians just praised are concerned, they say that they can indeed prove it with arguments which, they say, we BELIEVE will establish that they take the word Spirit in this way; but it is not worth the trouble to bring these arguments forward for Vedel's sake. Well! How much I am deprived of a good thing, since they are unwilling to bring these arguments forward for my sake! But they ought at least to have brought these arguments forward for their own sake and that of their followers. But let it be noted that they say they have arguments which they BELIEVE will establish this. Yet, to use their own words about themselves, speaking of this very matter, page 22: Could it not be that this appeared so to the Remonstrants, even though the matter was otherwise? It is certain that these arguments are trifling and empty, whatever they may be: for neither the shadow nor the trace of that thing is found in the words of the professors of Leiden. And truly, if the Arminians could have proved this, oh how those men, who snatch at and grab at anything, would not have let this opportunity pass by, by which they might have charged me with lying! That is clear from the fact that they want to accuse me there of lying and impudence, because I said that the Apostles too did not take the word Spirit in this way. Yet in this they quibble in vain. For the passages which the Arminians cite, from 2 Thessalonians 2:2 and 1 John 4:1, and the words of Dr. Beza of pious memory, are not contrary to me. For the word Spirit there is not used for the interpretations which a man persuades himself that he has from the Spirit of God, that is, either through the inspiration and suggestion of the Spirit or with the help of the divine Spirit. Rather it is used for the doctrines under the pretext of which the name of spiritual revelation is put forward; and also, by metonymy, for the one who says he is endowed with the gift of the Spirit to perform the office of prophet, as Mr. Beza rightly explains. In sum, those are not criticised in general who are persuaded that the Spirit of God has revealed such a doctrine to them, but those who put forward false opinions as true and, moreover, say or boast, and peddle them, that they have been revealed to them by the Spirit of God. These two things differ very greatly, and the matter is most evident. For when the Apostle says, 1 Thessalonians 2:2, that you be not quickly shaken in mind, nor troubled, neither by spirit nor by word, certainly the sense is not this: that you be not quickly moved from your mind neither by word, nor by those who are persuaded that they have been revealed the Holy Spirit's doctrine. For the Apostles too were persuaded, indeed most fully persuaded, that the Holy Spirit had revealed their doctrine to them. The same reasoning applies to 1 John 4:1. And the Arminians themselves know that this distinction is true and sound; they distinguish between being persuaded that an interpretation revealed to oneself is from God, and boasting of and peddling that revelation in the manner of a fanatic. For so in this very passage, Vindication, page 21: I scarcely believe, they say, that anyone is pious who does not at some time persuade himself of this, if after long and earnest prayer he has obtained some interpretation from God or from his Spirit, even if he does not boast of it or peddle it like a fanatic.

units.la: Porrò ut evincerent Arminiani libertatem Prophetandi Enthusiastis & fanaticis concedendam esse; usi fuerant instantiâ adversum Orthodoxos Theologos petitâ ex eo, quòd judicium nostrum de Spiritibus non sit ejusdem infallibilitatis cujus erat Apostolorum. Ad hoc ego responderam: non requiri ad Spirituum probationem quam Apostolus omnibus fidelibus imperat infallibilitatem extraordinariam, qualis erat in Prophetis & Apostolis divinitùs inspiratis: sed probationem Spirituum instituendam esse ex verbo Dei, cujus judicium infallibile est, & quod si sequimur, falli non possumus. Ad haec hi homines, respondent ita ut fateantur verum esse non requiri infallibilitatem & revelationem extraordinariam; sed & simul redeunt ad coccysmum suum contra me & Reformatos omnes: Nec ad Spiritus tui probationem, inquiunt, revelatione extraordinariâ opus est. Facilè instituí poterit ista tua ordinaria probatio etiam contra te, & momento eam instituent Pontificius qui te cruci, rogo, rota adjudicet; aut Lutheranus quite exilio multet &c. Repetunt quoque nugas suas de fallibilitate judicii humani: praeterea tenebrionem me vocant, ac mihi & Caeteris Reformatis tribuunt Spiritum fanaticum, tandem concludunt me semper recurrere ad verbum Dei; Vt anus ad armillam, ita ille semper recurrit ad verbum Dei p. 23.
units.tr: Furthermore, in order to prove that freedom of prophesying must be granted to enthusiasts and fanatical men, the Arminians had used an instance, directed against the Orthodox Theologians, drawn from the fact that our judgment about spirits does not have the same infallibility which the Apostles had. To this I had replied that for the testing of spirits, which the Apostle commands of all the faithful, one does not require the extraordinary infallibility which was in the Prophets and Apostles divinely inspired; rather, the testing of spirits is to be carried out from the Word of God, whose judgment is infallible, and if we follow it we cannot be deceived. To this these men reply, in such a way as to admit that it is true that neither infallibility nor extraordinary revelation is required; but at the same time they return to their clamour against me and all the Reformed: Nor, they say, is extraordinary revelation needed for the testing of your spirit. That ordinary test of yours can be easily set up even against you, and in a moment the Papists will set it up, who, I ask you, will adjudge you to the cross, the wheel, or the stake; or a Lutheran will fine you with exile, and so on. They also repeat their trifles about the fallibility of human judgment; moreover, they call me a benighted fellow and attribute a fanatical spirit to me and the other Reformed; finally, they conclude that I always have recourse to the Word of God: As an old woman to her bracelet, so he always has recourse to the Word of God, page 23. And they add that I and the other Reformed persuade ourselves that we are Orthodox and that our doctrine is true, and so on. Is this what it means to answer? Judge fairly, reader.

units.la: atque addunt me & caeteros Reformatos persuadere nobis, nos esse Orthodoxos & doctrinam nostram veram, &c. Estne hoc respondere? Iudica candide Lector.
units.tr: and they add that I and the other Reformed persuade us that we are the Orthodox and that our doctrine is true, etc. Is this how to answer? Judge fairly, reader.

units.la: 6. Sextum dogma est: Tales omnes interpretationes non esse peccatum, sed cum summa pietate conjunctas seu maxima reverentia Scripturae. Fatentur, & dicunt: Quasi vero ejusmodi interpretationes pio atque humili animo institutae peccatum esse possint. Ubi quid intelligant per interpretationes pio & humili animo institutas, notum est; nimirum, interpretationes ejusmodi quales sunt Socinianorum, quibus interpretationibus negatur Christum habere divinam naturam; in Deitate esse tres personas unius ejusdemque essentiae, &c. Ut autem id probent Arminiani, redeunt ad coccysmum suum de Vedelio cum suis, & fallibilitate judicii mei & Reformatorum reliquorum. Adduntque se non asseruisse eas interpretationes SEMPER cum pietate & quidem summa conjunctas esse. At ego non laboro de voce SEMPER. Sufficit quod dicunt ONMES tales interpretationes cum pietate summa conjunctas esse: At quae extra manifesta ista sunt interpretationes aliorum Scripturae sensuum, ea ad libertatem prophetandi pertinent, & cum Scripturae reverentia maxima conjuncta sunt. Apol. c. 24. f. 276. b. Et manifestissima est sententia eorum de errore & Haeresi, sic dicta ab Ecclesia tota quae Deum in tribus personis adorat: dum statuunt Errorem & Haeresin non esse peccatum: imo Haeresin eam etiam quam ipsi fingunt & nominant non esse peccatum quatenus error est.
units.tr: 6. The sixth dogma is: All such interpretations are not sin, but are joined with the highest piety or the greatest reverence for Scripture. They admit this and say: As if such interpretations, undertaken in a pious and humble spirit, could be sin. What they mean by interpretations undertaken in a pious and humble spirit is well known: namely, interpretations of the kind held by the Socinians, by which it is denied that Christ has a divine nature, and that in the Godhead there are three persons of one and the same essence, etc. In order to prove this, the Arminians return to their clamour about Vedel and his followers, and about the fallibility of my judgment and that of the other Reformed. And they add that they did not assert that those interpretations are ALWAYS joined with piety, and indeed with the highest piety. But I am not concerned about the word ALWAYS. It is enough that they say that ALL such interpretations are joined with the highest piety: But the interpretations of other senses of Scripture that lie outside these manifest ones pertain to the liberty of prophesying, and are joined with the greatest reverence for Scripture. Apology, ch. 24, p. 276 b. And their view of error and heresy, so called by the whole Church which worships God in three persons, is most manifest, since they hold that error and heresy are not sin: indeed, that even the heresy which they themselves invent and name is not sin, insofar as it is error.

units.la: 7. Septimum dogma est: Ab ejusmodi libertate prophetandi nihil periculi imminere. Fatentur, & tueri hoc quoque conantur coccysmo suo de Vedelio & Reformatis caeteris, quos dicunt Haereticos censeri ab aliis, & non habere infallibilitatem. Observetur autem me ibi accusasse Arminianos, quod αὐτοκατάκριτοι sint, seu ex proprio ore suo condemnati, dum agnoscunt injuriam factam veritati divinae redundare in ipsum Deum. Jam autem, dicebam, an non hoc est veritati divinae injuriam facere, cum ea Haereticorum & quorumcunque fanaticorum lubidini exponitur, ut quidem Arminiani faciunt inter alia praeclara sua doctrina de libertate prophetandi? Ad hanc accusationem gravissimam αὐτοκαταγνώσεως & oppressae veritatis divinae illi ne verbo quidem respondent, nec unquam se ab eo crimine purgare possunt. Nam si dicant forte, etiam Reformatis objici eos Haereticos esse; id quidem non est respondere sed inepte nugari, ut ostensum. Atque hoc etiam de doctrina eorum circa libertatem prophetandi. Itaque etiam ex hoc capite manifestissima est causa pessima & detestabilis Arminianonianorum; & patet me ipsis in eâ etiam parte injuriam nullam fecisse aut eos calumniatum esse. Fatentur enim, & defendere conantur dogmata sibi à me in cap. 3. lib. 1. Par. I. objecta.
units.tr: 7. The seventh dogma is: No danger threatens from such liberty of prophesying. They admit this too, and they try to defend it with their clamour about Vedel and the other Reformed, whom they say are regarded as heretics by others and do not possess infallibility. But let it be noted that I there accused the Arminians of being self-condemned (αὐτοκατάκριτοι), that is, condemned by their own mouth, since they acknowledge that the injury done to divine truth redounds upon God himself. Now, I was saying: Is it not to do injury to divine truth when it is exposed to the lust of heretics and of whatever fanatics, as the Arminians indeed do, among their other splendid doctrines, in their doctrine of the liberty of prophesying? To this most grave accusation of self-condemnation (αὐτοκαταγνώσεως) and of oppressed divine truth they do not respond even with a word, nor can they ever clear themselves of that charge. For if they perhaps say that the Reformed too are objected to as heretics, this is not an answer but a foolish trifling, as has been shown. And this holds also for their doctrine concerning the liberty of prophesying. Thus, even from this chapter, the most manifest cause of the Arminians is shown to be wretched and detestable; and it is clear that I have done them no injury in this respect, nor calumniated them. For they admit, and try to defend, the dogmas objected to them by me in chapter 3 of book 1, Part I.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: Examen Capitis Quarti Vindiciarum.
units.tr: Examination of the Fourth Chapter of the Vindiciae.

units.la: 1. Arminiani fatentur, & defendere impertinenter conantur dogma sibi objectum: Eum esse verum sensum literalem Scripturæ qui non solùm menti auctorû sed etiam rectæ rationi convenientissimus sit &c. 2. Arminiani contra conscientiam suam tergiversantur, sed frustrà, circa dogma sibi objectum, nimirùm in S. Cœnà mysterium nullum omninò esse, & realem communionem corporis & sanguinis Christi esse merum figmentum. Et esse istud figmentum profectum ab humanâ seu curiositate, seu superstitione, eorum, qui, postquam à phrasi Scripturæ semel discesserunt, admirationibus inexhaustis se pascere malunt, quàm claràveritatis sententiâ. Esse etiam istud dogma fontem horrendæ idololatriæ, quâ major concipi vix potest. 3. Fatentur, & contra conscientiam suam in alium sensum detorquent, dogma sibi objectum: Peritiores & accuratiores rerum æstimatores sacram cœnam vanitatis suspectam habere. 4. Fatentur se idcò doctrinam nostram de libero arbitrio & annexis capitibus rejicere; quia rationi non sit convenientissima. 5. Effugiis & corruptelis Arminianorum circa duo loca Apostoli occurritur. 6. Corollaria septem Auctoris frustrà ab Arminianis allatrata.
units.tr: 1. The Arminians admit, and feebly try to defend, the dogma put to them: that the true literal sense of Scripture is the one that agrees best not only with the mind of the authors but also with right reason, etc. 2. The Arminians, against their own conscience, evade, but in vain, the dogma put to them, namely that there is no mystery at all in the Holy Supper, and that the real communion of the body and blood of Christ is mere fiction. And that this fiction springs from human curiosity or superstition, of those who, once they have departed from the wording of Scripture, prefer to feed on endless wonders rather than on the plain sense of truth. That this dogma is also the source of a horrible idolatry, than which a greater can scarcely be imagined. 3. They admit, and against their own conscience twist into another sense, the dogma put to them: that skilled and more accurate judges of things regard the Holy Supper as suspect of vanity. 4. They admit that they therefore reject our doctrine of free will and the chapters connected with it, because it does not agree best with reason. 5. The evasions and distortions of the Arminians concerning two passages of the Apostle are met. 6. The seven corollaries of the author, barked at in vain by the Arminians.

units.la: 1. DOgma primum quod istis hominibus Capite Quarto l.1. Par.I. objeceram; est: Eum esse verum sensum literalem Scripturæ, qui non solùm menti auctoris, sed etiam rectæ rationi CONVENIENTISSIMVS sit. item: Documenta fidei rationi rectæ non disconvenire. item: Certissimam decisionem Controversiarum esse, quæ ex Scripturis clarissimis & rationibus à nullo non mentis suæ compote fieri potest: item, quæ fieri potest aut ex Scriptura aut ex recta ratione. Hæc objeceram ipsis. Illi Vindic. c. 4. fatentur, & defendere conantur: sed plane frivole, eo scilicet prætextu, quòd ratio profliganda non sit ex rebus fidei. Id quod, ut nemo negat, ita ad rem non facit. Nec enim ratio profligatur ex rebus fidei, quando negatur quòd mysteria fidei rationi rectæ per omnia conveniant. Habet enim ratio suum usum & quidem necessarium in rebus fidei, etiamsi hæ sint supra eam & non secundum eam, ut hi homines toti imbuti spiritu Socitiano (nam in hac etiam re eos cum Socinianis facere ostendi Par. III. Arc. lib. 1. cap. 4.) volunt. Sed de hac re ex professo & copiosissime egi tribus libris Rationalis Theologici.
units.tr: 1. The first dogma which I had put to these men in the fourth chapter of the first book of the first part is: that the true literal sense of Scripture is the one that agrees BEST not only with the mind of the author but also with right reason. Likewise: the articles of faith do not disagree with right reason. Likewise: the most certain decision of controversies is that which can be made from the clearest Scriptures and from reasons, by anyone who is in command of his mind; likewise: which can be made either from Scripture or from right reason. These things I had put to them. In the fourth chapter of their Vindiciae they admit them and try to defend them, but quite feebly, on the pretext, of course, that reason is not to be banished from the matters of faith. Nobody denies this, but it has nothing to do with the point. For reason is not banished from the matters of faith when it is denied that the mysteries of faith agree in every respect with right reason. Reason has its use, and indeed a necessary use, in the matters of faith, even if these are above it and not according to it, as these men, steeped wholly in the Socinian spirit (for I showed in Part III, Book 1, chapter 4 of the Arcana that in this matter too they agree with the Socinians), want. But I have treated this matter ex professo and at great length in three books of the Rationale Theologicum.

units.la: 2. Secundum ipsorum dogma est: Ideo in S. Cœna mysterium nullum omnino esse, & realem communionem corporis & sanguinis Christi (quam Ecclesiæ Euangelicæ omnes h. e. & Reformatæ & Lutheranæ agnoscunt) esse merum figmentum, quia rationi & Scripturæ non sit conforme ipsud mysterium. Et esse ipsud figmentum profectu ab humana, seu curiositate, seu superstitione, eorum qui, postquam a phrasi Scripturæ semel discesserunt, admirationibus inexhaustis se pascere malunt quam clara veritatis sententia. Esse etiam ipsud dogma fontem horrenda idololatriæ, qua major concipi vix potest. Hoc ipsis objeceram. At Arminiani, quia constrictos se vident, mire hic perplexi sunt; nam nec aperte fateri volunt, nec audent directe negare, itaq; armati maledicentia solita in me irruunt, dicunt infatuatum esse zelum meum, me cupere rationem rectam proscriptam; id quod hinc inde in hoc capite oggerunt. In quo quidem ex more suo calumniosissime agunt. Nam ipsi faciunt in Vindiciis suis lib. 1. c. 9. p. 52. mentionem Rationalis Theologici ante aliquot annis editi, & præ se ferunt se id legisse. In eo autem opere tribus libris integris uberrime & ex professo defendo non solum usum sed & necessitatem rationis in rebus fidei ac Controversiis Theologicis, atque ostendo in quo verus usus rationis circa eas consistat, in quo non ac speciatim eum non consistere in eo in quo Arminiani eum ponunt cum apertis Socinianis; & disputo sufficientissime adversum omnes eos qui usum rationis profligare conantur ex rebus fidei. Verba Arminianorum quibus mentionem Rationalis Thologici faciunt, hæc sunt: Conferatur Rationale Theologicum & scripta eorum qui id tentarunt, & apparebit eos cum ratione insanire, simulque ingenium suum ac tempus dilapidare voluisse. Hic utique præ se ferunt se legisse Rationale Thologicum. Quod, si id revera legerunt, certe contra conscientiam suam me accusant hinc inde quasi cuperem rationem rectam proscriptam; quandoquidem a sententia mea comprecomprehensâ illis tribus libris non discessi. Si autem id non legerunt, certè impudenter, protervè, & temerariè faciunt, quòd cum convitiis maledicentissimi isti homines me eo nomine reprehendere audent.
units.tr: 2. The second dogma of theirs is: therefore there is no mystery at all in the Holy Supper, and the real communion of the body and blood of Christ (which all the Evangelical churches, that is both the Reformed and the Lutheran, acknowledge) is mere fiction, because that mystery is not in agreement with reason and Scripture. And that this fiction springs from human curiosity or superstition, of those who, once they have departed from the wording of Scripture, prefer to feed on endless wonders rather than on the plain sense of truth. That this dogma too is the source of a horrible idolatry, than which a greater can scarcely be conceived. This I had put to them. But the Arminians, seeing themselves pressed, are strangely perplexed here; for they neither want to confess openly nor dare to deny directly, and so, armed with their usual slander, they fall upon me, saying that my zeal has run mad, that I wish right reason to be banished; which they heap up here and there in this chapter. In this they act most calumniously, as is their custom. For in their Vindiciae, book 1, chapter 9, page 52, they make mention of the Rationale Theologicum, published some years ago, and they let it be seen that they have read it. Yet in that work, in three entire books, I defend most fully and ex professo not only the use but also the necessity of reason in the matters of faith and in theological controversies, and I show in what the true use of reason in these consists, and that it does not consist, and especially not in what the Arminians place it in, together with the open Socinians; and I dispute most adequately against all those who try to banish the use of reason from the matters of faith. The words of the Arminians in which they mention the Rationale Theologicum are these: Let the Rationale Theologicum and the writings of those who attempted the same be compared, and it will appear that they were mad with reason, and wished at the same time to squander their wit and time. Here they certainly make it appear that they have read the Rationale Theologicum. If they really did read it, then they accuse me, against their own conscience, here and there, as if I wished right reason to be banished, since I have not departed from my view as comprehended in those three books. If, however, they did not read it, then they act shamelessly, insolently and rashly in daring to rebuke me under that name with the insults of these most slanderous men.

units.la: Sed pergunt: Verba Remonstrantium videantur, quae Vedelius ipse subiicit, & comperietur eum nescire quid dicat: Nam Remonstrantes, inquiunt, tantum asserunt, communionem & unionem istam realem cum physica corporis Christi substantia, quae in cibum animae cedat, NUSPIAM in SCRIPTURA finem coenae Dominicae statui NEC ULLA SOLIDA RATIONE niti: Eos vero qui id affirmant, mysterium ei attribuisse adeò magnum, ut illud nec mens ulla concipere, nec lingua effari possit. Vides, candide Lector, perplexitatem horum hominum. Ita enim fatentur, ut velint tamen videri negare, & ita negant ut velint videri affirmare. Nostrum est discutere has nebulas, quas Lectori offundere volunt. Videamus igitur, an non Arminiani ita doceant? quod fieri non potest, nisi verba eorum rursus Lectori ante oculos ponamus. Primùm igitur hic fatentur se dixisse, realem communionem & unionem cum Physica corporis Christi substantia nuspiam in Scriptura finem Coenae Dominicae statui aut ratione ulla solida niti. Hoc itaque probatione ulteriore opus non habet. Fatentur etiam, quantum ad hoc dogma attinet, se dixisse, eos qui communionem illam affirmant mysterium ei attribuisse adeò magnum ut illud nec mens ulla concipere nec lingua effari possit. De eo igitur quoque nec quaestio nec dubium est. Sed in hoc contra conscientiam suam agunt, quòd dicunt se hoc TANTUM dixisse. In quare eò graviorem reprehensiorem merentur, quòd ipsi sine ullo rubore & verecundiâ, cùm in conscientiâ suâ convicti sint falsitatis, invitant Lectorem ut videat verba ipsorum à me allegata: verba enim Remonstrantium videantur quae Vedelius ipse subiiciet, inquiunt. Videamus igitur verba eorum ex quibus apparebit eos non TANTUM illud quod falsi sunt dixisse, sed longè graviora. Ita enim Apol. c. 23. f. 250. b. de S. Coenâ loquuntur: Ut inquirendi omnis occasio praecideretur, mysterium ei attributum fuit, quod nec mens concipere, nec lingua effari potest, quo ipso admiratio ceremoniae hujus adeò aulla fuit, ut non minor ferè idololatria sequuta quàm sopita fuerit, &c. Observa hic primò quòd dicunt mysterium attributum fuisse S. Coenae in eum finem ut inquirendi omnis occasio praecideretur; quibus verbis indicant Orthodoxam illam doctrinam à Doctorum illorum qui avorum nostrorum tempore Ecclesiâs à Papatus erroribus reformârunt calliditate & versutiâ profectam esse, & propositam in eum finem, ut illâ ratione veritas suppressa jaceret. Deinde dicunt ex doctrinâ illâ Orthodoxâ, postquam jam idololatria Papalis sopita in plurimis locis esset, fluxisse & sequutam esse non minorem fere idololatriam quam Pontificiam. Item f. 251. a. Adduci sane non possunt Remonstrantes ut communionem talem cum physica corporis Christi substantia finem Coenae Dominicae faciant, rati sufficere adeoque tutissimum esse ut ad Scripturae instar loquantur, & incomprehensibilia, ineffabilia illa mysteria, quae humana seu curiositas seu superstitio, in hoc tam simplice, tam plano & a nullo non ingenio facile perceptibili ritu finxit potius quam repperit, iis relinquant qui postquam a simplice scriptura phrasi semel discesserunt, admirationibus inexhaustis se pascere malunt quam clara veritatis sententia. Vides eos primo μιμήσει seu imitatione ironica sententiae Orthodoxae, deridere & rejicere eam: Incomprehensibilia, ineffabilia illa mysteria iis relinquunt, &c. Deinde dicunt esse ea mysteria humana seu curiositatis seu superstitionis figmenta. Tertio carpunt eos qui orthodoxam hanc doctrinam de communione realli corporis & sanguinis Christi tuentur: nam ajunt eos a simplice Scriptura phrasi discessisse & malle se inexhaustis admirationibus (vides, optime Lector, quam scoptice!) pascere quam clara veritatis luce. Pergunt: Nec dubitant quin ex isto fonte emanaverit hodieque adhuc fluat ingens illa idololatria apud complures, quae major concipi vix potest. Nimirum magnorum mysteriorum quae huic ritui subesse credantur apprehensio peperit admirationem, quam adoratio e vestigio subsequuta est, totaque illa pompatica circumgestatio, quam in ecclesia Pontificia, non sine lacrymis adspicere potest Christianus, & in caeteris Ecclesiis tanta tamque superstitiosa vanitas, ut Coena hujus usurpatio veluti panacea quaedam habeatur, & praesentissimorum scelerum ac mortalium omnium peccatorum remedium & antidotum. En eos dicentes ex doctrina illa de reali communione corporis & sanguinis Christi jam olim fluxisse idololatriam Pontificiam deplorandam; & In caeteris Ecclesiis (Evangelicas intelligunt) tantam tamque superstitiosam vanitatem ut habeatur pro remedio peccatorum. Eos autem per caeteras Ecclesias intelligere Evangelicas patet exinde; nam quantum ad Socinianos attinet illi cum Arminianis, seu potius hi cum illis sentiunt. Ita enim Socinus Epist. de Ecclesia p. 253. Nec vero est in hoc ritu alicujus divinae rei ulla datio seu ministratio. Sic enim proprie loqui oportet. Et ut Arminiani sacram coenam, quia mysterium in coena nullum agnoscunt, simplicem & a nullo non ingenio facile perceptibilem ceremoniam vocant, ut vidimus; ita & Socinus ibidem ob eandem causam (adeoque longe aliam quam Augustinus & alii Orthodoxi mysterium hoc intellectu facile esse dicunt) Neque enim, inquit, parabilissima haec & simplicissima Cerimonia Apostolis ut Apostolis, &c. Judicet jam cet jam Lector, an'ne Arminiani candidè agant, an verò Deo & hominibus illudere studeant, an'non denique in propriâ conscientiâ convicti sint, & me ipsis hoc dogma jure objecisse, & se mihi dum ob eam causam convitiis me onerant injuriam facere etiam in hac parte contra conscientiam suam.
units.tr: But they go on: Let the words of the Remonstrants be considered, which Vedel himself subjoins, and it will be found that he does not know what he is saying. For the Remonstrants, they say, merely assert that that communion and union with the physical substance of the body of Christ, which passes into the food of the soul, is NOWHERE laid down in Scripture as the purpose of the Lord's Supper, nor rests on ANY SOLID REASON. But those who affirm it have attributed to it a mystery so great that no mind can conceive it, nor tongue express it. You see, kind reader, the perplexity of these men. For they confess in such a way that they wish nevertheless to seem to deny, and they deny in such a way that they wish to seem to affirm. It is our task to dispel these clouds, which they want to pour over the reader. Let us see, then, whether the Arminians do not teach thus; which cannot be done unless we set their words again before the reader's eyes. First, then, here they confess that they said: the real communion and union with the physical substance of the body of Christ is nowhere laid down in Scripture as the purpose of the Lord's Supper, nor rests on any solid reason. This, therefore, needs no further proof. They also confess, as far as this dogma is concerned, that they said: those who affirm that communion have attributed to it a mystery so great that no mind can conceive it, nor tongue express it. Concerning this, therefore, there is neither question nor doubt. But in this they act against their own conscience, in that they say they have said only THIS. Therefore they deserve a heavier and more serious rebuke, in that they, without any blush or shame, though convicted by their own conscience of falsehood, invite the reader to see their words as I have quoted them: for let the words of the Remonstrants be considered, which Vedel himself subjoins, they say. Let us then look at their words, from which it will appear that they have said not only what is false, but things far more grave. For in the Apology, chapter 23, page 250 b, they speak thus about the Holy Supper: That every occasion for inquiry might be cut off, a mystery was attributed to it which neither mind can conceive nor tongue express, by which very wonder this ceremony became so great that scarcely less idolatry followed than had been put to sleep, etc. Observe here first that they say a mystery was attributed to the Holy Supper in order that every occasion of inquiry might be cut off; by which words they indicate that that Orthodox doctrine arose from the cunning and craft of those teachers who reformed the Church from the errors of the Papacy in the times of our forefathers, and was put forward with the aim that, by this method, the truth might lie suppressed. Next they say that from that Orthodox doctrine, after Papal idolatry had already been put to sleep in very many places, there flowed and followed an idolatry scarcely less than the Papistical. Likewise on page 251 a: The Remonstrants cannot indeed be persuaded to make such a communion with the physical substance of the body of Christ the purpose of the Lord's Supper, thinking it sufficient, and indeed most safe, to speak as Scripture does, and to leave those incomprehensible and unspeakable mysteries, which human curiosity or superstition, in this so simple, so plain and easily perceived by every wit rite, has feigned rather than discovered, to those who, once they have departed from the simple phrasing of Scripture, prefer to feed on endless wonders rather than on the clear sense of truth. You see that, first, by ironic imitation [μιμήσει] of the Orthodox view, they mock and reject it: they leave those incomprehensible and unspeakable mysteries, etc. Then they say that those mysteries are figments of human curiosity or superstition. Thirdly, they carp at those who defend this Orthodox doctrine of the real communion of the body and blood of Christ; for they say that these have departed from the simple phrasing of Scripture and prefer to feed on endless wonders (you see, best reader, how mocking!) rather than on the clear light of truth. They go on: Nor do they doubt that from that source has flowed, and even today still flows, that huge idolatry among many, than which a greater can scarcely be conceived. Namely, the apprehension of the great mysteries which are believed to lie under this rite has produced wonder, which adoration immediately followed, and the whole pompous procession which a Christian can behold, not without tears, in the Papal Church, and in the other Churches so great and so superstitious a vanity, that the use of this Supper is held as a kind of panacea, and a remedy and antidote for the most present sins and all mortal sins. Behold them saying that from that doctrine of the real communion of the body and blood of Christ there long ago flowed the Papal idolatry to be deplored; and that in the other Churches (they mean the Evangelical ones) there is so great and so superstitious a vanity that it is held as a remedy for sins. That they mean by the other Churches the Evangelical ones is clear from this: for as far as the Socinians are concerned, they agree with the Arminians, or rather the Arminians agree with them. For so Socinus, in the Epistle on the Church, page 253: Nor indeed is there in this rite any giving or ministering of a divine thing. For it must be spoken of properly in this way. And just as the Arminians, because they acknowledge no mystery in the Supper, call the Holy Supper a simple ceremony, easily perceived by every wit, as we have seen; so too Socinus, in the same place, for the same reason (and therefore, quite differently from Augustine and the other Orthodox, who say this mystery is easily understood by the intellect) says: For this most easily prepared and most simple ceremony was not given to the Apostles as Apostles, etc. Let the reader now judge whether the Arminians act candidly, or rather seek to mock God and men, or whether, finally, they are not convicted by their own conscience, and whether I have rightly put this dogma to them, and whether, while they load me with insults for that reason, they do me an injustice in this part too, against their own conscience.

units.la: 3. Tertium quod objeceram ipsis est, quod dicunt : Peritos & accuratos rerum æstimatores sacram (cænam vanitatis suspectam habere. In hac re illud notaveram, quòd eos qui sacram Cœnam vanitatis suspectam habent peritiores atque accuratiores rerum æstimatores appellant; cùm contra omnis homo pietatis studiosus & amans, eos qui S. (cœnam vanitatis suspectam habent, pro nebulonibus & atheis habere debeat. Quid enim? dicebam, institutionem Christi, Sacramentum gratiæ Dei tam augustum, vanitatis suspectum habere? Et tales nebulones tanquam peritos & accuratos rerum æstimatores venditare, esse hoc pietatem an atheismum docere? Hæc ego ibi. Hic verò rursus videte insignem proterviam & fraudulentiam; quæ ut speciem habeat, & ut videantur incautis & à se seductis hominibus bonæ causæ suæ certissimi esse, rursus convitiis me incessunt. Videamus rem. Dicunt se hoc tantum dixisse in verbis à me allegatis, eos qui communionem realem corporis & sanguinis Christi affirmant, mysterium (cœna attribuisse adeo magnum, ut illud nec mens ulla concipere nec lingua effari posset, eaque re occasionem dedisse peritioribus ritum hunc vanitatis suspectum habendi SIC VIDELICET USURPATUM. Quæ ultima verba (sic videlicet usurpatum) etiam charactere diverso à reliquo textu scribunt, ut hominibus persuadeant verba ista esse ab ipsis in Apologiâ usurpata, & à me malâ fide omissa. Et profectò nemo aliter judicare posset; qui ipsorum responsum videre contentus, Apologiam ipsam ex quâ verba eorum desumsi, non aspiciat. Postquam igitur ista verba assuissent, & mea verba quæ modò exhibui, quibus de istâ impietate eorum ac profanitate stupendâ conqueror, subjecissent, inquiunt: Quis hic non prima statim fronte supinam quandam insciitiam ne quid gravius dicam animadvertit? Nam aliud longè est, ritum hunc seu S.Cœnam Dominicam totam vanitatis suspectam reddere: aliud ritum istum sic intellectum & usurpatum suspectum reddere, & quando ac quamdiu aliter non concipitur, etiam totum ritum tanquam ritum Christo indignum, suspectum reddere vanitatis. Quid enim? Si quis cordatus ritum Cœna, &c. Hic unusquisque videt eos me carpere, quòd hæc verba sic videlicet usurpatum non respexerim sed præterierim. At hic rursus pessimâ fide ac indicibili fraude contra propriam conscientiam agunt. Nam inspiciatur Apologia, & manifestum erit, nec verba ista sic videlicet usurpatum, nec sensum eorum in ea reperiri, sed esse impostu-ram hominum istorum qua elabi conantur, quia se constri-ctos vident & reos manifestae impietatis. Verba enim Apologiae quod attinet, haec sunt cap. 23. sol. 250.b. Atque ut inquirendi omnis occasio praecideretur, mysterium ei attributum fuit, quod nec mens concipere nec lingua effari potest, quo ipso admiratio ceremoniae huius adeo aucta fuit, ut non minor fere idololatria secuta quam sopita fuerit, & quod caput rei est, peritioribus atque accuratis rerum aestimatoribus ritus hic alioquin per se obvius ac facilis nescio cujus vanitatis suspectus & adversariis omnibus ludibrio propinatus fuerit. Videt hic unusquisque primo verba haec sic videlicet usurpatum nequaquam in Apologia existere. Sensum quod attinet, eum etiam verba ista (ritus hic alioquin, &c.) non patiuntur. Nam dum dicunt, ritus hic alioquin &c. quis non videt eos non loqui de sacro hoc ritu sic usurpato, sed in se & per & se considerato: Nam expresse dicunt: Peritioribus atque accuratioribus rerum aestimatoribus ritus hic alioquin PERSE obvius ac facilis nescio cujus vanitatis suspectus, &c. fuerit. Itaque ne quidem illum sensum patiuntur verba ista. Sed sensus hic est; opinionem seu doctrinam Euangelicorum de reali communione corporis & sanguinis Christi, ansam praebuisse peritioribus & accuratioribus rerum aestimatoribus ipsam totam Sacram coenam vanitatis suspectam habendi. Et sic sensus iste quem Euangelici tribuunt S. Coenae non est objectum judicii de vanitate Coenae, sed causa efficiens. Ac magis etiam patet insignis haec fraus ex ratione qua addunt Arminiani in vindiciis suis, p. 26. Cum enim dixissent: aliud est Coenam totam vanitatis suspectam reddere, aliud eam sic usurpatam & intellectam suspectam reddere vanitatis. Subjiciunt immediate: Quid enim? Si quis cordatus, inquiunt, ritum Coenae prout a Pontificiis usurpatur, attentius consideret, an non facile in istam cogitationem incidere potest, eum vanum, superstitiosum, idololatricum, Christo indignum, imo commentitium esse? Nihil dubito, quin tu ipse, Vedelie, id facile fieri posse credas. Cur? quia tam multa absona, absurda, & a recta omni ratione aliena ex eo consequuntur, ut fieri vix possit, quin ab eo usurpando quivis reddatur alienior, quamdiu rectiorem de eo usurpando sensum ex mente Christi perspectum non habet. Hanc rationem dum Arminiani proferunt, omnino contra conscientiam faciunt. Norunt enim se non loqui iis verbis Apologiae de Missa Papistica & opinione Pontificiorum de transsubstantiatione; sed de sententia Evangelicorum circa communionem realem corporis & sanguinis Christi. Patet illud non solum ex toto contextu, sed ex hac ipsa periodo, ubi dicunt hac sententia Euangelicorum factum, ut non minor fere idololatria sequuta quàm sopita fuerit. Itaque Apologia non loquitur de ritu hoc prout à Pontificiis usurpatur, sed de ipsâ verâ sacrâ coenâ, quam vanitatis suspectam Arminiani in Apologiâ dicunt esse peritioribus & accuratioribus rerum æstimatoribus, ob sententiam istam Evangelicorum. Patet deinde etiam ex ratione quam in ipsâ Apologiâ subtexunt verbis istis egregiis. Cùm enim dixissent factum esse ut peritioribus atque accuratis rerum æstimatoribus ritus hic alioquin per se obvius ac facilis, nescio cujus vanitatis suspectus,& adversariis omnibus ludibrio propinatus fuerit: causam addunt immediatè, non profectò illam quam in Vindiciis contra conscientiam suam afferunt; sed longè aliam. Neque enim dicunt in Apologiâ: si quis ritum coena prout à Pontificiis usurpatur, consideret, &c. Sed causam ponunt in naturâ doctrinæ Evangelicæ de communione corporis & sanguinis Christi; imò quod magis est in naturâ communionis ipsius cum ipsâ corporis & sanguinis Christi physici substantiâ. Hanc communionem dicunt nullum fructum dare posse, ex eâ nullum fructum spiritualem proficisci posse. Nam, inquiunt loco allegato Apologiæ, obsecro, communio illa cum ipsa corporis & sanguinis Christi physici substantia, quem fructum dare potest, aut quem spiritualem in animi nostra effectum, in primis cùm sit communio cum corpore mortuo & sanguine ejus effuso? Nec enim est communio cum Christo integro, Spiritu vivificato predito, sed cum ipsius cadavere. Quæ profectò horrenda sunt: quibus hi homines Messalianorum seu Enthusiastarum hæresin ex inferis revocant, qui simulantes Orthodoxam Religionem, cum Orthodoxis communicabant eo prætextu quod sacra coena non prosit nec obsit, ut videre est apud Theodoretum lib. 5. c. 10. Quibus similes erant Armenii Hæretici, qui dicebant communionem nostram nihil esse, teste Nicephoro lib. 18. c. 53. Verùm enimverò hanc quoque hæresin à Socino suo didicerunt qui in Epistolâ allegatâ de Ecclesiâ inquit, ut paulò ante vidimus: Nec vero est in hoc ritu, alicujus divina rei ulla datio seu ministratio. Sic enim proprie loqui oportet.
units.tr: 3. The third point I had objected to them is that they say: Those who are skilled and careful judges of things regard the holy Supper as suspect of vanity. On this point I had noted that they call those who regard the holy Supper as suspect of vanity "more skilled and more careful judges of things; whereas every man who is zealous and a lover of piety ought to regard those who hold the holy Supper suspect of vanity as scoundrels and atheists. For what?" I said, "Is it to hold the institution of Christ, a sacrament of God's grace so august, suspect of vanity? And to pass off such scoundrels as skilled and careful judges of things, is this teaching piety or atheism?" So I said there. But here again see their remarkable impudence and deceit, which, so that it may have an appearance, and so that men who are unwary and led astray by them may think them certain of their good cause, they again assail me with abuse. Let us look at the matter. They say they said only this in the words I quoted: "those who affirm the real communion of the body and blood of Christ have attributed to the mystery of the Supper so great a thing that no mind can conceive it nor tongue express it, and so have given occasion to the more skilled to hold this rite suspect of vanity, THUS, OF COURSE, USED." These last words (thus, of course, used) they also print in a different type from the rest of the text, so as to persuade men that these words were used by them in the Apology and omitted by me in bad faith. And indeed no one could judge otherwise who is content to look at their reply and does not look at the Apology itself from which I took their words. After they have set down those words, and have added my words which I have just given, in which I complain of their astonishing impiety and profanity, they say: "Who here does not at once notice, at first sight, a certain crass ignorance, not to say something more serious? For it is one thing to make this rite, or the holy Lord's Supper, wholly suspect of vanity; it is another to make that rite, as understood and used in this way, suspect, and, as long as it is not conceived otherwise, to make the whole rite suspect of vanity as a rite unworthy of Christ. For what? If any man of sense should consider the rite of the Supper, etc." Here everyone sees that they blame me for not looking at, but passing over, these words thus, of course, used. But here again they act with the worst faith and unspeakable deceit against their own conscience. For let the Apology be inspected, and it will be plain that neither the words thus, of course, used nor their sense is found in it, but that this is the trickery of those men which they try to slip out of, because they see themselves pressed and charged with manifest impiety. As for the words of the Apology, they are in chapter 23, page 250b: "And that every occasion of inquiry might be cut off, a mystery was attributed to it which no mind can conceive nor tongue express; by this very fact the admiration for this ceremony was so increased that an idolatry not much less followed than was quieted, and, what is the heart of the matter, to the more skilled and careful judges of things this rite, otherwise obvious and easy in itself, was made suspect of I know not what vanity and offered as a mockery to all adversaries." Everyone sees first that these words thus, of course, used do not exist at all in the Apology. As for the sense, the words themselves (this rite otherwise, etc.) do not allow it either. For when they say "this rite otherwise, etc.," who does not see that they are not speaking of this sacred rite so used, but of it considered in itself and through itself? For they say expressly: "to the more skilled and more careful judges of things this rite, otherwise obvious and easy in itself, was made suspect of I know not what vanity, etc." So these words do not even allow that sense. But the sense is this: the opinion or doctrine of the Evangelicals about the real communion of the body and blood of Christ gave occasion to the more skilled and more careful judges of things to hold the whole holy Supper itself suspect of vanity. And so the sense which the Evangelicals attribute to the holy Supper is not the object of a judgement about the vanity of the Supper, but its efficient cause. This deceit is shown even more clearly by the argument which the Arminians add in their Vindiciae, p. 26. For when they had said: "It is one thing to make the whole Supper suspect of vanity, another to make it suspect of vanity when so used and understood." they immediately add: "For what? If any man of sense, they say, should consider more carefully the rite of the Supper as it is used by the Papists, could he not easily fall into the thought that it is vain, superstitious, idolatrous, unworthy of Christ, indeed made up? I do not doubt that you yourself, Vedel, believe this can easily happen. Why? Because so many absurd and unreasonable things, alien to all right reason, follow from it that it can scarcely happen that anyone who uses it does not become more estranged from it, as long as he does not have a more correct sense of its use, perceived from the mind of Christ." When the Arminians put forward this argument, they act entirely against their conscience. For they know they are not speaking in those words of the Apology about the Papal Mass and the Papists' opinion about transubstantiation, but about the opinion of the Evangelicals concerning the real communion of the body and blood of Christ. That is clear not only from the whole context but from this very sentence, where they say that by this opinion of the Evangelicals an idolatry came about not much less than the one that was quieted. Therefore the Apology does not speak of this rite as it is used by the Papists, but of the true holy Supper itself, which the Arminians in the Apology say is suspect of vanity to the more skilled and more careful judges of things, on account of that opinion of the Evangelicals. It is clear also from the reason which they add in the Apology itself after those striking words. For when they had said that it came about that this rite, otherwise obvious and easy in itself, was made suspect of I know not what vanity to the more skilled and careful judges of things, and was offered as a mockery to all adversaries, they immediately give a cause, certainly not the one they put forward in the Vindiciae against their conscience, but a quite different one. For they do not say in the Apology: "if anyone considers the rite of the Supper as it is used by the Papists, etc." But they place the cause in the nature of the Evangelical doctrine of the communion of the body and blood of Christ; indeed, what is more, in the nature of that very communion with the substance of the physical body and blood of Christ. They say this communion can give no fruit, and that no spiritual fruit can come from it. "For," they say in the passage of the Apology cited, "I ask, what fruit can that communion with the very substance of the physical body and blood of Christ give, or what spiritual effect in our minds, especially since it is communion with a dead body and with its poured-out blood? For it is not communion with the whole Christ, endowed with the living Spirit, but with his corpse." These things are truly horrible, by which these men call back from hell the heresy of the Messalians or Enthusiasts, who, pretending to the Orthodox religion, communed with the Orthodox on the pretext that "the holy Supper neither profits nor harms," as may be seen in Theodoret, book 5, chapter 10. Similar to them were the Armenian heretics, who said "our communion is nothing," as Nicephorus testifies, book 18, chapter 53.
