But indeed they learned this heresy too from their Socinus, who in the letter cited about the Church says, as we saw a little earlier: "Nor indeed is there in this rite any giving or ministering of a divine thing. For thus it is proper to speak."

units.la: Cæterùm ut nullus omninò scrupulus Lectori hæreat, sed ut is plenissimè intelligat Arminianos de ipsâ seu totâ sacrâ coenâ in se consideratâ & prout à Christo instituta est loqui: sciat hoc non insolitum esse istis hominibus. Similiter enim loquuntur de articulo Resurrectionis mortuorum. Non credunt Arminiani Resurrectionem corporis esse Resurrectionem hujus ipsius corporis; ut ostendimus Arcanorum parte primâ, & infra amplius patebit, adeoque etiam in eâ parte Socinianorum hæresi addicti sunt. Inter alia argumenta quæ afferunt in Responsione ad Excerpta Clarissimorum DD. Proff. Leydensium, etiam hac utun- tur pag.122: Hac ratione veluti uno ictu ansa praeciditur innumeris non minus difficillimis quam curiosis ineptisque quaestionibus, quae apta nata sunt fidem & veritatem TOTIUS ARTICULI DE RESURRECTIONE mortuorum PLANE suspectam reddere ac dubiam.
units.tr: But so that the reader may have no scruple at all, and may fully understand that the Arminians are speaking of the whole sacred supper considered in itself and as Christ instituted it, let him know that this is not unusual for these men. They speak in the same way about the article of the resurrection of the dead. The Arminians do not believe that the resurrection of the body is the resurrection of this very body, as we have shown in the first part of the Arcana, and as will become clearer below. Thus in this respect too they are attached to the heresy of the Socinians. Among the other arguments they bring forward in their Reply to the Excerpts of the most distinguished professors of Leiden, they also use this one (p. 122): By this reasoning, as with one blow, the handle is cut off from countless questions no less difficult than curious and foolish, which are fitted by nature to make the faith and truth of the WHOLE ARTICLE OF THE RESURRECTION of the dead CLEARLY suspect and doubtful.

units.la: Patet itaq; praeter profanitatem & impietatem Arminianorum ministrorum, rursus fraudulentia & improbitas eorum, quâ contra conscientiam suam incrustare volunt impietatem suam, per quam habent eos pro peritioribus & accuratis rerum aestimatoribus qui sacram coenam vanitatis suspectam habent. Huic insigni specimini conscientiae & αὐτοκατακρισίας Arminianorum diutius insistere volui, quia diligenter & probe est observandum.
units.tr: It is plain, then, that besides the profanity and impiety of the Arminian ministers, there is also their deceitfulness and wickedness, by which they wish to varnish their impiety against their own conscience, so that they regard themselves as more skilled and accurate judges of things, who hold the sacred supper to be suspect of vanity. I wanted to dwell longer on this striking example of the conscience and self-condemnation [αὐτοκατακρισίας] of the Arminians, because it must be observed carefully and honestly.

units.la: Quod addunt isti homines, me ipsos nebulones &c. impudenter vocasse, nae faciunt in eo quoque contra conscientiam suam. Nam hoc saltem dixi, eos qui sacram coenam vanitatis suspectam habent, non esse laudandos tanquam peritos & accuratos rerum aestimatores, sed habendos pro Atheis & nebulonibus; ac Arminianos ministros, dum ita eos commendant, non docere pietatem sed Atheismum. Verba mea clariora sunt, quam ut ea Arminiani negare possint. Sed placuit ipsis me convitii facti accusare, ut praetextum haberent qualemcunque infamis & diabolicae maledicentiae, quâ non solum adversum me, sed omnes Ecclesias Reformatas earumque Doctores, imo adversum omnes Reges, Principes, Magistratus qui blasphemias Socinianorum tolerare nolunt, speciatim contra Illustrissimos Ordines Generales in responso suo usi sunt. Ego, ut dixi, neminem appellavi nebulonem, quamvis non defit in orbe Christiano inter alios praecipue quidam qui hoc nomen & pejus mereatur, & qui tandem me & alios bonos forte coget ut eum isto potius quam alio nomine libere designemus, cuius rei justissimam rationem Deo & omnibus hominibus optima conscientia reddere poterimus, habentes ante oculos nostros praeeuntem in simili negocio Spiritum Sanctum, cum laudatissimis exemplis veteris & modernae Ecclesiae.
units.tr: As for what these men add, that I impudently called them scoundrels etc., they act against their own conscience in this too. For I said only this: that those who hold the sacred supper to be suspect of vanity are not to be praised as skilled and accurate judges of things, but are to be regarded as atheists and scoundrels; and that the Arminian ministers, while they commend such men in this way, are teaching not piety but atheism. My words are too clear for the Arminians to be able to deny them. But they were pleased to accuse me of having uttered an insult, so that they would have some pretext, of whatever kind, for their infamous and diabolical slander, with which they have attacked not only me but all the Reformed Churches and their teachers, indeed all kings, princes and magistrates who refuse to tolerate the blasphemies of the Socinians, and in their reply they have especially attacked the most illustrious States General. I, as I said, have named no one a scoundrel, although in the Christian world there are not lacking, among others, certain particular men who deserve this name and worse, and who may at last force me and other good men to designate them freely by this name rather than by another. For this matter we can give a most just account to God and to all men with the best conscience, having before our eyes the Holy Spirit, who went before us in a similar matter, together with the most praiseworthy examples of the ancient and modern Church.

units.la: 4. Intuleram ex praecedentibus, neminem jam mirari debere eos, qui de S. coena ita sentiunt ob causam allatam, etiam doctrinam nostram de praedestinatione, vocatione &c. ob eandem causam rejicere, quia rationi convenientissima non sit, seu non secundum rationem. Fatentur, & dicunt se recte facere in eo; habere enim se non solum rationem sed & Scripturam Sacram praeeuntem. Hic quod de ratione dicunt, libenter ipsis do de ratione sua corrupta & male sana; nam rationi sanae non contraria est doctrina nostra sed eam superat ut & reliqua omnia mysteria fidei faciunt, quæ si ad rationis sanæ normam exigantur, ita ut rejiciantur nisi ei per omnia conveniant, actum est de iis omnibus, speciatim ac præcipuè de mysterio Trinitatis, unione duarum naturarum in Christo, & satisfactione Christi. Atque hæc quidem causa est cur Sociniani aperti & simulatores in hunc lapidem impegerint. Quod ajunt Scripturam sacram sibi suffragari, illud salsissimum est. Qui enim cum judicio & attentè legit ipsorum argumenta ut & responsiones eorum ad nostra, deprehendet omnia tandem resolvi in hoc salsissimum & Pelagianum principium: Necessarium & liberum sibi invicem simpliciter repugnare: seu tolli libertatem arbitrii Ad hoc principium detorquent omnia loca Scripturæ ex quibus ipsi argumentantur, & confugiunt tandem in responsionibus ad loca quæ nos afferimus; sequuti in eo exemplum Pelagii & reliquiarum ejus, quas Prosper Aquitanicus sic vocat. Atque hoc est quod ipsi dicunt, ut ostendimus Parte Tertiâ Arcanorum, omnem controversiam quinquarticulariam revocari tandem (ab ipsis scilicet qui nobis controversias illas notorias initiò moverunt) ad definitionem liberi Arbitrii. Hoc obiter monere visum est. Nam de eâ re in præsens contendere cum iis & supervacaneum est, & mihi non propositum. Satis de eâ disputatum fuit. Et manifestissimum est tum ex iis quæ alii quidem Orthodoxi Theologi scripsere adversum eos, tùm ex Partibus Quatuor Arcanorum, atque ex Vindiciis seu responso quod primæ parti oppositerunt, eam controversiam quam Ecclesiis Reformatis super iis articulis moverunt, non nisi prætextum esse impiorum & execrandorum dogmatum quibus Libertinismum in doctrinâ,& per Libertinismum introducere conantur blasphemias Turcicas Socinianorum. Unde causæ ipsorum improbitas,& litis quam super iis articulis initiò moverunt iniquitas, ab omnibus luce clarius meridianâ deprehendi potest.
units.tr: 4. I had inferred from what went before that no one ought now to be surprised that those who think this way about the holy supper, for the reason given, also reject our doctrine of predestination, calling, etc., for the same reason: that it is not most agreeable to reason, or not according to reason. They confess this, and say that they do right in it; for they claim to have not only reason but also Holy Scripture going before them. Here, as to what they say about reason, I readily grant them their corrupt and ill-sound reason. For our doctrine is not contrary to sound reason but surpasses it, as all the other mysteries of the faith do; and if these were measured by the rule of sound reason, so that they were rejected unless they agreed with it in every respect, then all of them would be finished, and especially and above all the mystery of the Trinity, the union of the two natures in Christ, and the satisfaction of Christ. And this is indeed the reason why the open Socinians and the dissemblers have stumbled over this stone. As for their claim that Holy Scripture supports them, that is most absurd. For whoever reads with judgment and attention their arguments, and their replies to ours, will find that everything is in the end resolved into this most absurd and Pelagian principle: that the necessary and the free are simply opposed to each other, or that freedom of the will is abolished. To this principle they twist all the passages of Scripture from which they argue, and at last they take refuge in replies to the passages we cite; in this they follow the example of Pelagius and his remnants, whom Prosper of Aquitaine so calls. And this is what they themselves say, as we have shown in Part Three of the Arcana: that the whole quinquarticular controversy is at last traced back (by those, namely, who first raised those notorious controversies against us) to the definition of free will. I thought it worth noting this in passing. For it is both superfluous and not my purpose to contend with them about this matter at present. Enough has been disputed about it. And it is most manifest, both from what other orthodox theologians have written against them, and from the four Parts of the Arcana, and from the Vindiciae, or reply which they set against the first part, that the controversy which they have raised against the Reformed Churches over those articles is nothing but a pretext for impious and accursed doctrines, by which they try to introduce libertinism into doctrine, and through libertinism the Turkish blasphemies of the Socinians. Hence the wickedness of their cause and the injustice of the dispute which they first raised over those articles can be perceived by all, clearer than the midday light.

units.la: 5. Porrò ostenderam Arminianos injuriam facere doctrinæ nostræ de quinq; articulis.Nam ex eo quod factum,decretum,judicium,doctrinam aliquam percipere non possumus,seu rationem & connexionem cum sapientiâ & justitiâ introspicere, ex eo, dicebam, inferendum non esse, stultitiam in talibus esse aut injustitiam &c. Et confirmabam illud exinde quia judicia Dei inscrutabilia & viæ ejus impervestigabiles sunt, teste Apostolo Rom.11. Simulque addideram responsum ad exceptionem eorum quâ in Apologiâ locum eum Pauli conantur corrumpere. Hic illi, (postquam, ut Lectorem turbarent & fallerent, perturbâssent & lacerâssent omnia ea quæ à me aliquot paginis proposita fuerant) respondent p. 29. me Dictatorem & non disputatorem agere, & rationes non afferre, nec refutare rationem quam ibi attulerint. Verum enim vero hoc primò impertinens est. Nam, ut monueram in ipso ingressu Partis primæ Arcanorum, propositum mihi non fuit disputare cum ipsis aut quæstionem juris movere; sed saltem enarrationem & quasi historiam texere dogmatum eorum, hoc est ostendere quid Arminiani ministri credant aut non credant. Interim tamen simul indicaveram, me interdum ubi speciem aliquam habeant dogmata eorum quæ imponere simplicioribus possint, uno atque altero verbo palam facturum falsitatem eorum. Deinde falsum est, me probationem non attulisse responsi mei ad exceptionem istam, ut unusquisque, qui locum inspicere vult, videre potest. Ideò enim dixi hominem non posse percipere rationem mysteriorum omnem seu connexionem eorum cum justitiâ, rectitudine, sapientiâ &c. Dei, quia Deus revelavit ea tantum in quæstione An sit; in quæstione autem quomodo sit, aut omnino non revelare voluit, aut non plenè & perfectè. Falsum etiam est me ad rationem quam in Apologiâ adferunt c. 17. f. 177. b. non respondisse. Dicunt loco allegato Apologiæ, Apostolum non indicare judicia Dei talia esse, ut eorum æquitas ac multitudo intelligi à nobis non possit, cum judicia ista Dei nobis revelantur. Hoc probare conantur ex eo, quia Apostolus Paulus admiratus fuit sapientiam Dei, Ergo eam intellexit, & in iis sapientiam singularem penitus perspexit. Respondi enim, ex admiratione ista Pauli sequi intelligi, adeòq; ab Apostolo intellectam esse, eam sapientiam ac rectitudinè tantum in quæstione An sit, non autem in quæstione Quomodo sit. Ad hanc responsionem meam reponere aliquid firmi & solidi debuissent Arminiani si potuissent. Nam quod p. 28, dicunt me ineptire in descriptione illius quod est secundum rationem; & addunt secundum rationem esse illud tantum quod non est repugnans rationi: id verò utrumque falsum est. Etenim ego non descripsi id quod est secundum rationem, sed id quod est supra rationem, adeòque in descriptione quam non attuli ineptire non potui. Deinde, ut aliquid sit secundam rationem, non sufficit, ut non sit repugnans rectæ rationi (alioquin etiam id quod est supra rationem foret secundum rationem, id quod ineptissimum est ac salsissimum ut ostendi parte Tertia lib. 1. c. 4.) sed etiam requiritur ut ejus ratio & connexionis veritas ex ratione reddi possit.
units.tr: 5. Further, I had shown that the Arminians do an injustice to our doctrine of the five articles. For I said that from the fact that we cannot perceive the deed, decree, or judgment, or the doctrine of anything, or see into its reason and connection with wisdom and justice, it must not be inferred that there is folly or injustice in such things, and so on. And I confirmed this by the fact that the judgments of God are unsearchable and his ways past finding out, as the Apostle witnesses (Rom. 11). At the same time I had added a reply to their objection, by which in the Apology they try to corrupt that passage of Paul. Here they (after they had, in order to disturb and deceive the reader, confused and torn apart everything that I had set forth over several pages) reply on p. 29 that I play the dictator and not the disputant, and that I bring forward no arguments and refute no argument which they have brought forward there. But this, in the first place, is beside the point. For, as I had warned at the very beginning of the first part of the Arcana, it was not my purpose to dispute with them or to raise a question of right; but only to give an account, and as it were a history, of their doctrines, that is, to show what the Arminian ministers believe or do not believe. Meanwhile, however, I had also indicated at the same time that, wherever their doctrines have some appearance by which they can impose on simpler people, I would make their falsity plain in a word or two. Secondly, it is false that I have not brought forward a proof of my reply to that objection, as anyone who wishes to look at the passage can see. For I said that man cannot perceive the reason of all the mysteries, or their connection with the justice, uprightness, wisdom, etc., of God, because God has revealed them only in the question whether they are; but in the question how they are, he has either not willed to reveal them at all, or not fully and perfectly. It is also false that I did not reply to the argument they bring forward in the Apology, ch. 17, fol. 177 b. They say in the cited place of the Apology that the Apostle does not indicate that the judgments of God are such that their equity and multitude cannot be understood by us, since those judgments of God are revealed to us. They try to prove this from the fact that the Apostle Paul admired the wisdom of God; therefore he understood it, and fully perceived its singular wisdom in them. For I replied that from that admiration of Paul it follows that it was understood, and therefore understood by the Apostle, but only that wisdom and uprightness in the question whether it is, not in the question how it is. To this reply of mine the Arminians ought to have set something firm and solid, if they could have. For as to what they say on p. 28, that I talk nonsense in describing what is according to reason, and add that what is according to reason is only that which is not contrary to reason, both of these claims are false. For I did not describe what is according to reason, but what is above reason, and so I could not talk nonsense in a description I did not give. Next, for something to be according to reason, it is not enough that it is not contrary to right reason (otherwise what is above reason would also be according to reason, which is most absurd and most foolish, as I showed in Part Three, book 1, ch. 4); it is also required that the truth of its reason and connection can be rendered from reason.

units.la: Vindicaveram etiam p. 30. locum 1. Cor. 1. 23. à corruptelâ quâ Apol. c. 1. f. 37. a. eum locum depravant. Respondent me petere principium. Sed id falsum est. Nam illi ibi loci contendunt, sapientes hujus mundi intellexisse sensus Evangelij; & probant ex eo quia eam doctrinam pro stultitia habebant: verum enim vero id quod probare nituntur, ad rem non facit; prout etiam omnia ea quæ in Apologiæ illo loco f. 36. & 37. nugantur impertinentia sunt, & statum quæstionis non attingunt. Deinde probatio illa a stulto judicio Ethnicorum petita, quam stulta sit ecquis non videt? Etenim primo potest aliquis etiam pro stulto habere sermonem quem non intelligit. Deinde sequi ex eo plus & ad summum non potest, quam eos intellexisse sensum Grammaticum seu significationem vocum, id quod etiam puer potest qui res non intelligit. Falsum etiam est quod dicunt ibi, sapientes hujus mundi omnia utilitate rerum mundanarum metiri solere. Contrarium enim testatur res ipsa in plurimis sapientioribus, qui mero virtutis (quam talem esse putabant) nullo autem commodorum hujus seculi studio ducebantur. Hi profecto sensus Evangelij non poterant pro stultitia habere ideo, quod illos non nisi homines qui commodis vitæ suæ studere non sciunt probatuti essent, ut Arminiani volunt. Alia in præsens non addam.
units.tr: I had also vindicated, on p. 30, the text 1 Cor. 1:23 from the distortion by which the author of the Apology, at c. 1, f. 37a, twists that passage. They reply that I am begging the question. But that is false. For they there contend that the wise men of this world understood the sense of the Gospel, and they prove it from the fact that they regarded that doctrine as foolishness. But the very thing they try to prove has nothing to do with the matter; and likewise everything they trifle with in the Apology at that place, pp. 36 and 37, is beside the point and does not touch the state of the question. Moreover, who does not see how foolish that proof, drawn from the foolish judgment of the Gentiles, is? For, first, a man may regard as foolish a discourse he does not understand. Next, it follows from that at most only that they understood the grammatical sense or the meaning of the words, which even a child can do without understanding the matter. It is also false what they say there, that the wise men of this world are wont to measure everything by the usefulness of worldly things. The thing itself bears witness to the contrary in many of the wiser men, who were led by pure virtue (as they thought it to be), and not at all by any concern for the advantages of this age. Such men certainly could not have regarded the sense of the Gospel as foolishness on the ground that it was approved only by men who do not know how to pursue the advantages of their own lives, as the Arminians want. I will add nothing else for the present.

units.la: Cætera quæ p. 27. 28. 29. nugantur de usu rationis in Theologia & natura mysteriorum quæ dicunt me ignorare, partim falsa sunt, in quibus illi nobis produnt nova quædam Arcana sua, de quibus capiteegimus; partim impertinentia, & quæ ego ab his Magistris non discam. Qui volet, legere potest quæ in Rationali Theologico de vero ac falso usu rationis in mysteriis fidei pertractavimus.
units.tr: The rest of what they trifle with on pp. 27, 28 and 29, concerning the use of reason in theology and the nature of the mysteries, which they say I do not understand, is partly false, and in it they reveal to us some new secrets of their own, which we have dealt with in the chapter; partly irrelevant, and things which I shall not learn from these masters. Whoever wishes may read what we have treated in the Rational Theology concerning the true and false use of reason in the mysteries of faith.

units.la: 6. Addideram etiam Corollaria septem quæ illi dicunt redire eo, quod Arminiani ideo hanc doctrinam suam de usu rationis tuerentur, ut tuto convellere possint omnia ista mysteria fidei, quæ de Trinitate & Prædestinatione, in Ecclesia traduntur contra Hæreticos & alios errantes. Sed falsum est eo redire ista omnia, ut videre est unicuique legenti septem illa Corollaria. Ad primum igitur Corollarium, quo ostendi, eos etsi quandoq; dicant Scripturam esse solam regulam fidei, tamen hac doctrina de usu rationis non solum Scripturam sed etiam rationem normam constituere; ad hanc, inquā, accusationem gravissimam nihil respondent.
units.tr: 6. I had also added seven corollaries, which they say come down to this: that the Arminians defend this doctrine of theirs about the use of reason so that they may safely overthrow all those mysteries of faith concerning the Trinity and predestination which the Church hands down against heretics and other erring persons. But it is false that all these things come down to that, as anyone reading those seven corollaries can see. As for the first corollary, in which I showed that, although they sometimes say Scripture is the only rule of faith, nevertheless by this doctrine of the use of reason they set up reason as well as Scripture as the norm, they make no answer to this most serious charge.

units.la: Ad Secundum Corollarium quo ostendi eos omnis generis Hæresibus & fanaticis opinionibus portam aperire: ideo enim Hæretici v. g. Antitrinitarii mysteria fidei negant, quia secundum rationem non sunt &c. Respondent illi se hoc dogma de usu rationis in mysteriis fidei, quod nimirum mirùm omnia debeant esse secundùm rationem, tueri, ne quicquam temerè asseratur de mysteriis quod recta ratio absurdum ac falsum esse deprehendit, atque ita Hæreticis ansa præripiatur calumniandi; denique ut temerariis istis assertoribus frænum injiciatur quo retineantur, ne cùm mysteriis istis agitur, præter sacram Scripturam quicquam audacter statuant &c. Quibus verbis etiam novum arcanum nobis pandunt, quod vidimus eodem capite Quarto Partis Tertiæ.
units.tr: As for the second corollary, in which I showed that they open the door to heresies of every kind and to fanatical opinions: for heretics, for example the Antitrinitarians, deny the mysteries of faith precisely because they are not according to reason, and so on. They reply that they defend this doctrine of the use of reason in the mysteries of faith, namely that everything ought to be according to reason, so that nothing rashly asserted about the mysteries may be what right reason finds absurd and false, and so the heretics are deprived of an occasion for slander; and finally, that a bridle may be placed on those rash assertors to restrain them, lest, when dealing with those mysteries, they boldly set down anything beyond Holy Scripture, and so on. In these words they also reveal to us a new secret, which we have seen in the same fourth chapter of Part III.

units.la: Tertio Corollario indicavi, quæ'nam vera causa sit, propter quam Arminiani mysterium Trinitatis prout controversum est inter nos & Antitrinitarios negant esse eductam è Scripturâ per evidentem consequentiam: quia scilicet rationi non est conformis ista doctrina. Ad hoc etiam nihil respondent.
units.tr: In the third corollary I pointed out what the true cause is for which the Arminians deny that the mystery of the Trinity, as it is disputed between us and the Antitrinitarians, has been drawn from Scripture by evident consequence: namely, because this doctrine is not in conformity with reason. They make no answer to this either.

units.la: Quarto indicavi fundamentum quo nixi Arminiani jam per multos annos doctrinam Reformatarū Ecclesiarum de Prædestinatione &c. oppugnarint. Nimirùm quia ab initio statuendum sibi putárunt dogmata controversa, si secundùm rationem non sint, non esse vera. Ad hoc hic quidem & suo loco nihil respondent; sed sufficit, quòd paulò ante falsi sunt, se etiam propter hanc causam ea nostra dogmata oppugnare; de quo paulò ante & ipsi § 4. egimus.
units.tr: Fourthly, I pointed out the foundation on which the Arminians, leaning, have for many years assailed the doctrine of the Reformed Churches concerning predestination and so on. Namely, because they thought at the outset that controverted dogmas, if they are not according to reason, are not true. Here, and in its proper place, they make no answer to this; but it is enough that, as we said a little earlier, they are false in claiming that they assail our dogmas for this reason too, which we also treated a little earlier, in § 4.

units.la: Quintò ostendi, neminem mirari debere eos nostram illam doctrinam de Prædestinatione &c. rejicere ac damnare, qui ita ut diximus de S. Cœnâ judicant. Ad hanc rem quam bis attigeram quid respondeant vidimus eâdem sectione.
units.tr: Fifthly, I showed that no one ought to wonder that they reject and condemn our doctrine of predestination and so on, since they judge concerning the Holy Supper as I have said. What they answer to this matter, which I touched on twice, we have seen in the same section.

units.la: Sextò dixi sequi exinde neminem scandalizari debere, h. e. nostram illam doctrinam condemnare aut rejicere propter absurda illa horrenda quæ Arminiani exinde eliciunt: quandoquidem ea non fluunt ex nostrâ doctrinâ, sed ex præjudicio ipsorum quo statuunt eam doctrinam demum veram esse quæ secundùm rationem est &c. Ad hoc etiam nihil reponunt. Nisi quis forte velit hûc referre quæ calumniantur pag.30. me & alios Reformatos Theologos furere ad conspectum rationis veluti ad Gorgonis caput &c. Certè nemo rationis usum ac necessitatem in Theologiâ ita amplè & sanè commendavit ac vindicavit scriptis publicis quàm Reformati Theologi: qui interim volunt eam limitibus suis se continere debere.
units.tr: Sixthly, I said that it should follow from this that no one ought to be scandalized, that is, to condemn or reject our doctrine on account of those horrible absurdities which the Arminians draw from it, since these do not flow from our doctrine but from their own prejudice, by which they hold that only that doctrine is true which is according to reason, and so on. They reply nothing to this either. Unless perhaps someone wishes to refer here what they slander me and other Reformed theologians for on p. 30: that we rage at the sight of reason as at the head of the Gorgon, and so on. Certainly no one has so fully and soundly commended and vindicated in public writings the use and necessity of reason in theology as the Reformed theologians, who nevertheless wish that it should keep itself within its own limits.

units.la: Septimum denique Corollarium eò redit: ne quis temerè dogma aliquod tanquam falsum, impium, Diabolicum rejiciat, eò quòd talia vel talia absurda exinde sequantur. Sed si negare vult doctrinam aliquam veram esse &c. ante omnia certus sit doctrinam eam verbo Dei contrariam esse. Quod ut certò scire possit eum non à rationis absurdis quæ ei attribuere potest, sed à verbo Dei incipere debere, adeoque non debere progredi hoc modo : Hæc doctrina absurda est, Ergò verbo Dei repugnat. Sed hoc modo: Hæc doctrina verbo Dei repugnat. Ergò est absurda. in summâ, dicebam incipiendum esse in judicio de dogmatis fidei non à ratione, sed à verbo Dei &c. Quid his sanius ac verius dici potest? Interim tamen insaniam perfectam hoc vocant hi homines, & dicunt hoc consilium perniciosum esse; quod probant eâ calumniâ quòd solo rectæ rationis odio illud à me dicatur, item quòd hoc non levem suspicionem injiciat animis BONORUM, doctrinam Christi absurditatibus non paucis laborare. Judica Lector, qualis consequentia hæc sit? & consídera profanitatem horum hominum qui BONOS vocant illos qui doctrinam sanctissimam Christi vanitatis suspectam habent. Addunt verò præcludi hoc modo Atheis & Judæis viam ad Christianismum. Atqui hoc impertinens esse cùm ipsi fateantur; cur hoc argumento igitur utuntur? Fatentur enim me Christianis hoc consilium dare, non Atheis aut Judæis: Verùm enimverò, inquiunt pag. 30. de Christianis loquor, inquies. Et certè expresse dixeram: Hoc consilium sequimini Christiani populi &c. Unde vides, optime Lector, quales Sophistæ & rabulæ hi sint, qui solent multa nugari, quæ ipsi impertinentia esse sciunt. Sed de hac re alibi pluribus egimus.
units.tr: Finally, the seventh corollary comes down to this: that no one should rashly reject any dogma as false, impious or diabolical because such or such absurdities follow from it. But if someone wishes to deny that some doctrine is true, above all let him be certain that the doctrine is contrary to the Word of God. In order to know this for certain, he must begin not from the absurdities which he may attribute to reason, but from the Word of God, and so must not proceed in this way: This doctrine is absurd, therefore it is contrary to the Word of God; but in this way: This doctrine is contrary to the Word of God, therefore it is absurd. In sum, I said that judgment about the dogmas of faith must begin not from reason but from the Word of God, and so on. What could be said that is saner and truer than this? Yet these men call it utter madness, and say that this counsel is pernicious; which they prove by the slander that it is said by me out of mere hatred of right reason, and also that this counsel casts no slight suspicion into the minds of the GOOD, that the doctrine of Christ labours under not a few absurdities. Judge, reader, what kind of consequence this is! And consider the profanity of these men, who call good those who hold the most holy doctrine of Christ open to suspicion of vanity. They add that by this method the way to Christianity is closed to atheists and Jews. But this is irrelevant, since they themselves admit it; why then do they use this argument? For they concede that I give this counsel to Christians, not to atheists or Jews. But truly, they say on p. 30, you will say that I speak of Christians. And certainly I had expressly said: Follow this counsel, Christian people, and so on. From this you see, best reader, what sophists and wranglers these are, who are accustomed to trifle much, things which they themselves know to be irrelevant. But we have treated this matter at greater length elsewhere.

units.la: Addunt p. 31. etiam Christianis suspectum debere esse hoc consilium, & multa ibi deblatterant quibus novum nobis Arcanum produnt impietatis suæ, ut vidimus eodem cap. 4. Part. III. lib. 1. §. 3. Quæ ibi nugantur de argumentis desumtis ab absurdo, quibus ipsi nos utimur in disputando ad rem non faciunt. Non enim quæstio est, an liceat uti isto argumentandi genere, sed quæstio est de ordine quo adhiberi debeat. Ex his jam patet, non solùm firma stare Corollaria illa, quæ quia res continent diligenter notandas, veri cupidus Lector non male fecerit, si postquàm ea ab his hominibus frustrà oppugnata sunt, semel relegere non gravetur. Patet etiam ex omnibus quæ diximus in hoc capite, nos etiam capite 4. Par. I. lib. 1. bonâ fide egisse cum Arminianis, contra quàm illi calumniantur in frontispicio præsertim libri sui.
units.tr: On p. 31 they add that this counsel should also be suspect to Christians, and there they babble much by which they reveal to us a new secret of their impiety, as we have seen in the same chapter 4 of Part III, book 1, §3. What they trifle with there concerning arguments drawn from the absurd, which they themselves use in disputing against us, does not bear on the matter. For the question is not whether it is lawful to use that kind of argument, but the question concerns the order in which it ought to be employed. From all this it is now plain that not only do those corollaries stand firm, which, since they contain matters to be carefully noted, the lover of truth would not do amiss to reread once they have been vainly assailed by these men. It is also plain from everything we have said in this chapter that we also dealt in good faith with the Arminians in chapter 4 of Part I, book 1, contrary to their slander, especially on the title-page of their book.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CAP. V.

units.la: Examen Capitis V. Vindiciarum.
units.tr: Examination of Chapter V of the Vindiciae.

units.la: I. Arminiani fatentur & defendere conantur ea quae ipsis objecta erant circa dogmata quae Haereßiarcham seu damnati nominis auctorem habent. 2. Manifesta veritas quae sit secundum Arminianos. 3. Sentiunt se eodem jure posse Socini doctrinam sequi quam Calvini. 4. Corollarium Auctoris vindicatur. Arminiani non negant se Calvinum habere pro Haeretico, Socinum autem non habere pro Haeretico.
units.tr: I. The Arminians admit, and try to defend, the things objected to them concerning the doctrines held by the heresiarch, that is, the author of the condemned name. 2. What the manifest truth is according to the Arminians. 3. They think they may follow the doctrine of Socinus by the same right as that of Calvin. 4. The Author's corollary is vindicated. The Arminians do not deny that they hold Calvin to be a heretic, but they do not hold Socinus to be a heretic.

units.la: I. IN hoc capite objeceram istis hominibus, quòd, cùm ipsis objectum esset à Clarissimis Profes. Theol. Leydensibus dogma quoddam Socinianum, ipsi responderint, se non curare si maxime Socinus, Servetus, Pelagius &c. sit primus ac solus auctor alicujus dogmatis. Item; quòd, cùm ipsis objectum esset eos sub pacis nomine Socinianam haeresin introducere velle, responderint: se pensi non habere accusationem Socinianismi. Item, sefusque deque habere quodcunque tandem invisum nomen sententiae ipsorum praescribatur. Item, quòd, cùm aliâ occasione ipsis objectum esset ab iisdem Orthodoxis Theologis sententiam eorum Pelagianam fore, seu eos sic in Pelagii castra transituros, quòd, inquam, responderent: Quantum crimen medius fidius si hoc omninò verum foret! Item, quòd, cum aliud dogma Socinianum ipsis objectum esset, responderent: Sed esto, ex Socino haec desumta sint, quid tum? Cum Socino itaque sentiunt hac in parte Remonstrantes. Bene habet. Socinus ergo in hac re bene sentit scripsitque. Item, cùm rursus illud objectum ipsis esset alià occasione, responderent: Papa! quantum crimen! &c.
units.tr: I. In this chapter I had objected to these men that when the most distinguished professors of theology at Leiden had charged them with a certain Socinian doctrine, they replied: that they did not care even if Socinus, Servetus, Pelagius and so on were the first and sole author of some doctrine. Likewise, when they were charged with wanting to introduce Socinian heresy under the name of peace, they replied: that they had no concern for the accusation of Socinianism. Likewise, they make light of whatever hateful name may at last be assigned to their opinion. Likewise, when on another occasion the same orthodox theologians objected that their view would be Pelagian, or that they would thus go over to the camp of Pelagius, they answered (I say): What a crime, upon my word, if this were altogether true! Likewise, when another Socinian doctrine was objected to them, they replied: But grant that these things are taken from Socinus, so what? Therefore the Remonstrants agree with Socinus in this part. Well and good. Socinus, then, thinks and writes well in this matter. Likewise, when that charge was again brought against them on another occasion, they replied: Oh Pope! What a crime! etc.

units.la: Haec sibi à me objecta Arminiani nequaquam negant sed fatentur, ac defendunt hoc praetextu se loquutos esse de manifestâ veritate. Verùm iste praetextus eos non juvat. Nam quae est ista manifesta veritas de quâ loquuntur? Est veritas talis, cujus auctor primus ac solus est Socinus, Servetus, Pelagius. Verum hoc esse patet ex verbis à me allegatis ex Apolog. Exam. Cens. Praef. f. 11. b. Nec referre, inquiunt, crederemus, si Auctor ejus primus ac solus fuisset Socinus, aliusve quivis e trivio Christianus. Tanti est Remonstrantibus manifesta veritas, ut susque deque habeant, sive Socini, sive Serveti, sive Pelagii, sive alterius alicujus exosissimi hominis nomen ei praescribatur. Est veritas talis, cujus duces sunt Haeretici: Sequendum itaque est ubi prae præit veritas, necex ducibus veritas, sed ex veritate duces æstimandi sunt. Nec refert quo nomine aut titulo nigri sunt. Responf. ad Excerp. DD. Proff. Leyd. p. 15. Sic igitur ultimis his verbis ne quidem Hæreticos verè sic dictos excipiunt. Est veritas talis, quam non Ecclesia Orthodoxa sed ipsi soli cum Hæreticis illis profitentur. Ita enim, cùm dixissent de hac materiâ loquentes, se Adamantem (veritatem intelligunt) non rejecturos etiamsi illum in sterquilinio reperirent; objectionem anticipantes respondent: Neque verò arrogantia eorum tribui debet, quòd adamantes ipsos se videre sibi persuadeant, quos alii non vident. Quis enim arrogantem eum vocet, qui quod suis oculis videt, se videre sibi persuadet? Nemo alienis oculis videt, nemo alienis auribus audit: Quisque suis ut credat, æquum est. Nimium abjecti animi, nimis servilis ingenii est, non sapere nisi ad alienum arbitrium. ibid. Veritas manifesta talis, quàm quis scripturis maximè consentaneam veritatem esse adhibito omni ingenio ac judicio suo deprehendit & amplectitur, etiamsi totus orbis refragetur, quemadmodum refragari constat totum Orbem Christianum blasphemiis Antitrinitariorum. Ita enim manifestam veritatem ibidem p. 14. describunt: At cùm consensionis rationem habendam esse negant Remonstrantes, hoc tantum volunt, manifestam veritatem & Scripturarum auctoritatem pluris faciendam esse quàm Doctorum omnium vel centumviralia suffragia, neque cuiquam vitio verti debere, si eam quam Scripturis maximè consentaneam veritatem esse adhibuto omni ingenio ac judicio suo deprehendit, amplectatur, etiamsi totus, ut ita loquamur, orbis refragetur. Quod quàm periculosum sit, postquam veritatis lux per prædicationem Evangelii ante annos centum & ultra quasi postliminio reducta & per totum orbem hactenus dispersa est, prudens Lector facilè intelligit. Et si hoc verum est, Antitrinitariis profecto vitio verti non debent dogmata eorum quæ blasphema, execranda & Hæretica esse totus orbis Christianus judicat. Atque hoc est, quod Arminiani volunt; utpote qui statuunt Socinianos non peccare istis blasphemis dogmatis suis, ut ostendimus Par. III. lib.1, c. 2. Veritas denique manifesta talis, quam quivis mentis suæ compos intelligere potest: Usque adeò amant Remonstrantes Reformatam Religionem (Vide optime Lector quales Hypocritæ sint hi Socinani simulatores) ut ei attributum quicquam nolint, quod non manifesta est veritatis, & ad gloriam Reformationis pertinere non statim à quovis mentis suæ compote intelligi potest. ibid. p. 23. Qualis manifesta veritas Socinianis apertis & simulatoribus est, Christum non habere naturam divinam; non fuisse antequam nasceretur ex Maria virgine &c. Ita enim Socinus cùm dixisset, eum cùm verus homo sit, non posse simul esse æternum Deum, ait: Quis tàm hebes ac rudis est, qui, si animum adverterit, id itasse habere, perspicuè non cernat, & aliis aperte demonstrare non queat? Socin. animadv. Posnan. assert. 22. §. 2. p. 86. item : ipsos cœcos videre posse quàm monstrosa sibique nullâ ex parte consentanea doctrina sit Trinitatis assert. 25. §. 1. p. 93. item, ipsi sensui communi patet unam numero essentiam tres personas esse non posse ib. §. 2. p. 94.
units.tr: The Arminians by no means deny these things that I have objected to them; they admit them and defend them on the pretext that they have spoken of a manifest truth. But this pretext does not help them. For what is this manifest truth they speak of? It is a truth whose first and sole author is Socinus, Servetus or Pelagius. That this is so is clear from the words I quoted from the Apology, the Examination of the Censure, preface, f. 11 b: Nor, they say, would it matter to us if its author had been Socinus alone, or any other common Christian. So much does manifest truth count with the Remonstrants that they make light of whether the name of Socinus, Servetus, Pelagius or of any other most hated man is attached to it. It is a truth whose leaders are heretics: One must therefore follow where truth goes before, and truth is not to be judged by its leaders, but leaders are to be judged by the truth. Nor does it matter by what name or title they are called black. Answer to the Excerpts of the Professors of Leiden, p. 15. So by these last words they do not even exclude those who are truly called heretics. It is a truth which the orthodox Church does not profess, but which they alone profess together with those heretics. For when they had spoken on this subject, they said that they would not reject the adamant (meaning the truth) even if they found it in a dunghill; anticipating an objection, they answer: Nor should their arrogance be imputed to them, because they persuade themselves that they see adamants which others do not see. For who would call arrogant a man who persuades himself that he sees with his own eyes what he sees? No one sees with another's eyes, no one hears with another's ears. It is fair that each should believe with his own. It is too abject a spirit and too servile a mind not to be wise except at another's pleasure. Ibid. A manifest truth of this kind is one that someone, applying all his talent and his own judgment, discovers and embraces as the truth most consonant with the Scriptures, even if the whole world objects, just as it is well known that the whole Christian world objects to the blasphemies of the Antitrinitarians. For thus they describe the manifest truth in the same place, p. 14: But when the Remonstrants deny that consensus is to be taken into account, they only mean that manifest truth and the authority of the Scriptures are to be valued above all the teachers or the votes of a hundred men; and that no one ought to be blamed if he embraces what he has discovered, by applying all his talent and judgment, to be the truth most consonant with the Scriptures, even if the whole world, so to speak, objects. How dangerous this is, a prudent reader easily understands, since the light of truth, brought back as if by right of return through the preaching of the Gospel a hundred years and more ago, has hitherto spread through the whole world. And if this is true, the Antitrinitarians ought not to be blamed for their doctrines, which the whole Christian world judges to be blasphemous, execrable and heretical. And this is what the Arminians want, since they hold that the Socinians do not sin by these blasphemous doctrines of theirs, as we have shown in Part III, book 1, ch. 2. Finally, a manifest truth of the kind that anyone in his right mind can grasp: So greatly do the Remonstrants love the Reformed Religion (let the reader see well what hypocrites these Socinian pretenders are) that they do not want anything attributed to it which is not manifest truth and which cannot at once be understood by anyone in his right mind to pertain to the glory of the Reformation. Ibid., p. 23. Such is the manifest truth for the open and pretending Socinians: that Christ does not have a divine nature; that he did not exist before he was born of the Virgin Mary, etc. For when Socinus had said that, since he is a true man, he cannot at the same time be the eternal God, he says: Who is so dull and crude that, if he gives his mind to it, he does not clearly see that this is so, and cannot clearly demonstrate it to others? Socinus, Animadversions on Posnan, assertion 22, §2, p. 86. Likewise: that the blind themselves can see how monstrous and in no way consistent with itself the doctrine of the Trinity is, assertion 25, §1, p. 93. Likewise: it is evident to common sense itself that three persons cannot be one essence numerically, ibid., §2, p. 94.

units.la: Ita igitur frustrà defendere conantur ea quæ ipsis à me objecta erant. Unum præterire non possum, quod p. 32. 33. Vindic. dicunt me Chrysostomum pro Hæretico habere. In eo quoque falsum illos dicere patet exinde, quòd Chrysostomum in eo ipso loco Catholicum appellavi: etsi quia Pelagius virus suum tunc nondum sparserat, securius loquutus fuerit de Libero arbitrio, ut Augustinus eum cum aliis Patribus merito excusat.
units.tr: Thus they try in vain to defend the things I objected to them. There is one point I cannot pass over: on pp. 32–33 of the Vindiciae they say that I hold Chrysostom to be a heretic. That they say this falsely is clear from the fact that in that very passage I called Chrysostom Catholic; though, because Pelagius had not yet spread his poison, he spoke more safely about free will, as Augustine rightly excuses him along with the other Fathers.

units.la: 4. Porrò Corollarii loco conquestus fueram quòd Calvinum & Socinum conjungerent; ac dixeram eos, cùm dicunt; Socinus, Calvinus nomina sunt sectarum, jungere Calvinum ideò cum Socino ut videri possint eodem jure sequi doctrinam Socini, quàm eam quam Calvinus proposuit. Hoc illi nequaquam negant h. e. se id eo fine facere; saltem arrodunt quod dixeram, non esse conjungendos duos istos Doctores, nam Socinum Hæreticum fuisse non autem Calvinum; etsi Arminiani Socinum pro Hæretico non habeant, Calvinum autem pro tali habeant. Respondent illi p. 33. 1. Nullam esse consequentiam; Socinus Hæteticus fuit, non autem Calvinus: Ergò Calvinus non est nomen sectæ. Atqui hæc mea conclusio non fuit, sed ista: Ergò Calvinus non erat jungendus cum Socino. 2. Vtuntur coccysmo illo suo solito de pari jure eorum qui alium Hæreseos accusant, & ejus qui Hæreseos accusantur; item de Vedelio cum suis. Et non negant se Socinum non habere pro Hæretico, Calvinum autem pro Hæretico habere. Deinde ostenderam, Calvinum non esse nomen sectæ, ibi illi inter alias nugas quæ ad rem non faciunt, convitiis, sarcasmis & scommatis responsionis loco utuntur, & irrident omnes Reformatos: Nempe, inquiunt, vos fideles estis & non Calviniani. Cateri infideles, & aut Socinianí &c. & dicunt eos vicissim nos pro infidelibus habere, tandem me insaniæ arguunt & ad medicos remittunt. Et sic præclarè scilicet partibus suis etiam in isto quinto capite Vindiciarum defuncti sunt. Nunc ex dictis patet me Capite etiam Quinto Par.I. lib. 1. nihil ipsis per calumniam affinxisse.
units.tr: 4. Further, by way of a corollary, I had complained that they joined Calvin and Socinus together; and I had said that when they say, Socinus and Calvin are names of sects, they join Calvin with Socinus so that it may seem that they can follow the doctrine of Socinus by the same right as that which Calvin proposed. They by no means deny this, that is, they do it for that purpose; at least they carp at what I had said, that these two teachers should not be joined, for Socinus was a heretic but Calvin was not, although the Arminians do not hold Socinus to be a heretic while they hold Calvin to be one. They reply on p. 33: 1. There is no consequence: Socinus was a heretic, but Calvin was not; therefore Calvin is not the name of a sect. But my conclusion was not this, but that: Therefore Calvin ought not to be joined with Socinus. 2. They use their usual cry about the equal right of those who accuse another of heresy and of those who are accused of heresy; likewise about Vedelius and his followers. And they do not deny that they do not hold Socinus to be a heretic, but do hold Calvin to be a heretic. Then I showed that Calvin is not the name of a sect. Here, among other trifles that have nothing to do with the matter, they use insults, sarcasms and mockery in place of an answer, and they mock all the Reformed: Namely, they say, you are faithful and not Calvinists. The rest are unfaithful, and either Socinians, etc. And they in turn say that we hold them to be unfaithful, and at last they accuse me of madness and send me off to the doctors. And so, no doubt, they have admirably discharged their parts even in this fifth chapter of the Vindiciae. Now from what has been said it is clear that in Chapter Five too of Part I, book 1, I have falsely charged them with nothing.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: Examen Capitis VI. Vindic. Lib. I.
units.tr: Examination of Chapter VI of the Vindiciae, Book I.

units.la: 1. Arminiani nihil hic negant eorum omnium quae ipsis illo capite obiecta fuere. 2. Fraus Arminianorum agentium contra propriam conscientiam. 3. Haeresis Marcionitica Apellae ex inferis resuscitata ab Arminianis.
units.tr: 1. The Arminians deny nothing here of all those things that were objected to them in that chapter. 2. The fraud of the Arminians, acting against their own conscience. 3. The Marcionite heresy of Apelles, raised from the dead by the Arminians.

units.la: 1. OBjeceram Arminianis haec ipsorum dogmata: Ea tantum esse necessaria creditu ad salutem, quae extra controversiam sunt inter Christianos, sive quae apud omnes in confesso sunt. Ea quae non ab omnibus Christianis videntur seu agnoscuntur, non esse simpliciter clara sive manifesta. Imo quaedam quae ab Haereticis, & sic ab omnibus non agnoscuntur; tamen Reformatis, Lutheranis, Pontificiis clara sunt, & ab ipsis pro veris, quaedam etiam pro Necessariis habentur, non extare in Scriptura, imo ne hilum quidem. De simplicitate Dei ne iota quidem in Scriptura esse. Nullum locum in Scriptura esse, unde appareat Patres Veteris Testamenti in Iesum Christum credidisse. Sed ea esse clara & manifesta quae apud omnes Christianos in confesso sunt, sive ab omnibus agnoscuntur. Necessaria esse pauca, ita ut omnia controversa exinde excludantur. Ea pauca Necessaria esse tria tantum; nimirum fidem divinorum promissorum, obedientiam divinorum mandatorum, & debitam Scripturis reverentiam. Ea sola esse firmiter constanterque credenda.
units.tr: 1. I had charged the Arminians with these doctrines of theirs: That only those things are necessary to be believed for salvation which are beyond controversy among Christians, or which are admitted by all. Those things which are not seen or acknowledged by all Christians are not simply clear or manifest. Indeed, some things which are not acknowledged by heretics, and so not by all, yet are clear to the Reformed, the Lutherans and the Papists, and are held by them as true, and some even as necessary, are not found in Scripture, nor even a trace of them. That there is not even a jot of the simplicity of God in Scripture. That there is no passage in Scripture from which it appears that the fathers of the Old Testament believed in Jesus Christ. But that those things are clear and manifest which are admitted among all Christians, or acknowledged by all. That the necessary things are few, so that all controverted matters are thereby excluded. That these few necessary things are only three: namely, faith in the divine promises, obedience to the divine commands, and due reverence for Scripture. That these alone are to be firmly and constantly believed.

units.la: Quid ad haec Arminiani? Negantne? Nequaquam vero; sed postea quam, quia se constrictos vident, convitia mihi solita cum impudentia dixissent, omnia ad unum revocant & illud defendunt. Verba ipsorum fideliter referam, ut unus quisque de conscientia horum hominum judicare possit. Sic igitur caput hoc ordiuntur, non praemissa dogmatum enumeratione: Spongia hic opus est, Nullum enim lineamentum bona aut sanae mentis vel artis hic est. Huc omnia redeunt: Remonstrantes affirmant ea tantum esse praecise ad salutem scitu ac creditu necessaria, quae vel ex claris atque apertis Scripturarum verbis vel, per evidentem & sole clariorem consequentiam necessaria esse cuivis mentis tantum sua compoti constare potest, eaque pauca esse ex Theologorum Reformatorum, inprimis ex Regis Magnae Britanniae & Molinaei disertâ confessione evincunt, quippe qui id non tantum totidem verbis declarant, sed & addunt; omnia necessaria Scripturis tam clare atque aperte definita esse, ut nulla alia interpretatione egeant. Ita boni hi viri statuum quaestionis formant.
units.tr: What do the Arminians say to this? Do they deny it? Not at all; but after they see that they are pressed, they pour out their usual insults at me with impudence, and then they bring everything back to this one point and defend it. I shall report their words faithfully, so that each one may judge the conscience of these men. They begin this chapter thus, without any listing of doctrines: A sponge is needed here, for there is no outline here of any good or sound mind or art. All of it comes down to this: The Remonstrants affirm that only those things are strictly necessary to be known and believed for salvation which can be grasped either from the clear and plain words of Scripture or by an evident consequence, clearer than the sun, which is necessary for anyone who is in possession of his own mind; and they prove that these things are few from the explicit confession of the Reformed theologians, especially of the King of Great Britain and of Molinaeus, who not only declare this in so many words but also add that all the things necessary are defined in Scripture so clearly and plainly that they need no other interpretation. In this way these good men frame the state of the question.

units.la: 2. Hic profecto nemo est, qui non videat fraudem eorum, & eos contra protra propriam conscientiam suam Lectori velle imponere. Quis enim ex statu quaestionis ut illi eum formant, unquam possit colligere me reliqua illa objecisse ipsis, quae ipsi non exprimunt? Quis non videt eos saltem minimam partem status quaestionis proponere, quam tamen ne ipsam quidem sincere sed fraudulenter proponunt, ut mox videbimus? Nam cur ne verbo quidem mentionem faciunt horrendorum istorum caeterorum dogmatum quae ipsis objeci in capite isto & modo enumeravi? Cur ad ea nihil respondent? Cur dissimulant? Cur non meminerunt horum: Ea esse tantum necessaria ad salutem quae extra controversiam sunt inter Christianos, sive quae apud omnes in confesso sunt? Quaedam quae a Lutheranis, Reformatis, Pontificiis pro manifesta veritate Scriptura, imo quaedam etiam pro Necessariis habentur, non extare in Scriptura? Speciatim Adorationis Spiritus S. ne indicium quidem manifestum in Scriptura exstare, imo ne hilum quidem? De Simplicitate Dei ne jota quidem in Scriptura esse? Nullum locum in Scriptura tota esse, unde appareat Patres Veteris T. in I. Christum credidisse? Necessaria ita pauca esse, ut omnia controversa inde excludantur? Ea pauca necessaria tria esse haec tantum, nimirum fidem divinorum promissorum &c. Haec sola esse firmiter constanterque credenda? Haec debebant expressisse in statu quaestionis. Sed hoc non faciunt: quod diligenter observetur; hujus enim usus erit in sequentibus. Notandum igitur eos capite 6. in quo ostendi & probavi e variis locis Apologiae eos non agnoscere nulla dogmata controversa pro Necessariis ad salutem; eos, inquam, illud ne verbulo quidem negare. Unde unusquisque videt me injuriam ipsis in hac etiam parte nequaquam fecisse; & intelligit exinde bonitatem causae Ecclesiarum Reformatarum, contra vero pessimam fidem & desperatam causam horum hominum, cujus in conscientia sua convicti sunt, & nihilominus eam contra propriam conscientiam defendunt. Dixi autem, illos ne illam quidem partem status quaestionis sincere proponere. Nam eam ita fraudulenter exhibent, ac si Serenissimus M. Britanniae Rex & Cl. Molinaeus & caeteri Theologi Reformati cum iis facerent circa doctrinam de paucitate Necessariorum, quod falsum esse & longe aliam esse mentem illorum ostendi capite allegato Partis Primae; ad quam rem hi homines ne unico verbo respondent, & tamen cramben eandem impudenter audent reponere. Unde mihi aestimet aliquis conscientiam horum hominum. Deinde ita proponunt testimonia atque auctoritatem allegatam, ac si ego improbassem sententiam Serenissimi Regis & Theologorum Orthodoxorum. Hinc etiam immediate subjiciunt: Hac non confutat Vedelius, sed tantum tantum indicat. Quid de hujus opinionis veritate aut falsitate sentiendum sit, cap. 10. lib. 1. dabitur dicendi locus, inquit. In quâ re fraus etiam ipsorum manifestissima est. Nam ego ne verbulo quidem improbavi eam sentientiam; sed approbavi. Arminianorum autem opinionem quæ longè alia est, detestatus sum & cum omnibus piis ex animo detestor. In reliquâ parte istius sui capitis conantur probare opinionem suam de evidentiâ dogmatum necessariorum ineptis coccysmis suis contra judicium fallibile Ecclesiæ & contra Vedelių cū suis, ut loqui ipsis libet impertinentissimè.
units.tr: 2. Surely there is no one here who does not see their fraud, and their wish to impose on the reader, against their own conscience. For who, from the state of the question as they frame it, could ever gather that I had objected to them those other points which they do not express? Who does not see that they set out only the smallest part of the state of the question, and even that they present not sincerely but fraudulently, as we shall soon see? For why do they not so much as mention those horrible other doctrines which I objected to them in this chapter and listed in order? Why do they answer nothing to them? Why do they conceal them? Why do they not recall these: That only those things are necessary for salvation which are beyond controversy among Christians, or which are admitted by all? That some things, which are held by the Lutherans, the Reformed and the Papists to be the manifest truth of Scripture, and indeed some even as necessary, are not found in Scripture? Specifically, that not even a clear indication of the worship of the Holy Spirit exists in Scripture, indeed not even a trace? That there is not even a jot of the simplicity of God in Scripture? That there is no passage in the whole of Scripture from which it appears that the fathers of the Old Testament believed in Jesus Christ? That the necessary things are so few that all controverted matters are excluded thereby? That these few necessary things are only these three, namely faith in the divine promises, and so on? That these alone are to be firmly and constantly believed? They ought to have expressed these in the state of the question. But they do not do this; and this must be carefully noted, for its use will appear in what follows. It must therefore be noted that in chapter 6, where I showed and proved from various passages of the Apology that they do not acknowledge any controverted doctrines as necessary to salvation, they do not deny this, I say, even by a single word. From this everyone sees that I have in no way wronged them in this respect either, and understands from it the goodness of the cause of the Reformed Churches, and on the contrary the very wicked faith and desperate cause of these men, of which they are convicted in their own conscience, and yet which they defend against their own conscience. I have said, moreover, that they do not sincerely set out even that part of the state of the question. For they present it so fraudulently, as if the most serene King of Great Britain, the illustrious Molinaeus and the other Reformed theologians had taken this view of the doctrine concerning the paucity of necessary things. I have shown that this is false and that their mind is quite different, in the chapter cited in Part One; to which these men do not reply with a single word, and yet they dare shamelessly to serve up the same old scrap again. Let anyone judge the conscience of these men from this. Then they set out the testimonies and the authority cited in such a way as if I had disapproved of the opinion of the most serene King and of the orthodox theologians. Immediately after this they add: Vedelius does not refute this, but only merely indicates. What is to be thought of the truth or falsity of this opinion will be given its place in chapter 10 of Book 1, he says. In this matter their fraud is also most manifest. For I did not disapprove of that opinion by even a single word, but approved it. But the opinion of the Arminians, which is quite different, I have detested and with all pious men I detest it from my heart. In the rest of that chapter they try to prove their opinion about the evidence of the necessary doctrines with their silly quibbles, against the fallible judgment of the Church and against Vedelius and his fellows, as they are pleased to speak most impertinently.

units.la: 3. Hoc saltem Corollarii loco addam, Arminianos doctrinâ illâ suâ de tribus Necessariis dogmatis ex inferis revocare abominandam hæresin Marcionitarum, quæ, ut in diversas sectas & partes divisa erat, ita cujusdam partis Marcionitarum dux erat Apelles Hæreticus verus pater Libertinorum. Is docebat inter alia, ut testatur vetustissimus Scriptor Ecclesiasticus Rhodon apud Eusebium lib. 5. cap. 13. non debere Christianos sollicitos esse de controversiis fidei; unumquemque enim Christianum in suâ opinione seu religione servari posse; ad salutē quippe sufficere fidem in Iesum Christum & studium bonorum operum: σωθῆναι μὲν ἐκ τῆς πίστεως τὸν ἐσταυρωμένον ἠλπικότας ἀπεφαίνετο μόνον ἐαν ἐν ἔργοις ἀγαθοῖς ἐλέγχοντας; h. e. salvatum enim iri eos qui fiduciam suam in Christum collocassent, dummodo in bonis operibus versari sedulo deprehendantur. Quod certè manifestum facit, eum à suis exegisse etiam reverentiam debitâ Scripturis sacris. Harum enim reverentiam includit is qui dicit fidem in I. Christum & studium bonorum operum necessarium esse ad salutem; quandoquidem ex illis fides in Christum hauritur & studium bonorum operum discitur. Quare nec tertium illud dogma ad salutem Necessarium Apelles negavit; adeoque non erravit in quæstione an sit; quamvis erraverit in Quæstione quid sit, & quomodo sit honoranda, non secus ac alii Hæretici Veteres & recentes; quorum quidam libros quosdam Scripturæ addunt & eos reverentur, quia putant Scripturam sacram esse; alii autem quosdam resecant, quia putant eos Scripturam sacram non esse, sed infra Majestatem ac dignitatem Scripturæ subsidere. Unde etiam πολλὴν ἀπουδὴν ait Rhodon h. e. multum laboris insumsit Apelles, ut ostenderet libros Mosis & reliquos Veteris Testamenti non esse de Canone. Id quod non fecisset secundum hypothesin Arminianorum, nisi Scripturam sacram speciatim V. T. summopere reveritus fuisset. Absque eâ enim reverentiâ contemtim habuisset omnia, & manum non vertisset ut ostenderet quæ Scriptura sacra esset quæ non, ut Arminiani loquuntur
units.tr: 3. By way of a corollary I will add this much: by that doctrine of theirs about three necessary doctrines, the Arminians revive from the dead the abominable heresy of the Marcionites, which, though it was divided into various sects and parties, nonetheless had as the leader of one part of the Marcionites the heretic Apelles, the true father of the Libertines. He taught, among other things, as the most ancient ecclesiastical writer Rhodon testifies in Eusebius, book 5, chapter 13, that Christians ought not to be anxious about controversies of faith; for each Christian could be kept in his own opinion or religion, since faith in Jesus Christ and zeal for good works were sufficient for salvation: He declared that those who had placed their hope in the crucified one would be saved, provided they were found to be diligent in good works [σωθῆναι μὲν ἐκ τῆς πίστεως τὸν ἐσταυρωμένον ἠλπικότας ἀπεφαίνετο μόνον ἐαν ἐν ἔργοις ἀγαθοῖς ἐλέγχοντας]; that is, for those who had put their trust in Christ would be saved, provided they were found to be busy in good works. This certainly makes clear that he also required of his followers due reverence for the holy Scriptures. For whoever says that faith in Jesus Christ and zeal for good works are necessary for salvation includes that reverence for Scripture; since faith in Christ is drawn from Scripture, and zeal for good works is learned from it. Therefore Apelles did not deny that third doctrine, which is necessary for salvation either; and so he did not err on the question whether it is, although he erred on the question what it is and how it is to be honoured, just as other heretics both ancient and recent did; some of whom add certain books to Scripture and revere them because they think them to be holy Scripture, while others cut away certain books because they think they are not holy Scripture but fall below the majesty and dignity of Scripture. Hence Rhodon also says that Apelles took much effort [πολλὴν σπουδήν] to show that the books of Moses and the rest of the Old Testament were not of the canon. He would not have done this according to the hypothesis of the Arminians, unless he had greatly revered the holy Scripture, especially the Old Testament. For without that reverence he would have despised everything, and would not have taken the trouble to show which Scripture was holy and which was not, as the Arminians speak

units.la: { } quantur de iis qui sensum Scripturæ sacræ corrumpunt, Vindic. lib. I. c. 3. p. 23. Et docebat Apelles idem quod Sociniani aperti & nostri simulatores impiissimi sentiunt, nimirum esse tantùm unam personam Deitatis, Patrem videlicet. &, ut videas eum in conscientiâ suâ non aliter statuisse (id quod secundùm Arminianos constituit etiam innocentiam quam tantopere in Hæreticis commendant) jurabat Rhodoni se ita animo sentire ut dicebat. In hoc igitur uno etsi melior sit sententia Arminianorum quàm Apellæ, quòd scilicet omnes Scripturas recipiunt, id quod non faciebat Apelles, tamen putabat se eâ ratione tribuere Scripturæ reverentiam quam debebat. Et sub illâ latitudine reverentiæ debitæ Scripturis, non minùs latere potest Anabaptista aut alias quicunque Hæreticus, qui Vetus Testamentum sub hoc aut illo prætextu rejicit, ac interim profitetur & plane credit se debitam Scripturis reverentiam exhibere, non autem alios qui omnes Canonicos libros rejiciunt. Nec enim definiunt Arminiani quæ'nam sit illa reverentia Scripturæ, simpliciter necessaria ad salutem. Itaque nullus est Hæreticus qui non sub prætextu ac latitudine tertii dogmatis, ut & duorum priorum necessariorum, latere possit. Nullus enim est Hæreticus qui non ea tria dogmata profiteatur h. e. ore scriptisque de se protestetur & ab aliis exigat; nimirùm, fidem promissorum divinorum, obedientiam divinorum mandatorum, & debitam Scripturis sacris reverentiam. Ex quo vel solo manifestum fit, quid Arminiani ministri moliantur in negocio Religionis. Sic igitur etiam ex hoc capite patet, me bonâ fide cum istis hominibus egisse, & nihil iis per calumniam affinxisse, quandoquidem ipsi nihil hîc negant eorum quæ iis objeceram.
units.tr: {  } speak of those who corrupt the sense of Holy Scripture, Vindic. lib. I, c. 3, p. 23. Apelles also taught what the Socinians openly hold and what our most impious dissemblers think: that there is only one Person of the Deity, namely the Father. And so that you may see that he did not hold otherwise in his own conscience (which, according to the Arminians, also makes innocent the very thing they commend so highly in heretics), he swore to Rhodon that he felt in his mind just as he said. In this one point, then, the opinion of the Arminians is better than Apelles', since they accept all the Scriptures, which Apelles did not do; yet he thought that by this means he paid the reverence to Scripture that he owed. Under this broad notion of the reverence due to the Scriptures, an Anabaptist or any other heretic can equally lie hidden, one who rejects the Old Testament under this or that pretext and meanwhile professes, and plainly believes, that he shows the Scriptures the reverence due to them, while not so the others who reject all the canonical books. For the Arminians do not define what that reverence for Scripture is, which is simply necessary to salvation. Thus there is no heretic who cannot lie hidden under the pretext and broad sense of the third doctrine, as also of the two earlier necessary ones. For there is no heretic who does not profess those three doctrines, that is, who does not declare them of himself by mouth and in writing and demand them from others: namely, faith in the divine promises, obedience to the divine commands, and the reverence due to the holy Scriptures. From this alone it is clear what the Arminian ministers are plotting in the business of religion. So too from this chapter it is evident that I have dealt honestly with these men, and have falsely attributed nothing to them by calumny, since they here deny nothing of what I had objected to them.

units.la: CAP. VII. Examen Capitis Septimi.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII. Examination of the Seventh Chapter.

units.la: I. Tergiversatio, mala fides, & confessio Arminianorum circa dogma sibi objectum, nimirum: Mysterium Trinitatis nullos usus per se habere. Alia fraus eorum contra propriam conscientiam. Quâ pœnâ digni sint Arminiani ministri? 2. Arminianos in conscientiâ suâ convictos esse malæ causæ suæ, exemplum luculentissimum. 3. Arminianorum tergiversatio & confessio circa dogma dogma objectum sibi; quod nolint agnoscere mysterium Trinitatis pro Necessario ad salutem. 4. Arminiani negant Ecclesiam inde ab initio judicasse Orthodoxa dogmata notoria de Trinitate necessaria esse ad salutem. Ostenditur ex Antiquitate Ecclesiastica contra eos, in Niceno Concilio anathema dictum esse Ario. Aliis quibusdam cavillis eorum respondetur. 5. 6. Fatentur se docere doctrinam Orthodoxam circa mysterium Trinitatis, quam oppugnant Antitrinitarii, non esse eductam e Scriptura per consequentiam evidentem. Non negant Tyrannidis convitium quo proscindunt totam veterem & modernam Ecclesiam ob sententiam de Necessitate hujus doctrinae. Fatentur quod nolunt Anathema dicere Antitrinitario. Fatentur quod docent Antitrinitarios esse homines pios, piissimos sanctissimos. 7. Arminiani fraudem aliam quae ipsis objecta erat non negant. 8. Non negant se eo fine ita sentire de mysterio Trinitatis ut Antitrinitarios possint introducere in Ecclesiam Dei; sed illud ex Justino male defendunt. S. Ignatius Antiochenus vindicatus; nec non auctor liberatus ab ipsorum suspicione. 9. Fatentur convitium factum ab ipsis Symbolo Athanasii & approbant. 10. Non negant se aliter credere mysterium Trinitatis quam Ecclesia tota, quae Deum in tribus personis adorat. Eunomii Baptismus ex Socrate. Cognatio doctrinae de Mysterio Trinitatis & Baptismo ex Epistola Synodica Concilii Constantinop. apud Theodoretum.
units.tr: I. The evasion, bad faith and confession of the Arminians concerning the doctrine objected to them, namely that the mystery of the Trinity has no uses in itself. Another deceit of theirs against their own conscience. With what penalty the Arminian ministers deserve to be punished? 2. The Arminians, convicted by their own conscience of their bad cause, a most striking example. 3. The evasion and confession of the Arminians concerning the doctrine objected to them, that they are unwilling to acknowledge the mystery of the Trinity as necessary to salvation. 4. The Arminians deny that the Church from the beginning judged the orthodox and well-known doctrines of the Trinity to be necessary to salvation. This is shown against them from ecclesiastical antiquity: that at the Council of Nicaea an anathema was pronounced on Arius. Certain other of their quibbles are answered. 5. 6. They confess that they teach the orthodox doctrine concerning the mystery of the Trinity, which the Antitrinitarians oppose, is not drawn from Scripture by a plainly evident consequence. They do not deny the slander of tyranny by which they tear to pieces the whole ancient and modern Church because of its opinion on the necessity of this doctrine. They confess that they are unwilling to pronounce an anathema on an Antitrinitarian. They confess that they teach that Antitrinitarians are pious, most pious and most holy men. 7. The Arminians do not deny another deceit which was objected to them. 8. They do not deny that they hold such a view of the mystery of the Trinity for the purpose of being able to introduce Antitrinitarians into the Church of God; but they defend this poorly from Justin. Ignatius of Antioch is vindicated; and also the author is cleared of their suspicion. 9. They confess the slander made by them against the Creed of Athanasius and approve it. 10. They do not deny that they believe otherwise concerning the mystery of the Trinity than the whole Church, which worships God in three persons. The baptism of Eunomius from Socrates. The kinship of the doctrine of the mystery of the Trinity and of baptism from the Synodal Letter of the Council of Constantinople, in Theodoret.

units.la: 1. CApite Septimo objeceram Arminianis, primo, quod docent: Mysterium Trinitatis nullum usum ad fidem & pietatem habere per se, & ei peculiares usus tribuere esse figmentum & vacordiam. Hic Arminiani postquam scoptice exagitassent & derisissent materiam sanctissimam ac summe arduam quam in isto capite tracto, & per ludibrium dixissent profani hi homines: Minos & Rhadamanthus in hoc capite tribunal habent &c. respondent hoc falsum esse. Vide, optime Lector, insignem proterviam horum hominum, qua contra propriam conscientiam negant se dixisse, quod tamen dixerunt conceptis verbis. Dicunt hoc esse falsum, se hoc non docere. Atqui ego protuli verba ipsorum manimanifestissima, quæ, quia rem evidentissimam sine ullo pudore negant, nobis repetenda sunt. Notârant eos Cll. Proff. Leydd. quòd nullos usus Mysterii Trinitatis in suâ Confessione protulerant, respondent illi Apol. c. 3. f. 52. b. At quis insulsiorem aut imperitiorem censuram hic fieri posse cogitet? Usus enim doctrinæ de Deo præmissi fuerunt & quidem satis prolixè. Nunc vero hoc capite tantùm ostenditur, Deum illum se patefecisse sub tribus personis sive hypostasibus. Quis nisi vacors novos usus hic fingat? Quicunque enim hic fingentur usus, ii non fingentur sub alio conceptu quàm sub conceptu Deitatis. Persona aut persona simpliciter usum præbere non potest, nisi quatenus persona divina est. Divinitatis autem conceptus quos usus præbeat, jam antè præcedente capite indicatum erat. Ex his manifestum est Arminianos in suo hoc responso contra conscientiam suam dicere; se id in Apologiâ non docuisse. Provocant etiam ad rationem: Et ne relegem vos, Judices, ad libros, rationem audite: Mysterium Trinitatis creditu necessarium esse Remonstrantes hactenus asseruerunt & adhuc asserunt, ac proinde illud usum suum habere ut fateantur necesse est. Respondeo I. ex eo nequaquam sequi, me falsum dixisse, sed eos ἀσυσατα dicere & sibi ipsis contradicere. Sunt enim hæc ἀσυσατα h. e. simul non possunt consistere, esse necessarium, & tamen nullum usum habere; adeoque sequitur exinde eos αυτοκαταχρίτως esse. Quâ de re ipsos monui & convici cap. 7. Par. I. lib. 1. p. 51. 52. 53. 54. Quia igitur convicti sunt & deprehensos se vident non solùm à me sed etiam antea à Cll.DD. Proff. Leydd. hinc palliant sententiam suam in Responsione ad Excerpta modò laudatorum Theologorum (ad quæ hic adversus me provocant) & in Vindiciis suis, ac negant se ita docere in Apologiâ suâ: sed verba ipsorum evidentiora sunt, quàm ut persuadere hominibus possint Cll. Theol. Proff. Leydenses & me post illos falsum dixisse. 2. Inanis lusus est, quando dicunt se mysterium Trinitatis habere pro necessario ad salutem. Nam dicunt quidem se habere illud pro Necessario; & tamen nolunt illud habere pro necessario in suo vero sensu, ut clarius mox videbimus. Quid enim mysterium sive dogma, quid verba absque suo vero sensu? Adeoque non est nisi mera fraus & simulatio, quando hoc loco dicunt se habere mysterium Trinitatis pro necessario ad salutem. De quâ eorum simulatione ex professo egi Par. II. Arcan. lib. 1. cap. 4. ubi ostendi Arminianos Theologos esse simulatores Antitrinitarios etiam circa necessitatem mysterii illius prout extra controversiam est, & ex animo addictos esse hæresi ac blasphemiæ Socinianorum etiam in illâ re.
units.tr: 1. In the seventh chapter I objected to the Arminians, first, that they teach that the mystery of the Trinity has no use in itself for faith and piety, and that to attribute peculiar uses to it is a fiction and foolishness. Here the Arminians, after they had scornfully assailed and mocked the most holy and exceedingly difficult matter which I treated in that chapter, and had said in jest, these profane men: Minos and Rhadamanthus sit in judgment in this chapter, etc., reply that this is false. See, most kind reader, the remarkable shamelessness of these men, by which they deny, against their own conscience, that they said what they nevertheless said in so many words. They say it is false, that they do not teach this. And yet I have quoted their very manifest words, which, since they shamelessly deny a most evident matter, must be repeated by us. The illustrious professors of Leiden had noted that they had set out no uses of the mystery of the Trinity in their Confession; they answer in their Apology, chapter 3, folio 52 verso: But who could think that a more foolish or ignorant criticism could be made here? For uses of the doctrine of God were set out beforehand, and indeed quite fully. Now, in this chapter, it is only shown that God revealed himself under three persons or hypostases. Who but a fool would invent new uses here? For whatever uses are invented here, they will not be invented under any other concept than under the concept of the Deity. A person, or a person simply, cannot yield a use, except insofar as he is a divine person. But what uses the concept of the Divinity yields had already been indicated in the preceding chapter. From these things it is plain that the Arminians, in this their reply, speak against their own conscience when they say that they did not teach this in their Apology. They also appeal to reason: And, lest I send you back, Judges, to the books, hear the reasoning: the Remonstrants have hitherto asserted, and still assert, that the mystery of the Trinity is necessary to be believed, and therefore they must admit that it has its use. I reply, first, that it does not at all follow that I have said something false, but that they say inconsistent things [ἀσυσατα] and contradict themselves. For these things are ἀσυσατα, that is, they cannot stand together at the same time: that it is necessary, and yet that it has no use; and hence it follows that they are self-condemned [αυτοκαταχρίτως]. On this matter I warned them and convicted them in chapter 7, Part I, book 1, pp. 51, 52, 53, 54.
