Since therefore they have been convicted and see themselves caught out, not only by me but also earlier by the illustrious doctors, the professors of Leiden, they now cover up their opinion in their Response to the Excerpts of the theologians just mentioned (to which they appeal against me here) and in their Vindications, and they deny that they teach this in their Apology. But their words are too plain for the illustrious theology professors of Leiden, and for me after them, to be persuaded that they have said something false. 2. It is an empty game when they say that they hold the mystery of the Trinity as necessary to salvation. For they do indeed say that they hold it as necessary; and yet they are unwilling to hold it as necessary in its true sense, as we shall see more clearly shortly. For what is a mystery or doctrine, what are words, without their true sense? And so it is nothing but mere deceit and pretence when they here say that they hold the mystery of the Trinity as necessary to salvation. Concerning this pretence of theirs I treated expressly in Part II, Arcana, book 1, chapter 4, where I showed that the Arminian theologians are pretenders and Antitrinitarians, even concerning the necessity of that mystery as it lies beyond controversy, and are devoted in heart to the heresy and blasphemy of the Socinians even in that matter.

units.la: Pergunt in impostura suâ, &, quia vident se premi verbis manifestis ApoloApologiæ suæ, ajunt: Mutari terminos; se enim negare ex numero trium personarum per se considerato posse elici usus peculiares ad pietatem & bonos mores. Respondeo: Quod dicunt terminos mutari à Cll. Proff. Leydd. & à me, in eo profecto agunt contra conscientiam suam. Nam norunt sibi à modo laudatis Theologis objectum fuisse, non quod Trinitatis, ut est numerus, nullos usus proferrent; sed quod mysterii hujus & dogmatis nullos usus proferrent: Coronidis loco duo alia (sunt verba Cll. Proff. Leydd.) sunt observanda; primum est quod DOCTRINÆ hujus ac MYSTERII de S.S. Trinitate nullos usus proferant &c. Norunt etiam se respondere in Apologia, ipsum mysterium nullum usum habere, non autem numerum ternarium c. 3. §. 4. f. 52. b. At quis insulsiorem, inquiunt, aut imperitiorem censuram hic fieri posse cogitet? Usus enim doctrina de Deo premissi fuerunt & quidem satis prolixè. Nunc vero hoc capite tantum ostenditur Deum illum se patefecisse sub tribus personis sive hypostasibus. Quis nisi vacors novos usus hic fingat? Quicunque enim hic fingantur usus &c. Et postea ut probent mysterium Trinitatis nullum usum habere; afferunt in Apol. loco citato hoc argumentum; quia persona ut persona nullum usum habeat. Nec agitur cap. 3. Confessionis & Apologiæ de numero ternario saltem personarum, sed de toto mysterio Trinitatis, primo generatim §. 1. deinde speciatim de Patre §. 2. de Filio §. 3. de Spiritu S. §. 4. Quare speciem haberet effugium ipsorum, siquidem tantum de numero ternario ageretur locis allegatis. Et loquuntur Apologiæ cap. 3. de usu doctrinæ quam proposuerant Confess. cap. 3. At in Confessione proposuerunt doctrinam de S.S. Trinitate, ut etiam titulus ipse capitis illius indicat. Quod igitur Arminiani jam de Trinitate, ut numerus est, loquuntur, inane effugium est, & ad rem non facit. Et sic patet quoque terminos non mutatos esse à Cll. DD. Proff. Leydd. aut à me, sed ab ipsis Arminianis jam fraudulenter eos mutari. Sed hoc sophisma didicerunt ab Antitrinitariis apertis, qui simili modo doctrinam Orthodoxam de Trinitate eludere solent; ac argutantur Trinitatem non esse Deum quia Trinitas sit numerus; numerus autem non possit esse Deus seu essentia divina; adeoque Trinitatem ut numerum numerantem saltē seu abstractive considerant, ut hic simulatores Sociniani faciunt. Unde sequitur etiam, quod me invitant ut practicum aliquē usum ex numero triupersonarum, quâ tali, sive per se cōsiderato adducant impertinens esse. Quemadmodū etiam salsissimum est, quòd dicunt me numeri istius ita consiederati usum practicum conatum esse adducere, sed infeliciter perperam. Videte, inquiunt, quem usum adferat Vedelius: Non sufficit fidei Christianæ, ut homo sciat, se &c. Agunt etiam in hac parte fraudulenter & contra conscientiam suam. Nam ego nullum usum protuli, non quòd non possem, sed quia id instituti mei non fuit nec etiamnum est: quandoquidem, ut dixi, quæstio non est de usu numeri ternarii abstractivè considerati, sed de usu totius mysterii Trinitatis. Et verba mea quæ allegant, nõrunt ipsi à me prolata esse in eum finem, ut ostenderem eos perperam facere quòd huic mysterio nullos usus tribuant per se, sed tantum respectu doctrinæ de essentiâ Dei. Quasi verò, dicebam, Christiano sufficiat ad fidem pietatem & salutem usus habere ex conceptu Deitatis tantùm essentialiter non etiam personaliter considerata. Illos tantùm protulerant Arminiani, sed non protulerunt usus ex conceptu Deitatis personaliter, h. e. prout hæc vel illa persona a Deus est, considerata. Atqui hoc fidei Christianæ non sufficit, ut homo sciat se colere debere unum Deum &c. sed necessarium etiam ad salutem est, ut credat se debere colere & adorare Deum eum qui se in tribus personis revelavit, &c. His verbis in animo suo nõrunt me saltem hoc agere ut eos redarguam, quòd non protulerint usus ex conceptu Deitatis personaliter consideratæ, & me causam reddere cur eos usus proferre debuissent, nimirùm causam hanc, quia non sufficit fidei Christiana &c. Sed quia hæc refutare non potuerunt; & tamen videri volunt Vedelium refutâsse, hinc fraudulenter fingunt me istis verbis practicum usum velle afferre Trinitatis ut est numerus ternarius, & quidem usum talem quem Arminiani non expresserint in Doctrinâ de Deo absolutè consideratο; & verbosè ostendere conantur hunc non esse usum Trinitatis ut est numerus, & se hunc ipsum usum expressisse dicunt, se provocare ad partem libri, &, si ulterior probatio postuletur, ad Epistolam à me allegatam &c. Quibus omnibus quis non videt hos homines omnem honestatem & pudorem deposuisse, ac contra propriam conscientiam agere, in quâ convicti sunt malæ suæ causæ etiam in hac parte? Si enim convicti non sunt in conscientiâ suâ, cur non responderunt candidè & sincerè ad meum illud argumentum, quo effugium ipsorum dilui, per quod Cl. Theoll. Leydd. censuram eludere in hac re conati fuerunt. Nam quia Viri Clarissimi notârant illos, quòd nullos usus mysterii Trinitatis protulissent: illi eâ ratione effugere se posse rati sunt ut dicerent: nullos usus hic fingi posse quàm sub conceptu divinitatis. Divinitatis autem conceptus quos usus prabeat jam antè præcedente capite indicatum erat. Apol. cap. 3. f. 52. b. Ad hoc inane & putidum effugium ipsis responderam his verbis, quorum partem hic allegant: Quasi verò Christiano Christiano sufficiat ad fidem & pietatem &c. Quia igitur vident se constrictos teneri, & non possunt diluere responsum quo sophisma ipsorum everti; ideo dissimulant me ea verba responsi loco opposuisse ipsorum sophismati, & fingunt me hic usum voluisse proferre Trinitatis ut est numerus &c. Quid putant hi homines? Existimantne se semper Ecclesiæ & Reipublicæ coram Deo & Angelis ipsius illudere posse?
units.tr: They persist in their imposture, and since they see themselves pressed by plain words of their own Apology, they say: the terms are changed; for they deny that peculiar uses for piety and good morals can be drawn from the number of three persons considered in itself. I answer: that they say the terms were changed by the illustrious professors of Leiden and by me, they in truth do against their own conscience. For they know that the objection raised against them by the above-mentioned theologians was not that they offered no uses of the Trinity as a number, but that they offered no uses of this mystery and doctrine. As a crown (these are the words of the illustrious professors of Leiden), two other points are to be observed: first, that they offer no uses of this doctrine and mystery of the Holy Trinity, etc. They also know that in their Apology they replied that the mystery itself has no use, not that the number three has none (ch. 3, §4, fol. 52 b). But who, they say, could imagine a more foolish or ignorant criticism here? For the uses of the doctrine of God were set forth beforehand, and quite fully. Now, however, this chapter only shows that God has revealed himself under three persons or hypostases. Who but a fool would invent new uses here? For whatever uses are invented here, etc. And afterwards, to prove that the mystery of the Trinity has no use, they bring forward in the Apology, in the place cited, this argument: because a person as a person has no use. Nor does chapter 3 of the Confession and the Apology deal with the number three of the persons alone, but with the whole mystery of the Trinity: first in general, §1; then in particular, of the Father, §2; of the Son, §3; of the Holy Spirit, §4. Therefore their evasion would have some appearance only if the cited places dealt merely with the number three. And the Apology, chapter 3, speaks of the use of the doctrine which they had set out in Confession, chapter 3. But in the Confession they set out the doctrine of the Holy Trinity, as the very title of that chapter indicates. So what the Arminians now say about the Trinity as a number is an empty evasion and does not bear on the matter. And thus it is also clear that the terms were not changed by the illustrious doctors and professors of Leiden or by me, but by the Arminians themselves, who now change them fraudulently. But they learned this sophism from open Antitrinitarians, who in the same way are wont to mock the orthodox doctrine of the Trinity, and argue that the Trinity is not God because the Trinity is a number, and a number cannot be God or the divine essence; and so they consider the Trinity, as a number that numbers, only abstractly, as these Socinian pretenders do. Hence it also follows that they invite me to bring forward some practical use of the number of three persons as such, that is, considered in itself, as if it were irrelevant. Just as it is very absurd that they say I tried to bring forward a practical use of this number so considered, but unsuccessfully and wrongly. See, they say, what use Vedelius brings: it is not enough for Christian faith that a man knows that he, etc. In this part too they act fraudulently and against their own conscience. For I did bring forward no use, not because I could not, but because it was not and is not my purpose: since, as I have said, the question is not about the use of the number three considered abstractly, but about the use of the whole mystery of the Trinity. And the words of mine which they cite, they know were put forward by me with the aim of showing that they act wrongly in offering no uses of this mystery in itself, but only with respect to the doctrine of God's essence. As if, I was saying, it were enough for a Christian's faith, piety and salvation to have uses drawn from the concept of the Deity considered only essentially and not also personally. The Arminians had brought forward only those, but they did not bring forward uses from the concept of the Deity considered personally, that is, as this or that person is God. Yet this is not enough for Christian faith, that a man knows he ought to worship one God, etc.; it is also necessary for salvation that he believe he ought to worship and adore God who has revealed himself in three persons, etc. They know in their own minds that by these words I did only this: to refute them for not bringing forward uses from the concept of the Deity considered personally, and to give the reason why they ought to have brought forward such uses, namely this reason, because it is not enough for Christian faith, etc. But since they could not refute these points, and yet want to seem to have refuted Vedelius, they therefore fraudulently pretend that by these words I wish to bring a practical use of the Trinity as the number three, and indeed a use such as the Arminians did not express in the doctrine of God considered absolutely; and they strive at length to show that this is not a use of the Trinity as a number, and they say that they themselves expressed this very use, that they appeal to a part of their book, and, if further proof is demanded, to the letter I cited, etc. Who does not see from all this that these men have cast off all honesty and shame, and act against their own conscience, in which they are convicted of the badness of their cause, even in this part? For if they are not convicted in their own conscience, why did they not answer frankly and sincerely to my argument by which their evasion is refuted, by which they tried to evade the censure of the most distinguished theologians of Leiden in this matter? For since those illustrious men had noted that they had offered no uses of the mystery of the Trinity, they thought they could escape by saying: no uses can be invented here except under the concept of divinity. Now the uses which the concept of divinity affords had already been indicated in the preceding chapter. Apology, ch. 3, fol. 52 b. To this empty and foul evasion I had replied in the words, part of which they cite here: As if it were enough for a Christian, a Christian, for faith and piety, etc. Therefore, since they see that they are pressed hard and cannot refute the answer by which their sophism is overturned, they dissemble that I set those words against their sophism as a reply, and pretend that I here wished to bring forward a use of the Trinity as the number three, etc. What do these men think? Do they suppose they can always mock the Church and the commonwealth before God and his angels?

units.la: Contumeliam quâ præ rabie me afficiunt hoc loco, quia se respondere mihi non posse in conscientiâ suâ convicti sunt, cum reliquâ omni ipsorum maledicentiâ quâ utuntur adversum me,Deo ultori relinquo. Et quia hic pronunciant quâ pœna ego dignus sim & ad ferulam me condemnant ac per ludibrium præceptorem vocant: nihil aliud ipsis regeram quàm me non velle mihi arrogare potestatem decernendi quâ pœnâ digna sit eorum maledicentia,quâ non solùm adversum me sed omnes Ecclesias Reformatas,omnes piosDoctores,omnes denique Magistratus,Reges,Principes qui Antitrinitarios ferre nolunt, utuntur; hoc saltem dicam, eos ipsos jam ante hac pronunciâsse quâ pœnâ digni sint ob eam, dum ajunt se certos & persuasos esse se propter convitia cœlo proscriptum iri ex divina sententia formula Resp. ad Excerp. p. 20. Et quia hic me ad pœnam atque ignominiam corporalem etiam condemnant; nihil aliud regero quàm me dijudicandum relinquere omnibus Regibus, Principibus ac Magistratibus,speciatim Illustrissimis Ordinibus Generalibus & Celsissimo Principi Aurasionensi, imò omnibus omninò coetibus ac hominibus qui Deum in tribus personis adorant, quâ ferula aut pœnâ digni sint, qui docent,hanc blasphemiam Socinianorum Turcicam & Judaicam,nimirùm Iesum Christum non habere naturam divinam, & non fuisse antequam homo fieret, non esse peccatum; &,qui Orthodoxam doctrinam de mysterio Trinitatis simulant, ex animo autem blasphemiis illis Socinianorum addicti sunt, ac jurati hostes Filii Dei.
units.tr: The insult with which they treat me here in their rage, because they are convicted of being unable to answer me in their own conscience, together with all the other slander they use against me, I leave to God the avenger. And since they here pronounce what punishment I deserve, and condemn me to the rod, and mockingly call me "schoolmaster," I will reply only this: that I do not wish to claim for myself the power of deciding what punishment their slander deserves, slander which they use not only against me but against all the Reformed Churches, all the pious teachers, and finally all magistrates, kings and princes who refuse to tolerate Antitrinitarians. This much I will say: they themselves have already pronounced what punishment they deserve, by saying, that they are certain and persuaded that, on account of their reproaches, they will be cast out of heaven by divine sentence (Reply to the Excerpts, p. 20). And since here they also condemn me to bodily punishment and disgrace, I will reply only that I leave my judgment to all kings, princes and magistrates, especially the Most Illustrious General Estates and the Most Exalted Prince of Orange; indeed to all assemblies and all men who worship God in three persons, as to whether they deserve the rod or punishment, who teach that this blasphemy of the Socinians, Turkish and Jewish, namely that Jesus Christ does not have a divine nature, and did not exist before he became man, is no sin; and who feign the orthodox doctrine of the mystery of the Trinity, while in heart they are devoted to those blasphemies of the Socinians and are sworn enemies of the Son of God.

units.la: 2. Porrò ex eo quòd Arminiani in Apologiâ suâ docent, mysterium Trinitatis nullum usum per se habere, intuleram post Cll. DD. Proff. Leydd. sequi exinde mysterium Trinitatis non esse necessarium ad salutem; & probaveram illud tùm ex definitione Necessariorum ab Arminianis allatâ,tùm etiam ex re ipsâ. Etenim quod necessarium ad salutem est, id dicebam, profectò per se usum habet, imò usum maximum &c. & eâ occasione ostenderam quo sensu Arminiani in Epistolâ quâdam Hagam Comitis scriptâ profitentur se habere mysterium Trinitatis pro Necessario ad salutem: nimirùm eos habere id pro necessario saltem in illis terminis qui controversi non sunt inter nos & Socinianos, non autem habere id pro necessario in suo vero sensu quem Antitrinitarii oppugant. Unde sententiam Arminianorum redargui hoc modo: Nunc igitur, quaso, est'ne hoc habere dogma aliquod revera pro necessario ad salutem, & tamen ejus verum sensum non habere pro necessario? Quid dogma seu mysterium est, imo quid verba sunt absque vero suo sensu? &c. Hoc'cine enim est, aliquod dogma pro necessario habere, & tamen negare illius sensum, quem ipse fateris verum, necessarium esse? Et inde inferebam eos non habere mysterium Trinitatis pro necessario ad salutem, ut tota Ecclesia Christiana quae Deum in tribus personis adorat: & sic eos in Epistola illa illudere Proceribus Reip. & toti Orbi. Teneri igitur ipsos, siquidem serio velint cum tota Ecclesia Christiana agnoscere mysterium hoc pro necessario ad salutem, ut condemnent ac rejiciant execrandam & pestilentissimam hanc opinionem, nimirum mysterium illud non esse necessarium in suo vero sensu &c. Ad haec quae maximi sunt momenti, videamus quid respondeant hi homines? Post verba enim petulantissima illa & improbissima quibus me prae rabie contumeliose habent, subjungunt immediate: Exceptiones tamen ejus contra Epistolam Remonstrantium, an'non graviore censura dignae sint etiam atque etiam perpendite. Quis haec verba legens non judicaret eos exordium facere confutationis instituendae & responsionis ad ea quae modo commemoravi? Sed quid faciunt? sicco pede transeunt illa, & accedunt ad aliud dogma sibi a me objectum: Ad secundum ergo caput, inquiunt, accusationis veniamus, in quo agitur de mysterio Trinitatis quatenus &c. Quid? Estne hoc refutare? Est'ne hoc negocium tantum serio agere? Inter alia quae ibi expositi, propositi argumentum gravissimum adversus doctrinam eorum qua statuunt mysterium Trinitatis non esse necessarium ad salutem in suo vero sensu, seu prout in Controversia est inter nos & Antitrinitarios. Argumentum in eo consistit: Quod est necessarium ad salutem, illud est necessarium in suo vero sensu. At dogma Trinitatis est necessarium ad salutem. Ergo est necessarium in suo vero sensu. Minor est Arminianorum in Epistola allegata, ut & in hoc capite 7. Vindiciarum. Majorem probavi hoc modo: Quid enim dogma seu mysterium est, imo quid verba sunt absque suo vero sensu? &c. Hoccine est aliquod dogma pro Necessario habere, & tamen negare illius verum sensum quem ipse fateris verum, necessarium esse? Ad hoc argumentum plane invictum Arminiani nihil aliud reponunt; quam: Exceptiones tamen ejus contra Epistolam Remonstrantium, an'non graviore censura digni sint, etiam atque etiam perpendite. Veniamus ad aliud &c. Quis hic non videt Arminianos constrictos teneri, imo in conscientia sua convictos esse? Sed de hac impostura eorum egimus etiam nonnihil Par. III. Prolegom. c. 5. quemodmodum etiam Par. II. lib. 1. c. 4. causam indicavi cur non re-sponderint ad istud argumentum; quæ quidem causa in eo posita est, quia si respondissent nimis manifeste detexissent simulationem suam & Socinianismum, tum circa veritatem illius mysterii prout controversum est, tum circa necessitatem illius prout extra controversiam est.
units.tr: 2. Further, since the Arminians in their Apology teach that the mystery of the Trinity has no use in itself, I had inferred, following the learned professors at Leiden, that it follows from this that the mystery of the Trinity is not necessary to salvation. I had proved this both from the definition of necessary things given by the Arminians and from the matter itself. For what is necessary to salvation, I said, certainly has a use in itself, indeed the greatest use, etc. On that occasion I had also shown in what sense the Arminians, in a certain letter written to the Count of The Hague, profess that they hold the mystery of the Trinity to be necessary to salvation. Namely, they hold it to be necessary at least in those terms which are not in dispute between us and the Socinians, but they do not hold it to be necessary in its true sense, which the Antitrinitarians oppose. Hence I refuted the Arminians' opinion in this way: Now then, I ask, is it really to hold some doctrine as necessary to salvation, and yet not to hold its true sense as necessary? What is a doctrine or mystery, or indeed what are words, without their true sense? And so on. For is this not to hold some doctrine as necessary, and yet to deny that its sense, which you yourselves admit is true, is necessary? And from this I inferred that they do not hold the mystery of the Trinity as necessary to salvation, as the whole Christian Church does, which adores God in three persons; and thus in that letter they mock the nobles of the Republic and the whole world. They are bound, therefore, if they seriously wish to acknowledge with the whole Christian Church that this mystery is necessary to salvation, to condemn and reject this accursed and most pestilential opinion, namely that that mystery is not necessary in its true sense, etc. Let us see what these men reply to these matters of the greatest weight. After those most insolent and shameless words with which they abuse me insultingly out of rage, they immediately add: Consider again and again whether his objections to the Remonstrants' Letter deserve a more severe censure. Who, reading these words, would not judge that they are making a start at conducting a refutation and a reply to what I have just mentioned? But what do they do? They pass these things by with dry feet and turn to another doctrine objected to them by me: Let us come, they say, to the second head of the accusation, in which the question concerns the mystery of the Trinity, insofar as, etc. What? Is this to refute? Is this to deal seriously with the matter? Among other things that I set out there, I put forward a most weighty argument against their doctrine, which holds that the mystery of the Trinity is not necessary to salvation in its true sense, or as it is in controversy between us and the Antitrinitarians. The argument consists in this: What is necessary to salvation is necessary in its true sense. But the doctrine of the Trinity is necessary to salvation. Therefore it is necessary in its true sense. The minor premise is the Arminians' in the letter cited, as also in the seventh chapter of the Vindiciae. I proved the major premise in this way: For what is a doctrine or mystery, or indeed what are words, without their true sense? And so on. Is it to hold some doctrine as necessary, and yet to deny that its true sense, which you yourselves admit is true, is necessary? To this argument, which is wholly unanswerable, the Arminians reply nothing except: Consider again and again whether his objections to the Remonstrants' Letter deserve a more severe censure. Let us come to another point, etc. Who here does not see that the Arminians are bound and indeed convicted in their own conscience? But we have also dealt somewhat with this imposture of theirs in Part III, Prolegomena, chapter 5, just as in Part II, book 1, chapter 4, I indicated the reason why they did not reply to that argument. That reason lies in this: if they had replied, they would have revealed far too clearly their pretence and their Socinianism, both concerning the truth of that mystery as it is in dispute, and concerning its necessity as it is outside the dispute.

units.la: Saltem hoc addam, quod probè observandum est, quia exinde hos homines intus & in cute nosse unusquisque poterit. Dicunt nonnunquam speciatim in hac ipsa materia, se, si melius edoceantur & erroris convincantur, statim cessuros & veniam petituros, gratias acturos meliora docenti. Sed hoc merum ludibrium est. Prout ex hoc exemplo patet, ubi vides, optime Lector, eos convictos esse, & nō habere quod respondeant. Nihilominus tamen errorem non agnoscunt, sed tantum præ rabie quòd constricti sint me convitiis petunt, & Lectorem fallere studeant, ne is deprehendat malam ac desperatam causam ipsorum. Judica nunc quisquis es Lector, quid speri de his hominibus in futurum sit concipiendum?
units.tr: I will add only this, which must be carefully observed, because from it everyone will be able to know these men inside and out. They sometimes say, especially on this very matter, that if they were better taught and convinced of their error, they would immediately give way and ask pardon, giving thanks to the one who teaches them better. But this is pure mockery. As this example makes plain, you see, best Reader, that they are convicted and have nothing to answer. Nevertheless they do not acknowledge their error, but only, out of rage that they are constrained, attack me with insults and strive to deceive the Reader, so that he may not perceive their wicked and desperate cause. Judge now, whoever you are, Reader, what hope can be conceived of these men for the future?

units.la: 3. Secundum dogma quod bonis his viris objeceram consistit in mysterio illo considerato ut est controversum inter nos & Antitrinitarios. Hæc enim sunt verba mea, non autem ut fraudulenter ea allegant, ac si in eâ parte accusationis agerem de mysterio illo non simpliciter considerato uti expresse est revelatum in Dei verbo sed ut est controversum inter nos & Antitrinitarios. Quæ verba malitiose ideo inferciunt, quia statuunt dogmata illa quæ ab Antitritinariis oppugnantur, nō expresse in Scriptura esse revelata, h.e. ita ut cuivis obvia sint, cui salte sanu sinciput est, id quod ipsis est expresse revelatum esse in Scriptura. Ea dogmata sunt: in una essentiâ divinâ esse tres personas, I. Christum esse Deum ab æterno, I. Christum esse genitum ex substantiâ Patris, seu ὁμοούσιον, sive coëssentialem esse Patri; Christum habere non solùm naturam humanam, sed etiam divinam: Spiritum S. esse personam Deitatis: Spiritum S. esse adorandum. Hæc dogmata dixeram, Ecclesia tota Christiana inde ab initio in hunc usque diem contra Hæreticos judicavit esse necessaria ad salutem, ac contrarium illis statuentes tanquam Hæreticos anathemate percussit. At hodie Remonstrantes nolunt ea agnoscere pro necessariis ad salutem. Hic respondent: falsum est quòd No-LINT Remonstrantes ea agnoscere pro necessariis: Aliud enim est, nolle; aliud non audere afferere, nec sententiam suam interponere: Et addunt, se dubitare saltem de hac re & in medio eam relinquere. Ac postea contendunt, Ecclesiam totam inde ab initio non habuisse ea dogmata pro necessariis, nec anathemate percuspercussisse negantes illa: ac quantum attinet ad illud, quòd non audent asserere dogmata illa esse necessaria ad salutem, remittunt Lectorem ad Responsionem suam ad Excerpta DD. Proff. Leydd. in quâ copiosissimè exponunt causas cur non agnoscant ea dogmata pro necessariis & sic anathema non possint dicere Antitrinitariis.
units.tr: 3. The second doctrine that I had objected to these good men consists in that mystery considered as it is in controversy between us and the Antitrinitarians. For these are my words, not as they fraudulently cite them, as if in that part of the accusation I were dealing with that mystery not simply considered as it is expressly revealed in God's Word, but as it is in controversy between us and the Antitrinitarians. They insert these words maliciously because they maintain that those doctrines which the Antitrinitarians attack are not expressly revealed in Scripture, that is, not so plain that they are obvious to anyone who has a sound mind, which is what, for them, is expressly revealed in Scripture. These doctrines are: that there are three persons in the one divine essence; that Christ is God from eternity; that Christ is begotten of the substance of the Father, or homoousios, that is, co-essential with the Father; that Christ has not only a human nature but also a divine nature; that the Holy Spirit is a person of the Godhead; that the Holy Spirit is to be adored. I had said that the whole Christian Church, from the beginning until this day, has judged these doctrines to be necessary to salvation against the heretics, and has struck with anathema those who hold the contrary as heretics. But today the Remonstrants are unwilling to acknowledge them as necessary to salvation. Here they reply: It is false that the Remonstrants are UNWILLING to acknowledge them as necessary. For it is one thing to be unwilling; it is another not to dare to assert, nor to put forward one's opinion. And they add that they doubt at least this matter and leave it open. Afterwards they contend that the whole Church from the beginning did not hold those doctrines as necessary, nor did it strike with anathema those who denied them. As far as it concerns the claim that they do not dare to assert that those doctrines are necessary to salvation, they refer the Reader to their Reply to the Excerpta of the learned professors at Leiden, in which they set out at great length the reasons why they do not acknowledge those doctrines as necessary, and so cannot pronounce anathema against the Antitrinitarians.

units.la: Verùm enim verò quis non videt inanem vitilitigationē & tergiversationem esse; dum ajunt falsum esse quòd dico Eos Nolle &c? Et quis non videt exemplum proterviæ ipsorum de quâ Par. III. lib. 1. c. 6. egimus, quâ negant se dixisse quod non totidem literis & syllabis dixerunt, etiamsi rem doceant, & contrarium non rejiciant aut improbent? Nam mihi perinde est, quâ voce utantur, dummodo de re constet, quæ in eâ est; nimirùm eos non agnoscere ea dogmata pro Necessariis. Id quod negare non possunt, nec etiam negant: quandoquidem profitentur se dubitare & judicium suum suspendere de hac re. Certè qui dubitat an aliquid verum sit aut necessarium; ille non agnoscit id pro vero aut necessario. Ne tamen Arminiani de voce Nolle conquerantur: ecquis non videt me merito dixisse eos Nolle asserere ea dogmata pro necessariis: quia ipsi dicunt se non audere id asserere? Certè qui non audet asserere aliquid, & praeterea non asserit aliquid, is certè non vult id asserere, eo ipso quia non audet asserere nec asserit. Quòd magis est ipsi expresse dicunt se Nolle. Non enim damnare Volunt Remonstrantes quemquam, nisi quem Christus Dominus eorum aut expresse damnat &c. quæ sunt ipsissima verba eorum de hac ipsâ re Apol. c. 1. f. 32. b. Jam autem Arminianis idem est (& quidem merito) dogma aliquod habere pro necessario ad salutem, & damnare aliquem sive anathema denunciare ei qui id dogma non agnoscit. Item cap. 3. Apol. f. 53. b. de hac eâdem re dicunt: Stabat jam Animo Remonstrantium hac sententia, nulli doctrinæ, nulli homini anathema dicere nisi cui Deus ipse anathema dicit &c. His adde, quòd, ut sectione praecedente vidimus, etiamsi illis luculentissimè & solidissimè ostensum sit, ea dogmata esse necessaria ad salutem, etiamsi ad illud argumentum à me allatum nihil respondere possint, adeoque in conscientiâ suâ convicti sint: tamen malunt dictamini propriæ suæ conscientiæ repugnare, quàm Sacrosanctæ Trinitati gloriam dare, & fateri ea dogmata esse necessaria ad salutem. An'non igitur merito dixi eos Nolle ea agnoscere pro necessariis ad salutem? An'non hoc est Nolle, more eorum qui in sensum reprobum dati sunt? Cæteroquin quòd dicunt se ἐπίσχειν seu dubitare saltem & judicium suum suspendere de hac re; ibi qualis dubitatio ea fit, facile intelligi potest si attendas ad ea quæ dicunt in Responsione ad Excerp. Cll. DD. Proff. Leydd, ubi causas reddunt, cur non possint anathema denunciare Antitrinitariis. Primam causam reddunt hanc p. 41. Quòd CERTUM SIT iis qui sic errant, in Scriptu-ris nusquam nec diserte atque in terminis, neque per manifestam consequentiam a-nathema dici. Quod autem in Scripturis non est, etiamsi verissimum sit, necessa-rium tamen dogma non esse ipsi Doctores in Synopsi suà asserunt. Secundam cau-sam hanc reddunt: Quòd causas errandi non leves habere videantur Socinianî, propter quas error eorum à pertinaciâ, ac proinde ab hæreseos culpâ, quæ sine pertinaciâ nulla est, à Doctoribus ipsis liber atque immunis censeri DEBET. Si CERTUM est, Scripturam non dicere Antitrinitariis anathema; item si DEBENT Antitrinitarii liberi atque immunes censeri ab hæreseos culpâ: profectò dubitandi locus nullus est. Ex quo apparet, qualis sit dubitatio eorum in hac re: nimirùm talis, quâ certi sint sententiam no-stram in Scripturâ non contineri, nec diserte nec per consequentiam manifestam; & quâ statuunt Ecclesiam non DEBERE anathemate ferire Antitrinitarios. Accedit his quòd in eâdem Resp. ad Excer. p. 84. dicunt: Vt in iis, qui illas propositiones (h. e. dogmata Orthodoxa quæ negant Antitrinitarii) aut ignorant, aut negant, aut in dubium vocant, manifestam culpam esse credant, ADDUCI Remonstrantes NON POSSUNT. Insuper in Vindiciis lib. 1. capite hoc ipso 7. p. 38. dicunt; Remonstrantes ODERUNT istos audaces assertores & damnatores in tàm ardua re. Denique Antitrinitarios habent pro hominibus, piis, piissimis, sanctissimis, statuunt eos non peccare blasphemis istis dogmatis & opinionibus suis, iis vitam æternam decernunt. Quæ omnia profectò facere non possent, nisi animo fixam haberent hanc sententiam, ea dogmata Orthodoxa non esse necessaria ad salutem. Est'ne igitur hoc dubitare, an verò potiùs simpliciter veram sententiam rejicere & improbare? Unde patet istos homines saltem mitiore vocabulo & modo loquendi palliare studere genuinam sententiam suam, quâ simpliciter statuunt illa dogmata non esse necessaria ad salutem, & tegere eam velle, ut non nuda appareat turpitudo illius. In summa hi homines nihil minus quàm candidè & honestè agunt in negocio salutis & Religionis. Quid in cæteris minoris momenti negociis faciant? Pudeat illos.
units.tr: But who does not see that this is empty wrangling and evasion, when they claim it is false that I say they are unwilling, and so on? And who does not see the shamelessness of them, which I discussed in Part III, book 1, chapter 6, where they deny having said what they did not say in precisely the same letters and syllables, even though they teach the same thing and do not reject or disapprove of the contrary? For it makes no difference to me what words they use, provided the matter is settled, namely that they do not acknowledge these doctrines as necessary. They cannot deny this, and they do not deny it, since they profess that they doubt and suspend their judgment on the matter. Certainly, whoever doubts whether something is true or necessary does not acknowledge it as true or necessary. Yet lest the Arminians complain about my use of the word "unwilling": who does not see that I rightly said they are unwilling to assert these doctrines as necessary, since they themselves say that they do not dare to assert it? Certainly, whoever does not dare to assert something, and in addition does not assert it, is surely unwilling to assert it, precisely because he does not dare to assert it and does not assert it. Moreover, they expressly say that they are unwilling. For the Remonstrants are not willing to condemn anyone, unless Christ the Lord expressly condemns him, and so on; these are their very words on this matter, in the Apology, chapter 1, folio 32b. Now for the Arminians it is the same thing (and rightly so) to hold some doctrine as necessary to salvation and to condemn anyone, or to pronounce anathema on him who does not acknowledge that doctrine. Likewise, in chapter 3 of the Apology, folio 53b, they say on this same matter: this opinion already stood in the mind of the Remonstrants: to pronounce anathema on no doctrine and no man, except him to whom God himself pronounces anathema, and so on. Add to this that, as we saw in the preceding section, even though it has been shown to them most brilliantly and most solidly that these doctrines are necessary to salvation, and even though they cannot answer the argument I brought forward, and so are convicted in their own conscience, they still prefer to act against the dictate of their own conscience rather than give glory to the most holy Trinity and confess that these doctrines are necessary to salvation. Have I not therefore rightly said that they are unwilling to acknowledge these as necessary to salvation? Is this not unwillingness, after the manner of those who have been given over to a reprobate mind? Moreover, as to their claim that they suspend judgment [ἐπίσχειν], or at least doubt and suspend their judgment on this matter, what sort of doubt it is can easily be understood if you attend to what they say in the Response to the Excerpts of the most learned professors of Leiden, where they give the reasons why they cannot pronounce anathema on the Antitrinitarians. They give the first reason on page 41: It is CERTAIN to those who so err that nowhere in the Scriptures is anathema pronounced, either expressly and in terms, or by manifest consequence. But what is not in the Scriptures, even if it is most true, is not a necessary doctrine, as the teachers themselves assert in their Synopsis. They give the second reason: The Socinians seem to have causes of error that are not slight, on account of which their error is to be regarded by the teachers themselves as free and exempt from obstinacy, and therefore from the guilt of heresy, which does not exist without obstinacy. If it is CERTAIN that Scripture does not pronounce anathema on the Antitrinitarians; and if the Antitrinitarians OUGHT to be regarded as free and exempt from the guilt of heresy: then surely there is no room for doubt. From this it appears what sort of doubt they have in this matter: namely, such that they are certain that our opinion is not contained in Scripture, neither expressly nor by manifest consequence, and by which they hold that the Church OUGHT not to strike the Antitrinitarians with anathema. To these things is added that in the same Response to the Excerpts, page 84, they say: As for those who either are ignorant of those propositions (that is, the orthodox doctrines which the Antitrinitarians deny), or deny them, or call them into doubt, they believe there is manifest fault; the Remonstrants CANNOT BE LED to that view. Moreover, in the Vindications, book 1, chapter 7 of this very work, page 38, they say: The Remonstrants HATE those bold assertors and condemners in so arduous a matter. Finally, they regard the Antitrinitarians as men, pious, most pious, most holy; they hold that these men do not sin by their blasphemous doctrines and opinions, and they decree eternal life for them. All of these things they surely could not do, unless they held firmly in their mind this opinion, that these orthodox doctrines are not necessary to salvation. Is this then to doubt, or rather simply to reject and disapprove the true opinion? Whence it is plain that these men strive, at least by a milder word and manner of speaking, to disguise their genuine opinion, by which they simply hold that those doctrines are not necessary to salvation, and they wish to cover it up so that its nakedness does not appear. In sum, these men act in no way less candidly and honestly in the matter of salvation and religion. What they do in other matters of lesser moment? Let them be ashamed.

units.la: 4. Porrò quia dixeram Ecclesiam inde ab initio in hunc usque diem dogmata ista judicâsse necessaria ad salutem, & contrarium illis statuentes tanquam Hæreticos anathemate percussisse: Hic isti homines adeò protervi sunt, ut pag. 37. id negare audeant, contra consensum omnium Theologorum, Lutheranorum, Reformatorum, Pontificiorum, & contra testimonium totius antiquitatis Ecclesiasticae, ex quâ videre est Ecclesiam inde ab initio omnia ista & singula dogmata, statim simul acquis ea in dubium vocare ausus esset & oppugnare, declarâsse se habere ea pro Necessariis ad salutem, & contrarium sententes tanquam Haereticos condemnasse; ut Ebionem, Cerinthum, Marcionem, Paulum Samosatenum, Arium, Sabellium, Photinum, Macedonium &c. Et tamen audent me hi homines impudentiae arguere eo nomine; quod Epitheton an mihi an ipsis competat, Lector ex dictis judicabit.
units.tr: 4. Furthermore, since I had said that the Church from the beginning until this day has judged these doctrines to be necessary to salvation, and has struck with anathema as heretics those who held the contrary, these men are so shameless that on page 37 they dare to deny it, against the consensus of all theologians, Lutheran, Reformed, and Papist, and against the testimony of all ecclesiastical antiquity. From this it can be seen that the Church from the beginning, as soon as anyone dared to call into doubt and oppose any of these doctrines, all of them and each one, declared that it held them as necessary to salvation, and condemned as heretics those who thought otherwise: for example Ebion, Cerinthus, Marcion, Paul of Samosata, Arius, Sabellius, Photinus, Macedonius, and so on. And yet these men dare to accuse me of impudence on this account; the reader will judge from what has been said to whom the epithet more properly belongs.

units.la: Probare autem id quod dixere conantur hi Sophistae hoc modo: Tantum abest, ut Patres ante Concilium Nicenum omnes ea dogmata necessaria judicaverint, ut si scripta eorum videantur, eorum multos ea ignorasse & longe secus de Trinitate quam multo post sentiri coeptum est, sensisse haud obscure intelligatur. Anathemata vero ante Concilium Nicenum contra eos usurpata fuisse, adeo absurdum est ut de ipso Concilio Niceno dubitetur, an anathemate Arius in eo sit percussus. Tum prolixè demonstratum est (in Resp. scilicet ad Excerp.) ex Justino Martyre, eos etiam qui Jesum non nisi nudum hominem credebant ac profitebantur, in communionem admissos fuisse & Ecclesiae Christianae accensitos.
units.tr: Now these sophists try to prove what they have attempted to say in this way: So far is it from being the case that all the Fathers before the Council of Nicaea judged these doctrines necessary, that if their writings are looked at, it is plainly understood that many of them were ignorant of these doctrines and thought quite differently about the Trinity from how it began to be thought much later. That anathemas were used against them before the Council of Nicaea is so absurd that it is doubted whether Arius was struck with anathema at that Council itself. Then it was demonstrated at length (namely in the Response to the Excerpts) from Justin Martyr that even those who believed and professed that Jesus was nothing but a mere man were admitted to communion and counted among the Christian Church.

units.la: Hic, praeterquam quod nobis novum Arcanum impietatis suae produnt (quo sentiunt doctrinam Orthodoxam de Trinitate demum coepisse cum Concilio Nicéno, adeoque simulationem suam ac Socinianismum in eo mysterio produnt, quemadmodum ostendi Arcan. Par. III. lib. 1. cap. 7. §. 1.) etiam salsissimum est, & commune ipsis cum Socinianis apertis mendacium; Patres veteres dissentire a dogmatis illis Orthodoxis quae Antitrinitarii oppugnant, aut ea ignorasse; prout saepe contra Antitrinitariorum illud impudens commentum ostenderunt Theologi eorum coetuum qui Deum in tribus personis adorant. Quod ajunt de ipso Concilio Niceno dubitari an anathemate Arius in eo percussus fuerit; & inde inferunt absurdum esse quod dixi Ecclesiam inde ab initio Antitrinitariis anathema dixisse, hic mihi vide improbitatem horum hominum, qui audent hoc argumenti loco afferre & in genere dicunt dubitari de eâ re; cum tamen ipsi non assentiantur illis qui de eâ re dubitant, quos recte fecisset si nominassent, nam Orthodoxorum nullus eam rem unquam negavit. Ita enim in Responsi. ad Excerp. p. 70. Sunt qui negant Anathema ullum in Synodo Nicenâ dictum esse; rectene an secus, aliorum esto judicium. Ubi, quod profitentur se dubitare de eâ re, & aliis eam dijudicandam candam relinquere, summam arguit eorum imperitiam antiquitatis Ecclesiasticæ, & ostendit quàm parum eruditionis habeant hi perturbatores Belgii, & superbissimi contemtores omnium Ordinum & hominum mortuorum æquè ac vivorum qui ab ipsis dissentiunt. Contrarium enim patet ex Symbolo Nicéno ut videre est apud Theodor. lib. 1. c. 12. Nicephorum Call. lib. 8. c. 17. Socratem lib. 1. c. 5. Item ex Epistolâ Synodicâ ejusdem Concilii apud eundem lib. 1. c. 6. cui Socrates subjungit verba hæc ob rem præsentem notanda: ἐν τῳ̂ τῇ τ̂ σωοδικ̂ ὁμο-λογῆ φανερὸν καθίσταν, ὅτι μόνον Ἀρειον & τὰς ὁμοιοδόξες αὐτῷ ἀνεθεματίσαν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰς λέξεις τῆς δόξης αὐτῷ h. e. Ex hac Concilii Epistola planum fit, eos non solum Ario & ejus secta fautoribus, verum etiam verbis perversa opinionis ipsius anathema dixisse. Patet etiam ex Epistolâ S. Athanasii, qui interfuit Concilio, scribentis ad Constantinum Magnum, fieri non posse ut Arius cum suis pristino gradui restitueretur, quòd impossibile esset τὰς ἀπαξ τῶν πίστιν ἀθετήσαντας ἢ ἀναθεματισθέντας eos qui semel fidem evertissent, & quibus anathema denunciatum esset, postliminio gradum suum recuperare. apud eundem Socratem lib. eodem cap. 20. Denique, patet idem ex eâdem formulâ fidei, seu Symbolo Nicéno repetito ex Epistolâ Synodicâ ejusdem Athanasii & reliquorum Episcoporum Ægyptiorum ad Jovinianum Imperatorem; cui formulæ subjiciunt Episcopi Orthodoxi etiam suum testimonium: διὰ τοῦτο γὰρ καὶ ἀναγκαῖον ἡ ἡ ἐν Νικαίᾳ Συνόδος ἀνεθεμάτισε τὴν τοιαύτην αἵρεσιν: ob hanc causam enim, ut modò diximus, etiam Synodus Nicæna anathema denunciavit huic Hæresi; apud Theodor. lib. 4. c. 3. Testimonia plura nolo adducere.
units.tr: Here, apart from the fact that they reveal to us a new mystery of their impiety (by which they feel that the orthodox doctrine of the Trinity only began with the Council of Nicaea, and so they reveal their dissimulation and their Socinianism on this mystery, as I have shown in Part III, book 1, chapter 7, section 1), what they say is also most absurd, and is a lie they share with the open Socinians: that the ancient Fathers dissented from those orthodox doctrines which the Antitrinitarians oppose, or were ignorant of them. Their theologians, of the assemblies that worship God in three persons, have often shown against that shameless fiction of the Antitrinitarians that this is false. As for their statement that it is doubted whether Arius was struck with anathema at the Council of Nicaea itself, and their inference from it that it is absurd of me to say that the Church from the beginning pronounced anathema on the Antitrinitarians, here see the impudence of these men, who dare to bring this forward as an argument and say in general terms that the matter is doubted, when they themselves do not agree with those who doubt it. They would have done well to name them, for none of the orthodox has ever denied this. Thus they say in the Response to the Excerpts, page 70: There are those who deny that any anathema was pronounced at the Synod of Nicaea; whether rightly or not, let others judge. Here, in that they profess to doubt this matter and leave it for others to decide, it reveals their great ignorance of ecclesiastical antiquity, and shows how little learning these disturbers of Belgium have, and how most arrogant they are in despising all orders and all men, dead as well as living, who differ from them. For the contrary is plain from the Nicene Creed, as can be seen in Theodoret, book 1, chapter 12; Nicephorus Callistus, book 8, chapter 17; Socrates, book 1, chapter 5. Likewise from the Synodal Letter of the same Council, in the same Theodoret, book 1, chapter 6, to which Socrates adds these words, worth noting for the present matter: In the Synodal Letter of the Council it became plain that they anathematized not only Arius and his like-minded supporters, but also the words of his perverse opinion [ἐν τῷ τῆς συνοδικῆς ὁμολογίᾳ φανερὸν καθίστασαν, ὅτι μόνον Ἀρείου καὶ τὰς ὁμοδόξους αὐτῷ ἀνεθεμάτισαν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰς λέξεις τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ]. It is also clear from the letter of St Athanasius, who was present at the Council, writing to Constantine the Great, that it is not possible for Arius and his followers to be restored to their former rank, because it is impossible for those who have once overthrown the faith, or who have been struck with anathema [τοὺς ἅπαξ τὴν πίστιν ἀθετήσαντας ἢ ἀναθεματισθέντας], to recover their rank by right of return; in the same Socrates, same book, chapter 20. Finally, the same appears from the same formula of faith, or Nicene Creed, repeated from the Synodal Letter of this same Athanasius and of the rest of the Egyptian bishops to the Emperor Jovian, to which formula the orthodox bishops also add their testimony: For this reason, as we have just said, the Synod of Nicaea also necessarily pronounced anathema on this heresy [διὰ τοῦτο γὰρ καὶ ἀναγκαῖον ἡ ἐν Νικαίᾳ Σύνοδος ἀνεθεμάτισε τὴν τοιαύτην αἵρεσιν]; in Theodoret, book 4, chapter 3. I do not wish to adduce more testimonies.

units.la: Quod dicunt se prolixè DEMONSTRASSE ex Justino Martyre eos qui negabant divinam naturam Christi in communionem Ecclesiæ admissos fuisse, salsissimum est. Etenim ipsi Arminiani in conscientiâ suâ norunt se id ex Justino non DEMONSTRASSE, seu istud argumentum ex Justino apodicticum non esse. Ne quis de eâ re dubitet, en confessionem ipsorum propriam. Nam postquam in loco illo Responsionis ad Excerpta adduxissent pag. 41. 42. rationes septem propter quas non possunt adduci ut Socinianis anathema dicant, addunt p. 43. 44. 45. 46. octavam rationem illam petitam ex Justino Martyre, & concludunt eâdē p. 46. de istâ octavâ ut & cæteris septem rationibus: Atqui hæ inter alias sunt rationes, quæ errantibus istis obstant, quò minus recepta de Trinitate sententia subscribere se posse affirment; quæ etsi PRORSUS APODICTICÆ NON SINT; tales tamen Remonstrantibus videntur, ut non levem causam præbere errantierrantibus possint cur in errore suo, five pertinacia culpa permanere credi debeant. Et sic manifestum est, omnia ea quae Arminiani p. 43. 44. 45. 46. de loco illo Justini deblatterant, non esse nisi meras nugas, & detorsionem ac corruptelam Justini.
units.tr: It is utterly absurd of them to say they have demonstrated from Justin Martyr that those who denied the divine nature of Christ were admitted into the communion of the Church. The Arminians themselves know in their own conscience that they have not demonstrated this from Justin, and that this argument from Justin is not apodictic. Lest anyone doubt it, here is their own confession. After they had adduced, in that part of their Response to the Excerpts (pp. 41–42), seven reasons why they cannot be brought to pronounce anathema on the Socinians, they add on pp. 43–46 an eighth reason taken from Justin Martyr. They conclude about this eighth reason, as about the other seven, on p. 46: Yet these are among the other reasons which stand in the way of these erring men, so that they cannot affirm that they can subscribe to the received doctrine of the Trinity. Although they are NOT ENTIRELY APODICTIC, they nevertheless seem to the Remonstrants such that they can give the erring no slight cause to believe that they ought to remain in their error through the guilt of obstinacy. It is therefore plain that everything the Arminians babble on pp. 43–46 about that passage of Justin is nothing but mere trifles, a distortion and a corruption of Justin.

units.la: Postea homines isti cavillantur id quod dixeram eos callide dicere se non agnoscere dogmata ista Orthodoxa esse necessaria ad salutem propter evidentem consequentiam. Et ostenderam eos callide formare statum quaestionis, ac si scilicet nos supponeremus ea dogmata esse simpliciter necessaria propter evidentem consequentiam qua e Scripturis eliciuntur. Hanc dicebam non esse veram consequentiam; primo enim multa dogma e Scripturis eliciuntur per evidentem consequentiam, quae tamen constat non esse necessaria ad salutem; deinde, fundamentum propter quod dogma aliquod est necessarium ad salutem aut verum etiam, nunquam est consequentia evidens: sed verum fundamentum, ob quod dogma aliquod verum esse credimus, dicebam esse quia fundatur seu continetur in verbo Dei; cur autem necessarium esse credimus, fundamentum esse inquiebam, quia verus sensus ille controversus est ipse literalis sensus partis verbi Dei quae necesaria est ad salutem, qualis quidem ratio est horum dogmatum Orthodoxorum de Trinitate. Haec ego ibi. Ad quae illi multa ineptissime deblatterant pag. 38. 39. 40. & quidem ad primum respondent: Magnum me hercule acumen! Vedelius dignus est ut propter istud fœnum edat. Idem totidem verbis agnoscunt Remonstrantes eodem folio &c. & alia convitia addunt. Vides, optime Lector, indolem insolentissimam istorum hominum, qui ideo mihi convitia dicunt quia dixi aliquid ad explicandam mentem Orthodoxorum Theologorum, quod adeo verum est ut ipsi id fateantur; & quod ego non dixi ab iis negari, sed perperam nobis opponi.
units.tr: Afterwards these men carp at what I had said: that they cunningly say they do not acknowledge these Orthodox doctrines to be necessary to salvation on account of evident consequence. I had shown that they cunningly frame the state of the question, as if we supposed these doctrines to be simply necessary on account of the evident consequence which is drawn from the Scriptures. I said this was not a true consequence. First, many doctrines are drawn from the Scriptures by evident consequence which it is certain are not necessary to salvation. Second, the ground on account of which some doctrine is necessary to salvation, or even true, is never an evident consequence. The true ground on account of which we believe a doctrine to be true, I said, is that it is founded on or contained in the Word of God. And why we believe it to be necessary, I said, the ground is that the true sense in dispute is the literal sense of that part of the Word of God which is necessary to salvation. This is indeed the case with these Orthodox doctrines of the Trinity. So much I said there. To this they babble a great deal, most ineptly (pp. 38–40). To the first point they reply: Great acumen, by God! Vedelius is worthy to publish it for the sake of that hay. The Remonstrants acknowledge the same thing in the same words on the same page, etc., and they add other insults. You see, most excellent reader, the most insolent disposition of these men. They revile me because I said something to explain the mind of the Orthodox theologians, and that is so true that they themselves confess it. I did not say that it was denied by them, but that it was wrongly opposed to us.

units.la: Ad secundum respondent: Consequentiam evidentem & directam enunciationem esse unum & idem apud omnes Theologos. id quod non nisi valde catachrestice dictum verum esse potest. Si enim proprie sumantur termini isti, vel pueri logici norunt aliud esse consequentiam enunciationis, item argumenti alicujus, & aliud esse ipsam enunciationem aut argumentum. Ego autem terminum consequentiae proprie & more usitato sumsi, M. Episcopio autem suam significationem relinquo, qui satis ostendit non uno in loco se magis imbutum Socinianarum blasphemiarum fœcibus quam philosophiae fontibus irrigatum esse. Addunt deinde, consequentiam evidentem etiam esse fundamentum propter ter quod dogma aliquod est necessarium; & in eum finem afferunt consequentiam ex Galat. 5. 22. Atqui sermo mihi erat de consequentiâ quæ est opus rationis, ut expresse ibi dico, non de eâ quæ est ipsius Spiritus Sancti, qualis est ista consequentia Apostoli. De quâ re etiam ex professo egi in Rationali Theologico, & ostendi discrimen inter consequentias divinas ac humanas; & illas, non has, dixi esse fundamentum fidei. præterea pandunt novum arcanum quoddam impietatis suæ, quod Par. III. lib 1. c. 4. §. 4. vidimus, & quo statuunt fidem Christianam niti opere aliquo rationis. Insuper negant, id quod dixi, esse fundamentum veritatis aut necessitatis dogmatis alicujus: & probationis loco redeunt ad coccysmum suum contra Reformatos; dicunt unumquemque sic posse fingere sensum literalem quem volet, cùm tamen ego de vero sensu seu qui revera talis est loquutus sim; & tandem, post novum quoddam aliud arcanum, quo negant dogma hoc Iesum Christum esse filium Dei unigentium esse necessarium ad salutem, de quo egimus Par. II. lib. 1. cap. 4. §. 1. rursus testantur affectum suum ardentissimum erga Antitrinitarios, & tantum non plorant ideo quia anathema ipsis dicitur. Id quod faciunt hoc prætextu suo solito, quem ubivis inculcant; Nimirum crudelem rem esse, perdere anathematizatione tot myriadas hominum velle. Verum enimvero iste prætextus frivolus est, quo palam faciunt se nondum didicisse nec ex Scripturâ sacrâ nec ex Praxi Ecclesiæ veteris quis finis anathematizationis sit. Finis is est, non perditio sed salus quâ errantis, quâ eorum qui in errore nondum sunt constituti. Salus errantis; ut scilicet is, motus detestatione fidelium quam incurrit, & metu pœnæ æternæ cui se obnoxium facit territus, in viam redeat atque convertatur. Finem hunc docet Apostolus 1. Cor. 5. 6. ubi dicit se tradere incestuosum Sathanæ ad exitium carnis, ut spiritus salvus sit illo die Domini Iesu. Salus non errantium, ut scilicet illi, præmoniti judicio publico & gravissimo Ecclesiæ, caveant sibi ab hæresi illâ, adeoque eâ non inficiantur; quem finem intendit ibidem Apostolus v. 6. 7. An nescitis, inquit, paululo fermenti totam massam fermentari? Expurgate igitur vetus fermentum &c. Hunc posteriorem finem respicit Socrates lib. 7. c. 35. in descriptione anathematizationis, ubi de Nestorio loquitur: κοινῇ μὲν τῇ ψήφῳ πάντες οἱ κληρικοὶ αὐτὸν ἀνεθεμάτισαν· ἔτω δὲ οἱ χριστιανοὶ καλεῖν εἰώθαμεν τὴν κατὰ τὸ βλασφήμως ψῆφον, ὅταν αὐτὴν ὥσπερ ἐν σήλῃ ἀναστήσαντες φανερῶς τοῖς ἅπασι καλὰ στήσωμεν. Itaque communi calculo omnes Clerici eum anathematizarunt. Ita enim nos Christiani vocamus sententiam contra blasphemum latam, quando eam tanquam in coluin columna elevatam & affixam omnibus conspicuam constituimus. Sed hoc M. Episcopius Socinianus simulator se ignorare ostendit, qui tantum erudi-tionis quantum pietatis habet.
units.tr: To the second point they reply that an evident consequence and a direct proposition are one and the same among all theologians. That can be true only in a very catachrestic sense. If these terms are taken properly, even schoolboys in logic know that the consequence of a proposition, or of some argument, is one thing, and the proposition or argument itself is another. But I took the term "consequence" properly and in its customary sense. I leave M. Episcopius his own meaning, who sufficiently shows that on more than one occasion he has been steeped in the dregs of Socinian blasphemies rather than watered from the fountains of philosophy. They then add that an evident consequence is also the ground on account of which some doctrine is necessary, and to that end they cite the consequence from Gal. 5.22. But my discussion concerned the consequence which is the work of reason, as I say expressly there, not that which belongs to the Holy Spirit himself, such as is the consequence of the Apostle in that passage. I treated this matter ex professo in the Rationale Theologicum, and showed the difference between divine and human consequences. I said it is the former, not the latter, that are the ground of faith. Moreover, they unfold a new secret of their impiety, which we saw in Par. III, lib. 1, cap. 4, §4, and by which they affirm that the Christian faith rests on some work of reason. Furthermore, they deny what I said, that it is the ground of the truth or necessity of some doctrine. By way of proof they return to their cackling against the Reformed, saying that each person may feign whatever literal sense he likes, whereas I spoke of the true sense, the one which really is such. Finally, after yet another new secret, by which they deny that this doctrine, that Jesus Christ is the only-begotten Son of God, is necessary to salvation (which we discussed in Par. II, lib. 1, cap. 4, §1), they again testify their most ardent affection for the Antitrinitarians, and they almost weep because anathema is pronounced on them. They do this under their usual pretext, which they inculcate everywhere: namely, that it is a cruel thing to wish to destroy so many myriads of men by anathematization. But this pretext is truly frivolous, and by it they openly show that they have not yet learned, either from holy Scripture or from the practice of the ancient Church, what the purpose of anathematization is. The purpose is not destruction but salvation: the salvation of the one who errs, and of those who are not yet settled in error. The salvation of the one who errs is this: that he, moved by the detestation of the faithful which he incurs, and frightened by the fear of the eternal punishment to which he makes himself liable, may return to the way and be converted. The Apostle teaches this purpose at 1 Cor. 5.6, where he says he delivers the incestuous man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus. The salvation of those who do not err is this: that those men, warned by the public and most grave judgment of the Church, may beware of that heresy and so not be infected by it. The Apostle intends this end in the same place, vv. 6–7: Know ye not, he says, that a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump? Purge out therefore the old leaven, etc. Socrates (Hist. 7.35) has this latter end in view in his description of anathematization, where he speaks of Nestorius: all the clergy with common vote anathematized him [κοινῇ μὲν τῇ ψήφῳ πάντες οἱ κληρικοὶ αὐτὸν ἀνεθεμάτισαν]. For thus we Christians are accustomed to call the sentence pronounced against the blasphemer, when we set it up openly for all to see, as on a raised pillar [οὕτω δὲ οἱ χριστιανοὶ καλεῖν εἰώθαμεν τὴν κατὰ τοῦ βλασφήμου ψῆφον, ὅταν αὐτὴν ὥσπερ ἐν στήλῃ ἀναστήσαντες φανερῶς τοῖς ἅπασι καλὰ στήσωμεν]. But M. Episcopius, the Socinian pretender, shows that he does not know this, though he has as much erudition as he lacks piety.

units.la: Denique jubent ut probem sensum istum Orthodoxum mysterii Tri-nitatis esse sensum illius literalem: sd quod tamen (ut Arcan. Par.I.lib.1. c. 7. p. 57. monueram) Ecclesia tota inde ab initio ad hunc usque diem ex Scripturâ ipsâ probat, eo ipso, quia nullum alium sed eum ipsum esse verum sensum perpetuo ex verbo Dei ostendit. Sed de hac re egimus e-tiam Par. III. lib. 1. c. 7. §. 2.
units.tr: Finally, they bid me prove that this Orthodox sense of the mystery of the Trinity is its literal sense. But this (as I had warned in Arcan. Par. I, lib. 1, c. 7, p. 57) the whole Church, from the beginning up to this day, proves from Scripture itself, precisely because it constantly shows from the Word of God that this, and no other, is the true sense. But we have discussed this matter also in Par. III, lib. 1, c. 7, §2.

units.la: 5. Objeceram ipsis etiam quod dogmata ista Orthodoxa quæ Anti-trinitarii oppugnant, negant seu non agnoscunt educta esse è Scriptura per evidentem consequentiam. Item quod Tyrannidis convitio proscin-dunt totam Ecclesiam veterem & modernam quæ Deum in tribus per-sonis adorávit & adorat; eò quod statuit ista dogmata esse necessaria ad salutem. Denique quod nolunt Hæreticis Antitrinitariis anathema dice-re. Hæc etiam non negant, sed fatentur, ac Lectorem remittunt ad Re-sponsionem ad Excer. DD. Proff. Leydd. in quâ persistunt in doctrinâ eâ Apologiæ; atque inter alia de Evidentiâ eorum dogmatum ita loquun-tur ibi p. 84. Quare cùm hæc ita se habeant, nemo homo est, qui non facile vi-det, oaufàs non leves esse cur Remonstrantes dubitare se dicant, an propositiones illæ censendæ sint in numero illarum quæ per evidentem consequentiam ex Scripturis deducuntur, sive quæ sine manifestâ hominis culpâ ignorari, in dubium vocari aut negari non possunt. Sed de hac re vide etiam, si libet, Par.III. lib.1.c.7.§.3. ubi etiam ostendimus hos homines in hac quoque parte αὐτοκαταχρίτως esse.
units.tr: I had also objected to them that the orthodox dogmas which the Antitrinitarians oppose they deny, or do not acknowledge, to be drawn from Scripture by evident consequence; likewise that they tear to pieces with the insult of tyranny the whole ancient and modern Church, which has worshipped and worships God in three persons, because it holds those dogmas to be necessary to salvation; and lastly that they are unwilling to pronounce anathema on the heretical Antitrinitarians. These things too they do not deny, but confess, and they refer the reader to their Response to the Excerpts of the Professors of Leiden, in which they persist in the doctrine of their Apology. Among other things, about the evidence of those dogmas, they speak thus there, p. 84: "Wherefore, since these things are so, there is no one who does not readily see that the reasons are not slight why the Remonstrants say they doubt whether those propositions are to be counted among those which are deduced from Scripture by evident consequence, or which cannot be ignored, called in doubt, or denied without manifest fault of the man." But on this matter see also, if you like, Part III, book 1, ch. 7, §3, where we also showed that these men are [αὐτοκαταχρίτως] self-condemned in this part too.

units.la: 6. Aliud dogma ipsorum est; quod eos qui negant Trinitatem, ac divinam naturam Christi &c. dicunt esse homines pios, piissimos, sanctissimos; eos vivere ex præscripto Euangelii &c. & dixeram Antitrinitarios apertos non melius potuisse suæ sectæ patrocinari, quàm hic Arminiani illis pa-trocinantur, dum eos ob pietatem tantopere commendant. Non ne-gant, sed defendunt, & in eum finem ablegantscum præcedentibus Le-ctorem ad Responsionem illam suam ad Excerpta; in quibus dicunt su-perlativos eos gradus non ita præcisè esse sumedos. Sed hoc ipsos non ju-vat quàmdiu eos in positivo gradu pro piis habent; & quamdiu eorum pietatem scilicet participant. Vide etiam Par. III. lib. 1. cap.7. §. 5.
units.tr: 6. Another of their doctrines is that those who deny the Trinity and the divine nature of Christ, etc., are pious, most pious, most holy men, who live according to the precept of the Gospel, etc. I had said that open Antitrinitarians could not have defended their own sect better than these Arminians defend them, when they commend them so highly for their piety. They do not deny this but defend it, and to that end they send the reader, together with the preceding passages, to their Reply to the Excerpts, where they say that these superlatives are not to be taken so strictly. But this does not help them, so long as they count such men as pious in the positive degree, and so long as they share in their piety. See also Part III, book 1, chapter 7, §5.

units.la: 7. Objeceram quoque ipsis fraudem, quâ statum quæstionis (nimi-rùm cur anathema non dixerint Hæresibus & Hæreticis Sabellianis, A-rianis, rianis, Photinianis, Samosatenianis &c) studiosè involverint in Apol. c. 3, f. 53. a. b. ac si quæstio esset de modis illis per intellectionem, per voluntatem, de distinctione reali &c. cùm tamen quæstio sit & fuerit de rejiciendis & damnandis blasphemis dogmatis atque hæresibus; ut ipsi coguntur fateri &c. Non negant hanc fraudem, & ne verbo quidem respondent. Observetur eos eâdem fraude uti denuò in eâdem re in Respons. ad Excerp. p. 39. &c. Objeceram pariter eâdem occasione p.60. 61. similem fraudem in eâdem materiâ in Epist. Hagam Comitis scriptâ. Hanc fraudem suam etiam non negant & nihil respondent.
units.tr: 7. I had also charged them with fraud, in that they cunningly obscured the state of the question (namely, why they had not pronounced anathema on the heresies and heretics of the Sabellians, Arians, Photinians, Samosatenes, etc.) in their Apology, chapter 3, fol. 53 a–b, as though the question concerned those modes of intellection and volition, the real distinction, and so on, whereas the question is and always has been about rejecting and condemning blasphemous doctrines and heresies, as they themselves are compelled to admit. They do not deny this fraud and do not answer it even with a word. Let it be noted that they use the same fraud again on the same point in the Reply to the Excerpts, p. 39 etc. I had likewise charged them, on the same occasion, pp. 60–61, with a similar fraud on the same matter in the letter written to Count Hagen. They do not deny this fraud either, and answer nothing.

units.la: 8. Objeceram ipsis, quòd dogmata talia non habeant pro Necessariis, eo fine, ut Hæreticos Antitrinitarios in Ecclesiam Dei introducant. Hoc etiam nequaquam negant. Ostenderam autem illud ex eo, quòd persuadere volunt hominibus, ex Justini loco impudentissimè detorto, veterem Ecclesiam Christianam communione coluisse cum illis qui negabant Christum habere naturam divinam. Id quod falsum esse, & contrà non coluisse Ecclesiam veterem cum illis communionem docueram ex S. Ignatio, ex quo patet jam 40 aut 50 annis ante Iustinum Ecclesiam Christianam detestatam fuisse eos, qui statuebant Christum esse nudum hominem, seu habere tantum naturam humanam non autem divinam. Hic dicunt 1 Epistolas illas censeri suppositititias à multis, aut esse saltem interpolatas. 2. Ex Epistolâ ad Philadelphenses constare auctorem detestari eos qui Christum nudum hominem esse dicebant, verùm non eos qui Christum non agnoscebant unius ejusdemque essentiæ divinæ cum Patre, sed Christum verum Deum esse agnosci volebant, sed alium tamen à Creatore universi. 3. Arianos his Epistolis errorem suum infersisse, dicunt constare ex Epist. ad Tarsenses & Philippenses, ubi, inquiunt, nimis clara & aperta vestigia & lineamenta Arianismi esse: Qui ista dicta, ajunt p. 42. conciliare volunt distinctione scholastica inter unitatem personalem & essentialem, illi profecto torquere malunt veterum scripta ad hypothesin suam, quàm sine præjudicio expendere. Ad hæc respondere supervacaneum ducerem, nì adderent: Quid? an Vedelium nostrum tortorem istum futurum male ominor? Tùm verò vos ei torturam scriptorum suorum pro pœnâ destinate Iudices. Quia igitur ominantur me futurum detortorem Ignatii, uno verbo ostendendum est eos malè sibi ominari. Nam quòd attinet ad primum quod excipiunt, de eo videatur Apologia nostra Ignatii Epistolis & nostris in eundem Excercitationibus præfixa. Ad secundum respondeo Ignatium rejicere & condemnare hæreses quæ suo tempore jam erant qualis est Ebionitarum qui naturam divinam Christi negabant, quam Hæresin Sociniani aperti & simulatores sequuntur. Arii Hæresis ducentis annis & ultra post Ignatium exorta fuit. Ad 3. dico Arianos non corrupisse Epistolas Ignatii; nec Arianismi vestigia in iis esse. Quem in finem opus non habent, ut metuant ne futurus sim tortor Ignatii in locis allegatis. Nam antequam Arminiani Iustini illo loco (cujus corruptelæ hunc locum Ignatii oppositi) abuterentur in Apologia sua quam ediderunt anno trigesimo; ostendi ego vere, candide, & sine ulla detorsione anno vigesimo tertio hujus seculi in Notis meis Criticis ad Ignatium eum locum non esse corruptum ab Arianis. Verba mea in notis Criticis in Epist. ad Trallens. lit. g. p. 125. hæc sunt, quæ ideo addam, ut videant Arminiani & unusquisque; intelligat me non futurum tortorem Ignatii contra eos, sed verum & candidum interpretem fuisse mentis ipsius jam ante omnationem illam Arminianorum: Taxat Ignatius Haereticorum dogma, qui non distinguebant essentiam divinam in tres personas, sed unam dicebant esse personam tantum. Contra Ignatius docet esse Patrem, Filium & Spiritum S. unum unitate essentiæ, sed non unum unitate personæ. Sic ad Tarsenses taxantur pariter Haeretici qui dicebant quod Christus sit ὁ ἐπὶ πάντων θεὸς Deus super omnia h.e. quod Christus sit ipsa persona Patris: ut in eadem Epistola clarius id repræsentatur cum confutatur haeresis illa: ἡ ὅτι οὐκ αὐτὸς ἐστιν ὁ ἐπὶ πάντων θεὸς ἀλλ' ὁ υἱὸς ἐκεῖνος, & quod ipse non sit super omnia Deus ET PATER, sed filius ipsius. Id probat locis Scripturæ quibus persona Patris a Persona Filii distinguitur. Igitur nihil est in his locis, quod aut absurdum sit, ut quidam putant, aut ARIANORUM haresi aspiretur. Hæc ego ibi. Ex quibus manifestum est, meum & mei similium ingenium atque indolem non esse contentionis studio contra Arminianos hæc vel illa loca Scripturæ aut Patrum ad nostra præjudicia (quæ per Dei gratiam nulla sunt) detorquere, ut ipsi faciunt: sed solius veritatis divinæ & causæ Dei vindicandæ studio ac necessitate ab iis dissentire. Mihi profecto ante undecim annos in mentem venire non potuit Arminianos olim depravaturos esse ista loca aut Ignatij aut Iustini, & ea vel alia mihi adversus ipsos vindicanda esse.
units.tr: 8. I had charged them that they do not hold such doctrines to be necessary, with the aim of introducing the Antitrinitarian heretics into the Church of God. This they by no means deny. I had shown this from the fact that they wish to persuade people, from a passage of Justin most shamelessly distorted, that the ancient Christian Church maintained communion with those who denied that Christ has a divine nature. I had shown from St Ignatius that this is false, and that on the contrary the ancient Church did not hold communion with such men, since already forty or fifty years before Justin the Christian Church had detested those who held that Christ was a mere man, or had only a human nature and not a divine one. Here they say, first, that those Epistles are considered spurious by many, or are at least interpolated. Second, that from the Epistle to the Philadelphians it is clear that the author detested those who said Christ was a mere man, but not those who did not acknowledge Christ as of one and the same divine essence with the Father, while wishing Christ to be acknowledged as true God, though distinct from the Creator of the universe. Third, they say it is clear from the Epistles to the Tarsians and the Philippians that the Arians inserted their error into these Epistles, since, they say, there are there very clear and open traces and outlines of Arianism: Those who wish to reconcile these sayings, they say on p. 42, by the scholastic distinction between personal and essential unity, prefer surely to twist the writings of the ancients to their own hypothesis rather than weigh them without prejudice. I would think it superfluous to reply to these things, were it not that they add: What? Is it an ill omen that our Vedelius will be such a torturer? Then you appoint him, as a penalty, to the torture of their writings, as judges. Since, then, they fear by their omen that I will be a distorter of Ignatius, it must be shown in one word that they are mistaken in their omen. For as to the first point they raise, let the reader consult our Apology, prefixed to our Epistles of Ignatius and to our Exercitations on the same. As to the second, I reply that Ignatius rejects and condemns heresies that already existed in his time, such as that of the Ebionites, who denied the divine nature of Christ, a heresy which open and disguised Socinians follow. The heresy of Arius arose more than two hundred years after Ignatius. As to the third, I say that the Arians did not corrupt the Epistles of Ignatius, nor are there any traces of Arianism in them. Therefore they have no need to fear that I shall be a torturer of Ignatius in the passages cited. For before the Arminians abused that passage of Justin (whose corruption I opposed to this passage of Ignatius) in their Apology, which they published in the thirtieth year, I showed truly, candidly, and without any distortion, in the year twenty-three of this century, in my Critical Notes on Ignatius, that the passage had not been corrupted by the Arians. My words in the Critical Notes on the Epistle to the Trallians, letter g, p. 125, are these, which I add so that the Arminians and everyone may see, and understand, that I am not going to be a torturer of Ignatius against them, but was a true and candid interpreter of his own mind, even before that Arminian fabrication: Ignatius censures the doctrine of the heretics who did not distinguish the divine essence into three persons, but said that there is only one person. On the contrary, Ignatius teaches that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are one in unity of essence, but not one in unity of person. So in the Epistle to the Tarsians the heretics are likewise censured who said that Christ is ὁ ἐπὶ πάντων θεὸς [God over all], that is, that Christ is the very person of the Father; as this is set out more clearly in the same Epistle when that heresy is refuted: ἡ ὅτι οὐκ αὐτὸς ἐστιν ὁ ἐπὶ πάντων θεὸς ἀλλ' ὁ υἱὸς ἐκεῖνος [that he is not himself God over all, but that Son], and that he himself is not God over all AND FATHER, but his Son. He proves this by passages of Scripture in which the person of the Father is distinguished from the person of the Son. Therefore there is nothing in these passages that is either absurd, as some think, or smacks of the heresy of the ARIANS. So far I wrote there. From these words it is plain that my nature and disposition, and that of those like me, is not to distort these or those passages of Scripture or of the Fathers against the Arminians, in a spirit of contention, to fit our prejudices (which, by the grace of God, we do not have), as they do. Rather, we dissent from them out of zeal for divine truth alone and out of the necessity of defending the cause of God. Indeed, eleven years ago it could not have come into my mind that the Arminians would one day corrupt these passages of Ignatius or of Justin, and that I would have to defend them or others against them.

units.la: 9. Objeceram quoque ipsis maledicentiam & contemtum quo utuntur adversus Athanasium & Symbolum ipsius, quia anathema dicit Antitrinitariis; dum scribunt Apol. Exam. præf. f. 6. b. Quare nihil dubitamus profiteri Athanasium limitem juris hujus prætergressum esse, quando Symbolo suo SUPERBAM istam præfationem præscripsit; Quicunque vult salvus esse &c. Hoc etiam non negant; sed agnoscunt, & dicunt me putare ista male esse ab ipsis dicta, sed se haec flocci facere. Sed non novum est Arminianorum hoc de Symbolo isto judicium. Sequuntur enim in eo, fratres suos Antitrinitarios apertos, qui Symbolum istud Athanasii vocant Sa-thanasii, item Symbolum Antichristi.
units.tr: 9.
