I had also charged them with the slander and contempt they show toward Athanasius and his Creed, because it pronounces anathema on the Antitrinitarians; while they write in the Apology, Examination, preface, fol. 6 b: Wherefore we do not doubt to declare that Athanasius overstepped the bounds of this right when he prefixed to his Creed that PROUD preface: "Whosoever will be saved," etc. They do not deny this either, but acknowledge it, and say that I think these things were said badly by them, but that they make nothing of them. But this judgment of the Arminians on that Creed is not new. For in this they follow their open Antitrinitarian brethren, who call that Creed of Athanasius Sathanasii, the Creed of Satan, and also the Creed of Antichrist.

units.la: 10. Denique conquestus eram, eos longè aliter de mysterio Trinitatis sentire, seu aliter illud credere quàm tota Ecclesia quæ Deum in tribus personis adorat. Etenim Ecclesia tota agnoscit Mysterium de Trinitate necessarios suos usus habere in fide & vitâ ad salutem: id quod Arminiani in Apologiâ suâ negant, quorum effugia circa hanc rem paulò ante diluimus. Præter hoc etiam Ecclesia Christiana dogmata Antitrinitariis opposita habet pro necessariis ad salutem & sic mysterium Trinitatis habet pro necessario in suo vero sensu: at Arminiani ea pro Necessariis agnoscere, & consequenter mysterium illud in suo vero sensu pro Necessario habere nolunt. Ecclesia Christiana anathema dicit Hæreticis negantibus illa dogmata: Arminiani negant anathema illis dicendum esse, sed contra habent eos pro hominibus piis, piissimis, sanctissimis, & salutem æternam illis blasphematoribus decernunt. Ecclesia Christiana recipit Symbolum Athanasii simpliciter; at non Arminiani. Ecclesia Christiana Spiritum S. adorandum statuit, at non Arminiani. Ecclesia per consequens Deum in tribus personis adorat: At hi homines de Deo in tribus personis adorando ne hilum quidem in Scripturâ esse dicunt. Ecclesia Christiana firmiter constanterque credenda esse ea dicit, idque fide divinâ sine ullâ variatione circa ea, in iis Religionem Christianam positam dicit: at Arminiani ea non habet pro Necessariis, & sic contrarium in reliquis illis sentiunt. Insuper conquestus fui, eos fiduciam in tres personas Deitatis collocandam, & invocationem ac cultum earum labefactare; nec non Baptismi, quo in nomen trium personarum baptizamur, substantiam plusquàm convellere, quandoquidem secundùm ipsos per evidentem consequentiam illa doctrina Orthodoxa probari non potest, & Antitrinitarii salvari possunt in suâ Hæresi. Ad hæc quid Arminiani? Non negant, imò ne hiscere quidem audent. Atqui hæc crimina sunt gravissima, & nequaquam toleranda in iis qui tantopere de Religionis Christianæ amore ac studio gloriantur.
units.tr: 10. Finally, I complained that they think quite differently about the mystery of the Trinity, or believe it otherwise than the whole Church, which worships God in three persons. For the whole Church acknowledges that the mystery of the Trinity has its necessary uses in faith and life for salvation; this the Arminians deny in their Apology, and we have a little earlier refuted their evasions on this matter. Besides this, the Christian Church holds the doctrines opposed to the Antitrinitarians to be necessary for salvation, and so holds the mystery of the Trinity to be necessary in its true sense; but the Arminians are unwilling to acknowledge those doctrines as necessary, and consequently are unwilling to hold that mystery in its true sense to be necessary. The Christian Church pronounces anathema on heretics who deny those doctrines; the Arminians deny that anathema is to be pronounced on them, but on the contrary count them pious, most pious, most holy men, and decree eternal salvation for those blasphemers. The Christian Church receives the Creed of Athanasius without qualification; the Arminians do not. The Christian Church holds the Holy Spirit to be worthy of worship; the Arminians do not. Consequently the Church worships God in three persons; but these men say that there is not the slightest trace in Scripture of worshipping God in three persons. The Christian Church says that these things are to be believed firmly and steadfastly, and with divine faith, without any variation, and it holds the Christian religion to rest on them; but the Arminians do not count them necessary, and so think otherwise about the rest. Moreover, I complained that they undermine the trust to be placed in the three persons of the Deity, and the invocation and worship of them; and that they more than shake the substance of baptism, in which we are baptized into the name of the three persons, since, according to them, that orthodox doctrine cannot be proved by necessary consequence, and Antitrinitarians can be saved in their heresy. To these charges what do the Arminians say? They do not deny them; indeed they do not even dare to open their mouths. Yet these are the gravest crimes, and by no means to be tolerated in men who boast so much of their love and zeal for the Christian religion.

units.la: Unde etiam unusquisque pius videt se cavere sibi debere à Baptismo quem hi homines administrant. Nam qui ita de mysterio Trinitatis sentiunt, speciatim illud non esse eductum è verbo Dei per necessariam consequentiam, illi profectò sincerè &verè non possunt baptizare in Trinitatem, tatem, h. e. tres personas Deitatis. Hoc Ariani Eunomiani agnoscentes, non baptizabant in Trinitatem sed in Christi mortem, ut videre est apud Socratem lib. 5. c. 23. οὐ γὰρ εἰς τὴν τελείαν, ἀλλ' εἰς τὸν τῆς χρι-στῆ βασιλείαν θάνατον. non in Trinitatem sed in Christi mortem baptizant. Ratio est: quia in quem baptizatur aliquis, in ejus ut veri & æterni Dei cultum obligatur. Hoc videbant Eunomiani, itaque in Trinitatem baptizare noluerunt. Et nexus est indissolubilis ac cognatio summa doctrinæ Orthodoxæ de Mysterio Trinitatis cum baptismo nostro. Unde veteres Patres Concilii Constantinopol. sub Gratiano & Theodosio, ex eo etiam æstimarunt veritatem doctrinæ illius Orthodoxæ, quòd Baptismo conformis sit, & doceat credere in nomen Patris Filii & Spiritus Sancti; ut testantur in libello suo Synodico apud Theod. lib 5. c. 9. ubi dicunt: istam fidem Nicenam ab omnibus approbari debere προσεθυλάττειν ... ut qua omnium antiquissima est, & conformis Baptismo & docet nos credere in nomen Patris & Filii & Spiritus Sancti. Ex his omnibus apparet quàm turpiter se dent Arminiani in hoc capite. Alii modi quibus hi homines dissentiunt ab Ecclesiâ totâ quæ Deum in tribus personis adorat, à nobis expositi sunt Par. III. lib. 1. cap. 7. Patet etiam ex dictis me nihil ipsis per calumniam affinxisse etiam capite. 7 Par. I. lib. 1. quandoquidem dogmata sibi à me in eo objecta nequaquam negant.
units.tr: Hence every pious person also sees that he must beware of the baptism these men administer. For those who think in this way about the mystery of the Trinity, and especially who hold that it is not drawn from the Word of God by necessary consequence, cannot truly and sincerely baptize into the Trinity, that is, into the three persons of the Godhead. The Arians and Eunomians, recognising this, did not baptize into the Trinity but into the death of Christ, as may be seen in Socrates, book 5, chapter 23: οὐ γὰρ εἰς τὴν τελείαν, ἀλλ' εἰς τὸν τῆς Χριστοῦ θάνατον ("for they baptize not into the perfect (Trinity), but into the death of Christ"). The reason is that whoever is baptized into a name is bound to the worship of that God who is true and eternal. The Eunomians saw this, and so they refused to baptize into the Trinity. There is an indissoluble bond and a close kinship between the orthodox doctrine of the mystery of the Trinity and our baptism. Hence the ancient Fathers of the Council of Constantinople under Gratian and Theodosius also judged the truth of that orthodox doctrine from this, that it agrees with baptism and teaches us to believe in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit. So they testify in their synodal letter, reported by Theodoret, book 5, chapter 9, where they say that this Nicene faith ought to be approved by all, προσεθυλάττειν ... ut qua omnium antiquissima est, & conformis Baptismo & docet nos credere in nomen Patris & Filii & Spiritus Sancti ("to hold fast to it, since it is the most ancient of all, agrees with baptism, and teaches us to believe in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit"). From all this it appears how shamefully the Arminians act in this chapter. The other ways in which these men dissent from the whole Church, which worships God in three persons, have been set out by us in Part III, book 1, chapter 7. It is also clear from what has been said that I have not falsely attributed anything to them, even in chapter 7 of Part I, book 1, since they by no means deny the doctrines I objected to them there.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CAP. VIII.

units.la: Examen Capitis Octavi.
units.tr: Examen Capitis Octavi.

units.la: 1. Arminiani contra conscientiam suam fallunt circa statum quæstionis. Maledicentia eorum contra omnes Reformatos. 2. Arminianos contra conscientiam suam negare ostenditur hoc dogma suum esse: Nulla dogmata controversa inter Christianos esse necessaria ad salutem. 3. Insignis alia impostura eorum, dum contra conscientiam suam negant se docere in Apologia: Necessaria dogmata ea tantum esse quæ apud omnes in confesso sunt. 4. Eorum impostura alia circa Necessaria dogmata controversa. Eos illâre veterum Hæreticorum praxin imitari ex collatione cum antiquiantiquitate Ecclesiastica ostenditur. 5. Eos non amplius fidem mereri in negocio Religionis, quando dicunt se hoc vel illud credere, ostenditur. 6. Non juvari causam eorum levitate & simulatione ipsorum in Religionis negocio docetur. 7. Præcipuum scopum eorum in Libertinismo esse introductionem blasphemiarum Socinianarum ostenditur. 8. Eos in limitatione quâ hic circa dogmata controversa utuntur, rursus contra propriam conscientiam agere probatur. Ulterius examen istius limitationis. 9. Exempla dogmatum controversorum necessariorum ab Arminianis allata ponderantur. 10. Fatentur se docere: Controversa vera dogmata non esse firmiter constanterque credenda. 11. Fatentur ea esse credenda tantum certitudine humanâ. 12. Non negant, dogmata quæ rudibus pariter atque imperitis obvia non sunt, qualia ipsis sunt dogmata Orthodoxa opposita Antitrinitariis non sine periculo credi. 13. Non negant, se docere; de rebus controversis nihil esse decidendum, quod firmiter & constanter Orthodoxis omnibus sit credendum. 14. Fatentur, quod docent, licere contradicere veris dogmatis controversis. 15. Item, quod homines docent dubitare de rebus fidei. Item quæ ipsis objecta erant de contemtu & explosione dogmatum controversorum etiam maximi momenti. Item, licere sententiam mutare in horas imò infinities circa dogmata controversa: Religionem veram inter infinitas adeoque horarias variationes circa controversias manere posse salvam &c. 16. Quomodo ad hæc omnia respondeant Arminiani.
units.tr: 1. The Arminians deceive, against their own conscience, about the state of the question. Their slander against all the Reformed. 2. It is shown that the Arminians deny against their own conscience that this is their doctrine: no controverted doctrines among Christians are necessary to salvation. 3. Another notable imposture of theirs, when they deny against their own conscience that they teach in the Apology: the only necessary doctrines are those that are admitted by all. 4. Another of their impostures concerning controverted necessary doctrines. It is shown from a comparison with ancient Church history that they imitate the practice of the ancient heretics. 5. It is shown that they no longer deserve credit in matters of religion when they say that they believe this or that. 6. It is taught that their cause is not helped by their levity and their pretence in matters of religion. 7. It is shown that their chief aim in Libertinism is the introduction of Socinian blasphemies. 8. It is proved that in the qualification they use here concerning controverted doctrines they again act against their own conscience. A further examination of this qualification. 9. Examples of controverted necessary doctrines brought forward by the Arminians are weighed. 10. They confess that they teach that controverted true doctrines are not to be held firmly and constantly. 11. They confess that these are to be believed only with human certainty. 12. They do not deny that doctrines which are not equally obvious to the untrained and the unlearned, such as the Orthodox doctrines opposed to the Antitrinitarians, are believed not without danger. 13. They do not deny that they teach that nothing is to be decided about controverted matters that all Orthodox persons must firmly and constantly believe. 14. They confess that what they teach is that it is lawful to contradict true controverted doctrines. 15. Likewise that they teach that men should doubt matters of faith. Likewise the charges brought against them of contempt and rejection of controverted doctrines, even of the greatest importance. Likewise that it is lawful to change one's opinion every hour, indeed countless times, about controverted doctrines, and that true religion can remain safe amid endless and hourly variations on controversies, etc. 16. How the Arminians answer all these things.

units.la: 1. IN hoc Capite antequam ad rem veniant, verbosè (ut scilicet exactè & amplè me refutâsse videantur) statum quæstionis obscurare conantur. Dicunt: Quicunque Remonstrantes in scriptis suis disputârunt de dogmatis necessariis rectè dijudicandis à non Necessariis, ea Nullo Alio Fine disputarunt quàm ut primum ac præcipuum Reformationis dogma solidè assertum irent contra Pontificios; videlicet Scripturam sacram perspicuam claram atque dilucidam esse in omnibus ad salutem scitu ac creditu necessariis, ita ut omnia necessaria vel πρῶτος & κατὰ λέξιν in ea expressa sint, vel ex ea per evidentem & tem & omnibus obviam consequentiam deduci possint.
units.tr: 1. In this chapter, before they come to the matter, they try in a wordy way (so that they may seem to have refuted me exactly and fully) to obscure the state of the question. They say: whatever Remonstrants have disputed in their writings about rightly distinguishing necessary doctrines from unnecessary ones, they disputed with no other end than to firmly establish the first and chief dogma of the Reformation against the Papists: namely, that Holy Scripture is perspicuous, clear and plain in all things necessary to be known and believed for salvation, so that all necessary things are either expressed in it first and word for word [πρῶτος καὶ κατὰ λέξιν], or can be deduced from it by an evident consequence, obvious to all.

units.la: Verum salsissimum est, eos nullo alio fine id fecisse. Nam in conscientia sua convicti sunt, se id alio longe fine fecisse, nimirum ut tolerantiam mutuam h. e. spiritualem communionem cum errantibus, praecipue Antitrinitariis ea ratione sancirent. Verum esse hoc patet ex ad Lectorem quam praefationi Apologiae suae immediate subjiciunt: A necessariis non necessaria dogmata sollicite ex animi sui sententia distinxerunt, ut, quae ad pacem & mutuam tolerantiam Christianorum coetuum pertinere putant, Christiano orbi representarent. Nempe hac via sectis, schismatis ac factionibus quibus passim fervet Christi populus, optime ac tutissime occurri posse persuasissimum habent. Quae autem sit illa tolerantia & qualis, patet ex quatuor Partibus Arcanorum, nimirum ea, per quam hoc agunt praecipue ut blasphemias Turcicas Socinianorum in Ecclesiam Dei introducant, & tempora nobis Ariana reducant, eadem arte qua olim Ariani usi sunt, de qua S. Hieronymus in Chronico ad annum 364. ubi inquit: Omnes pene toto orbe Ecclesia SUB NOMINE PACIS & Regis (h. e. Constantii Imperatoris auctoritate) Arianorum consortio polluuntur. Hic est verus finis doctrinae ipsorum de Necessariis distinguendis a non Necessariis; quem finem ut consequi possint, necessarium sibi putarunt ut corrumperent doctrinam Ortdodoxam de perspicuitate Scripturae.
units.tr: But it is most absurd that they did this "with no other end." For in their own conscience they stand convicted that they did it with a quite different end, namely that they might by that means sanction mutual tolerance, that is, spiritual communion with the erring, especially the Antitrinitarians. That this is true is clear from the address to the Reader which they place immediately after the preface of their Apology: They have carefully distinguished necessary doctrines from unnecessary ones according to the judgment of their own mind, so that they might present to the Christian world those things which they think pertain to the peace and mutual tolerance of Christian congregations. For they are most firmly persuaded that by this way the sects, schisms and factions by which the people of Christ everywhere seethe can be met most well and most safely. What that tolerance is, and of what kind, is clear from the four parts of the Arcana: namely, the tolerance by which they above all work to introduce into the Church of God the Turkish blasphemies of the Socinians and to bring back Arian times to us, by the same art by which the Arians once used it. Of this St. Jerome speaks in his Chronicle under the year 364, where he says: Almost the whole Church throughout the world, UNDER THE NAME OF PEACE and of the King (that is, by the authority of the Emperor Constantius), is polluted by fellowship with the Arians. This is the true end of their doctrine of distinguishing necessary from unnecessary things. In order to attain this end they judged it necessary to corrupt the Orthodox doctrine of the perspicuity of Scripture.

units.la: Consistit autem doctrina Orthodoxa in eo; Scripturam sacram per se & in se esse perspicuam, claram, evidentem, non solum in omnibus iis quae necessaria sunt simpliciter ad salutem, sed etiam in omnibus iis quae absolute necessaria non sunt, etiamsi claritas illa & evidentia non omnium promiscue hominum oculis pateat. Qui quod veritatem doctrinae Orthodoxae non perspiciunt, causa non est posita in Scriptura, sed in ipsorum aut ignorantia & caecitate, aut malitia, aut negligentia & socordia; non secus ac, quod solis lumen non potest cerni a quovis, causa non est in Sole sed in caeco posita, aut in alio impedimento quod homini vel ab ipso vel ab aliis objicitur. Cum igitur Scriptura Sacra omnia dogmata fidei perspicue contineat, sequi exinde dicimus primo, eam solam sufficere ad decisionem Controversiarum fidei, adeoque non opus esse supplemento supremi seu praetorii judicii Ecclesiae; secundo eam cum fructu ad fidei & vitae directionem a populo seu a quovis legi posse. Haec est Orthodoxa sententia de perspicuitate Scripturae, quam Evangelici omnes Romanensibus opponunt. Hanc doctrinam corrumpunt jam Arminiani. Docent enim in Apologia, Necessaria omnia in Scriptura sacra non solùm in se evidentia & clara esse, sed etiam OMNIBUS qui Christiani esse volunt & sensu tantùm communi præditi sunt, sanum-que sinciput habent, obvia, & apud omnes in confesso esse, adeòque extra controversiam posita. Hæc est doctrina Apologiæ ipsorum, ut jam jam videbimus. Hanc doctrinam ut nullus Reformatorum unquam professus est; ita ego taxavi, & inter Arcana Arminianismi retuli, non autem doctrinam Orthodoxam & fundamentum Reformationis, prout more suo calumniosè & sine pudore dicunt p. 43. Qui ut nostræ sententiæ partem hanc eludant, quæ in eo consistit, esse Scripturam evidentem & perspicuam, etsi non omnibus hominibus evidens sit, relabuntur ibidem ad coccysmum suum contra Vedelium & reliquos Reformatos: At evidens est consequentia, inquies, sed non omnibus. Esto. Quibus non? Non cæcis. Esto. Quinam isti sunt non cæci? Pontificii ne? Non. Socinani? Apage sis, Quinam ergo? Vedelius cum electis suis Borboritis. Tityre tu patula &c. Ubi, præter petulantiam quâ hic lasciviunt ex Tityro Virgiliano, non est prætereundum convitium impudentissimum & atrocissimum horum hominum erga doctrinam & Ecclesiam Reformatam. Qui Borboritæ fuerint notum est; Hæretici nimirùm omnium maximè turpissimi & infames tàm in doctrinâ quàm in vitâ spurcissimâ. Unde etiam Borboritæ à cœno seu luto vocati fuêre qui aliàs Gnostici dicebantur. Nonnulli eos Borboritas vocant, ait Augustinus, quasi cœnosos, propter nimiam turpitudinem quam in suis mysteriis exercere dicuntur, lib. de hæresibus, hæresi 6. Quæso, annon habent Reformati & Magistratus & Doctores & populi tàm Belgæ quàm exteri causam justam etiam apud illustrissimos Ordines Generales conquerendi, non solùm de impietate sed & petulantiâ ac maledicentiâ incomparabili horum hominum, & rogandi ut eam quâ par est severitate compescant?
units.tr: The Orthodox doctrine, however, consists in this: that Holy Scripture is perspicuous, clear and evident in itself and by itself, not only in those things which are simply necessary to salvation, but also in those things which are not absolutely necessary, even if that clarity and evidence do not lie open to the eyes of all men without distinction. If some do not perceive the truth of Orthodox doctrine, the cause is not placed in Scripture, but in their own ignorance and blindness, or malice, or negligence and sloth; just as, since the light of the sun cannot be seen by everyone, the cause is not in the sun but in the blind man, or in some other obstacle that is put in a man's way either by himself or by others. Since, therefore, Holy Scripture plainly contains all the doctrines of faith, we say that it follows from this, first, that it alone is sufficient for deciding the controversies of faith, and so there is no need of a supplement from the supreme or praetorian judgment of the Church; second, that it can be read with profit by the people, or by anyone, for the direction of faith and life. This is the Orthodox view of the perspicuity of Scripture, which all Evangelicals oppose to the Romanists. The Arminians now corrupt this doctrine. For they teach in their Apology that all necessary things in Holy Scripture are not only evident and clear in themselves, but also are obvious to ALL who wish to be Christians and who have only common sense and a sound head, and are admitted by all, and therefore placed beyond controversy. This is the doctrine of their Apology, as we shall soon see. No Reformed writer has ever professed this doctrine; and so I have censured it and listed it among the Arcana of Arminianism, and not the Orthodox doctrine and foundation of the Reformation, as they falsely and shamelessly say in their usual manner, p. 43. And in order to mock the part of our view which consists in this, that Scripture is evident and perspicuous, even if it is not evident to all men, they relapse there into their jeering against Vedelius and the other Reformed: "But the consequence is evident," you will say, "yet not to all." Granted. To whom not? Not to the blind. Granted. Who then are these who are not blind? The Papists? No. The Socinians? Get away! Who then? Vedelius with his chosen Borborites. "Tityrus, you under the spreading beech," etc. Here, apart from the impudence with which they wanton with Virgil's Tityrus, we must not pass over the most shameless and atrocious abuse of these men against the doctrine and Church of the Reformed. That the Borborites were is well known: heretics most vile and infamous above all, both in doctrine and in most foul living. Hence also the Borborites, called from mud or filth, who were otherwise called Gnostics. Some call them Borborites, says Augustine, as if miry, on account of the great filthiness which they are said to practise in their mysteries, in his book on heresies, heresy 6. I ask, do not the Reformed, both the magistrates and the teachers and the people, Belgian as well as foreign, have just cause to complain even before the most illustrious General States, not only of the impiety but also of the petulance and incomparable slander of these men, and to ask that they be restrained with the severity that is due?

units.la: 2. Veniamus jam cum Arminianis ad dogmata ipsis à me objecta. Primum dogma quod ipsis objeceram hoc est: Nulla dogmata inter Christianos controversa esse necessaria ad salutem, Imò nec ea etiam dogmata quæ in futurum controverti possunt, esse necessaria ad salutem. Quid Arminiani ad hoc respondent? Fidem tuam, Vedelie! Controversa dogmata intelligunt Remonstrantes non alia, quàm quæ idcirco controversa sunt, quòd ea nec φανερῶς nec per evidentem omnibusque obviam consequentiam in Scripturâ continentur, cujusmodi tu necessaria esse posse asseris &c. Alterum est, se credere dogmata quædam controversa esse necessaria ad salutem v. g. an idololatria sit, si quis imaginem Dei aut Sanctorum formet & coram ea se incurvet, genua flectat, eam adoret, & ei supplicia supplicia ac vota sua faciat: Item an idololatria sit, id, quod sensibus omnibus pal-pari potest non esse nisi merum panem, adorare atque invocare tanquam ipsum Christum Deum ac hominem? Enimvero, inquiunt, per evidentem & omni-bus obviam consequentiam concludi potest indubitato, id non esse Deum nec ado-randum, quod sensus omnes docent esse creaturam vilissimam. Item, an opera bo-na sint necessaria ad salutem &c. Item, an liceat errantes homines, quamvis vita sint proba, panis corporalibus adeoque morte etiam crudelissima afficere: Hoc enim καλὸν τὸ ῥητὸν directe repugnat legi Christi regia, qua charitatem proximi adeo severe sancivit, ut inimicis benefacere, & pro fratribus a perditione aeterna liberandis animam nos ponere jusserit. Similia, inquiunt plura sunt. Pari modo respon-dent lib. 2. c 1. p. 62. ubi inter alia dicunt: Falsum est Remonstrantes asse-ruisse ea tantum quae extra controversiam sunt apud omnes Christianos coetus, esse necessaria ad salutem &c. Item eodem cap. p. 64. vocant hoc vanum & commentitium fundamentum quo nixus disputem adversus eos. ibidem vocant πρῶτον ψεῦδος primum & fundamentale mendacium meum, ut & cap. 5. p. 119. & cap. 6. p. 128. 129.
units.tr: We come now, with the Arminians, to the dogmas that I objected to them. The first dogma I had charged them with is this: No dogmas controverted among Christians are necessary to salvation; indeed, not even those dogmas which may in future be controverted are necessary to salvation. What do the Arminians answer to this? By your faith, Vedelius! The Remonstrants understand by controverted dogmas only those which are controverted because they are not contained in Scripture either φανερῶς [plainly] or by a clear consequence obvious to everyone, which you assert may be necessary &c. The second answer is that they believe some controverted dogmas are necessary to salvation, for example, whether it is idolatry if someone forms an image of God or of the saints, bows before it, bends the knee, worships it, and makes supplications and vows to it. Likewise, whether it is idolatry to adore and invoke as Christ himself, God and man, what all the senses show to be nothing but mere bread. Indeed, they say, it can be concluded with certainty, by a clear consequence obvious to all, that what all the senses teach to be the most worthless creature is not God and is not to be worshipped. Likewise, whether good works are necessary to salvation &c. Likewise, whether it is lawful to punish erring men with bodily bread, even with the cruelest death, though their lives be upright. For this saying καλὸν τὸ ῥητὸν [the fine saying] directly contradicts the royal law of Christ, which so strictly enjoined love of neighbour that it commanded us to do good to enemies and to lay down our souls for brethren to be freed from eternal perdition. There are, they say, many similar cases. They answer in the same way in book 2, chapter 1, page 62, where among other things they say: It is false that the Remonstrants have asserted that only those things which are beyond controversy among all Christian assemblies are necessary to salvation &c. Likewise in the same chapter, page 64, they call this an empty and fabricated foundation on which I rest my dispute against them. In the same place they call it πρῶτον ψεῦδος [the first lie], my first and fundamental falsehood, and so also in chapter 5, page 119, and chapter 6, pages 128 and 129.

units.la: Negant igitur Arminiani se ita docuisse. Bone Deus! Quorsum hi homines tandem delabuntur? Putantne se Deo, se hominibus omnibus semper illudere posse? Videamus enim an hoc dogma ipsorum sit necne? Negant illi hoc loco, se ita in Apologia docuisse. Observa, candide Lector, eos ne verbulo quidem illud negasse capite sexto in quo proba-vi candide, fideliter, amplè non meis sed ipsorum verbis, eos id in Apo-logia saepe docere. Nunc in hoc capite octavo demum illud negant. Causam facile unusquisque videt. Nam si capite sexto id negassent, facil-lime ipsorum fraus deprehensa fuisset ab unoquoque qui saltem oculos conjecisset in Arcanorum illud caput meum; quandoquidem, ut dixi, eos id docere in Apologia clarissime ibi loci ostendi: Itaque distulerunt negocium in hoc caput, in quo non probo amplius illud, sed tantum ut antea probatum suppono. Quare putarunt fraudem & nequitiam suam non adeo facile hic deprehensum iri.
units.tr: The Arminians therefore deny that they so taught. Good God! To what lengths do these men finally slide? Do they think they can always mock God and all men? Let us see whether this is their doctrine or not. They deny here that they so taught in the Apology. Observe, candid reader, that they did not deny it even in a single word in chapter six, where I proved candidly, faithfully and fully, not from my words but from theirs, that they often teach this in the Apology. Only now, in this eighth chapter, do they deny it. Anyone can easily see the reason. For had they denied it in chapter six, their deceit would have been most easily detected by anyone who had at least glanced at that chapter of mine in the Arcana; since, as I said, I showed there most clearly that they teach this in the Apology. So they postponed the matter to this chapter, in which I no longer prove it but assume it as already proved. They thought their fraud and wickedness would not so easily be detected here.

units.la: Etiamsi autem Lectorem ad Partem I. lib. 1. cap. 6. ablegare possem atque ipsi curam committere integritatis meae etiam in hac parte, tamen sublevandi illius causa & ut res eo minus extra dubium constituatur, repetā paucis loca quaedam Apologiae ex quibus rei veritas manifesta fiet. In Apologia igitur Exam. Cens. praefat. sol. 6. b. Necessaria & quae aperti juris sunt seu aperte in Scripturis decisa contradistinguunt simpliciter iis quae Controversa sunt: uti in Necessariis & quae aperti juris sunt, nimis parum est parum est si dicatur, Nos hoc credimus verum esse: Asseverantius loquendum est, hoc credendum est. Anathema qui id non credit: Ita in iis quæ Controversi juris sunt, nimium dicitur &c. Item clarius adhuc: Quasi vero quisquam sit, qui libertatem hanc extendi velit in infinitum. De Hæreticis quæritur, non qui ea quæ in Scripturis aperte decisa sunt convellere audent, sed qui ea quæ Controversa sunt aut controverti possunt, in dubium vocant. Apol.c.24. f. 276. b. Videtis hic eos expresse negare, dogmata Controversa esse aperte decisa, & è necessariorum censu excludere omnia ea quæ controversa sunt. Similiter non necessaria & Controversa pro synonymis ponunt. Sic enim Apol.Exam Cens. præf. f. 5. a. dicunt se, quando docent nihil esse decidendum seu definiendum quod firmiter constanterque omnibus Orthodoxis credendum sit, loqui de formulis iis quæ versantur circa dogmata non præcise creditu necessaria, quaque inter Christianos controversa, ac proinde aliis quam Scripturæ puris putis verbis (observa Characterem dogmatum non necessariorum seu de quibus inter Christianos controvertitur) concepta sunt. De hujusmodi ergo formulis quæritur, quomodo optime, tutissime atque utilissime concipi possint, ac debeant. An sic, ut in iis præcise definiatur, quid de singulis controversis dogmatis constanter firmiterque Orthodoxis omnibus credendum sit? An vero ut in ipsis declaretur simplicibus atq; innoxiis verbis, quid ii, qui eas pro suis agnoscunt, de singulis controversiis sentiant ac credant. Rursus alibi. Necessaria nullo negocio a quolibet Christiano sensu communi tantum prædito æstimari possunt. In cæteris si quid aut definit, aut reticet aut in medio ponit Declaratio Remonstrantium, liberam dissentionem permittunt, & libertatis indulgentia pacem redimendam esse existimant. Apol. Conclus. f. 301. a. Similiter c. 24. f. 176. b. ajunt; ea quæ aperte in Scripturis decisa sunt (qualia modo vidimus Necessaria esse secundum Arminianos) negari non posse ab eo qui Christianus esse vult, aut cui sanum sinciput est. Qui ea negare vult, aut in controversiam vocare is eo ipso Hæreticus non est, sed Hæretico multo deterior, imo profanus & Religionis Christianæ contemtor. Item c. 25. f. 301. b. libertatem in dubium vocandi omnia qualiacunque dogmata controversa vocant liberas, amicas, serias collationes, & privilegium omnium Christianorum: Liberæ, inquiunt, amicæ, seriæ de rebus controversis QUALIBUSCUNQUE collationes privilegium Christianorum omnium sunt. Speciatim autem tribus quæ extra controversiam sunt inter Christianos cœtus comprehendunt dogmata Necessaria: Necessaria, inquiunt, dogmata voco, quæ ex officio nobis in Evangelio præscripto necessario tenenda ac facienda sunt, ut æterna salutis participes evadamus; quæ TRIBUS his comprehendo: fide divinorum promissorum, obedientia divinorum præceptorum, & debita & debita Scripturis (quibus praeter promissa ac praecepta alia omnia divina oracula comprehendo) reverentia. Apol. praefat. c. 1. b. Item dicunt, necessaria esse pauca QUAE APUD OMNES IN CONFESSO SUNT. Nam cum Orthodoxi Theologi censuissent eos, quod tantum pauca Necessaria ad salutem dixissent, nec tamen ea indicâssent seu expressissent; respondent illi Exam. Cens. praef. f. 12. a. Affirmantium (loquuntur de Orthodoxis Theologis) est probare: Negantibus (Remonstrantibus) sufficit, si dicant se non videre, unde aut quo modo praeter pauca ista QUAE APUD OMNES IN CONFESSO SUNT, alia plura adhuc necessaria esse ostendi aut elici possit. Ita in Apologia docent de Necessariis, & ea ratione illa a non Necessariis distinguunt. Et (quod etiam monui cap. 6. lib. 1. Par. I.) ne quis putet doctrinam hanc de distinctione Necessariorum & non Necessariorum ipsis temere excidisse; sciat ipsos sollicite & ex animi sententia ea ita distinxisse. ita enim ipsi fatentur in Apologiae ad Lectorem, cujus mentionem paulo ante fecimus: A Necessariis non Necessaria dogmata SOLLICITE EX ANIMI SUI SENTENTIA distinxerunt, ut, quae ad pacem & mutuam Christianorum coetuum tolerantiam pertinere putant, Christiano orbi repraesentarent. Et dicunt se id fecisse ob tolerantiam mutuam suam: Nempe hac via sectis, schismatis ac factionibus quibus passim fervet Christi populus, optime ac tutissime occurri posse PERSUASISSIMUM HABENT. Sic itaque manifestissimum est Arminianos docere in Apologia sua: Nulla dogmata quae aut controversa sunt, aut in futurum controverti possunt inter Christianos esse necessaria ad salutem; adeoque eos contra propriam conscientiam agere dum negant se id docuisse, & me ideo malae fidei accusare audent. Sed non solum ita docent in Apologia sua, verum etiam post editam Apologiam nec non primam Partem Arcanorum idem docent in Responsf. ad Excerp. Cll. D. D. Proff. Leydd. p.61. ubi, cum necessaria ad salutem ea tantum esse dixissent quae clare atque aperte de mysteriis divinis traduntur in Scripturis, declarant to clare atque aperte per phrasin prout jacent. Jam autem prout jacent in Scriptura, certe extra controversiam & apud omnes in confesso sunt. Sic enim ibi: Sexcenta talia ex Cypriano, Nazianzeno, Nysseno, Ambrosio, Chrysostomo, aliisque Patribus, proferri possent, quae manifeste demonstrant, Patres illos in thesi judicasse, sufficere ad salutem, ut ea quae clare atque aperte de mysteriis divinis traduntur in Scriptura, speciatim de Trinitatis mysterio, ac nominatim in Baptismi formula, humili ac devota mente credantur prout jacent. Et ne quis putet eos hoc ultimum ex illorum Patrum, (quibus tamen bus tamen id quod dicunt in mentem nunquam nec calamum venit) hypothesi dicere, non autem ex sua mente, sciat eos p.66.67. dicere Scriptores istos non tantum ea in parte non errasse, sed ea quae Scripserunt verissima esse &c.
units.tr: Although I could refer the reader to Part I, book 1, chapter 6, and leave to him the care of my integrity even in this part, yet, to relieve him and so that the matter may be placed beyond doubt, I shall briefly repeat certain passages of the Apology from which the truth of the matter will be plain. In the Apology, then, in the Examen of the Censure, preface, page 6, column b, they simply distinguish the necessary things, and those which are plain in law, or plainly decided in Scripture, from those which are controverted: As regards the necessary things and those which are plain in law, it is too weak to say, "We believe this to be true." It must be spoken more assertively: "This must be believed. Anathema to him who does not believe it." So in those things which are of controverted law, it is said too much &c. Likewise, more clearly still: As if there were anyone who wished this liberty to be extended to infinity. The question concerns heretics, not those who dare to overthrow what has been plainly decided in Scripture, but those who call into doubt what is controverted or can be controverted. Apology, chapter 24, page 276, column b. You see here that they expressly deny that controverted dogmas have been plainly decided, and exclude from the list of necessary things all those which are controverted. Likewise they treat "not necessary" and "controverted" as synonyms. For in the Apology, Examen of the Censure, preface, page 5, column a, they say that when they teach that nothing is to be decided or defined which must be firmly and constantly believed by all the Orthodox, they are speaking of those formulas which concern dogmas not strictly necessary to believe, and which are controverted among Christians, and which are therefore expressed in other than the pure words of Scripture (note the mark of dogmas not necessary, or about which there is controversy among Christians). Concerning such formulas, then, the question is how they can best, most safely and most usefully be framed and ought to be framed. Should it be so that in them is strictly defined what must be constantly and firmly believed by all the Orthodox about each controverted dogma? Or rather that in them is declared, in simple and harmless words, what those who acknowledge them as their own think and believe about each controversy. Again elsewhere: Necessary things can be recognised without any trouble by any Christian endowed merely with common sense. In other matters, if the Remonstrant Declaration either defines something, or is silent, or places something in the middle, they permit free dissent, and think peace must be purchased by the indulgence of liberty. Apology, Conclusion, page 301, column a. Similarly, in chapter 24, page 176, column b, they say: Those things which are plainly decided in Scripture (such as we have just seen are necessary according to the Arminians) cannot be denied by anyone who wishes to be a Christian, or who has a sound head. He who wants to deny them, or call them into controversy, is not thereby a heretic, but far worse than a heretic, indeed a profane man and a despiser of the Christian religion. Likewise, chapter 25, page 301, column b, they call the liberty of calling into doubt all dogmas of whatever kind that are controverted free, friendly, serious conferences, and the privilege of all Christians: "Free, they say, friendly, serious conferences about controverted things, of WHATEVER KIND, are the privilege of all Christians." Particularly, they include under three heads the necessary dogmas which are beyond controversy among Christian assemblies: "I call necessary dogmas, they say, those which by the duty prescribed to us in the Gospel must necessarily be held and done, so that we may become sharers in eternal salvation. These I include under three heads: faith in the divine promises, obedience to the divine precepts, and due reverence for the Scriptures (under which I include all other divine oracles besides promises and precepts)." Apology, preface, chapter 1, column b. Likewise they say the necessary things are few, WHICH ARE ADMITTED BY ALL. For when the Orthodox theologians judged that, since they said only a few things were necessary to salvation, yet had not indicated or expressed them, they answered in the Examen of the Censure, preface, page 12, column a: It is for those who affirm (the Orthodox theologians are speaking) to prove. It is enough for those who deny (the Remonstrants) to say that they do not see how or in what way other things besides those few, WHICH ARE ADMITTED BY ALL, can be shown or drawn out as necessary. Thus in the Apology they teach about the necessary things, and by this reasoning distinguish them from the non-necessary. And (as I also noted in chapter 6 of book 1, Part I) lest anyone think that this doctrine of the distinction between necessary and non-necessary things slipped from them by chance, let him know that they made this distinction carefully and from their own judgement. For they themselves confess this in the Apology's address to the reader, which I mentioned a little earlier: They have carefully distinguished the non-necessary dogmas from the necessary, FROM THEIR OWN JUDGEMENT, so that they might set before the Christian world those things which they think pertain to peace and mutual tolerance among the Christian assemblies. And they say they did this for the sake of their mutual tolerance: In this way, they are most firmly persuaded, the sects, schisms and factions with which the people of Christ everywhere boil can be best and most safely met. Thus it is most manifest that the Arminians teach in their Apology: No dogmas which are either controverted, or can in future be controverted, among Christians are necessary to salvation. And so they act against their own conscience when they deny that they taught this, and dare on that account to accuse me of bad faith. But they not only teach this in their Apology; even after the Apology was published, and also the first Part of the Arcana, they teach the same in their Answer to the Excerpts of the Most Illustrious Doctors, the Professors of Leiden, page 61, where, having said that only those things are necessary to salvation which are clearly and plainly delivered in Scripture concerning the divine mysteries, they explain clearly and plainly by the phrase as they lie (prout jacent). Now certainly things as they lie in Scripture are beyond controversy and admitted by all. For there they say: Six hundred such passages could be cited from Cyprian, Gregory Nazianzen, Gregory of Nyssa, Ambrose, Chrysostom and other Fathers, which plainly demonstrate that those Fathers judged in principle that it is sufficient for salvation that those things which are clearly and plainly delivered in Scripture concerning the divine mysteries, especially the mystery of the Trinity, and by name in the formula of baptism, be believed with a humble and devout mind as they lie. And lest anyone think that they say this last thing from the hypothesis of those Fathers (though the thing they say never came into their mind or onto their pen), not from their own mind, let him know that they say, on pages 66 and 67, that those writers not only did not err in that part, but that what they wrote is most true &c.

units.la: 3. At, inquiet aliquis, Arminiani hic expresse fatentur se quaedam Controversa pro Necessariis habere. Primo enim illud limitatione ista sua manifestum faciunt. Deinde etiam exempla proferunt quaedam dogmatum controversorum quae necessaria esse dicunt. Respondebo primum ad utrumque simul, deinde ad utrumque sigillatim ac seorsim. Dico igitur primo hanc doctrinam non esse in Apologia, sed plane contrariam, & sic illos in eo quod hic dicunt sibi contradicere. h. e. iis quae in Apologia docent. Verum hoc esse patet, ex iis locis quae inde modo protulimus; ex quibus patet eos nulla controversa inter coetus Christianos habere pro Necessariis, sed tantum ea quae apud omnes in confesso sunt. Hanc responsionem praevidere facile potuerunt Arminiani malae suae fidei sibi conscii, itaque praeoccupant; sed ita ut a fraudulentissimo ingenio suo nequaquam discedant. Aiunt enim p. 45. Vindic. At hoc non convenit cum sententia Remonstrantium, inquit Vedelius: Nam quae apud omnes in confesso sunt de illis controversia non potest esse. At necessaria apud omnes in confesso sunt. Et respondent: Minor haec non est Remonstrantium. Aliud enim est dogmata necessaria in Scripturis tam clara esse ut palpari ab omnibus possint ac debeant, aliud omnes ea sic palpare, & caetera quae subjiciunt; quibus significant multos claudere oculos ad claram lucem veritatis. Dicunt igitur se non dixisse Necessaria esse ea quae apud omnes in confesso sunt. Deus bone, quam hi homines abutuntur patientia tua & Procerum Reipublicae! qui dum etsi in conscientia sua convicti sint, se totidem verbis dixisse ea quae totidem verbis ipsis objiciuntur, tamen adeo inhoneste agunt (ut jam de pietate aut amore veritatis nihil dicam quam utramque pedibus dudum sese conculcasse palam faciunt in Vindiciis praesertim suis) ut contra propriam conscientiam in omnium hominum conspectu, non curantes se ab omnibus impositurae singularis convinci posse, negare audeant se id scripsisse. Cujus rei ut dubium nullum apud quenquam superfit, repetam verba ista eorum quae paulo ante allegavi. Censuerant Cll. DD. Proff. Leydd. eos in Censura praefat. Confessionis, quod paucissima (quae qualia sint vidimus) ad salutem scitu necessaria esse scripsissent. Arminiani contra Apol. Exam. Cens. praef. f. 12. a. dicunt, debuisse igitur Theologos modo laudatos ostendere quaenam sint illa plura necessaria ad ria ad salutem, hoc enim oneris incumbere non sibi sed illis: Sed qui praeter pauca ista alia adhuc multo plura scitu ac creditu necessaria esse asserunt, iis declarandi ac probandi onus incumbit: Affirmantium (loquuntur de Orthodoxis Theologis illis) est probare; Negantibus (loquuntur de se) sufficit, si dicant se non videre, unde aut quomodo praeter pauca ista, QUAE APUD OMNES IN CONFESSO SUNT, alia plura adhuc necessaria esse ostendi aut elici possit. Quare cum a Remonstrantibus Censor exigit, ut singulatim, quaenam ista necessaria dogmata sint definiant, iniquissimum petit, ut probandi onus, quod sibi incumbere novit, ab humeris suis dimoveat, & interim eos suspicione gravet, quasi manifestissime necessaria dogmata convellant ac rescindant. Hi homines, Optime Lector, saepe me, quia vere ipsis dixi quid in recessu habeant, & ulcus eorum purulentissimum presli (ex quo jam in Vindiciis eorum tantum puris & foetoris emanavit) impudentem vocant, dicunt me omni pudori epicedium scripsisse, imo nonnullibi ajunt me in sensum reprobum traditum esse &c. Quaeso judica vel ex his, cuinam ista epitheta competant? Antea in genere negarant se docuisse, Nulla dogmata inter Christianos controversa esse necessaria ad salutem: in qua re eos contra conscientiam agere ostendi. Nunc in specie negant se docuisse; ea tantum esse Necessaria quae apud omnes in confesso sunt. Nullam'ne plane habent rationem honestatis, pudoris, candoris, in negocio hoc gravissimo, quod Religionis est? Quod magis est, nullam'ne habent rationem amplius conscientiae suae, quae ipsis dictat, ipsos convincit, me vere iis dogma hoc objecisse, & eos contra propriam conscientiam id negare? Deus bone, ni homines hi resipiscant, quam desperatus & damnatus erit exitus eorum; quandoquidem contra propriam conscientiam in Religionis negocio agunt; & Belgium totum, imo totum orbem tam improbe & nefarie turbant! Quo in statu erit conscientia ipsorum aliquando tempore mortis! imo quo in statu ipsi tunc erunt! Profecto Deus non patitur sibi illudi. Meminerint fortassis aliquando eorum quae jam dico, & quae coram Deo, coram Angelis, coram omnibus hominibus jam contra ipsos testor; imo quae ipsorum conscientia propria in hoc negocio contra eos testatur. Hoc unum est quod respondeo.
units.tr: 3. But, someone will say, the Arminians here expressly admit that they hold certain controverted points to be necessary. For first, they make this clear by their own qualification, and second, they bring forward examples of controverted doctrines which they say are necessary. I will answer both points together first, and then each separately. I say, then, first, that this doctrine is not in the Apology but is plainly contrary to it, so that they contradict themselves in what they say here, that is, in what they teach in the Apology. That this is so is clear from the passages I have just quoted, from which it appears that they hold no controverted matter among Christian communities to be necessary, but only those things which are agreed upon by all. The Arminians, who were conscious of their bad faith, could easily foresee this answer, and so they forestall it, but in such a way that they never depart from their most fraudulent cleverness. For they say on p. 45 of the Vindiciae: "But this does not agree with the opinion of the Remonstrants, says Vedelius: for there can be no controversy about those things which are agreed upon by all. But necessary things are agreed upon by all." And they reply: "This minor premise is not the Remonstrants' view. For it is one thing that the necessary doctrines are in Scripture so clear that they can and ought to be grasped by all, and another that all do grasp them, and the rest they add, by which they mean that many close their eyes to the clear light of truth." So they say they did not say that the necessary things are those agreed upon by all. Good God, how these men abuse your patience and that of the leaders of the Commonwealth! Although they are convicted in their own conscience, they nevertheless act so dishonourably (not to mention piety or love of truth, which they have long since trampled underfoot, as they plainly show especially in their Vindiciae) that, against their own conscience, in the sight of all men, not caring that they can be convicted of a singular imposture by everyone, they dare to deny that they wrote it. So that there may be no doubt about this matter among anyone, I shall repeat their own words which I quoted a little earlier. The most learned professors of Leiden had judged in their Censure of the preface to the Confession that they had written that very few things (of what kind they are we have seen) are necessary to salvation to know. The Arminians, on the contrary, in their Apologia Examen Censurae, preface, p. 12 a, say that the aforementioned theologians ought therefore to have shown which the many other things are that are necessary to salvation, for this burden lies not on them but on those others: "But those who assert that, besides these few things, many other things are yet necessary to be known and believed, upon them lies the burden of declaring and proving. It is for those who affirm (they speak of those orthodox theologians) to prove; it suffices for those who deny (they speak of themselves) to say that they do not see how, or in what way, besides these few things WHICH ARE AGREED UPON BY ALL, many others might still be shown or deduced to be necessary. Therefore, when the Censor demands of the Remonstrants that they define singly which these necessary doctrines are, he asks the most unjust thing: that he should shift from his own shoulders the burden of proof, which he knows lies on him, and meanwhile burden them with suspicion, as if they were overturning and tearing down the most manifestly necessary doctrines." These men, best of readers, often call me shameless, because I have truly told them what they hold in reserve, and I have pressed on their most purulent ulcer (from which, in their Vindiciae, nothing but pus and stench has come out). They say that I have written an epitaph for all shame; indeed, they say in some places that I have been given over to a reprobate mind, and so on. Please judge, even from these things, to whom such epithets properly belong. Before, they had denied in general that they had taught that no controverted doctrines among Christians are necessary to salvation; in this matter I have shown that they act against their conscience. Now they deny in particular that they taught that only those things are necessary which are agreed upon by all. Do they have no regard at all for honour, shame, and candour in this most weighty business, which concerns religion? What is more, do they have no further regard for their conscience, which dictates to them and convicts them that I truly charged them with this doctrine, and that they deny it against their own conscience? Good God, unless these men repent, how desperate and damned their end will be, since they act against their own conscience in a matter of religion, and so wickedly and shamelessly disturb the whole of Belgium, indeed the whole world! What will their conscience be like at some time at the hour of death! Indeed, what will they themselves then be like! Surely God does not allow himself to be mocked. Perhaps they will at some time remember these things which I now say, and which I call to witness against them before God, before the angels, before all men; indeed, which their own conscience bears witness against them in this matter. This is the one thing I answer.

units.la: 4. Secundo dico Arminianos non solum sibi ipsis contradicere, nec non in hoc illudere Deo & hominibus, quod contra conscientiam suam negant se in Apologia docere Ea tantum esse Necessaria ad salutem quae apud omnes in confesso sunt; verum etiam alia ratione. Nam dicunt quidem jam in Vindiciis suis se agnoscere quaedam dogmata Controversa necessfa necessaria ad salutē: sed hoc plane illusorium est. Etenim ea Necessaria ad salutem talia esse docent, ut simul doceant; ea talia esse absque quibus homo salvari possit; talia, propter quæ damnatio denuncianda non sit illi qui ea negat: talia propter quæ anathema dicendum ei non est, etsi ita clara sint, ut ne Atheus quidem ea negare possit, nisi hominem exuat; talia quæ ab ipso Deo non sunt decisa: & quæ alia iis tribuunt, quæ manifestum faciunt eos dicis saltem causā, & nomine tenus, quò mundo imponant, Controversa quædam pro Necessariis habere; revera autem ea negare. De qua re amplè egimus Par. II. lib. 2. c. 1. Annon hoc est rursus Deo & hominibus illudere?
units.tr: 4. Second, I say that the Arminians not only contradict themselves, and in this mock God and men, by denying against their conscience that in the Apology they teach that only those things are necessary to salvation which are agreed upon by all; but also for another reason. For they do indeed say in their Vindiciae that they now acknowledge certain controverted doctrines as necessary to salvation; but this is quite illusory. For they teach that those things necessary to salvation are such that at the same time they teach: they are such that a man can be saved without them; such that for denying them a man is not to be condemned; such that for denying them he is not to be anathematized, even though they are so clear that not even an atheist could deny them, unless he put off his humanity; such as have not been decided by God himself; and they attribute other things to them which make it plain that they hold certain controverted matters to be necessary only in name and for the sake of appearance, so as to deceive the world, while in fact they deny them. We have treated this matter at length in Part II, book 2, chapter 1. Is this not once again mocking God and men?

units.la: Sed ita facere ex re suâ esse putárunt. In Apologiâ negant dogmata quædam controversa esse Necessaria ad salutem: at in vindiciis in speciem profitentur & præ se ferunt (sed illusorie ut modò ostendimus) se agnoscere quædam dogmata controversa pro Necessariis ad salutem. In Apologiâ protestantur se sollicitè magno cum studio & ex animi sui sententiâ doctrinam suam declarasse ac propositisse quid credant: In vindiciis verò, quia vident rerum suarum usum postulare ut dicant se non hoc sed contrarium credere, contrarium se credere dicunt. Quâ in re imitantur veteres Hæreticos, qui modò hanc doctrinam modò contrariam protestabantur se sequi; modò asseverabant se ita credere, modò contrà declarabant se nunquam ita credidisse, sed contrarium tenuisse & tenere; prout scilicet videbant sectæ suæ res & suum emolumentum id requirere, imò non dubitabant sæpè propriæ suæ sententiæ anathema dicere: atque interim eam animo retinebant, & ubi commodum aut tutum putabant, spargebant. Timotheus Colon episcopus Constantinopolitanus sub Anastasio I. Imperatore Eutychianus erat, eam hæresin animo fovebat & docebat. Quo facto, ut cùm Episcopum quendam ordinare vellet, episcopus ille resiliret, dicens; Timotheum Eutychiamum esse & Synodum Chalcedonensem rejicere. ibi Timotheus; anathema sit, inquit, cuilibet homini Synodum Chalcedonensem rejicienti. Res ad Imperatorem perfertur, qui Timotheum ad se accersitum acriter reprehendit. Ille verò negat factum strenue, ut hic nostri Arminiani, & addit: anathema sit cuilibet homini approbanti Synodum Chalcedonensem. Videatur Theodorus Anagnostes Collect. lib. 2. Similiter Petrus Mongus Alexandrinus Episcopus sub Zenone Imperatore Eutychianus fuit; mox docuit orthodoxam fidem cum res ejus postularent. Paulò post rursus damnat eam & rejicit Concilium Chalcedonense. Mos iterum contrà in Epistolâ ad Acacium Episcopum Orthodoxum Constantinopolitanum declarat se Orthodoxorum sententiam amplecti, & negat se damnâsse Concilium Chalcedonense & rejecisse doctrinam veram. Denique alio tempore postea, rebus sic postulantibus ipsius, rursus damnat Concilium Chalcedonense & fidem Orthodoxam. Vnde rectè Evagrius eum vocat κάτωρον ἢ παλίμβολον ἡ τῆς καιροῖς συνδιαπεφυλμένον. cothurnum, versatilem, & temporibus inservientem lib. 3. cap. 13. 16. 17. 22. Marcionitæ Hæretici habebant circa res fidei γνώμην ἀσυσατον versatilem mentem & cui secum non conveniebat, ait Rhodon antiquissimus Scriptor Ecclesiasticus apud Eusebium lib. 5. c. 13. Vnde etiam per consequens inter ipsos variæ dissensiones erant; quales brevi forte, volente Domino, ob eandem causam inter Arminianos erumpent. Hæc versutia & fraus Hæreticorum veterum (de quâ pluribus egimus lib. 2. de prudentiâ veteris Ecclesiæ) non ignoranda est, ut hodie à simili impostura nobis cavere possimus, & iis fidem nequaquam adhibeamus qui ita in Religionis negocio ludunt.
units.tr: But they thought it advantageous to their cause to act in this way. In the Apology they deny that certain controverted doctrines are necessary to salvation; but in the Vindiciae they profess in appearance, and display openly (but in a deceptive way, as we have just shown), that they acknowledge certain controverted doctrines as necessary to salvation. In the Apology they protest that they have carefully, with great zeal and in accordance with their own mind, declared and set forth their doctrine and what they believe; but in the Vindiciae, because they see that the interest of their affairs requires them to say that they do not hold this but the contrary, they say that they believe the contrary. In this they imitate the ancient heretics, who by turns protested that they followed this doctrine and then the contrary; sometimes they asserted that they believed thus, and at other times they declared that they had never believed thus, but had held and still hold the contrary; as they saw, of course, that the affairs and advantage of their sect required it. Indeed, they did not hesitate often to pronounce anathema on their own opinion, while in the meantime they kept it in their heart, and where they thought it convenient or safe, they spread it abroad. Timothy Aelurus, bishop of Constantinople, was under the Emperor Anastasius I an Eutychian; he nourished that heresy in his mind and taught it. When he wished to ordain a certain bishop, that bishop refused, saying that Timothy was an Eutychian and rejected the Council of Chalcedon. Then Timothy said: "Let him be anathema who rejects the Council of Chalcedon." The matter was brought to the Emperor, who sharply rebuked Timothy when he was summoned to him. But Timothy vigorously denied the deed, as our Arminians do here, and added: "Let him be anathema who approves the Council of Chalcedon." See Theodore the Reader, Collection, book 2. Similarly Peter Mongus, bishop of Alexandria, was an Eutychian under the Emperor Zeno; soon, when his affairs required it, he taught the orthodox faith. A little later he again condemned and rejected the Council of Chalcedon. Again, in a letter to Acacius, orthodox bishop of Constantinople, he declared that he embraced the opinion of the orthodox and denied that he had condemned the Council of Chalcedon or rejected the true doctrine. Finally, at another time afterwards, when his affairs again required it, he once more condemned the Council of Chalcedon and the orthodox faith. Hence Evagrius rightly calls him "a buskin, a changeable man, serving the times" [κάτωρον ἢ παλίμβολον ἡ τῆς καιροῖς συνδιαπεφυλμένον], book 3, chapters 13, 16, 17, 22. The Marcionite heretics had, concerning matters of faith, "an unstable mind, one which did not agree with itself" [γνώμην ἀσυσατον], says Rhodo, a very ancient ecclesiastical writer, in Eusebius, book 5, chapter 13. Hence also, as a consequence, there were various dissensions among them; such, perhaps, as will shortly break out among the Arminians for the same cause, if the Lord wills. This cunning and fraud of the ancient heretics (of which we have treated at greater length in book 2 of On the Prudence of the Ancient Church) must not be ignored, so that today we may guard ourselves against such imposture, and never give credence to those who play in this way with matters of religion.

units.la: 5. Itaque si quis Hæreticus Antitrinitarius aut fautor & socius eorum negat, quod conceptis verbis dixit, ac protestatur se id non dixisse aut scripsisse, hanc suam mentem non esse, se contrarium dicere & credere &c. non miretur quisquam hoc hodie contingere. Sciat id novum non esse, sed sæpius in Ecclesiâ veteri contigisse, & esse artem ac versutiam hominum Hæreticorum ac Turbonum; quare iis fidem non adhibeat, sed caveat sibi sollicitè ab eorum impostu-ris, & pro officii sui ratione operam det ne nocere possint Ecclesiæ ac Reipublicæ, & ad scopum improbum quem sibi proposuerunt pervenire. Cùm itaque Arminiani Theologi hac arte & versutiâ utantur jam circa doctrinam de Necessariis, manifestum est eos nullam fidem amplius mereri apud ullum virum honestum in negocio Religionis; quandoquidem fidem omnem sibi ipsis adimunt, dum ita contra cõscientiam negant se dixisse & docuisse quæ dixisse & docuisse in conscientiâ suâ convicti sunt coràm Deo & coràm hominibus; item dum affirmant se hoc docuisse, cùm tamen contrarium ejus se docuisse in conscientiâ suâ norint, & omnes homines in eâ re falsitatis ipsos convincere possint. Hoc secundum est quod respondeo.
units.tr: 5. So if any Antitrinitarian heretic, or a supporter and associate of theirs, denies what he has said in so many words, and protests that he did not say or write it, that this is not his mind, that he holds and believes the contrary, and so on, no one should be surprised that this happens today. Let him know that it is not new but has often happened in the ancient Church, and that it is the craft and cunning of heretics and troublemakers. Therefore he should not give them credence but should guard himself carefully against their deceptions, and, as his duty requires, take care that they cannot harm the Church or the commonwealth or reach the wicked goal they have set for themselves. Since the Arminian theologians now use this same craft and cunning in the doctrine of Necessary things, it is plain that they deserve no further trust from any honest man in matters of religion. They strip themselves of all credit when they deny, against their conscience, that they have said and taught what they have been convicted, before God and before men, of saying and teaching in their own conscience; and likewise when they affirm that they taught this, although they know in their own conscience that they taught the contrary, and all men can convict them of falsehood on this point. This is the second point of my reply.

units.la: 6. Tertiò: Quid juvat Arminianos ministros, quòd hic dicunt se agnoscere dogmata quædam controversa pro Necessariis ad salutem, v. g. panem non esse adorandum, Hæreticis nullâ plane corporali coercitione esse resistendum (cujus posterioris contrarium tenent non solùm Pontificii sed etiam Lutherani & Reformati) adeoque eos qui contrarium tenent errare in Necessariis? Hoc, inquam, eos nequaquam juvat, nec crimine liberat: quamdiu hos quidem dicent errare in Necessariis;de Socinianis autem seu Antitrinitariis Haereticis nolunt dicere eos errare in Necessariis: adeoq; quamdiu nolunt fateri dogmata illa Orthodoxa de S.S. Trinitate opposita Antitrinitariis esse necessaria ad salutem. Eo enim testatum faciunt se nolle quidem in Tolerantia sua mutua & fraternitate ac unione spirituali comprehendere & pro membris Ecclesiae Dei habere praeter Pontificios & Reformatos, etiam Lutheranos: sed tamen in tolerantia sua mutua & fraternitate ac unione spirituali comprehendere & pro verae Ecclesiae membris habere eos qui Turcicas & Judaicas illas blasphemias Socinianorum profitentur, nimirum Christum non habere naturam divinam sed tantum humanam; cum non extitisse antequam conciperetur in utero virginis &c.
units.tr: 6. Thirdly: What good does it do the Arminian ministers that they here say they acknowledge certain controverted doctrines as necessary to salvation, for example that bread is not to be adored, and that heretics are not to be resisted by any bodily coercion (the Papists, and not only they but also the Lutherans and the Reformed, hold the contrary of this latter point), and therefore that those who hold the contrary err in necessary things? This, I say, does not help them at all, nor does it free them from the charge. As long as they say that these men err in necessary things, but are unwilling to say that the Socinians or Antitrinitarian heretics err in necessary things, and so long as they are unwilling to admit that those orthodox doctrines about the Holy Trinity, opposed to the Antitrinitarians, are necessary to salvation, they show by this that they do indeed wish, in their mutual toleration, brotherly fellowship and spiritual union, to include, and to regard as members of the Church of God, besides the Papists and the Reformed, also the Lutherans; but in that same mutual toleration, brotherly fellowship and spiritual union they also include, and regard as true members of the Church, those who profess those Turkish and Jewish blasphemies of the Socinians, namely that Christ has not a divine nature but only a human one, and that he did not exist before he was conceived in the womb of the virgin, etc.

units.la: Ex quo jam patet quis praecipuus scopus sit Arminianorum in doctrina de Necessariis & non Necessariis, tam ea quam in Apologia & Confessione quam ea quam in his suis Vindiciis proposuerunt: nimirum efficere pedetentim (quod etiam efficient, Deo obcontemtum Religionis nobis irato, ni servi Dei tam in Republica quam in Ecclesia ipsis omnibus modis pro officii ratione serio, fortiter, magnanimiter, vigilanter se ipsis opponant) ut libere vigeant & doceantur Turcicae istae blasphemiae in his provinciis, ex his in vicinas (ut fieri solet quemadmodum maxime ex veteris Ecclesiae experientia patet) regiones, & mox alibi propagentur: quandoquidem dogmata orthodoxa Antitrinitariis opposita non videntur ipsis Necessaria ad salutem; & Antitrinitarii sunt homines pii, piissimi, sanctissimi secundum Arminianos, ac non obligantur deponere conscientiam suam erroneam, non peccant istis blasphemiis suis, non Haeretici sunt; adeoque non feriendi anathemate nec ab Ecclesia Dei procul arcendi. Tu Deus optime Maxime respice Ecclesiam tuam oculo propitio, & libera eam ab impiissimis his & pestilentissimis hominibus, propter gloriam nominis tui ac Filii tui Iesu Christi. Amen. Et vicinae regiones caveant sibi ab istis hominibus, praecipue autem Anglia. Huic enim hi homines maxime insidiantur. Consistunt autem insidiae ipsorum speciatim in praetextu quinque articulorum; prout tristis experientia Ecclesiarum & Provinciarum Belgii docet. Harum damnis, calamitatibus, periculis sapiant, qui suis sapere nolunt.
units.tr: From this it is now clear what the principal aim of the Arminians is in their doctrine of necessary and unnecessary things, both in the one they set out in their Apology and Confession and in the one they have now set out in these their Vindications. It is to bring about, little by little (and they will bring it about, with God angry at our contempt for religion, unless the servants of God, both in the commonwealth and in the Church, oppose them in every way, seriously, bravely, magnanimously and vigilantly, as their office requires), that these Turkish blasphemies may flourish freely and be taught in these provinces, and from here spread to the neighbouring regions (as usually happens, as the experience of the ancient Church shows especially well), and soon be propagated elsewhere. For the orthodox doctrines opposed to the Antitrinitarians do not seem to them necessary to salvation; and according to the Arminians the Antitrinitarians are pious, most pious and most holy men, and are not bound to abandon their erroneous conscience, they do not sin by these blasphemies of theirs, they are not heretics, and therefore they are not to be struck with anathema nor kept far from the Church of God. You, most good and great God, look upon your Church with a favourable eye, and free it from these most impious and most pestilent men, for the glory of your name and of your Son Jesus Christ. Amen. And let the neighbouring regions beware of these men, and especially England, for these men lay their snares chiefly for her. Their snares consist especially in the pretext of the five articles, as the sad experience of the Churches and Provinces of Belgium teaches. Let those who are unwilling to be wise at their own expense be wise from their losses, calamities and dangers.

units.la: 8. Atque haec quidem ad utrumque simul h. e. & ad limitationem & ad Exempla illa conjunctim ac generatim considerata dicta funto. Nunc seorsim respondebo ad prius quod dicunt; nimirum ad limitationem qua hic utuntur, dicentes se asseruisse ea omnia qua inter Christianos controversa sunt idcirco, quod nec aperte in Scripturis expressa sit eorum necessitas nec per evidentem & omnibus sana mentis obviam consequentiam ex Scripturis eliciantur, non esse ad salutem praecise creditu aut scitu Necessaria, quae sunt verba ipsorum quibus in hac re utuntur lib. 2. cap. 2. p. 62. Dico igitur Arminianos etiam in hac parte contra conscientiam suam agere, dum dicunt se asseruisse in Apologia sua ea omnia qua inter Christianos controversa sunt idcirco &c. Nam falsum est eos unquam hoc dixisse seu asseruisse, sive ista limitatione ullibi usos esse aut in Apologia, aut in Confessione, aut in Responsionibus quas varias ediderunt ad Excerpta Cll. D.D. Theoll. Leydd. aut alibi inde ab edita Apologia. id quod eo magis mirum est, quia dicunt omnia ea quae in prima parte Arcanorum objeci illis, jam antea ipsis objecta & a se refutata fuisse, me nihil novi omnino ipsis objecisse &c. Pag. 2. Vindic. dicunt: nihil ibi occurrere non protritum, obsoletum ac pervulgatum & pag. 3. An dixit quicquam indictum, aut quod majorem veri speciem habet, quam quod hactenus uno pene ore clamarunt omnes Remonstrantium adversarii? Item: nec vola nec vestigium novum est. Et p. 4: Ne γω quidem est, quod non aperte censuerunt atque impegerunt Remonstrantibus Professores Leydenses etsi non sine manifesta calumnia &c. Nihil hic nisi crambe eadem est; quam recoxit Vedelius &c. Mazam a Professoribus aliisque pistam repinsuit &c. Item ibid. ajunt me earevelasse quae palam atque in aperto est multo ante lippis ac tonsoribus indicata fuisse, quaque idcirco pueri & qui nondum are lavantur apprime comperta habuerunt, tanquam ungues digitosque suos. Item, mihi respondere dicunt esse toties actum agere velle & in eodem semper pistrino circumagi. Et p. 5. Serram hanc toties reciprocavimus contra adversarios; saxum hoc toties volvimus ac revolvimus, ut iam nova Apologia opus non sit. Item; si novis armis, si aliis argumentis quis nos adoriatur, en lubentes adsumus in harenā &c. At si quis se cum iisdem armis telisque alio tantum fuco delibutis ostentet in arena &c. interiistos est hic Vedelius, qui cum non nisi eadem & multoties inculcata & conculcata regerat &c. Videtis hic Arminianos afferere me nihil novi ipsis objecisse, & se omnia ea jam ante hac refutasse antequam sibi a me objicerentur. Quod si ita est, ecqui igitur factum ut ista limitatione antehac nunquam usi fuerint? Nec dicere possunt, se tunc ad illud alia ratione respondisse, nunc autem etiam hac responsione uti. Nam monstrare in aeternum non possunt se unquam ullo modo aut verbulo ad illud antehac responrespondisse. ita igitur falsissimū est quod dicunt: Remonstrates adseruisse ea omnia quae inter Christianos controversa sunt idcirco quod nec aperte in Scripturis &c.
units.tr: 8. These things, then, are to be taken as said both together, that is, considered jointly and generally, with respect to both the limitation and those examples. Now I will reply separately to what they say first, namely to the limitation they use here, saying that they asserted all those things which are controverted among Christians for this reason, that their necessity is not clearly expressed in Scripture, nor is it drawn from Scripture by an evident consequence obvious to every sound mind, so that they are not strictly necessary to be believed or known for salvation; these are their own words, which they use on this point in book 2, chapter 2, page 62. I say, therefore, that the Arminians act against their own conscience in this part too, when they say that they asserted in their Apology all those things which are controverted among Christians for this reason, etc. For it is false that they ever said or asserted this, or that they ever used this limitation anywhere, either in the Apology, or in the Confession, or in the Responses which they published in various forms against the Excerpts of the very learned Doctors of Theology of Leiden, or anywhere else since the Apology was published. This is all the more remarkable because they say that everything which in the first part of the Arcana I objected to them had already been objected to them before and refuted by them, and that I had objected nothing new to them at all, etc. On page 2 of the Vindications they say: nothing occurs there that is not worn out, obsolete and commonplace; and on page 3: Has he said anything unheard of, or anything that has a greater appearance of truth than what all the adversaries of the Remonstrants have hitherto cried out with almost one voice? Likewise: there is no new wing or trace of it. And on page 4: There is not even a γῶ [a crumb] that the Leiden professors have not openly thought and pressed upon the Remonstrants, though not without manifest calumny, etc. This is nothing but the same cabbage, which Vedelius has warmed up again, etc. He has rekneaded a mash kneaded by the professors and others, etc. Likewise in the same place: they say that I have revealed what is plain and open, which was pointed out long ago to bleary-eyed men and barbers, and which boys and those not yet washed in the bath have thoroughly known, like their own nails and fingers. Likewise they say that my reply is that it is always the same to wish to act and to be driven round in the same mill. And on page 5: We have so often moved this saw back and forth against our adversaries; we have so often rolled and rerolled this stone, that there is now no need of a new Apology. Likewise: if anyone attacks us with new weapons, with other arguments, behold, we gladly stand in the arena, etc. But if anyone presents himself in the arena with the same weapons and missiles only smeared with another colour, etc., this Vedelius is undone, who, since he brings back nothing but the same things, trampled and repeatedly pressed in, etc. You see here that the Arminians assert that I objected nothing new to them, and that they had refuted all those things before they were objected to them by me. If that is so, then why did they never use this limitation before? Nor can they say that they answered that objection then by another method and now also use this answer. For they can never show that they ever answered it in any way, or with a single word, before. So it is most false what they say: the Remonstrants asserted all those things which are controverted among Christians for this reason, that they are not clearly expressed in Scripture, etc.

units.la: Secundò, non constanter loquuntur in his Vindiciis de Controversis dogmatis non necessariis h. e. de eâ re de quâ quæstio est. Nam interdum dicunt se loquutos fuisse de iis Controversis, quæ controversa sunt idcirco quia ipsa non aperte continentur in Scripturâ ut hoc loco, interdum dicunt, quæ controversa sunt idcirco quia eorum necessitas non aperte in Scripturâ est expressa ut lib. 1. cap. 3. p. 19. & lib. 2. c. 2. p. 62. Interdum, quæ idcirco controversa sunt, quia eorum seu veritas seu necessitas non aperte in Scripturâ est decisa ut lib. 2. c. 5. p. 11. Quæ certè à se invicem non parum differunt, ut unusquisque videt. Nam ut aliud est necessitas, aliud veritas; ita aliud est dicere veritatem non esse expressam alicujus dogmatis in Scripturâ, aliud necessitatem, aliud denique seu necessitatem seu veritatem ejus non esse expressam in Scripturâ. Deinde falsum est idcirco quædam dogmata in Controversiam vocari, quia eorum necessitas non sit aperte decisa in Scriptura. Nam omnia quæ inter Christianos in Controversiam vocantur ab errantibus, ideo in Controversiam vocantur ab iis, quia putant eorum veritatē in Scripturis non contineri, seu ea vera non esse, cum tamen eorum non solùm veritas sed etiam sæpè necessitas aperte in Scripturâ decisa sit, ut patet ex controversiis quas Antitrinitarii circa mysterium Trinitatis nobis movent. Et ob hanc causam & quidem solàm Antitrinitarii sive Socinians vocant in controversiam dogmata Orthodoxa de Trinitate. Quod verum esse ipsi fatentur Vindic. lib. 2. c. 3. p. 85. ubi ajunt se ideo suspendere judicium suum de Necessitate dogmatum illorum controversorum in mysterio illo, ne leviter ex unâ parte damnent infinitas hominum myriadas, qui dogmata ista aut ignorant aut in dubium vocant aut negant NULLO ALIO argumento adducti, quàm quòd ea nec in Scripturis possint deprehendere, nec ut rationi rectæ convenientia comprehendere. Nec potest aliquis excipere; imò ea dogmata ideò controversa esse, quia necessitas eorum aperte non expressa sit in Scripturâ: nam si necessitas eorum aperte expressa esset in Scripturâ tunc non vocarentur in controversiam à quoquam. Hoc, inquam excipi non potest. Nam non convenit cum ipsorum novâ hypothesi, quâ hic statuunt in controversiam vocari quædam à Pontificiis &c. quam necessitatem dicunt aperte in Scripturâ decisam esse.
units.tr: Secondly, in these Vindiciae they do not speak consistently about controversies over non-necessary dogmas, that is, about the very matter in question.
