Sometimes they say they have spoken of those controversies which are controverted because the doctrines themselves are not openly contained in Scripture, as in this place. Sometimes they say those which are controverted because their necessity is not openly expressed in Scripture, as in book 1, chapter 3, p. 19, and book 2, chapter 2, p. 62. Sometimes they say those which are controverted because either their truth or their necessity is not openly decided in Scripture, as in book 2, chapter 5, p. 11. These things certainly differ from one another not a little, as anyone can see. For as necessity is one thing and truth another, so it is one thing to say that the truth of some dogma is not expressed in Scripture, another that its necessity is not, and another again that either its necessity or its truth is not expressed in Scripture. Next, it is false that certain dogmas are called into controversy because their necessity is not openly decided in Scripture. For all the things that are called into controversy among Christians by those who err are so called because they think their truth is not contained in the Scriptures, or that they are not true. Yet not only their truth but often also their necessity is openly decided in Scripture, as is plain from the controversies which the Antitrinitarians raise against us concerning the mystery of the Trinity. For this reason, and indeed only the Antitrinitarians or Socinians call the Orthodox doctrines of the Trinity into controversy. That this is true they themselves confess, Vindiciae book 2, chapter 3, p. 85, where they say they therefore suspend their judgment about the necessity of those controverted dogmas in that mystery, lest they rashly condemn on one side infinite myriads of men who either are ignorant of those dogmas, or call them in doubt, or deny them, moved by NO OTHER argument than that they cannot find them in Scripture or grasp them as agreeing with right reason. Nor can anyone object otherwise: indeed, those dogmas are controverted because their necessity is not openly expressed in Scripture. For if their necessity were openly expressed in Scripture, they would not be called into controversy by anyone. This, I say, cannot be objected. For it does not agree with their new hypothesis, by which they here maintain that certain things are called into controversy by the Papists etc., whose necessity they say is openly decided in Scripture.

units.la: Tertiò, limitationem hanc non patitur materia subjecta de quâ agunt. Sunt enim ἀσυμβατα seu consistere simul non possunt hæc duo: nimirum limitatio ista quam hic afferunt, & quod hoc quidem in loco dicunt: Controversa quaedam esse Necessaria ad salutem. Nam si quaedam necessaria ideo in controversiam non vocantur, quia eorum aut veritas aut necessitas est aperte in Scripturis decisa; tum necesse est, ut etiam sit causa aliqua propter quam Necessaria quaedam controversa fiunt seu in controversiam vocantur. Hanc causam dicunt Arminani positam esse in affectibus, praejudiciis, adeoque voluntate hominum. Ita dicunt hoc loco p. 45. Similiter in dedicatoria Epistola sub finem dicunt: Necessaria omnia ita clare & perspicue in Scriptura contineri, ut a quovis mentis sua compote & praejudicio affectibusque non praeoccupato possint intelligi. Ita & alibi saepius in his Vindiciis. Atqui Arminiani talia quae ideo non intellig:untur quia affectus & praejudicia obstant, in Apologia dicunt non esse simpliciter evidentia seu omnibus obvia sed tantum aliquibus, mihi, tibi. Ita enim cap. 24. f. 280. a. At rationes sunt, inquies, luce meridiana clariores, quibus non assentiri pertinacia est. At, inquam, aliud est simpliciter rationes esse luce meridiana clariores, aliud mihi tibique clariores: Persaepe enim quod mihi clarum & solis radio scriptum videtur, aliis nocte & tenebris ipsis obscurius videtur. Nec mirum: judicia enim aut pro captu aut pro affectu variant. γλαυκωμα saepe in animo est, quod rem aliter atque aliter apparere facit. Intus apparens prohibet alienum. Vides, optime Lector eos expresse dicere, ea non esse omnibus obvia & simpliciter evidentia quae ob affectus & praejudicia non possunt intelligi. Iam autem talia h. e. quae non sunt simpliciter evidentia h. e. omnibus obvia & sole meridiano clariora Arminiani non habent pro Necessariis. Manifestum igitur est Arminianos in hac etiam parte ἀσύγχυτα dicere, quae in aeternum conciliari ab ipsis non possunt. Haec de priore membro limitatione scilicet illa dicta sunto.
units.tr: Thirdly, the subject matter they treat does not allow this limitation. For these two things are ἀσυμβατα [incompatible], that is, cannot stand together: namely this limitation which they here bring forward, and what they say in this place, that certain controverted things are necessary to salvation. For if certain necessary things are not called into controversy because either their truth or their necessity is openly decided in Scripture, then it must follow that there is also some cause on account of which certain necessary things become controverted, or are called into controversy. The Arminians say this cause lies "in affections, prejudices, and so in the will of men." So they say here at p. 45. Similarly, near the end of the dedicatory epistle they say: "All necessary things are so clearly and perspicuously contained in Scripture that they can be understood by anyone who is master of his mind and not preoccupied by prejudice or affections." So also quite often elsewhere in these Vindiciae. But the Arminians, in their Apologia, say that such things as cannot be understood because affections and prejudices stand in the way are not simply evident or obvious to all, but only to some: to me, to you. For so in chapter 24, f. 280 a: "But the arguments, you will say, are clearer than midday light, and it is obstinacy not to assent to them. But I reply: it is one thing for arguments to be simply clearer than midday light, another for them to be clearer to me and to you. For often what seems clear to me and written in the rays of the sun seems more obscure to others, even in night and darkness. Nor is this surprising: for judgments vary according to capacity or according to affection. γλαύκωμα [a cataract] is often in the mind, which makes a thing appear one way or another. The inward appearance prevents the outward." You see, best reader, that they expressly say those things are not obvious to all and not simply evident which cannot be understood on account of affections and prejudices. Now the Arminians do not hold such things to be necessary, that is, things not simply evident, not obvious to all and clearer than the noonday sun. It is therefore manifest that the Arminians in this part too say things ἀσύγχυτα [that cannot be mingled together], which they can never reconcile. These things are to be said concerning the first member of the limitation.

units.la: 9. Ad alterum venio, nimirum ad exempla quae hic afferunt, quibus ostendere volunt se controversa quaedam dogmata pro Necessariis habere. Hic possem ego copiose perspicue & solide ostendere; ea exempla pugnare non solum, ut vidimus, cum doctrina eorum de Necessariis quam paulo ante ex Apologia protulimus, sed etiam cum aliis dogmatis Apologiae ipsorum; ut v. g. de iis quae ῥητῶς in Scripturis continentur de libertate prophetandi, de mutua tolerantia &c. Sed brevitatis studio ea omittam. Saltem hoc commemorabo de iis Exemplis in genere, ea pugnare cum doctrina Vindiciarum. Pugnant enim primo cum doctrina eorum de judicio humano circa errores & Haereses, ac cum Praxi qua respondent quando ipsis objicitur doctrinam aliquam erroneam & speciatim ciatim Hæreticam esse. Docent enim nullum dari infallibile judicium de erroribus aliorum. Aliud est hæresibus, inquiunt, & schismatibus omnibus januam aperire, aliud iis aperire januam, qui nullo infallibili judicio convinci possunt, quòd placita eorum hæreses sint. Apol. c. 25. f. 298. b. Et quando ipsis objicitur verbum Dei docere hanc vel illam opinionem erroneam aut Hæreticam esse; regerunt; Quo judice? an quia tu ineptissimus homo ita censes? Quâ auctoritate? Quid si tibi ille regerat vicissim, sensum quem tu Scriptura verum ac genuinum sensum esse dicis, pessimum ac plane detortum sensum esse, & libertatem istam ejusmodi pravos sensus verbo divino adfingendi ac Scripturam detorquendi tibi tuisque permitti non debere, quid dices mi nugator? Vindic. c. 3. p. 23. 24. item, De Hæreticis loquor, inquies, & fanaticis hominibus. At talem te censent tuosque à quibus libertatem istam tibi concedi postulas in Germania, Gallia, Italia &c. Fac illos tibi regerere Diabolicam licentiam esse quam postulas &c. an non quod tute tibi intrivisses hoc tibi exedendum foret? Parce in posterum tibi & sapere disce tuo bono ac malo. (Contra te ipsum ubique & contra solem loqueris, nisi infallibilitatem tibi arroges & Papista fias, jubeasque omnes credere veritatis definitionem & libertatis circumscriptionem tibi tuisque jure divino competere &c. eâdem p.24. Item p.20. Cum falli possis in eo ipso de errore aliorum judicio, ex tuâ propriâ concessione, & confessione fieri potest ut veritati divinae ostium occludas &c. Et hoc modo atque hac Praxi Arminiani in Vindiciis istis suis hinc inde utuntur. Eadem est ratio doctrinæ & Praxeos eorum de pari jure omnium cœtuum: Qui tibi tuisque Hæretici sunt, iis & tu cum tuis Hæreticus es. Nec enim minus Pontificio, Lutherano, Anabaptista Hæreticus est Calvinista quàm huic illi. Itaque si libertatem istam iis non permittendam censes, ut eam illi tibi non permittant eodem jure & lege æquum putes necesse est, nisi forte hic speciale privilegium allegare possis. cap.3. p. 20. & alibi sæpissimè. Hoc eodem modo si quis Pontificius, Lutheranus, Reformatus ipsis in hac causâ respondeat, quid regerent Arminiani? Nam si regere velint, veritatem & necessitatem dogmatum suorum quæ istis exemplis continentur in Scripturis ῥητῶς exstare, hanc rem in eâ aperte decisam esse; negabunt illi. Si Magister Episcopius regerat rem hanc negari non posse, veritatem hanc esse claram, regerent illi vestigia ejus sequuti: quo judice? qua auctoritate? an quia tu Episcopi homo maledicentissime & blasphemator Socinianæ ita judicas? Quid si nos tibi contra regeramus tuum dogma, quod tu verum esse & necessarium dicis, salsissimum esse, quid dices mi nugator? Tu putas nos errare in Necessariis: at alii censent te cum tuis errare in Necessariis. Contra te ipsum ubique & contra solem loqueris, nisi infallibilitatem tibi ibi arroges, & jubeas omnes credere veritatis ac necessitatis definitionem tibi tuisque divino jure competere &c. Si ita praxi & verbis Arminianorum edoctus Pontificius aut alius ipsis regerat, quid dicent? An forte necessariam & omnem controversam veritatem ab unoquoque decidi posse, qui praejudicio aut affectu non est occupatus? At si hoc verum est; tunc corruit sophisma illud quo sexcenties in suo Responso adversum Partem primam Arcanorum utuntur. Rursus, si ob praejudicium aut affectum decidi non potest illud dogma ab omnibus, Ergo secundum doctrinam Apologiae, ut vidimus, dogma tale necessarium non est.
units.tr: 9. I come to the second point, namely the examples they bring forward, by which they wish to show that they hold certain controverted dogmas to be necessary. Here I could show copiously, clearly and solidly that these examples fight not only, as we have seen, with their doctrine of necessary things which we have just brought forth from the Apologia, but also with other dogmas of their Apologia: for instance, concerning those things which are expressly [ῥητῶς] contained in Scripture, concerning freedom of prophesying, mutual tolerance, etc. But for the sake of brevity I will omit these. At least I will mention this about those examples in general, that they fight with the doctrine of the Vindiciae. For they fight first with their doctrine of human judgment concerning errors and heresies, and with their practice by which they answer when some erroneous and especially heretical doctrine is objected to them. For they teach that no infallible judgment exists concerning the errors of others. "It is one thing," they say, "to open the door to all heresies and schisms, another to open the door to those who cannot be convicted by any infallible judgment that their opinions are heresies." Apol. c. 25, f. 298 b. And when it is objected to them that the Word of God teaches that this or that opinion is erroneous or heretical, they retort: "By whose judgment? Is it because you, most inept man, think so? By what authority? What if that man retorts to you in turn that the sense which you call the true and genuine sense of Scripture is the worst and plainly twisted sense, and that this freedom of attaching such perverse senses to the divine word and twisting Scripture ought not to be permitted to you and yours? What will you say, my trifler?" Vindiciae c. 3, p. 23, 24. Likewise: "You will say I speak of heretics and fanatical men. But those from whom you ask this freedom in Germany, France, Italy etc. judge you to be such a one, and yours. Suppose they retort to you that the licence you demand is diabolical etc.: would it not be that what you yourself have brewed must be eaten by you? Spare yourself in future, and learn to be wise to your own good and harm." (You speak against yourself everywhere and against the sun, unless you claim infallibility for yourself and become a Papist, and order everyone to believe that the definition of truth and the circumscription of liberty belong to you and yours by divine right etc.) The same, p. 24. Also p. 20: "Since you can be mistaken in that very judgment about the error of others, by your own concession and confession, it can happen that you shut the door to divine truth etc." And in this way, and by this practice, the Arminians in their Vindiciae use it here and there. The reasoning of their doctrine and practice concerning the equal right of all assemblies is the same: "Whoever are heretics to you and yours, to them you too with yours are heretics. For a Calvinist is no less a heretic to a Papist, a Lutheran, an Anabaptist, than they are to him. So if you think this liberty should not be granted to them, it is necessary that you think it fair that they should not grant it to you by the same right and law, unless perhaps you can allege a special privilege here." c. 3, p. 20, and very often elsewhere. In the same way, if some Papist, Lutheran or Reformed man should answer them in this cause, what would the Arminians reply? For if they wish to reply that the truth and necessity of their dogmas, which are contained in these examples, expressly exist in Scripture, and that this matter is openly decided there, the others will deny it. If Master Episcopius says this cannot be denied, that this truth is clear, the others, following his footsteps, would reply: "By whose judgment? By what authority? Is it because you, Episcopius, most abusive man and blasphemer, a Socinian, judge so? What if we in turn retort that your dogma, which you say is true and necessary, is most false? What will you say, my trifler? You think we err in necessary things, but others think you and yours err in necessary things. You speak against yourself everywhere and against the sun, unless you claim infallibility for yourself there, and order all to believe that the definition of truth and necessity belongs to you and yours by divine right" etc. If a Papist or someone else, taught by the practice and words of the Arminians, should reply to them thus, what will they say? Perhaps that every controverted truth, and every necessary one, can be decided by anyone who is not occupied by prejudice or affection? But if this is true, then that sophism falls by which they so often use in their Response against the First Part of the Arcana. Again, if that dogma cannot be decided by all on account of prejudice or affection, then, according to the doctrine of the Apologia, as we have seen, such a dogma is not necessary.

units.la: Deinde pugnant exempla illa cum eo argumento quo saepissime tam in Apologia & Resp. ad Excerp. quam in vindiciis solent uti, ut ostendant dogmata aliqua v. g. ea quae opposita Antitrinitariis sunt, non esse Necessaria ad salutem, & anathema non esse dicendum aut damnationis calculum ferendum adversum Antitrinitarios: Nam si hoc admittatur, inquiunt Vindic. lib. 1. cap. 7. p. 40. tum aeterna mortis sententia ferenda est de plano non in eos tantum qui contra sentiunt, quorum ingens turba est, sed etiam in myriades hominum innocentissimorum, qui sensum istum literalem (orthodoxa dogmata Antitrinitariis opposita, quae ego dixeram esse sensum literalem partis verbi Dei necessariae ad salutem) aut ignorant aut non percipiunt, aut, quia non plane de eo constat, ulteriorem eius probationem postulant, nullius alterius criminis aut culpae rei: Hoc si vobis placet, judices, quae ergo & quot mortium genera sufficient excarnificandis innumeris innoxiis animabus in gratiam inclementissimorum istorum hominum, qui tam leviter in comitia eunt de capitibus hominum & non minus promtam ac paratam habent sententiam aeternae maledictionis quam lanii malleum suum quo boves mactant, animal sine fraude dolo-que? Quid si Pontificius, Lutheranus, Reformatus id retorqueat in Arminianos, quibus in Apologia & nonnunquam etiam in Vindiciis quando causae suae id expedire putant, unum idemque est dogma aliquod esse necessarium vel non necessarium ad salutem & propter id anathema denunciandum vel non denunciandum esse; ac dicat: Si hoc admittatur, judices, dogmata haec (nimirum Panem Eucharisticum non esse adorandum; imagines Dei & sanctorum non esse faciendas & adorandas, Haereticis nulla corporali coercitione esse resistendum) esse necessaria ad salutem; tum aeterna mortis sententia ferenda est de plano non in eos tantum qui contra sentiunt, quorum ingens turba est, sed etiam in myriades hominum innocentissimorum qui necessitatem istam & pistōs illa dogmata in Scriptura exstare ignorant &c. Sic omnes Reformati, Lutherani, Pontificii qui fuerunt & qui sunt aeternum damnabuntur, quorum tamen inmen infinitis major numerus est, quam Socinianorum quibus commiserationis affectu parcunt Arminiani, quem non habent erga omnes eos coetus qui Deum in tribus personis adorant. Hoc si vobis placet, aeterna morti & maledictioni expositae erunt infinita myriades in gratiam istorum inclementissimorum hominum &c. Ita si respondeatur Arminianis quid regerent? Nam argumenti istius Arminiani nervus consistit in affectu & commiseratione. Itaque negare non possunt Arminiani, Pontificium, Reformatum aut Lutheranum ex hypothesi ipsorum argumentari; nisi minus commiseratione Arminianorum digni sint Reformati, Lutherani, Pontificii quàm Sociniani. Et profecto omnes eos qui Deum in tribus personis adorant pejore in loco apud Arminianos esse ob doctrinam de Haereticorum coercitione qualibet corporali, constat tàm ex aliis, tàm ex eo quòd Arminiani nullum dogma inveniunt in sectâ Socinianâ quae Trinitatis mysterium oppugnat, propter quod anathema ipsis dicere velint; sed contrà eos coetus qui Deum in tribus personis adorant plura dogmata inveniunt propter quae anathema ipsis dicunt. Ex quo vel solo hos homines nosse licet. Atque haec de istis exemplis in genere dicta sufficiant.
units.tr: Next, these examples rely on the same argument that the Arminians very often use in their Apology and in the Response to the Excerpta, and also in the Vindiciae, to show that certain doctrines, for instance those opposed to the Antitrinitarians, are not necessary to salvation, and that no anathema should be pronounced, nor any sentence of damnation passed, against the Antitrinitarians. For if this is admitted, they say in Vindiciae, book 1, chapter 7, p. 40, then the sentence of eternal death must be passed outright not only on those who think otherwise, who form a huge crowd, but also on myriads of most innocent men who either are ignorant of or do not grasp that literal sense (the orthodox doctrines opposed to the Antitrinitarians, which I had said were the literal sense of a part of the Word of God necessary to salvation), or who, since they are not plainly certain of it, demand further proof of it, and are guilty of no other crime or fault. If this pleases you, judges, what kinds of death, and how many, will be enough to butcher countless innocent souls, to gratify those most merciless men who go so lightly to the assembly to judge the lives of men, and who have their sentence of eternal condemnation as ready and to hand as the butcher has his mallet with which he kills oxen, an animal without fraud or guile? What if a Papist, a Lutheran or a Reformed man turned this argument against the Arminians? In the Apology, and sometimes also in the Vindiciae, whenever they think their cause requires it, the Arminians hold that one and the same doctrine is either necessary or not necessary to salvation, and that on that account an anathema is or is not to be pronounced. Such a man could say: If this is admitted, judges, these doctrines (namely, that the Eucharistic bread is not to be adored; that images of God and of the saints are not to be made and adored; that heretics are not to be resisted by any bodily coercion) are necessary to salvation; then the sentence of eternal death must be passed outright, not only on those who think otherwise, who form a huge crowd, but also on myriads of most innocent men who are ignorant that this necessity exists and that these doctrines are to be found in Scripture, etc. So all the Reformed, Lutherans and Papists who have been and who are will be eternally damned, although in truth their number is far greater than that of the Socinians, whom the Arminians spare out of a feeling of pity, a pity they do not have towards all those assemblies that worship God in three persons. If this pleases you, countless myriads will be exposed to eternal death and curse, to gratify these most merciless men, etc. If the Arminians were answered in this way, what would they reply? For the strength of this argument of the Arminians rests on feeling and pity. Therefore the Arminians cannot deny that the Papist, the Reformed man or the Lutheran reasons from their own premise, unless the Reformed, the Lutherans and the Papists are less deserving of the Arminians' pity than the Socinians are. And indeed it is evident, both from other things and from the fact that the Arminians find no doctrine in the Socinian sect, which attacks the mystery of the Trinity, on account of which they would wish to pronounce an anathema on them, but on the contrary they find many doctrines in the assemblies that worship God in three persons on account of which they pronounce an anathema on them, that all who worship God in three persons stand in a worse position among the Arminians, because of the doctrine of the coercion of heretics by any bodily means. From this alone one may know these men. But let what has been said in general about these examples suffice.

units.la: Quod speciatim attinet ad dogma controversum de Necessitate bonorum operum quoad praesentiam; quia peculiare Arcanum malitiae & improbitatis horum hominum in eo exemplo continetur; de eo egimus Arcan. Par. III. lib. 2. c. 8. §. 9.
units.tr: As for the controverted doctrine of the necessity of good works as to their presence, since a particular mystery of the malice and wickedness of these men is contained in that example, we have dealt with it in Arcanum, Part III, book 2, chapter 8, §9.

units.la: Quod vero concernit dogma de Haereticorum coercitione corporali; ego jam dudum antequam responsum suum conciperent contradictionem hanc ipsorum animadverteram, quâ se ipsos involvunt dum docent in Apologia Nullum dogma Controversum esse necessarium ad salutem; & tamen eos damnant imò anathema Maranatha denunciant in Responf. ad Excerp. append. p. 128. qui Haereticidium (ut loquuntur Arminiani) h. e. qualemcunque corporalem Haereticorum coercitionem Probant, imò qui non improbant, non dissuadent. Hanc ipsorum contradictionem jam ante biennium & aliquot menses me observâsse testes mihi sunt non pauci eximii servi Dei praesertim in Hollandiâ, qui probè meminerunt me de istâ contradictione & ἀντικατάθεσις Arminianorum palpabilissimâ cum ipsis tùm temporis locutum esse. Itaque quoties dicunt Arminiani eos qui ita de Haereticorum coercitione sentiunt aeternùm damnatum iri; sciant se hujus improbitatis & malitiae à se ipsis in Apologiâ suâ convictos esse, in quâ docent: Nullum dogma inter Christianos controversum aut quod in futurum controverti possit esse necessarium ad salutem. Nam hoc quidem
units.tr: As for the doctrine of the bodily coercion of heretics, I had noticed this contradiction of theirs long before they conceived their response, by which they entangle themselves when they teach in the Apology that no controverted doctrine is necessary to salvation; and yet they condemn those who hold otherwise, and indeed pronounce the anathema Maranatha on them, in the Response to the Excerpta, appendix, p. 128, namely those who approve of heretic-killing (as the Arminians call it), that is, any bodily coercion of heretics whatever, or who do not disapprove of it, or do not dissuade from it. That I had observed this contradiction of theirs more than two years and some months ago, and had spoken about it with them at that time, as a most palpable self-contradiction of the Arminians, many distinguished servants of God, especially in Holland, are witnesses to me, and they remember it well. Therefore, whenever the Arminians say that those who think in this way about the coercion of heretics will be damned eternally, let them know that they are convicted by their own Apology of this wickedness and malice, in which they teach: No doctrine controverted among Christians, or one which may in future be controverted, is necessary to salvation. For this doctrine

units.la: K quidem dogma controversum est ut ipsi hic in Vindiciis fatentur. Quod ajunt illud ἐντὸς repugnare legi charitatis, falsum est, imò contrà, Arminianorum sententia repugnat ei Legi. Nam charitas erga proximum tàm errantem quàm non errantem requirit, ut Hæreticis à Magistratu resistatur. Atque hæc quidem de primo hoc dogmate Arminianorum objecto ipsis à me in illo capite prolixius dicere necessum fuit, quia hujus rei perpetuus usus in sequentibus erit. Subinde enim ad hanc fraudem recurrunt.
units.tr: is indeed controverted, as they themselves here admit in the Vindiciae. As for their claim that the opposite view is contrary to the law of charity, that is false; on the contrary, the opinion of the Arminians is contrary to that law. For charity towards a neighbour, whether he errs or not, requires that heretics be resisted by the magistrate. I have had to say rather more about this first doctrine of the Arminians, objected to them by me in that chapter, because the constant use of this matter will arise in what follows, for they keep returning to this deceit.

units.la: Addo saltem, quod p. 44. dicunt me afferere etiam ea posse esse Necessaria quæ per evidentem consequentiam in Scripturis non contineantur; id falsum est. Nam dixi quidem dogmata quædam esse necessaria etsi non contineantur in Scripturâ per consequentiam omnibus obviam cui saltem sanum sinciput sit &c. sed non dixi ea posse esse necessaria quæ in Scripturâ non continentur per evidentem consequentiam. Nam planè contrarium asserui lib. 1. par. I. c. 6. & alibi.
units.tr: I will add at least this: they say, on p. 44, that I assert that even those things may be necessary which are not contained in the Scriptures by evident consequence; that is false. For I did say that certain doctrines are necessary even if they are not contained in Scripture by a consequence obvious to everyone who has a sound head at least, etc.; but I did not say that those things may be necessary which are not contained in Scripture by an evident consequence. For I plainly asserted the opposite in book 1, part I, chapter 6, and elsewhere.

units.la: 10. Secundum dogma quod ipsis objeceram est: Controversa vera dogmata non esse firmiter constanterque credenda. Hoc non negant, sed saltem me insciitiæ arguunt & dicunt 1. se loqui de dogmatis veris controversis, sed non necessariis creditu. 2. de dogmatis quæ vera quis esse judicat, quod judicium tale sit ut errare possit p. 45. 46. &, ut loquuntur p. 47. cui falsum subesse potest. Respondeo, prius adversum me non facere, quia docent, ut ostendi, in Apologiâ suâ nulla controversa dogmata esse necessaria ad salutem. Posterius quoque inane effugium est. Nam Arminiani in Apologiâ suâ loquuntur de dogmatis quæ nó solùm aliquis putat vera esse, sed quæ etiam reverà talia sunt, prout patet non solùm ex verbis Apologiæ Exam Cens. præf. f. 6. b. quibus probavi Par. I. lib. 1. cap. 8. p. 68. eos ita docere: sed etiam ex eàdem Apol. f. 7. a. ubi postquam dixissent, asserenda ea esse firmiter, quæ Scriptura necessaria esse dicit totidem verbis aut per consequentiam evidentē & Sole clariorem omnibusque obviam, addunt: Qui circa CÆTERA ALIA OMNIA ita se gerit aut de iis non nisi cum modestâ præfatione contra alios dissentientes sententiam suam pandit, is non hæsitat &c. sed ita judicat ut judicium suum divino impar faciat &c. NIHIL firmiter constanterque credendum est in REBUS EIUSMODI de quibus controversia incidit inter doctos & pios (quales ipsis sunt Antitrinitarii) nisi cum hac lege &c. Videt unusquisque eos generaliter loqui de omnibus non necessariis, item de omnibus Controversis veris dogmatis quâ talia, seu prout sunt res, sive prout sunt objectum judicii nostri, non autem prout à judicio nostro hanc vel illam formam & conceptum sortiuntur.
units.tr: 10. The second doctrine I had objected to them is this: Controverted true doctrines are not to be believed firmly and steadfastly. They do not deny this, but merely accuse me of ignorance, and say, first, that they are speaking of true controverted doctrines which are not necessary to be believed; second, of doctrines which someone judges to be true, where that judgement is such that it may err, p. 45, 46, and, as they put it on p. 47, in which falsehood may lie hidden. I reply that the first point does not tell against me, because, as I have shown, they teach in their Apology that no controverted doctrines are necessary to salvation. The second is also an empty evasion. For in their Apology the Arminians speak of doctrines which not only someone thinks to be true but which are in fact really such, as is clear not only from the words of the Apology, Examen Censurae, preface, f. 6 b, by which I proved in Part I, book 1, chapter 8, p. 68 that they teach this way, but also from the same Apology, f. 7 a, where, after saying that those things are to be asserted firmly which Scripture declares necessary in so many words or by an evident consequence clearer than the sun and obvious to all, they add: He who conducts himself in the same way concerning ALL OTHER THINGS, or who sets out his opinion about them, and dissents from others only with a modest preface, does not hesitate, etc., but judges in such a way that his judgement is unequal to the divine one, etc. NOTHING is to be believed firmly and steadfastly in THINGS OF THIS KIND about which controversy has arisen among learned and pious men (such as the Antitrinitarians are to them), except under this condition, etc. Anyone can see that they speak generally of all non-necessary things, and likewise of all controverted true doctrines as such, that is, as they are in themselves, or as they are the object of our judgement, and not as they take on this or that form and concept from our judgement.

units.la: Porrò quia argumentatus eram hoc modo : Quod non est firmiter credendum, id non opus habet firmis argumentis : At dogmata Controversa, quale est illud de Spiritu S. adorando, non sunt firmiter credenda secundùm Arminianos : Ergò non opus habent firmis argumentis : Per consequens, quod dicunt in Epistolâ Hagam Comitis scriptâ, (se ideò ab adorationis cultu ad probandam Spiritus S. divinitatem argumentari in Apologiâ noluisse, quòd ipsis propositum fuerit non nisi firmis & solidis argumentis uti,) non esse nisi merum praetextum impietatis Socinianæ quâ in animo suo Spiritum S. non habent pro persona Deitatis. Hic verò Arminiani quia constricti tenentur & elabi non possunt, convicium mihi faciunt & malitiæ me accusant, atque addunt : Non dicunt Remonstrantes se argumentis firmis & solidis uti non posse ad id probandum, prout hic innuit Vedelius eos dicere. Argumentis enim tribus solidis usi sunt ad id probandum. Sed tantum dicunt, se istud argumentum quartum non adhibuisse, quia istud firmum & solidum esse demonstrare non possint &c. Iudicet Lector, an hoc sit argumentum meum solvere, & an tangat haec responsio vel majorem vel minorem vel Conclusionem argumenti mei. Et falsum est me illud innuisse quod hic dicunt. Nam hoc saltem indicavi : Quid enim, dicebam, opus est anxie laborare de argumentis firmis, ubi res non est firmiter credenda? De Spiritus S. adoratione quod addunt, de eo vidimus Par. III. lib. 1. cap. 8. §. 1.
units.tr: Moreover, since I had argued in this way: what is not firmly to be believed does not need firm arguments; but the controverted doctrines, such as that concerning the adoration of the Holy Spirit, are not firmly to be believed according to the Arminians; therefore they do not need firm arguments. Consequently, what they say in the letter written to the Count of The Hague (that they did not wish to argue from the worship of adoration to prove the divinity of the Holy Spirit in their Apology, because they had resolved to use only firm and solid arguments) is nothing but a mere pretext for Socinian impiety, by which in their minds they do not hold the Holy Spirit to be a person of the Godhead. Here the Arminians, since they are pressed and cannot escape, abuse me and accuse me of malice, and they add: The Remonstrants do not say that they cannot use firm and solid arguments to prove this, as Vedelius here hints that they say. For they used three solid arguments to prove it. But they only say that they did not employ this fourth argument, because they cannot demonstrate that it is firm and solid, &c. Let the reader judge whether this is an answer to my argument, and whether this reply touches my major premise, my minor premise, or my conclusion. And it is false that I hinted at what they here say. For I indicated only this: For why, I was saying, is there any need to labour anxiously over firm arguments, where the thing is not to be firmly believed? As to what they add about the adoration of the Holy Spirit, we have seen that in Part III, book 1, chapter 8, §1.

units.la: II. Aliud dogma ipsis objeceram hoc : Controversa vera dogmata esse credenda tantum certitudine humana. Hoc non negant; sed mihi convitia dicunt & addunt p. 47. se non loqui de certitudine humana quae rationibus nititur, oppositè ad fidem seu certitudinem quae verbo Dei nititur. At hoc est tergiversari. Nam certitudo quae, ut Arminiani hic dicunt, rationibus nititur, non autem ipsis oraculis divinis, non potest esse fides divina seu certitudo divina quae verbo Dei nititur. Et sufficit mihi quod dicunt Controversa vera dogmata esse credenda certitudine humana. Quâ in re nobis novum arcanum pandunt de quo egimus Par. III. lib. 1. cap. 8. §. 2.
units.tr: II. I had objected to them another doctrine, this one: Controverted true doctrines are to be believed only with human certainty. They do not deny this; but they abuse me with insults and add, on page 47, that they are not speaking of human certainty, which rests on reasons, as opposed to faith or certainty which rests on the Word of God. But this is to evade. For certainty which, as the Arminians here say, rests on reasons and not on the divine oracles themselves, cannot be divine faith or divine certainty which rests on the Word of God. And it is enough for me that they say controverted true doctrines are to be believed with human certainty. In this matter they reveal to us a new mystery, which we discussed in Part III, book 1, chapter 8, §2.

units.la: Aliud dogma ipsorum est : Controversa vera dogmata rationibus niti, sed quae ab oraculis divinis differunt. Agnoscunt, & dicunt se loqui de rationibus ex verbo Dei JUDICIO NOSTRO petitis, ibid. Atqui sermo est in Apologiâ de dogmatis veris controversis, quae re ipsa vera sunt, quibus per consequens falsum subesse non potest. Haec ego ostenderam cap. 8. Par. I. nititipsis oraculis divinis, non autem rationibus quae a divinis oraculis differunt. Ad hoc Arminiani respondere debuissent.
units.tr: Another doctrine of theirs is this: Controverted true doctrines rest on reasons, but reasons which differ from the divine oracles. They acknowledge this, and say that they are speaking of reasons drawn from the Word of God by OUR JUDGEMENT, ibid. But the Apology is concerned with controverted doctrines that are truly true in fact, and in which therefore falsehood cannot lie. I had shown this in chapter 8 of Part I: they rest on the divine oracles themselves, and not on reasons which differ from the divine oracles. To this the Arminians ought to have replied.

units.la: 12. Aliud dogma quod ipsis §. 4. objeceram est: Dogmata quae rudibus pariter atque imperitis obvia non sunt, qualia Arminianis sunt dogmata de Trinitate oppositá Antitrinitariis, non sine periculo credi. Item eos statuere controversum dogma non esse certissimum, sed opponere haec duo sibi invicem: & eos fidem controversorum dogmatum talem statuere, quae cum dubitatione conjuncta sit, prout isthaec omnia ex ipsorum in Apologia verbis luce clarius meridianâ ostendi.
units.tr: 12. Another doctrine which I had objected to them in §4 is this: Doctrines which are not equally obvious to the uneducated and the unskilled, such as the Arminians' doctrines on the Trinity, opposed to the Antitrinitarians, are not to be believed without danger. Likewise that they hold a controverted doctrine not to be most certain, but set these two things against each other; and that they hold the faith in controverted doctrines to be such as is joined with doubt. All these things I have shown, more clearly than the noonday light, from their own words in the Apology.

units.la: 13. Illa omnia, ut & dogma aliud a me productum, nimirum de rebus controversis nihil esse decidendum quod firmiter & constanter Orthodoxis omnibus sit credendum, non negant. Sed vide gloriosam admodum refutandi rationem! Fingunt me, qui contra confessionem & Apologiam eorum pro instituti mei ratione egi, contra nugas, quas modo in Vindiciis suis protulerunt, disputare sectione 4. & 5. & respondent uno verbo : Quae contra haec infert Vedelius sect. 4. & 5. ea ne speciem quidem habent. Et sic, contra ea ne hiscere quidem ausi, ad aliud dogma veniunt. Atqui ego contra ea non disputavi, quia nondum Vindicias suas ediderant, neque istas nugas vel in Apologia vel alibi protulerant: sed res mihi fuit tunc cum eorum Confessione & Apologia. Vide mihi, optime Lector, pudorem simul & conscientiam horum hominum!
units.tr: 13. They do not deny all these things, nor the other doctrine I put forward, namely that nothing is to be decided in controverted matters which all Orthodox believers must firmly and constantly believe. But see what a glorious way of refuting it they have! They pretend that I, who in accordance with my purpose argued against their Confession and Apology, am disputing in sections 4 and 5 against the trifles which they have just brought forward in their Vindications, and they reply in one word: What Vedelius infers against these in sections 4 and 5 does not even have the appearance [of truth]. And so, not daring even to breathe against them, they move on to another doctrine. But I did not dispute against them, because they had not yet published their Vindications, nor had they put forward those trifles either in the Apology or elsewhere; my business at that time was with their Confession and Apology. Consider, best reader, the shamelessness and the conscience of these men!

units.la: 14. Aliud ipsorum dogma est: Controversis dogmatis veris LICERE contradicere, & ea in dubium vocare. Fatentur. Et postquam fassi essent illud ipsum omne quod ego ex pluribus locis Apologiae circa hanc rem ipsis objeceram, & explicuissent quo sensu dicant LICERE contradicere veris dogmatis; nimirum: Licent quaedam, inquiunt, in quantum sine periculo salutis sic aut aliter credi possunt &c. adeo tamen sunt perversi & improbi ut audeant me eo nomine malae fidei accusare. Atque hinc, inquiunt, p. 48. colligere est, quam mala fide agat Vedelius, cum Remonstrantibus in fine hujus sectionis impietatem tribuit, quasi doceant non solum posse contradici veris dogmatis controversis absque iactura salutis, sed & LICERE id facere, cum id tam longe absit a mente Remonstrantium, quam coelum a terra. Optime Lector, quid facias his hominibus? Fatentur se docere, LICERE contradicere veris dogmatis, & tamen dicunt me malâ fide agere, quod dico eos docere LICERE contradicere veris dogmatis. Bone Deus, qualis horum hominum conscientia est! Et, ut magis videas, Lector, eos docere, LICERE contradicere veris dogmatis controversis; vocant hoc non solùm libertatem in Confessionis suæ Præfatione, item in Apologiæ variis locis à me allegatis; sed etiam, dum tribuunt eam omnibus Christianis, ac vocant liberas amicas & serias collationes, eam PRIVILEGIUM omnium Christianorum appellant: Libera, inquiunt, amica, seria, de rebus controversis Qualibuscunq; collationes, PRIVILEGIUM Christianorum omnium sunt. Apol. c. 25. f. 301. b.
units.tr: 14. Another doctrine of theirs is this: It is LAWFUL to contradict true controverted doctrines, and to call them into doubt. They confess it. And after they had admitted that very thing which I had objected to them from several places in the Apology on this point, and had explained in what sense they say it is LAWFUL to contradict true doctrines, namely: Some things are permitted, they say, so far as they can be believed in this or that way without danger to salvation, &c., they are nonetheless so perverse and wicked that they dare to accuse me of bad faith on this account. And from this, they say, p. 48, it may be gathered how much in bad faith Vedelius acts, when at the end of this section he attributes impiety to the Remonstrants, as if they taught not only that true controverted doctrines may be contradicted without loss of salvation, but that it is LAWFUL to do so, when this is as far from the mind of the Remonstrants as heaven is from earth. Best reader, what can you do with such men? They confess that they teach that it is LAWFUL to contradict true doctrines, and yet they say I act in bad faith because I say that they teach that it is LAWFUL to contradict true doctrines. Good God, what sort of conscience do these men have! And so that you may see more clearly, reader, that they teach that it is LAWFUL to contradict true controverted doctrines, they call this not only liberty in the Preface of their Confession, and in various places of the Apology cited by me, but also, while they attribute it to all Christians and call it free, friendly and serious conferences, they call it the PRIVILEGE of all Christians: Free, they say, friendly, serious conferences about any controverted matters whatever are the PRIVILEGE of all Christians. Apology, ch. 25, p. 301 b.

units.la: Addunt, si falsum sit quod dicunt, LICERE contradicere veris dogmatis, debere igitur me ostendere quæ sint dogmata ista quæ necessaria & quæ non necessaria sint. Id si non possim, tum optant mihi bonam mentem & non reprobam. Quasi verò hoc ad rem faciat, aut quasi liceat contradicere veris dogmatis non necessariis! Isti homines finem distinctionis Necessariorum & non Necessariorum putant esse, ut liceat liberè contradicere non Necessariis: cùm tamen veritati divinæ, seu necessaria seu non Necessaria sit ad salutem, nunquam contradicere liceat. Hoc enim est, nomen Domini temerè usurpare, eum mendacii arguere, Scripturam detorquere in alium sensum. Præterea superfluum atque ineptum est à nobis Reformatis postulare, ut ostendamus quæ dogmata necessaria & non necessaria sint. Constat enim quos cœtus nos habeamus pro Hæreticis, quos non; seu quibuscum communionem colendam aut non colendam esse statuamus. itaque stultum est postulare à nobis ut indicemus quæ dogmata habeamus pro Necessariis, quæ non.
units.tr: They add that if what they say is false, that it is LAWFUL to contradict true doctrines, then I ought to show which doctrines are necessary and which are not necessary. If I cannot do this, then they wish me a good mind and not a reprobate one. As if this had any bearing on the matter, or as if it were lawful to contradict true doctrines which are not necessary! These men think the purpose of the distinction between Necessary and non-Necessary doctrines is that it is lawful to contradict freely the non-Necessary ones, whereas it is never lawful to contradict the divine truth, whether it be necessary to salvation or not. For to do so is to take the name of the Lord in vain, to accuse Him of lying, and to twist Scripture into another sense. Moreover, it is superfluous and absurd to demand of us Reformed that we show which doctrines are necessary and which are not. For it is well known which assemblies we hold to be heretical and which not, or with whom we decide that communion is to be kept or not to be kept. Therefore it is foolish to demand that we indicate which doctrines we hold to be Necessary and which not.

units.la: Unum adhuc præterire hic non debeo. Distinguunt hic inter τὸ Licere. Nam ajunt, homonymia est in verbo licere. Licent quædam de quibus perinde est, sive hoc sive illud credas. Licent quædam quæ sine periculo salutis sic aut aliter credi possunt &c. Et addunt; se saltem hoc secundo sensu intelligere verbum illud licere, non autem primo. Verùm hoc falsum est, & sibi contradicunt. Nam statuunt etiam in Apologiâ licere in primo sensu contradicere dogmatis veris controversis. Ita enim circa controversiam quæ nobis intercedit cum Socinianis: Anne Decalogus perfectam vitæ normam contineat? respondent: Quid ad rem facit sive Christianus credat hoc sive id neget? Nam sive hoc sive illud credat, secundùm regulam illam ipsi vivendum est quam Christus tradit, sive ea perfectior sit vivendi Regula quàm lex tradit, sive non. Apol. c. 13. f. 142. a. Item circa controversias: An eadem species fuerit Ecclesia veteris Testamenti cum Ecclesia Novi Testi? An eadem fides in Iesum Christum præcepta fuerit sub V. Testamento quæ sub Novo? An eadem præcepta & promissa sint sub vetere Testam. quæ sub Novo, ALIASQUE Elus Generis Plures,&c. inquiunt. Quid hoc ad Christianum hominem facit, sive quaestiones illas sciat sive nesciat &c. Quicquid de istis dixeris, haud magnopere contendent Remonstrantes. Apol. c. 22. f. 232. Item de justitia Originali: Qualemcunque, inquiunt, justitiam Originalem Adamo & Evae tribueris cum Ecclesiis seu Reformatis, seu Romanensibus seu aliis quibuscunque, eam volentibus ac lubentibus Remonstrantibus Adamo & Evae attribueris; dummodo non dicas fuisse qualitatem qua posita impossibile fuerit Adamum peccare &c. c. 5. f. 60. b.
units.tr: There is one more thing I must not pass over here. They distinguish here between the senses of the word licere. For they say: There is an ambiguity in the word licere. Some things are permitted, about which it makes no difference whether you believe this or that. Some things are permitted which can be believed in this or that way without danger to salvation, &c. And they add that they understand that word licere at least in the second sense, and not in the first. But this is false, and they contradict themselves. For they also maintain in the Apology that it is lawful, in the first sense, to contradict true controverted doctrines. Thus, concerning the controversy which we have with the Socinians: Does the Decalogue contain the perfect rule of life? they reply: What does it matter to the point whether the Christian believes this or denies it? For whether he believes this or that, he must live according to that rule which Christ delivers, whether that rule of living is more perfect than the law delivers or not. Apology, ch. 13, p. 142 a. Likewise concerning controversies: Was the Church of the Old Testament the same kind as the Church of the New Testament? Was the same faith in Jesus Christ commanded under the Old Testament as under the New? Are the same commands and promises under the Old Testament as under the New, and several others of this kind, they say. What does this matter to a Christian man, whether he knows those questions or not, &c. Whatever you say about these, the Remonstrants will not contend greatly. Apology, ch. 22, p. 232. Likewise concerning original justice: Whatever kind of original justice you attribute to Adam and Eve, they say, along with the Churches, whether Reformed or Roman or any others, the Remonstrants are willing and glad that you attribute it to Adam and Eve; provided you do not say that it was a quality by which, once it was present, it would have been impossible for Adam to sin, &c. Ch. 5, p. 60 b.

units.la: 15. Dixeram etiam eos docere hominem ἐπίσχεσιν seu dubitare de rebus fidei, h.e. ita fluctuare ut nec affirmet nec neget aliquod dogma, sed dubitet quid statuendum sit. Non negant; sed asserunt & ideo convitiis me petunt. Ac quia dixeram eos judicium suum suspendere & dubitare in multis, circa omnia fere Religionis Christianae capita, respondent: Id sequenti capite confutabitur. Memor esto, Lector, hujus promissi. Nam mox videbis quam egregie me refutarint.
units.tr: 15. I had also said that they teach that a man practises ἐπίσχεσιν [suspension of judgement], or doubts about the matters of faith, that is, wavers so that he neither affirms nor denies any doctrine, but is unsure what ought to be held. They do not deny this; they assert it, and for that reason they attack me with insults. And since I had said that they suspend their judgement and doubt in many matters, on almost all the chief heads of the Christian religion, they reply: This will be refuted in the following chapter. Reader, remember this promise, for you will soon see how splendidly they refute me.

units.la: Objeceram ipsis etiam, quod doceant contemnere & explodere dogmata vera controversa, & quod adeo contemtim loquantur de iis ut ne quidem parcant quibusdam maximi momenti, imo quae necessaria sunt ad salutem & fundamentalia. Speciatim conquestus eram, quod adeo contemtim loquerentur de dogmatis Controversis cum Antitrinitariis circa mysterium Trinitatis, Item de Controversia de Peccato Originis, de paedobaptismo, de Coena Domini, de justificatione hominis coram Deo. Conquestus eram quod exsibilare & explodere docerent controversa quaedam dogmata vera maximi momenti, eo praetexu quod homo absque iis veram fidem habere, pie vivere, & salvus esse possit; prout controversiam, quae nobis cum Socinianis & Anabaptistis intercedit de perfectione legis moralis eo praetextu explodunt, quod res Gratia in eo sita non sint si Christianus id neget.
units.tr: I had also charged them with teaching that true controverted doctrines are to be despised and hooted down, and that they speak of them so contemptuously that they do not spare even some of the greatest importance, indeed those which are necessary to salvation and fundamental. In particular I complained that they spoke so contemptuously of the controverted doctrines with the Antitrinitarians concerning the mystery of the Trinity, and likewise of the controversy about Original Sin, infant baptism, the Lord's Supper, and the justification of man before God. I complained that they taught that certain true doctrines of the greatest importance were to be hissed down and exploded, on the pretext that a man can have true faith, live piously and be saved without them; as they explode the controversy which lies between us and the Socinians and Anabaptists concerning the perfection of the moral law, on the pretext that the matter is not one of grace if the Christian denies it.

units.la: Item objeceram ipsis dogmata eorum de mutatione sententiae circa controversa dogmata; statuunt enim licere habere Theologiam annuam, menstruam, horariam, seu mutare sententiam suam de rebus controversis quoties aliquis velit, imo in horas. Item, Religionem positam non esse in controversorum dogmatum firma fide: sed contra, Religionem veram inter infinitas adeoque horarias circa controversias variationes manere posse salvam atque illaesam. Perinde esse sive quis teneat sensum verum in rebus controversis sive falsum, ubi decisiones factae sunt quibus firmiter est adhaerendum. Nam utrumque fieri sine judicio, tantum casu. Et sic veram sententiam non magis profuturam huic, quam illi obsuturus sit suum error.
units.tr: Likewise I had charged them with their doctrines of changing opinion about controverted doctrines; for they lay down that it is lawful to have a theology for the year, for the month, for the hour, or to change one's opinion on controverted matters as often as one wishes, even hour by hour. Also, that religion does not consist in the firm faith of controverted doctrines; on the contrary, that the true religion can remain safe and unharmed amid endless, even hourly, variations on controversies. It makes no difference whether a man holds the true sense or the false in controverted matters, where decisions have been made to which one must firmly cling. For both come about without judgement, merely by chance; and thus the true opinion will profit this man no more than his error will harm that one.

units.la: 16. Denique omnes eos coetus qui errant circa qualiacunque controversa dogmata mata esse veram Ecclesiam. Ad hæc omnia his tribus sectionibus propositæ respondet nihil aliud, quàm: {catera quæ in hoc capite sunt, ex his facile æstimari possunt, & prolixè in Responsione Remonstrantium ad Specimen professorum Leydensium ventilata sunt. Egregia verò responsio & digna iis, qui calumniâ dicam mihi scripserunt in titulo libri sui. Nam quòd ajunt, hæc omnia quæ ipsis objeci ventilata ab ipsis fuisse in Resp. ad Excerp. D.D. Proff. Leydd. salsissimum est: nisi hoc sensu dicant, se in Responsione illâ profiteri eadem impia & profana dogmata sua; id quod verissimum est.
units.tr: 16. Finally, all those assemblies which err about any controverted doctrines are a true Church. To all these things, set out in these three sections, he replies nothing except: {The rest of what is in this chapter can easily be judged from these points, and has been thoroughly debated in the Remonstrants' Reply to the Specimen of the Leiden Professors. A splendid reply indeed, and worthy of those who wrote to me calumny on the title page of their book. For their claim that all these things I objected to them were debated by them in the Reply to the Excerpts of the Leiden Professors is most witty, unless they mean by it that in that Reply they profess the same impious and profane doctrines of theirs; which is most true.

units.la: Conclusionis loco, quia inter alia conquestus eram de scurrilitate (ubi quis non videt me longe mitiore vocabulo usum fuisse contra tantam improbitatem ac horrendam profanitatem?) eorum, quòd Electos quos sacra Scriptura filios Dei vocat, appellarint cap. 7. Apolog. f. 90. b. Electos ipsos filios albæ gallinæ (quemadmodum simili profanitate, ut hoc obiter addam, vocant Electos ipsos Iovis filios Respons. ad Excerp. p. 31.) illi non aliâ ratione satisfaciunt orbi Christiano quàm quod me convitiis onerant. Et, ut videantur causam habere maledicentiæ quâ erga me utuntur, dicunt: Convitia quæ passim intercurrunt, cum impietatem, scurrilitatem, & cætera Remonstrantibus tribuit, præterimus ut excrementa hominis parum sani &c. In quâ re eas contra conscientiam suam loqui constat. Nam ego honorificè cum iis egi contra meritum ipsorum: etsi impietatem eorum doctrinæ merito tribuerim, & de scurrilitate eorum bis conquestus fuerim. Sed vellent egregii hi homines impia dogmata, blasphema & exercanda spargere; & tamen cuperent ut nemo os contra ea aperiret, ac ea impia esse diceret. Sic igitur etiam inter alia apparet me nihil per calumniam Arminianis in isto capite tribuisse, quandoquidem nihil eorum negant quæ ipsis in eo objeci, excepto uno quod contra propriam suam conscientiam eos negare luce clarius meridianâ ostendi.
units.tr: By way of conclusion: since, among other things, I had complained of the buffoonery (where does anyone not see that I used a far milder word against such great wickedness and horrible profanity?) of their calling the Elect, whom Holy Scripture calls sons of God, the very sons of a white hen (ch. 7, Apology, f. 90 b.), as, by the same profanity, I may add in passing, they call the Elect the very sons of Jupiter (Reply to the Excerpts, p. 31), they satisfy the Christian world with nothing but loading me with insults. And, so that they may seem to have some reason for the abuse they heap on me, they say: We pass over the insults that everywhere intrude, when he attributes impiety, buffoonery and other things to the Remonstrants, as the excrement of a man not quite sound in mind, and so on. In this matter it is clear that they speak against their own conscience. For I have dealt with them honourably, contrary to their deserts; although I have rightly ascribed impiety to their doctrine, and twice complained of their buffoonery. But these splendid men would wish to spread impious, blasphemous and accursed doctrines, and yet they would want no one to open his mouth against them or to say that they are impious. Thus it also appears, among other things, that in this chapter I have attributed nothing to the Arminians by calumny, since they deny none of the things I objected to them in it, except one, which I have shown more clearly than noonday light that they deny against their own conscience.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CAP. IX.

units.la: Examen Capitis Noni lib. 1. Vindiciarum.
units.tr: Examination of the Ninth Chapter of the first book of the Vindiciae.

units.la: 1. Arminianorum tergiversatio & confessio circa dubitationem suam de omniprælentiâ Dei. 2. Arminiani non negant se dubitare de præscientiâ Dei circa futura contingentia. 3. Eorum tergitergiversatio circa dubitatione de Spiritu S. adorando Αὐτοναται-ρεσία ipsorum in hac re; seu eos proprio ex ore suo falsitatis convictos in eâ esse. 4. Fatentur se dubitare an Christus Mediator adorandus sit secundum divinitatem an humanitatem, seu quomodo communicatus sit ei honor adorationis. 5. Fatentur se dubitare de gentilium honestorum statu post hanc vitam. Dubitatio Arminianorum illa qualis, quàm contumeliosa & blasphema sit ostenditur, 6. Fatentur se dubitare de fine principali adventus Christi in carnem. 7. Fatentur se dubitare de octodecim & pluribus aliis dogmatis, quæ Orthodoxi contra Socinianos tuentur. 8. Respondetur effugiis tribus Arminianorum, quibus conantur evincere, etsi dubitent de illis dogmatis, tamen se Pyrrhonismum seu ἐποχὴν non invehere velle in Ecclesiam. Iohannis Philoponi Tritheita hæresis renovata à Socinianis & Arminianis. 9. Dissimilitudo dubitationis Orthodoxorum & Arminianorum.
units.tr: 1. Arminian evasion and admission concerning their doubt about the omnipresence of God. 2. The Arminians do not deny that they doubt the foreknowledge of God concerning future contingent things. 3. Their evasion concerning doubt about the adoration of the Holy Spirit. Their self-choice [Αὐτοναιρεσία] in this matter; that is, they are convicted of falsehood by their own mouth in it. 4. They admit that they doubt whether Christ the Mediator is to be adored according to his divinity or his humanity, that is, how the honour of adoration is communicated to him. 5. They admit that they doubt about the state of honourable Gentiles after this life. How such a doubt of the Arminians is shown to be insulting and blasphemous. 6. They admit that they doubt about the principal end of the coming of Christ in the flesh. 7. They admit that they doubt about eighteen and more other doctrines which the Orthodox defend against the Socinians. 8. An answer is given to three evasions of the Arminians, by which they try to prove that, even if they doubt those doctrines, they nevertheless do not wish to introduce Pyrrhonism or suspension of judgement [ἐποχή] into the Church. The Tritheism of John Philoponus, renewed by the Socinians and Arminians. 9. The difference between the doubt of the Orthodox and that of the Arminians.

units.la: CAPITE NONO Partis primæ Arcan. lib. 1.
units.tr: THE NINTH CHAPTER OF PART ONE OF THE ARCANA, BOOK 1.

units.la: 1. Capite Nono Partis primæ Arcan. lib. 1. ostenderam Theologos Arminianos non contentos, quod in genere dixerant licere dubitare de rebus fidei, seu judicium suum suspendere, ac in incerto hærere; etiam Praxi seu facto ipso id palàm fecisse. Idque in iis præsertim capitibus, quæ Ecclesiæ controversa sunt cum Antitrinitariis seu Socinianis. In his enim, cùm Ecclesia ex verbo Dei contra Hæreticos illos sentiat ac doceat, Arminiani malunt judicium suum suspendere quàm cum Ecclesiâ Dei adversum Hæreticos illos sentire. Ex quo manifestum fit unicuique, quo præcipuè fine & consilio doceant in genere Licere dubitare de rebus fidei; quia scilicet nolunt erronea & Hæretica dogmata Antitrinitariorum rejicere ac condemnare, sed malunt judicium suum, pro tempore quidem, suspendere.
units.tr: 1. In the ninth chapter of the first part of the Arcana, book 1, I had shown that the Arminian theologians were not content with having said in general that it is lawful to doubt the matters of faith, that is, to suspend one's judgement and remain in uncertainty; they had also openly done this in their practice and deeds. This was especially so in those chapters which the Church disputes with the Antitrinitarians or Socinians. For in these, since the Church teaches and holds according to the Word of God against those heretics, the Arminians prefer to suspend their judgement rather than to think with the Church of God against those heretics. From this it is plain to everyone for what chief purpose and intention they teach in general that it is lawful to doubt the matters of faith: namely, because they are unwilling to reject and condemn the erroneous and heretical doctrines of the Antitrinitarians, but prefer, for the present at least, to suspend their judgement.

units.la: Primò igitur objeceram, quòd circa doctrinam de Deo profitentur se dubitare; Anne Deus immensus & omnipræsens secundùm essentiam sit. Et dixeram eos in negativam partem cum Socinianis & Vorstio magis inclinare. Hic tergiversantur, & dicunt, falsum esse se in negativam partem magis inclinare; imò quia dicant in margine Apologiæ, se non negare Deum omnipræsentem esse secundùm essentiam significant (sunt verba eorum) se parti affirmativæ adhærere. Deinde se phrasi istâ secundùm essentiam tiam tiam non denotasse rem, sed modu rei h. e. atomicum & atopicum divinæ præsentiæ modum in spaciis omnibus etiā imaginariis. 3. per vocem ubiq; non tàm designare voluisse cœlum ac terram, quàm spatia imaginaria omnia quæ extra cœlum & terram sunt. 4. Remonstrantes in isto loco, inquiunt, non profitentur se suspendere judicium suum de rei veritate, sed de rei credendæ, id est, de modi istius præsentiæ atomici credendi necessitate. Ita illi. Verùm enim verò in his omnibus tergiversantur Arminiani contra conscientiam suam. Nam quod ad primum attinet, sciunt se in Apologiâ argumentis variis ita reddere causam cur non assentiantur affirmativæ parti, ut simul eam vehementissimo conatu ac variis argumentis oppugnent, contra negativam autem ne verbulum quidem proferant. Estne hoc adhærere parti affirmativæ; an verò inclinare in negativam? Iudicet unusquisque, an qui ex duobus enunciatis seu dogmatis contrariis affirmativam oppugnat, negativam autem non oppugnat, in affirmativam partem an negativam inclinet? & an'non Arminiani manifestè hic hominibus illudant? Quod ajunt, se non negasse affirmativam, ex eo non sequitur eos adhærere affirmativæ. Nam ut quis adhæreat parti affirmativæ, non sufficit ut non neget, & interim argumentis eam oppugnet; sed requiritur ut eam affirmet, & contrariam neget. Deinde, ut non negant affirmativam, ita non negant etiam contrariam. Quod ad secundum, tertium, & quartum attinet, nòrunt se in Apologiâ suâ conceptis verbis profiteri, se dubitare, an'ne Deus secundùm essentiâ (id quod hic, ut & in Apologiâ, vocant, non ex nostrâ doctrinâ, sed ex eâdem suâ profanitate ac petulantiâ quâ Electos filios Dei filios albæ gallinæ vocant, atomicum & atopicum divinæ præsentiæ modum in spaciis omnibus etiā imaginariis) in cœlo & in terrâ & ubivis præsens sit, adeóq; de rei veritate, non autè credendi absolutâ ad salutem necessitate loquutos esse. Ne quis dubitet, etsi me pigeat laboris illius, tamè verba Apologiæ adscribam. Ita enim c.2.f.42.b. Nec enim usquam in Scripturis legitur, Deum secundùm essentiam suam ubiq; esse, nedum Deum secundùm essentiam suâ esse extra cœlu & terram in spatiis omnibus etiam imaginariis. Remonstrantes cum Scriptura & ad Scripturæ formulâ, divinam omnipræsentiam agnoverunt, modum præsentiæ, utpote sibi incomprehensibilē & in Scriptura non expressum, definire non fuerunt ausi; rati sufficere, si intra Scripturæ locutionem starent, & ab intricatis scholarum litibus, de hoc præsentiæ modo in totū abstinerent, aut professione ignorantiæ sese subducerent. Nec mirum: usque adeò involuta & implicata est reddita lis hæc, ut vix quisquam bene sanus homo sub sole sit, qui postquàm omnia ad eam pertinentia acerrimè excussit, ita ut nihil ad decisionem faciendam reliquum fecisse videatur, tandem tamen fateri non debeat sibi deveniendum esse ad ingenuam istam voculam Nescio. Evanescit in concipiendo, nedum in ratiocinando mens, & gurgite difficultatum absorberi se sentit, ubi in quaestionis istius adyta penetrare incipit. Et bone Deus! quis atopicam & atomicam istam essentiam divina & personarum trium divinarum praesentiam, non dico tantum in coelo & terra, in cloacis, in idolis foedissimis, in diabolis, in inferno ipso; sed extra coelum & terram in spatiis etiam imaginariis, qua non constat ullam esse, & qua fingi necesse est, & ficta quid sint, intelligi non potest, sic comprehendit, ut non haereat, non stupeat, non tremat, non horreat? Quis ista cum dicit, intelligit? Ab istis sane facilis prolapsus est in Atheismum. Nam juxta illam thesin, sequitur hoc axioma: Quicquid est, id est Deus & essentia divina: Si quid aliud statuitur, quod Deus non est, atomica Dei praesentia laborat. Quod si qui tamen sunt, qui aliter censent, aut tam firmo judicio, ut difficultates has omnes possint superare, fruantur judicio suo. Remonstrantes decisionem illam suam esse nolunt, aut saltem eam necessariam esse non credunt, vel hoc unico argumento adducti, quod Scriptura eam nusquam faciat, idcirco malunt Deo eam relinquere & futuro isti seculo, in quo videbunt Deum sicuti est. Nescire liceat, qua non nisi periculose creduntur, & cum subtilitate summa disceptantur.
units.tr: First, then, I had objected that concerning the doctrine of God they profess that they doubt whether God is immense and omnipresent according to his essence. I had said that on this question they lean more towards the negative side with the Socinians and Vorstius. Here they evade, and say that it is false that they lean more towards the negative side; indeed, because they say in the margin of the Apologia that they do not deny that God is omnipresent according to his essence (these are their words), they signify that they adhere to the affirmative part. Then they say that by the phrase according to his essence they did not mean the thing, but the mode of the thing, that is, the atomic and atopic mode of the divine presence in all spaces, even imaginary ones. Third, by the word everywhere they wished to designate not so much heaven and earth as all the imaginary spaces which are outside heaven and earth. Fourth, they say, the Remonstrants in that place do not profess that they suspend their judgement about the truth of the thing, but about the necessity of believing the thing, that is, about the necessity of believing this atomic mode of presence. So they. But in truth, in all these points the Arminians evade against their own conscience. For as to the first point, they know that in their Apologia they so give their reason, by various arguments, for not assenting to the affirmative part, that at the same time they attack it with the greatest effort and with various arguments, while against the negative they do not utter even a word. Is this to adhere to the affirmative part, or rather to lean towards the negative? Let everyone judge whether one who, of two contrary propositions or doctrines, attacks the affirmative and does not attack the negative, leans towards the affirmative or the negative part; and whether the Arminians are not here plainly mocking men. That they say they did not deny the affirmative does not follow from this that they adhere to the affirmative. For that someone adhere to the affirmative part, it is not enough that he does not deny it while attacking it with arguments; he must affirm it and deny the contrary. Further, as they do not deny the affirmative, so they do not deny the contrary either. As to the second, third and fourth points, they know that in their Apologia they professed in express words that they doubt whether God is present in heaven and on earth and everywhere according to his essence (which they here, as also in the Apologia, call, not from our doctrine but from the same profanity and wantonness with which they call the elect sons of God the sons of the white hen, the atomic and atopic mode of the divine presence in all spaces, even imaginary ones), and so they spoke about the truth of the thing, not about the absolute necessity of believing for salvation. Lest anyone doubt it, though I am weary of that labour, I will add the words of the Apologia. For thus, in chapter 2, folio 42, side b: For nowhere in the Scriptures is it read that God is everywhere according to his essence, much less that God according to his essence is outside heaven and earth in all spaces, even imaginary ones. The Remonstrants acknowledged the divine omnipresence with Scripture and in the wording of Scripture; they did not dare to define the mode of presence, since it is incomprehensible to them and not expressed in Scripture; they thought it sufficient if they kept within the language of Scripture, and abstained altogether from the intricate quarrels of the schools about this mode of presence, or withdrew from it by a profession of ignorance. Nor is this surprising: this dispute has been so involved and entangled that scarcely any sound-minded man under the sun, who has thoroughly examined everything pertaining to it, so that nothing seems left to be done for a decision, yet does not at last have to confess that he must come to that ingenuous little word I do not know. The mind vanishes in conceiving, much less in reasoning, and feels itself swallowed up in the whirlpool of difficulties when it begins to penetrate the sanctuaries of that question. And good God! Who understands that atopic and atomic essence and presence of the divine and of the three divine persons, not only in heaven and earth, in sewers, in most foul idols, in devils, in hell itself; but outside heaven and earth in imaginary spaces as well, which it is not agreed that there are, and which must be feigned, and it cannot be understood what things feigned are, so comprehends it as not to stick, not to be astonished, not to tremble, not to shudder? Who understands these things when he says them? Certainly from these there is an easy slide into atheism. For according to that thesis there follows this axiom: Whatever is, is God and divine essence; if anything else is posited which God is not, the atomic presence of God is in difficulty. But if there are some who think otherwise, or with so firm a judgement that they can overcome all these difficulties, let them enjoy their judgement. The Remonstrants do not wish to make that decision of theirs, or at least do not believe it necessary, being led by this single argument alone, that Scripture nowhere makes it; therefore they prefer to leave it to God and to that future age, in which they will see God as he is. Let it be permitted to be ignorant of what is believed only at risk, and disputed with the greatest subtlety.

units.la: Videt hic unusquisque eos primo quatuor argumentis ita reddere causam ἀτοχίας suae, ut simul manifestissime oppugnent affirmativam partem, & veram sententiam, nimirum Deum secundum essentiam immensum, adeoque ubique seu Omnipraesentem esse. Primum argumentum est, quia Scriptura nullibi dicat Deum secundum essentiam ubique esse. Secundum, quia controversia haec sit inextricabilis. Tertium, quia nemo atopicam & atomicam istam praesentiam Dei in cloacis &c. (ita describunt Omnipraesentiam & immensitatem Dei homines hi) sine tremore & horrore cogitare possit. Quartum quia exinde facilis prolapsus in Atheismum sit. Alia argumenta addunt in Resp. ad Excerp. p. 87. 88. 89. Quibus accedit, quod orthodoxam sententiam turpibus, spurcis, absurdis vocibus ac phrasibus a se confictis proferunt, ut horrorem & abominationem sententiae nostrae, quae est omnium qui Deum in tribus personis adorant, concilient. Est ne hoc adhaerere ei, an vero eam oppugnare, non solum animosissime, sed etiam improbissime & petulantissime? Ex his omnibus patet eos contra conscientiam suam hoc etiam loco tergiversari. Obiter hac occasione, quia dicunt exinde facilem prolapsum in Atheismum esse, addam, tantum abesse ut ex sententia Orthodoxa prolapsus in Atheismum fit, ut contra ex sententia contraria facilem prolapsum in Atheismum esse constet. Hoc vidit Arnobius ex Scriptoribus antiquissimis lib. 6. Hoc est enim proprium Deorum (utitur Arnobius plurali numero ad captum Ethnicorum quibus cum illi res est) complere omnia visua, non partiliter ubiam sed ubique esse totos; non adesse, non abesse, non coenatum ad Æthiopas pergere, & post dies bisfenos privatum ad domicilium redire. Quod si ita non erit, tollitur omnis spes opis, & erit in dubio audiamini a diis necne, si quando res sacras ceremoniarum conficitis &c. Hoc de primo dogmate.
units.tr: Here everyone sees that first, by four arguments, they so give their reason for their irresolution [ἀτοχία] that at the same time they most plainly attack the affirmative part and the true opinion, namely that God is immense according to his essence and therefore everywhere, that is, omnipresent. The first argument is that Scripture nowhere says that God is everywhere according to his essence. The second, that this controversy is inextricable. The third, that no one can think of that atopic and atomic presence of God in sewers, etc. (so these men describe the omnipresence and immensity of God) without trembling and horror. The fourth, that from this there is an easy slide into atheism. They add other arguments in the Response to the Excerpta, pages 87, 88, 89. To these is added that they express the orthodox opinion in base, filthy, absurd words and phrases of their own invention, so as to win horror and abomination for our opinion, which is that of all who adore God in three persons. Is this to adhere to it, or rather to attack it, not only most boldly but also most wickedly and wantonly? From all these things it is plain that in this place too they evade against their own conscience. Incidentally, on this occasion, since they say that there is an easy slide into atheism from this, I will add that it is so far from being the case that a slide into atheism follows from the Orthodox opinion, that on the contrary it is clear that an easy slide into atheism follows from the contrary opinion. Arnobius saw this among the most ancient writers, book 6: For it is the property of the gods (Arnobius uses the plural to suit the understanding of the heathens with whom he was dealing) to fill all things with their sight, to be present not partially in one place but wholly everywhere; not to be absent, not to go away to the Ethiopians for dinner and after twelve days return privately home. But if it is not so, all hope of help is taken away, and it will be doubtful whether you are heard by the gods or not, whenever you perform the sacred rites of ceremonies, etc. So much for the first doctrine.

units.la: 2. Secundò objeceram ipsis, eos circa eundem articulum de Deo, doctrinam de praescientia Dei respectu futurorum contingentium problematicam facere, dum disquiri permittunt, an ne necessarium sit scitu scientiam istam Deo competere? Hoc etiam non negant, & ne verbo quidem respondent, sed ne mentione quidem illius facta transiliunt, ac dicunt; secundum dogma esse de Adoratione Spiritus Sancti.
units.tr: 2. Secondly, I had objected to them that on the same article concerning God they make the doctrine of God's foreknowledge of future contingent things problematic, since they allow it to be debated whether it is necessary to know that this knowledge belongs to God. They do not deny this, nor do they answer a word to it. They skip over it without even mentioning it and say that the second dogma is concerning the Adoration of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: 3. Tertiò igitur ipsis objeceram eos adorationem Spiritus S. inter non necessaria habere & eam nec affirmare nec negare. Respondent primò, se ante ostendisse quam ineptus sit Coccyfmus hic. Verùm enim verò Arminiani in praecedentibus omnibus nihil dixerunt de hac re, quàm quòd dixerant capite 8. p. 46. 47. se argumentum ab adorationis cultu ad probandam Spiritus S. divinitatem non attulisse, ideò quia istud non sit firmum ac solidum cùm in Scripturis non sit mandatum aut exemplum de adorando Spiritu S. aut adorato in terminis: & postulaverunt ibi à me ut probem hanc minorem: Atqui Spiritui S. debetur adorationis cultus ex praecepto divino, aut cultus adorationis ei tributus legitur in Scripturis. Estne hoc ostendere me ineptire? Deinde dicunt me falsum dicere: Nam, inquiunt, Remonstrantes Spiritum S. adorandum esse aperte profitentur, quia Deus est. Deitatem enim ejus probárunt tribus argumentis. Sed negant argumento isto se uti posse; Adorandus est Ergo est Deus. Quia antecedens argumenti istius nec praecepto nec exèplo ullo demonstrare possunt ex Scripturâ. Vide optime Lector proterviam horum hominum. Aiunt se affirmare Spiritum S. esse adorandum. Estne hoc affirmare Spiritum S. adorandum esse; quando dicunt: De Spiritu S. adorando ne hilum quidem in Scripturâ esse. De Patre, inquiunt, & Filio adorando Scriptura plena est: DE SPIRITUS. NE HILUM QUIDEM. Apol. c. 3. f. 51. b. & f. 51. a. dicunt: Adorationis Spiritus S. nullum mandatum, exemplum aut INDICIUM aliquod manifestum in Scriptura esse. Quod magis est, non solùm illius nullum manifestum indicium, sed ne indicium quidem aliquod in Scripturâ esse dicunt in Resp. ad Excerp. p. 50. Deinde esto, dixerint Remonstrantes indicium nullum esse, & vox Manifestum omittatur, dent itaque Doctores indicium aliquod ex Scripturis unde id liqueat. Nihil equidem gratius fecerint Remonstrantibus, qui illud hactenus reperire aut deprehendere, licet summo studio adnixi, non potuerunt. Neque enim id propterea negant à se repertum esse, quia illud studio ac dedita opera observare noluerunt, ut sic dogmatis de Trinitate autoritatem elevarent; sed quia id adhibita omni diligentia observare non potuerunt, gratulaturi sibi si illud reperirent, aut ab aliis repertum offerri sibi viderent. Atqui, inquiet Magister Episcopius, aut alius istius exedrae, Remonstrantes hic aperte profitentur Spiritum S. adorandum esse, quia Deus est.
