Respondeo 1. ex hoc non sequitur me falsum dixisse, sed eos in hac parte αὐτοκαλαχρῖτας esse, & è suo proprio ore convictos falsitatis, in eo quod in Apol. dicunt, item in Resp. ad Excerp. ne hilum quidem de adorando Spiritu S. in Scriptura esse; Item; nullum omnino indicium illius rei in Scriptura esse. Nam si Scriptura dicit Spiritum S. esse Deum, ut fatentur Arminiani, certè etiam Scriptura dicit Spiritum S. esse adorandum; quandoquidem expressum est mandatum in Scriptura Dominum Deum tuum adorabis, & illi soli servies. Deut. 6. 13. c. 10. 20. Matth. 4. 10. 2. dicunt hic se aperte profiteri Spiritum S. esse adorandum, & tamen in hoc ipso loco Vindiciarum immediatè subjiciunt: Sed negant Remonstrantes argumento isto se uti posse: Adorandus est Spiritus S. Ergo est Deus: quia antecedens argumenti istius nec praecepto nec exemplo ullo demonstrare possunt ex Scriptura. Item in hoc eodem capite Vindic. p. 54. negant hoc antecedens, Spiritus S. est adorandus, ex Scriptura solidè probari posse, & jubent me si vir sim illud probare: Da, inquiunt, hujus minoris probationem si vir es, & viceris si vel hilum dederis. Quid? estne hoc aperte profiteri, Spiritum S. adorandum esse, & tamen simul audere dicere: se nec praecepto nec exemplo ullo demonstrare posse ex Scriptura sacra eum adorandum esse, & solidè id probari non posse? Igitur Spiritus S. adoratur & adoratus fuit ab Ecclesia sine ullo praecepto aut exemplo Scripturae sacrae. Qualis est ille cultus, qualis illa Religio, cujus nec praeceptum nec exemplum in Scriptura est; de quâ ne hilum quidem in eâ est? Annon talis cultus idololatricus est? Sed de hac re videatur etiam Par. II. lib. 1. Arcan. cap. 3. §. 1. & par. III. lib. 1. cap. 8. §. 1. & cap. 9. §. 2.
units.tr: 3. Thirdly, then, I had objected that they hold the adoration of the Holy Spirit among things not necessary, and neither affirm nor deny it. They reply first that they had already shown how inept this calumny is. But in fact the Arminians in all their earlier writings said nothing on this matter except what they had said in chapter 8, pp. 46–47: that they had not brought forward the argument from the worship of adoration to prove the divinity of the Holy Spirit, because it is not firm and solid, since Scripture contains no command or example of adoring the Holy Spirit, or of the Spirit being adored, in so many words. And there they demanded that I prove this minor premise: But worship of adoration is due to the Holy Spirit by divine precept, or worship of adoration is read of as given to him in Scripture. Is this to show that I am being inept? Next they say that I speak falsely. For, they say, the Remonstrants plainly profess that the Holy Spirit is to be adored, because he is God. For they have proved his Deity by three arguments. But they deny that they can use this argument: He is to be adored, therefore he is God; because they cannot demonstrate the antecedent of this argument from Scripture, either by precept or by any example. Note well, reader, the shamelessness of these men. They say they affirm that the Holy Spirit is to be adored. Is this affirming that the Holy Spirit is to be adored, when they say: there is not so much as a trace in Scripture of adoring the Holy Spirit? Of the Father, they say, and the Son, Scripture is full of adoring: OF THE SPIRIT, NOT SO MUCH AS A TRACE. Apology, ch. 3, fol. 51b and fol. 51a, they say: there is no command, example, or manifest INDICATION of the adoration of the Holy Spirit in Scripture. What is more, in the Reply to the Excerpta, p. 50, they say that there is not even any indication at all in Scripture of it, not merely no manifest one. Next, grant that the Remonstrants said there is no indication, and the word manifest is left out; let the teachers then give some indication from the Scriptures by which this may become clear. Indeed they would do the Remonstrants no greater favour than to find or detect it, though they have striven with the utmost zeal and not been able to. For they do not deny that it has been found by themselves because they were unwilling to look for it with care and deliberate effort, so as to undermine the authority of the doctrine of the Trinity; but because, though they applied every diligence, they could not observe it, and would rejoice if they found it, or saw it offered to them as found by others. But, the Magister Episcopius or some other man of that school will say, the Remonstrants here plainly profess that the Holy Spirit is to be adored, because he is God. I reply, first, that it does not follow from this that I have spoken falsely; rather, they are autokalachritai [αὐτοκαλαχρῖταί], convicted of falsehood out of their own mouths, in what they say in the Apology, and likewise in the Reply to the Excerpta: that there is not so much as a trace in Scripture of adoring the Holy Spirit; and again, that there is no indication at all of this in Scripture. For if Scripture says that the Holy Spirit is God, as the Arminians admit, then surely Scripture also says that the Holy Spirit is to be adored, since there is an express command in Scripture: You shall worship the Lord your God, and serve him alone. Deut. 6:13; 10:20; Matt. 4:10. Second, they say here that they plainly profess that the Holy Spirit is to be adored, and yet in this very passage of the Vindiciae they immediately add: But the Remonstrants deny that they can use this argument: The Holy Spirit is to be adored, therefore he is God; because they cannot demonstrate the antecedent of this argument from Scripture, either by precept or by any example. Likewise in the same chapter of the Vindiciae, p. 54, they deny that this antecedent, the Holy Spirit is to be adored, can be solidly proved from Scripture, and they bid me, if I am a man, to prove it: Give, they say, a proof of this minor premise, if you are a man, and you will win if you give even a trace of it. What then? Is this plainly professing that the Holy Spirit is to be adored, and yet at the same time daring to say that they cannot demonstrate from holy Scripture that he is to be adored, and that this cannot be solidly proved? Therefore the Holy Spirit is adored, and has been adored by the Church, without any precept or example of holy Scripture. What sort of worship, what sort of religion is this, of which there is neither precept nor example in Scripture, and of which there is not so much as a trace in it? Is not such worship idolatrous? But on this matter see also Part II, book 1 of the Arcana, ch. 3, §1, and Part III, book 1, ch. 8, §1, and ch. 9, §2.

units.la: 4. Quartum est circa articulum de persona & officio Christi: ubi profitentur se dubitare an Christus Mediator adorandus sit secundùm divinitatem an humanitatem? Non negant Arminiani, sed postquam inscitiae pus in faciem mihi pro sua solita maledicentia conjecissent, fatentur & persistunt stunt in eâ dubitatione, ac declarant se velle se medios tenere in hac re in pacis ac concordiæ gratiam inter Lutheranos, Calvinistas, & Pontificios. Quæ quidem mera hypocrisis est. Constat enim quid pacis & concordiæ prætextu moliantur; nimirùm introductionem Socinianarū blasphemiarum. Itaquè quod hoc loco faciunt, id faciunt in gratiam fratrum suorum secundùm Spiritum quo reguntur, nimirùm Antitrinitariorum seu Socinianorum apertorum, qui Christum quidem dicunt adorandum sed non secundùm divinam naturam, quam negant Christum habere, verùm quatenus homo est, seu secundùm eos, Deus factus, sine naturâ divinâ.
units.tr: 4. Fourth, on the article concerning the person and office of Christ, they profess that they doubt whether Christ the Mediator is to be adored according to his divinity or his humanity? The Arminians do not deny this. But after they had, in their accustomed slander, thrown the filth of ignorance in my face, they admit it and persist in this doubt, and declare that they wish to hold a middle course on this matter, for the sake of peace and concord among the Lutherans, the Calvinists, and the Papists. This is mere hypocrisy. For it is clear what they are aiming at under the pretext of peace and concord: namely, the introduction of Socinian blasphemies. Therefore what they do in this passage they do for the sake of their brothers according to the Spirit by whom they are governed, namely the open Antitrinitarians or Socinians, who indeed say that Christ is to be adored, but not according to the divine nature, which they deny that Christ has, but insofar as he is man, or, according to them, God made without a divine nature.

units.la: 5. Quintum est: quòd Arminiani profitentur se dubitare an' ne Gentiles qui rectâ rationis ductu virtutem sunt sectati & voluptatibus omnibus pro virili renunciarunt in salvandorum ordine sint collocandi? Hoc etiam fatentur; & persistunt in eâ ἐποχὴ seu dubitatione. Et quia ego cum omnibus Evangelicis contrarium teneo; quandoquidem ex verbo Dei constat, nemini salutem æternam conferri à Deo nisi cui ea promissa est; promissa est autem credentibus saltem & infantibus in fœdere gratiæ constitutis. Ob hanc itaque causam me, loco omnium eorum qui veram sententiam hanc contra Arminianorum ἐποχὴν tuentur, plaustris convitiorum onerant, Apollinem tortorem (h. e. Diabolum) vocant, me feram ac crudam animam habere dicunt, crudelissimum hominem appellant; in Busiridis, Phalaridis, Dionysii consortium relegant; me sic Deum non nisi trucem, crudelem, & Phalaride quovis immaniorem fingere, cui voluptè sit ad gloriam (horreo dum has hominum istorum blasphemias scribo) crudelitatis suæ æternis flammis inferni mancipare non adultos modò sed & infantes. Et eâ occasione in S. Hilarium meum manus injiciunt, ubi de gratiâ singulari Dei erga filios suos ago, & contrà de justo judicio Dei erga adultos infideles & infantes Gentilium, Turcarum, & aliorum extra fœdus gratiæ constitutorum. Dicunt me Hilaria celebrare, dum ista scribo, choreas fortè etiam ducturum inter infantium ejulantium & gementium strepitus, me mœrorem ac pudorem simul omnē fronti detersisse; Christianum pectus alienum esse ab istis damnationibus; eas Tyrannos & Neronas decere &c. Imò tandem planè me damnant & versum accinunt: Misselle Doctor, si tibi placet: Quare tuumque nomen Theta sectilis signet. Et hæc omnia tanto cum furore debacchantur; ut quasi extra se sint, & nesciant ubi sint, prout ipsi agnoscunt. Addunt enim: Quò abeo? Abripior justo dolore in diverticulum. Et postea probant hanc suam ἐποχὴν auctoritate Veterum & recentiorum quorundam, quos dicunt statuisse Gentiles virtute praeditos salvos esse. Id quod partim verum, partim falsum est: de quâ re in Rationali Theologico, quantum instituti nostri ratio postulabat egimus; ad quod Arminiani non nisi per convitia respondent.
units.tr: 5. Fifth, the Arminians profess that they doubt whether the Gentiles who, guided by right reason, have pursued virtue and renounced all pleasures as far as they could, are to be placed in the order of the saved? They also admit this, and persist in that epochē [ἐποχή], or suspension of judgment. And because I hold, with all the Evangelicals, the opposite view, since it is clear from the Word of God that eternal salvation is conferred by God on no one except those to whom it has been promised; and it is promised to believers, at least, and to infants who are placed in the covenant of grace. For this reason, instead of me, and of all those who defend this true view against the Arminian epochē, they load us with wagonloads of insults. They call me Apollo the torturer (that is, the Devil); they say I have a savage and cruel soul; they call me the most cruel of men; they banish me to the company of Busiris, Phalaris and Dionysius; they picture me as a God who is nothing but fierce, cruel, and more monstrous than any Phalaris, one who takes pleasure in the glory (I shudder as I write these blasphemies of those men) of his cruelty in consigning to eternal flames of hell not only adults but infants too. And on this occasion they lay their hands on my S. Hilarius, where I treat of God's singular grace toward his sons, and on the contrary of God's just judgment toward unbelieving adults and the infants of Gentiles, Turks, and others placed outside the covenant of grace. They say that while I write these things I am celebrating the Hilaria, and perhaps will even lead the dance amid the din of wailing and groaning infants, and that I have wiped every trace of grief and shame from my brow; that a Christian breast is alien to such condemnations; that such things befit tyrants and Neros, and so on. Indeed, at last they condemn me outright and sing me a verse: Off with you, Doctor, if you please: so let your name be marked with a sectile theta. And they rage with all this fury, so that, as they themselves acknowledge, they seem beside themselves and do not know where they are. For they add: Where am I going? I am dragged off by righteous grief into a digression. And afterwards they support this suspension of judgment of theirs by the authority of some of the ancients and of more recent writers, whom they say have held that virtuous Gentiles are saved. This is partly true and partly false; on this matter we have treated it, as far as the plan of our work required, in the Rational Theology; to which the Arminians reply only with insults.

units.la: Ex his tria haec manifesta fiunt. Primò, quia ob doctrinam, quae omnibus Evangelicis tàmReformatis quàm Lutheranis communis est, me istis horrendis convitiis petunt, ea non me concernere solùm sed omnes Evangelicos. Deinde qualis sit haec ἐποχὴ seu dubitatio Arminianorum; nimirùm talis, quâ statuunt, Deum trucem, crudelem & Phalaride quovis immaniorem esse, & cui volupe sit ad gloriam crudelitatis suae aeternis flammis infernî mancipare homines, si Gentiles & infantes extra foedus gratiae constituti salutem aeternam non consequantur. Item, Christianum pectus alienum esse ab istis damnationibus; eas Tyrannos decere. Judicet unusquisque, an hoc sit dubitare; an verò plusquàm asserere? Et exinde discat quales sint dubitationes Arminianorum circa dogmata Socinianis opposita? Habuimus capite praecedente simile exemplum, necnon aliud in hoc ipso capite §. 1. & rursus aliud §. 8. Unde manifestum est, Arminianos ore quidem prae se ferre se tantùm dubitare, reverà autem & ex animo Socinianorum sententiae circa ea addictos esse. Tertiò sequitur, in posterum neminem amplius mirari debere, eos doctrinam nostram de praedestinatione & annexis rejicere; eò quòd, sequatur exinde Deum Busiride, Phalaride & Tyranno quovis crudeliorem esse. Qui eam consequentiam blasphemam eliciunt ex doctrinâ non meâ solùm, sed omnium Evangelicorum circa Gentilium statum post hanc vitam: illos mirum non est, eandem ex doctrinâ Reformatorum de Praedestinatione elicere. Quod ipsum Veritati doctrinae nostrae circa Praedestinationem & annexos articulos; contra falsitatem opinionis Arminianae circa eosdem articulos testimonium reddit luculentissimum.
units.tr: From these things three points become plain. First, since they attack me with these horrible insults on account of a doctrine common to all Evangelicals, both Reformed and Lutheran, they show that these insults concern not me alone but all Evangelicals. Second, we see what kind of suspension of judgement or doubt this is among the Arminians. It is of this sort: they hold that God is grim, cruel, and more savage than any Phalaris, and that he delights to hand over men to the eternal flames of hell to the glory of his cruelty, if Gentiles and infants, who are placed outside the covenant of grace, do not obtain eternal salvation. Likewise, they hold that a Christian heart is alien to these damnations and that such things befit tyrants. Let each judge whether this is doubting or rather asserting. From this let them learn what the Arminians' doubts are like concerning the doctrines opposed to the Socinians. In the preceding chapter we had a similar example, and another in this same chapter, §1, and yet another in §8. From these it is clear that the Arminians, while outwardly professing that they only doubt, are in truth and from the heart devoted to the Socinian opinion on these matters. Third, it follows that from now on no one should wonder that they reject our doctrine of predestination and its connected articles, since, they say, it would follow that God is more cruel than Busiris, Phalaris, or any tyrant. Those who draw that blasphemous conclusion from my doctrine, and from the doctrine of all Evangelicals concerning the state of the Gentiles after this life, are not to be wondered at for drawing the same conclusion from the Reformers' doctrine of predestination. This very fact bears the most striking witness to the truth of our doctrine concerning predestination and its connected articles, and against the falsehood of the Arminian opinion on the same articles.

units.la: 6. Sextum est: Arminianos dubitare an finis adventus Christi in carnem principalis sit, ut Legislator esset, nec'ne? Fatentur; & dicunt se etiamnum de eâ re dubitare; & titivillitio non emtitare velle utrum dicatur. Idque praetextu hujus sophismatis; quòd non sit necessarium ad salutem ut sciamus, quid primo, quid secundo, quid tertio loco credi debeat? Quasi verò quaestio hic sit, quid primo, quid secundo aut tertio loco credi debeat! Quaestio hic est de fine principali adventus Christi in carnem, seu, ut terminos logicos omittamus, de officio Christi, an'ne Christus in mundum venerit ut rit ut mediator & redemtor; an vero ut potius Legislator noster esset? seu, Quomodo Christus in Evangelio se nobis offerat, an ut Redemtor qui pro nobis satisfecit, an vero ut Legislator prout eum Iusiitiarii ac speciatim Socinianì considerant. Magnum hic negocium agitur, & cardo vertitur fidei, spei ac salutis nostræ. Id Arminiani sophismate suo, de eo quod primo, secundo, tertio loco credi debeat (de quo quæstio non est) frustrà eludere conantur.
units.tr: 6. The sixth point is this: the Arminians doubt whether the principal purpose of Christ's coming in the flesh was that he might be a Lawgiver, or not? They confess this, and say they still doubt it, and they do not want to quibble over what is said. They pretend this is justified by this sophism: that it is not necessary for salvation that we know what should be believed first, what second, and what third? As if the question here were what should be believed first, second, or third! The question here concerns the principal purpose of Christ's coming in the flesh, or, to leave aside logical terms, concerns the office of Christ: did Christ come into the world as mediator and redeemer, or was he rather to be our Lawgiver? Or, how does Christ present himself to us in the Gospel: as Redeemer who satisfied for us, or as Lawgiver, as the legalists and especially the Socinians regard him? A great matter is at stake here, and the hinge of our faith, hope and salvation turns on it. The Arminians try in vain to evade this with their sophism about what should be believed first, second, or third, which is not the question at all.

units.la: 7. Reliqua quod attinet, (sunt autem simul omnia dogmata numero octodecim, & quidem dogmata maximi momenti,) non negant etiam se de iis dubitare, sed fatentur, & Lectorem remittunt ad Responsionem ad Excerpta. Fatentur autem in Apologia se alia plura ejus generis, quæ à Socinianis oppugnantur, habere de quibus dubitent, ut Parte primâ Arcanorum lib. 1. cap. 9. ostendimus.
units.tr: 7. As for the rest (and all together these are eighteen doctrines, and indeed doctrines of the greatest importance), they do not deny that they doubt them too, but they confess it, and they refer the reader to their Answer to the Excerpts. In their Apology they confess that they have several other doubts of this kind, which are attacked by the Socinians, as we showed in Part One of the Arcana, book 1, chapter 9.

units.la: 8. Tot ac tanta dogmata Socinianis oppositá cùm profiteantur se in dubium vocare, atque hoc modo tàm praxi quàm doctrinâ suâ alios dubitare doceant: audent tamen negare pag. 53. 54. se ἐποχὴν seu Pyrrhonismum (nam perinde mihi est quo nomine dubitationes suas & impietatem in hac parte insigniri velint) introducere in Ecclesiam. Idque hoc prætextu egregio scilicet, quòd non de omnibus articulis fidei dubitent. Respondeo: Sufficit, quòd docent licere in genere in dubium revocare dogmata controversa ut patet ex præcedente capite. Accedit quod de octodecim & pluribus aliis ut ipsi fatentur, dogmatibus dubitant; & præcipuè quod horrendum est; an'ne eadem numero corpora sint resurrectura? Quod revera est ipsam resurrectionem mortuorum in dubium vocare, ut rectè judicat magnus ille servus Dei Iohannes Calvinus Institut. III. c. 6. §. 7. Et certè vetus Ecclesia tota habuit pro articulo fundamentali Religionis & causâ simul cur mortem læti obirent Martyres. Quæ res adeò notoria fuit inter Christianos veteres, ut etiam ad Ethnicos pervaserit. Hi enim dicebant Christianos spe resurrectionis horum suorum corporum novam doctrinam invexisse. Unde, ut Christianos refutarent, & spem illorum falsam ostenderent, cineres Martyrum dissipabant & in fluvium projiciebant Lugduni & Viennæ in Galliâ, ut ostenderent corpora hæc exsurgere non posse ἵνα ὡς ἐλέγχον ἐκεῖνοι μηδὲ ἐλπίδα χώραν ἀναστάσεως, ἐΦ' ᾗ πεποιθότες ξένην τινὰ καὶ καινὴν εἰσάγουσιν θρη-σκείαν, ἣ καταφρονοῦσι τ᾽ δεινῶν &c. ut, quemadmodum ipsi quidem dicebant, Christiani nullam spem habere possent resurrectionis, quâ confisi nobis introducunt novam Religionem & tormenta contemnunt &c. Nitebantur enim hoc argumento, mento, quòd dissipatæ corporis partes, in cineres redactæ, & in fluvium dispersæ restitui non possent; prout Confessores Lugdunenses sub Aurelio Vero apud Eusebium testantur lib. 5. cap. 1.
units.tr: 8. Although they profess that they call into doubt so many and such great doctrines opposed by the Socinians, and in this way teach others to doubt both in practice and in doctrine, they nevertheless dare to deny, on pages 53 and 54, that they introduce into the Church suspension of judgement [ἐποχὴν], or Pyrrhonism (for it makes no difference to me by what name they wish their doubts and impiety in this respect to be designated). And they do so under this excellent pretext, namely that they do not doubt all the articles of faith. I answer: it is enough that they teach it is lawful in general to call controversial doctrines into doubt, as is clear from the preceding chapter. In addition, they doubt, as they themselves confess, eighteen doctrines and many others; and especially, and this is horrible, whether the same bodies in number will rise again? This is indeed to call into doubt the resurrection of the dead itself, as that great servant of God, John Calvin, rightly judges in the Institutes, book III, chapter 6, §7. And certainly the whole ancient Church held it as a fundamental article of religion, and at the same time as the reason why the martyrs died gladly. This matter was so well known among the ancient Christians that it even reached the pagans. For they said that the Christians had introduced a new doctrine through hope in the resurrection of these their bodies. Hence, in order to refute the Christians and show their hope to be false, they scattered the ashes of the martyrs and threw them into the river at Lyons and Vienne in Gaul, so as to show that these bodies could not rise: [ἵνα ὡς ἐλέγχον ἐκεῖνοι μηδὲ ἐλπίδα χώραν ἀναστάσεως, ἐΦ' ᾗ πεποιθότες ξένην τινὰ καὶ καινὴν εἰσάγουσιν θρη-σκείαν, ἣ καταφρονοῦσι τ᾽ δεινῶν &c.] so that, as they themselves said, the Christians could have no hope of resurrection, in which, trusting, they introduce a strange and new religion and despise torments, etc. For they relied on this argument, that the scattered parts of the body, reduced to ashes and dispersed into the river, could not be restored, as the Lyons confessors under Marcus Aurelius bear witness in Eusebius, book 5, chapter 1.

units.la: Porrò observetur hîc Arminianos in Respons. ad Excerpta D.D. Proff. Leydd. p. 121. ita ἐπιχὴν suam circa hoc dogma de Resurrectione horum ipsorum corporum probare tribus argumentis, ut simul aperte veritatem illius convellere studeant. Rei gravitas requirit ut ea argumenta videamus in gratiam eorum qui ex animo pietatem amant. Primum argumentum eorum est: Scriptura nihil de ea expresse definivit. At hoc falsum est. Nam ubicunque Scriptura resurrectionem corporis docet, indicat Hoc ipsum corpus resurrecturum. Alienum enim, quod nunquam fuit resurgere non potest. Inspiciant Arminiani inter alia caput 1. Cor. 15. quod totum expresse resurrectionem hujus corporis asserit. Et si quidem in terminis volunt sibi rem hanc monstrari; habent ibi non solùm vocem Resurrectionis quæ, ut diximus, non competit corpori quod nunquam fuit, & nunquam mortuum est, sed & v. 53.54. legere possunt Hoc ipsum corpus resurrecturum: Oportet corruptibile Hoc &c. Secundum argumentum est: Non laborare articulum Symboli sive hoc sive illud dicatur: aliud est, inquiunt, caro, aliud hæc caro. Et, ut probent non laborare articulum Symboli, consider, pie Lector, argumentum memorabile Spiritus Arminiani: Et evincitur, inquiunt, hoc ex eo, quia olim Origenistæ fatebantur nos resurrecturos cum corporibus carneis; at non cum his in quibus anima nostra nunc degit. Bone Deus, quam perversa ingenia! probare auctoritate & suffragio Hæreticorum qui Origenistæ vocabantur articulum Symboli manere etiamsi hæc caro non resurgere dicatur! Ex doctrinâ & opinione tali propter quam inter alias Origenistæ Hæreseos notati sunt, prout videre est apud Augustinum libro de Hæresibus hær. 43. (qui ideo dicit eos negâsse resurrectionem mortuorum) argumentum causæ luæ accersere, an non hoc est argumentum ex inferno petere? An non Arminianorum res eò jam rediit, quemadmodum re ipsâ palàm faciunt, ut, quia è Scripturis suam impietatem stabilire non possunt, eò recurrant quò ille apud Poëtam: Flectere si nequeo superos Acheronta movebo? Et hi homines tamen audent dicere me in sensum reprobum datum esse. Judica, Orbis Christiane, inter nos & illos homines. Tertium eorum argumentum petitum exinde est; quòd hac ratione uno veluti ictu ansa præcidatur innumeris non minus difficilibus, quàm curiosis, ineptisque quæstionibus, quæ APTÆ NATÆ sunt fidem & veritatem TOTIUS articuli de ResurResurrectione mortuorū P L A N E suspectum reddere. Pigetme refellere impium hoc argumentum, quo dicunt verā & fundamentalem doctrinam de Resurrectione hujus corporis A n s A m praebere impietatis h.e. atheismi. item quòd atheorum hominum & impiorū objectionibus tantùm deferunt, ut A p t a s N a t a s esse dicant &c. denique, quòd ob impietatem hominum non comprehendentium veritatem articuli hujus & eum oppugnantium, ipsius articuli veritatem convellunt. Et observa, quòd Arminiani unum ictum vocant hanc suam impietatem. At hic ictus, si quid roboris habet, aptus est totam Religionem Christianam evertere. Annon enim infideles, libertini, Athei quivis, ex Religionis Christianae articulo quovis putant se ansam habere eum oppugnandi? Vide rursus, optime Lector, cum quibus monstris res nobis sit.
units.tr: Furthermore, let it be noted here that the Arminians, in their Answer to the Excerpts of the Reverend Professors of Leiden, p. 121, so prove their suspension [ἐπιχὴν] concerning this doctrine of the resurrection of these very bodies by three arguments, that at the same time they openly strive to overturn its truth. The gravity of the matter requires that we look at these arguments for the sake of those who love piety from the heart. The first argument of theirs is: Scripture has not expressly defined anything about it. But this is false. For wherever Scripture teaches the resurrection of the body, it indicates that this very body will rise again. For what never existed cannot rise again. Let the Arminians look, among other places, at 1 Corinthians 15, which as a whole expressly asserts the resurrection of this body. And if they want this matter shown to them in express terms, they have there not only the word resurrection, which, as we said, does not apply to a body that never existed and never died, but they can also read in verses 53 and 54 that this very body will rise again: This corruptible must put on… The second argument is: It does not affect an article of the Creed whether this or that is said: they say, flesh is one thing, this flesh another. And, to prove that it does not affect an article of the Creed, consider, pious reader, the memorable argument of the Arminian spirit: And it is proved, they say, from this, that the Origenists of old confessed that we shall rise with fleshly bodies, but not with those in which our soul now dwells. Good God, what perverse minds! To prove by the authority and support of heretics who were called Origenists that an article of the Creed remains even if it is said that this flesh will not rise! Are we to draw an argument for our cause from a doctrine and opinion of this sort, on account of which the Origenists were among others marked as heretics, as may be seen in Augustine's book On Heresies, heresy 43 (where he says that they denied the resurrection of the dead)? Is this not to seek an argument from hell? Has not the Arminians' affair by now come to this, as they plainly show in fact, that, because they cannot establish their impiety from the Scriptures, they resort to where that line of the poet leads: If I cannot bend the gods above, I will move Acheron? And yet these men dare to say that I have been given over to a reprobate mind. Judge, Christian world, between us and those men. Their third argument is drawn from this: that by this method, at one stroke as it were, a handle is cut off for countless questions no less difficult than curious and foolish, which are APTLY BORN to make the faith and truth of the WHOLE article of the resurrection of the dead PLAINLY suspect. Am I not troubled to refute this impious argument, by which they say that the true and fundamental doctrine of the resurrection of this body gives a HANDLE for impiety, that is, atheism; and also that they yield so much to the objections of godless and impious men that they say they are APT and BORN, and so on; and finally, that because of the impiety of men who do not grasp the truth of this article and attack it, they overturn the truth of the article itself? And observe that the Arminians call this their impiety one stroke. But this stroke, if it has any force, is fit to overthrow the whole Christian religion. For do not unbelievers, libertines, and atheists of every kind think they have a handle for attacking any article of the Christian religion? See again, excellent reader, with what monsters we have to deal.

units.la: Porrò, quia Arminiani his tribus argumentis convellunt veritatem articuli de Resurrectione h u i u s corporis, manifestum est eos in eâ re cum Socinianis ex inferis revocare haeresin non solùm modò memoratam Origenistarum, sed etiam Iohannis Philoponi Tritheitarum Coryphaei, qui sub Phoca Imperatore vixit, qui etiam veritatem hujus dogmatis oppugnavit, statuens non haec corpora resurrectura, sed Deum pro eis alia corpora creaturum, teste Nicephoro lib. 18. c. 47. Dicent Arminiani, se nihil statuere seu definire in hac re, ut & caeteris dogmatis. Sed hoc, inquam ego, est definire contra veritatem, quando eam argumentis oppugnant. Deinde veritatis divinae ea ratio hâc in parte est, quae ipsius Dei: Qui non est pro me, est contra me, ait Christus. Ita qui veritatem non agnoscit, is eam oppugnat. Veritatis divinae ea ratio est, ut perinde sit sive opprimas eam sive suppriimas. Utrobique ἀπιστία est seu infidelitas, sive in dubium voces sive neges quod Deus verum esse pronunciavit.
units.tr: Furthermore, since the Arminians attack the truth of the article on the resurrection of this body by these three arguments, it is plain that in this matter they are reviving, together with the Socinians, not only the heresy of the Origenists already mentioned, but also that of John Philoponus, the leader of the Tritheites, who lived under the emperor Phocas. He too attacked the truth of this doctrine, holding that these bodies would not rise again, but that God would create other bodies for them, as Nicephorus testifies, book 18, chapter 47. The Arminians will say that they lay down and define nothing in this matter, as in their other doctrines. But this, I say, is to define against the truth when they attack it with arguments. Moreover, the manner of dealing with divine truth is the same in this respect as God's own: "He who is not for me is against me," says Christ. So whoever does not acknowledge the truth opposes it. The rule for divine truth is that it makes no difference whether you suppress it or oppress it. In either case there is ἀπιστία [unbelief], that is, infidelity, whether you call into doubt or deny what God has declared to be true.

units.la: 9. Secundus praetextus Arminianorum est p. 53. 54. Si de quibusdam dubitare est Pyrrhonismus, quotus quisque Doctor erit qui ad Pyrrhoniorum familiam non pertinebit? quis est quem non aut fugiat aliquando aliquid aut fallat? Dubitationem omnem calumniari, est convitium facere mortalitati. Respondeo: Hoc ad rem non facit. Primò enim Orthodoxi Doctores etiam dubitare, imò ignorare se multa fatentur, ea praesertim quae in verbo Dei non sunt revelata, de quibus verum est quod Augustinus ait de Genesi ad lit. lib. 8. c. 9. praestat dubitare de occultis, quàm litigare de incertis. At nemo eorum dubitat de dogmatis fidei, & quidem tot ac tantis, quae cōtra hostes filii Dei h. e. Socinianos Ecclesia defendit. Sed contra faciunt Arminiani, qui dubitant, & profitentur se dubitare de istis tot ac tantis dogmatibus. Deinde, si Orthodoxus forte aliquis dubitet de dogmate aliquo; ille, si sapit, suas dubitationes non spargit in vulgus, non docet eas alios; sed Augustini consilium sequitur, dicentis: Qua vera esse perspexeris tene, & Ecclesiae Catholicae tribue; qua falsa, respue; qua dubia crede, donec aut respuenda esse, aut vera esse, aut semper credenda esse vel ratio doceat, vel praecipiat authoritas. de vera Relig. c. 10. Quod si forte fiat, ut quis de pluribus dogmatibus orthodoxis dubitet, ille sequi debet ejusdem Augustini exemplum, qui cum dubitaret de dogmatis controversis inter Orthodoxos & Manichaeos, non obiit docentis partes in Ecclesia, sed salte discipulum se praebuit diligentem & attentum auditorem Ambrosii, ut ipse testatur Confession. lib 6. cap. 3. At Arminiani contra faciunt; nam & dubitationibus suis impiis alios inficiunt, spargendo eas in vulgus; & cum de tot ac tantis dogmatibus dubitent, non intra discipulorum subsellia se continent, sed docendi officium, (quo a Magistratu privati sunt jure merito ut totus Orbis hodie manifeste videt) usurpant in Ecclesia; imo omnes alios Orthodoxos Doctores vivos & mortuos, qui ab ipsis dissentiunt, inscitiae, ignorantiae, erroris cum summa maledicentia & improbitate arguunt, totius Ecclesiae veteris judicium contra Antitrinitarios non curant, sed contemnunt; eos qui in Ecclesia docent & se ipsorum detestandis conatibus opponunt pro stupidis, bardis, bestiis habent, saepe etiam eos quorum non digni sunt vultus intueri. In summa nulla unquam sub coelo secta adeo arrogans & insolens fuit, quam hujus secta ministri sunt, quos tamen tantum eruditionis quam modestiae & pietatis habere vel ex hac Quarta Parte Arcanorum manifestissimum est. Denique Arminianorum dubitationes illae quid producunt boni? aut quid in illis solidi, quid acuminis est? Nihil profecto habent aliud quam τὰ ἐρεῖστικὸν seu sophisticam contentionem, quod etiam rusticus facere posset ut appositè Socrates de Aetii Haeretici Antitrinitarii disputandi genere loquitur, qui, cum solide & piae eruditionis nihil haberet, τὰ ἐρεῖστικὸν κατωρθω- μένον, ὅπερ ἂν ἐκ ἀγροικὸς τις πιθανὸν ἐν. dubia salte & contentiones movebat, quod etiam rusticus facile facere posset lib. 2. cap. 28. Haec de secundo praetextu.
units.tr: 9. The second pretext of the Arminians is at pp. 53, 54: If to doubt about certain matters is Pyrrhonism, how many teachers will there be who do not belong to the family of the Pyrrhonists? Who is there whom something does not at some time escape, or who does not make a mistake? To call every doubt into question is to cast reproach upon mortality. I answer: this has nothing to do with the matter. First, the orthodox teachers themselves confess that they doubt, indeed that they do not know, many things, especially those that have not been revealed in the Word of God, concerning which what Augustine says in his book on Genesis literally, book 8, chapter 9, is true: it is better to doubt about hidden things than to quarrel about uncertain ones. But none of them doubts the dogmas of the faith, and indeed so many and so great ones, which the Church defends against the enemies of the Son of God, that is, the Socinians. Yet the Arminians act contrary to this, for they doubt, and profess that they doubt, these so many and so great dogmas. Next, if some orthodox person happens to doubt some doctrine, he, if he is wise, does not spread his doubts abroad among the people, nor teach them to others; rather he follows the counsel of Augustine, who says: What you have perceived to be true, hold, and ascribe to the Catholic Church; what is false, reject; what is doubtful, believe until either reason teaches or authority commands that it is to be rejected, or that it is true, or that it is always to be believed. On True Religion, chapter 10. But if it happens that someone doubts several orthodox doctrines, he ought to follow the same Augustine's example, who, although he doubted the doctrines disputed between the orthodox and the Manichaeans, did not take on the role of a teacher in the Church, but at least showed himself a diligent disciple and attentive hearer of Ambrose, as he himself testifies in the Confessions, book 6, chapter 3. The Arminians, however, act otherwise: they infect others with their impious doubts, spreading them among the people; and although they doubt so many and so great doctrines, they do not keep themselves within the benches of the pupils, but assume the office of teaching in the Church, an office from which they have rightly been deprived by the magistrate, as the whole world now plainly sees. Indeed, they accuse all other orthodox teachers, living and dead, who dissent from them, of ignorance, unlearnedness and error, with great slander and wickedness; they disregard and despise the judgment of the whole ancient Church against the Antitrinitarians; those who teach in the Church and oppose their detestable attempts they hold to be stupid, boorish, and beasts, often even persons whose faces they are not worthy to look upon. In sum, no sect under heaven has ever been so arrogant and insolent as the ministers of this sect are, who nevertheless have as much of learning as of modesty and piety, which is most manifest even from this Fourth Part of the Arcana. Finally, what good do those Arminian doubts produce? Or what is solid or sharp in them? They have nothing at all but τὰ ἐρεῖστικὸν [the eristic art], that is, sophistical contention, which even a peasant could do, as Socrates aptly says of the manner of disputing of the Antitrinitarian heretic Aëtius, who, since he had nothing solid or of pious learning, τὰ ἐρεῖστικὸν κατωρθωμένον, ὅπερ ἂν ἐκ ἀγροικός τις πιθανὸν ἦν [the eristic art perfected, which a rustic could easily manage], but only raised doubts and quarrels, which even a peasant could easily do, book 2, chapter 28. So much for the second pretext.

units.la: Tertio ajunt: si de his dogmatibus non est dubitandum, probet Vedelius ea necessaria esse ad salutem. ibid. Quis non videt, quam inepta simul & impia sit Theologia Arminiana? Quasi scilicet tantum de illis, quae necessaria ad salutem sunt dubitare non liceat? Aut quasi causa propter quam aliquod dogma in dubium vocare non liceat, sit necessitas illius absoluta ad salutem? Cum causa illius propria & prima sit haec, quia est veritas divina, seu quia Dominus dixit, quia os Domini locutum est. Conclusionis loco videat æquus Lector, an Arminiani promisso suo steterint, an verò orbi illudant? Dixeram cap. 8. par. I. lib. 1. Arminianos judicium & fidem suam suspendere in pluribus gravissimi momenti controversiis. Respondent Arminiani cap. 8. & dicunt : id sequenti capite confutabitur. Estne hoc refutare, fateri omnia, nisi quòd ex octodecim accusationibus circa duo tantùm aliquantulùm, sed frustrà, tergiversantur?
units.tr: Third, they say: if one must not doubt these doctrines, let Vedelius prove that they are necessary to salvation. Ibid. Who does not see how both foolish and impious Arminian theology is? As if it were allowed to doubt only those things that are necessary to salvation! Or as if the reason for which it is not permitted to call some doctrine into question were the absolute necessity of that doctrine for salvation! Whereas its proper and primary cause is this: because it is divine truth, or because the Lord has said it, because the mouth of the Lord has spoken. By way of conclusion, let the fair reader see whether the Arminians have kept their promise, or whether they are mocking the world. I said in chapter 8, part I, book 1, that the Arminians suspend their judgment and faith in many controversies of the greatest weight. The Arminians reply in chapter 8 and say: This will be refuted in the following chapter. Is this to refute? To confess everything, except that, of the eighteen accusations, they wriggle out of two only somewhat, and that in vain?

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: Examen Capitis Decimi Vindic.
units.tr: Examination of the Tenth Chapter of the Vindication

units.la: 1. Arminiani non negant se docuisse cognitionem operum Dei non esse partem cultus divini; & argumentum pro vera sententia allatum sophisticè eludere conantur. 2. Distinctio de Necessitate dogmatum asserta contra sophisma ipsorum. 3. Diluuntur tredecim calumnia & falsitates Arminianorum quibus Reformatarum Ecclesiarum Doctores malignè gravant. Falsus & verus scopus Arminianorum.
units.tr: 1. The Arminians do not deny that they have taught that the knowledge of God's works is not part of divine worship, and they try to evade the argument brought for the true opinion by sophistry. 2. The distinction about the necessity of doctrines is maintained against their sophism. 3. Thirteen calumnies and falsehoods of the Arminians, with which they wrongly burden the teachers of the Reformed Churches, are refuted. The false and the true aim of the Arminians.

units.la: 1. CApite decimo objeceram, Arminianos docere : veram cognitionem Dei & illius operum non esse partem cultus Dei, sed tantum requisitum antecedens, quo etsi homo careat in illis omnibus quæ controversa sunt inter Christianos, tamen pius esse & salvari possit. Cùm tamen cognitio Dei in dogmatis quidem necessariis sit simpliciter necessaria ad salutem, & sic habeat absolutam necessitatem tàm medii quàm præcepti; in non necessariis autem sit necessaria necessitate absolutâ præcepti. Unde intuli hæc duo: primò, unumquemque facile jam intelligere posse quid sibi velint dum Theologiam suam dicunt esse practicam, nimirum eam quæ non requirit veram cognitionem DEI & operum illius in rebus controversis inter Christianos, seu veram cognitionem dogmatum controversorum, inter quæ tamen aliqua sunt ἁπλῶς necessaria ad salutem, modò credat promissionibus divinis, ea teneat quæ extra controversiam sunt inter Christianos, & mandata Dei observare studeat. Secundò, per consequens Arminianos imponere populis prætextu & specie pietatis, quam se docere præ se ferunt. Nam illi pietatem veram non profitentur aut docent qui magnam illius partem pedibus conculcant, dum docent hominem minem posse pie vivere & salvari sine cognitione verorum dogmatum controversorum, inter quae tamen aliqua sunt ἀπλῶς necessaria ad salutem; imò Haereticos negantes & oppugnantes ea pios esse, & salvos fieri &c.
units.tr: 1. In my tenth chapter I charged the Arminians with teaching that the true knowledge of God and of his works is not part of the worship of God, but only a prior requisite, which a man may lack in all those points that are disputed among Christians, and yet may be godly and be saved. Yet the knowledge of God, in the necessary doctrines, is simply necessary to salvation, and so has an absolute necessity both of means and of precept; but in the non-necessary doctrines it is necessary with the absolute necessity of precept. From this I drew two conclusions. First, anyone can now easily understand what they mean when they call their theology practical, namely that which does not require the true knowledge of God and of his works in the matters disputed among Christians, that is, the true knowledge of the disputed doctrines, among which some are simply [ἁπλῶς] necessary to salvation, provided a man believes the divine promises, holds what is beyond dispute among Christians, and takes care to observe God's commands. Second, consequently, the Arminians impose on the people under the pretext and appearance of godliness, which they profess to teach. For those do not profess or teach true godliness who trample underfoot a great part of it, while they teach that a man can live godly and be saved without knowledge of the true disputed doctrines, among which some are simply [ἁπλῶς] necessary to salvation; indeed, they hold that heretics who deny and attack these doctrines are godly and are saved, and so on.

units.la: Ad haec omnia antequam respondeant, fingunt se non intelligere quid mihi velim; cum tamen nihil clarius aut explicatius dici possit. Ego perspicuitati in omnibus libenter studeo, Arminianorum est ad instar omnium Haereticorum & Sophistarum sub verborum latibulis se involvere, ut, qui adversum eos disputat, plus laboris impendere necessum habeat in indaganda & penetranda fraudulenta mente illorum, quam in confutanda doctrina. Postea formant statum quaestionis: Contendit in hoc capite veram cognitionem Dei & operum ejus esse partem cultus Dei, non autem antecedens requisitum, & quidem quatenus cognitio illa opponitur studio bonorum operum. Hic quis non videt eos statum controversiae fraudulenter & mala fide proponere, ut ex collatione patet? Porro vocem opponitur adhibui significatione illa lata, qua etiam disparata seu diversa quae Logicorum filii vocant, opposita dicuntur: ut sensus sit cognitionem Dei contradistingui studio bonorum operum, seu distinctum esse ab eo, prout ibi loci ostendi.
units.tr: Before they answer all this, they pretend not to understand what I mean, although nothing could be stated more clearly or explicitly. I gladly strive for clarity in all things. It is the habit of all heretics and sophists, the Arminians included, to wrap themselves in the hiding-places of words, so that whoever disputes against them must spend more labour in searching out and penetrating their deceitful mind than in refuting their doctrine. Afterwards they frame the state of the question: He contends in this chapter that the true knowledge of God and of his works is part of the worship of God, and not a prior requisite, and indeed insofar as that knowledge is set over against the pursuit of good works. Who does not see here that they propose the state of the controversy fraudulently and in bad faith, as the comparison makes plain? Moreover, I used the word opposed in that broad sense in which things that are disparate or different, which the sons of the logicians call opposites, are said to be opposed; so the meaning is that the knowledge of God is distinguished from the pursuit of good works, or is distinct from it, as I showed in that place.

units.la: Inde respondere conantur; summa responsi illorum huc redit: Non negant se docuisse cognitionem veram Dei non esse partem cultus divini: & argumenta quae pro vera sententia attuli refutare volunt, & ut ea eludere possint, fingunt primo me sumere vocem cognitionis pro pura speculatione mentis, quae sit mera mentis passio, & contra hoc disputant p. 55. 56. Deinde quia vident se mihi injuriam facere (nam ipsi p. 57. dicunt objectionem sibi a me factam postulare alium sensum) fingunt p. 57. me vocem Cognitionis Dei sumere pro studio cognoscendi veritatem divinam, & contra hoc disputant p. 57. 58. Sed isthaec omnia ad rem non faciunt, & nihil aliud sunt quam sophistica contentio, ut accusationis veritatem effugiant, quam negare non audent. Nam vocem cognitionis Dei sumsi significatione illa ordinaria qua ipsi etiam utuntur in hoc capite p. 55. dum dicunt salutarem cognitionem Dei & operum illius. Dixi enim ego capite nono Par. I. Arc. lib. 1. p. 93. me intelligere cognitionem illam quae est prima pars fidei, quae fides primo est certa notitia atque assensus, deinde fiducia &c. Itaque per cognitionem intellexi nihil aliud, quam notitiam certam qua firmiter assentimur omnibus quae Deus nobis in verbo suo patefecit, ut Catechesis nostra loquitur in definitione fidei: dei: seu, verum de Deo sensum, & studium proficiendi ac crescendi magis ac magis in veritate divina, quâ significatione passim in Scripturâ sumitur. Itaque omnes istæ nugæ quibus Arminiani quatuor paginas complent impertinentes sunt.
units.tr: They then try to reply. The sum of their reply comes to this: they do not deny that they have taught that the true knowledge of God is not part of divine worship; and they wish to refute the arguments I have brought for the true opinion, and in order to evade them they pretend, first, that I take the word knowledge to mean the mere speculation of the mind, which is a bare passion of the mind, and against this they argue on pages 55 and 56. Then, because they see that they are doing me an injustice (for they themselves say on page 57 that the objection made by me demands another sense), they pretend on page 57 that I take the phrase knowledge of God to mean the pursuit of knowing divine truth, and they argue against this on pages 57 and 58. But all this has nothing to do with the matter; it is nothing but sophistical quarrelling, in order to escape the truth of the charge, which they dare not deny. For I took the word knowledge of God in that ordinary sense which they themselves also use in this chapter on page 55, where they speak of the saving knowledge of God and of his works. For I said in my ninth chapter of Part I of the Arminian controversy, book 1, page 93, that I understood that knowledge to be the first part of faith, which faith is first a sure knowledge and assent, then trust, etc. So by knowledge I understood nothing other than a certain knowledge by which we firmly assent to all that God has revealed to us in his word, as our Catechism speaks in its definition of faith; or the true sense of God, and the endeavour to advance and grow more and more in divine truth, in which sense it is commonly used in Scripture. So all those trifles with which the Arminians fill four pages are beside the point.

units.la: Manet igitur hæc veritas quam ostendi capite allegato ; nimirum: Arminianos docere in Apologiâ suâ veram cognitionem Dei & illius operum non esse partem cultus Dei, sed tantum requisitum antecedens, quo etsi homo careat in omnibus illis quæ controversa sunt inter Christianos, tamen pius esse & salvari possit; & per consequens Theologiam eorum Practicam impiam esse, & eos verbis prætexere & præ se ferre se pietatem docere, quam tamen revera nequaquam docent, quia bonam ejus partem pedibus conculcant doctrinâ illâ suâ de Cognitione Dei.
units.tr: Therefore the truth stands which I showed in the chapter cited, namely: that the Arminians teach in their Apology that the true knowledge of God and of his works is not part of the worship of God, but only a prior requisite, which a man may lack in all those points that are disputed among Christians, and yet may be godly and be saved; and consequently that their practical theology is ungodly, and that they cover it with words and profess to teach godliness, which in truth they by no means teach, because they trample underfoot a good part of it by their doctrine of the knowledge of God.

units.la: 2. Ex his jam etiam facilè dilui potest sophisma, quod nugis suis intexunt adversus id quod dixeram Cognitionem Dei esse necessariam sed diversimodè. Nam in dogmatis necessariis sive controversa illa sint, dicebam, sive non, simpliciter est Necessaria ad salutem, & sic absolutam habet necessitatem tàm medii quàm præcepti. In non necessariis autem non est necessaria necessitate absolutâ medii, sed tantum est necessaria necessitate absolutâ præcepti; ita ut quisq; eam inquirere teneatur, adeòque peccet si negligat, multò magis si eam oppugnet; & nemo dispensare possit contra istud mandatum, seu permittere alicui & licentiam dare sentiendi aut docendi contra id quod Deus de se & operibus suis revelavit.
units.tr: 2. From these things the sophism which they weave into their trifles against what I had said can now easily be dissolved: The knowledge of God is necessary, but in different ways. For in the necessary doctrines, whether those be disputed or not, I said, it is simply necessary to salvation, and so has an absolute necessity both of means and of precept. In the non-necessary doctrines, however, it is not necessary with the absolute necessity of means, but only with the absolute necessity of precept; so that everyone is bound to seek it, and so sins if he neglects it, much more if he attacks it; and no one can dispense with this command, or allow anyone or give him licence to think or teach against what God has revealed concerning himself and his works.

units.la: Hic utrumque membrum oppugnant. Et quidem priore loco posterius: Cùm non necessariorum, inquiunt, cognitionem necessariam esse dicit necessitate solâ præcepti & quidem necessitate absolutâ, quari potest quæ illa absoluta necessitas sit? an præcepti simpliciter, an præcepti sanciti comminatione mortis & promissione vitæ æternæ? Si hanc necessitatem intelligit, quomodo tùm præcepti hujus necessitas non est absoluta necessitas medii? Si istam &c. Respondeo: Quis non videt hos malè feriatos homines abuti otio suo? Quis enim unquam Evangelicus somniavit esse quoddâ præceptum Dei sine promissione & comminatione illâ? Nec tamen sequitur, si dogmata illa necessaria sint necessitate præcepti ita sanciti, illa fore necessaria necessitate absolutâ medii. Nam dogmata necessaria necessitate absolutâ medii, sunt, quorum contrarium si quis teneat, non potest salvari nisi iis renuntiet, seu ea deponat: Necessaria autem dogmata necessitate absolutâ præcepti sunt, quæ etsi Dominus propositurit in verbo suo adeòque ea teneri præceperit, ita ut nemo absque peccato ea negare aut oppugnare possit, tamen homo salvari potest, etsi iis dogmatis non renunciet seu ea non deponat, ac contrariam veritatem amplectatur. Salvatur autem non ita ut cum ista inobedientia cœlum ingrediatur, ( quod absurdum hîc p. 57. fingunt Arminiani ) nam in cœlum nihil impuri ingreditur, nec ullum mendacium; sed quia ei veniam peccatorum suorum omnium etiam sibi incognitorum Psalm. 19. 13. per veram fidem petenti, istud peccatum ob Christum non imputatur, id quod tollere peccatum Scriptura vocat.
units.tr: Here they attack both members. And indeed they attack the latter first: Since he says that the knowledge of the non-necessary doctrines is necessary by the necessity of precept alone, and indeed by absolute necessity, it may be asked what that absolute necessity is: is it of precept simply, or of precept sanctioned by the threat of death and the promise of eternal life? If he means the second, how is the necessity of this precept not an absolute necessity of means? If the first, etc. I answer: who does not see that these men, ill-occupied, abuse their leisure? For what evangelical has ever dreamed that there is any precept of God without promise and that threat? Nor does it follow, if those necessary doctrines are necessary by the necessity of a precept so sanctioned, that they will be necessary with the absolute necessity of means. For doctrines necessary with the absolute necessity of means are those whose contrary, if anyone holds it, he cannot be saved unless he renounces it, or gives it up. But doctrines necessary with the absolute necessity of precept are those which, although the Lord has set them forth in his word and so commanded that they are to be held, so that no one can deny or oppose them without sin, nevertheless a man can be saved even if he does not renounce those doctrines or give them up, and embraces the contrary truth. Yet he is not saved in such a way as to enter heaven with this disobedience (which the Arminians here, on page 57, falsely imagine as an absurdity), for nothing unclean enters heaven, nor any lie; but because, when he asks by true faith for forgiveness of all his sins, even those unknown to him (Psalm 19:13), that sin is not imputed to him on account of Christ, which Scripture calls taking away sin.

units.la: Alterum membrum quod attinet, ita sophisticantur : Cum necessariorum cognitionem necessariam esse asserit necessitate absoluta medii simul ac præcepti, tum necesse est ut cognitionem illam accipiat vel simpliciter atque absolute ut cognitio est (id est pura puta speculatio & passio, ut ipsi quidem loquuntur, mentis) vel prout significat studium ac laborem sedulum cognoscendi illa. Si hoc posteriore modo accipit, uti objectio facta postulat, tum quaero &c. Respondeo uno verbo, me neutro modo sumere; sed, ut dixi, pro ipsa notitia & firmo assensu una cū studio magis ac magis proficiendi in veritate agnita. Sic concidunt omnes nugæ ipsorum quas ibi proferunt. Videri etiam possunt quæ de his diximus Par. III. lib. 1. c. 10. ubi ad reliquam partem sophismatum ipsorum, tribus, quod ajunt, verbis respondimus.
units.tr: As for the second member, they argue sophistically: Since he asserts that the knowledge of necessary things is necessary with absolute necessity both as a means and as a precept, it must follow that this knowledge is received either simply and absolutely as knowledge (that is, as pure speculation and a passive state of the mind, as they themselves put it), or as signifying the earnest study and diligent labour of knowing those things. If he takes it in the latter sense, as the objection requires, then I ask, etc. I answer in one word that I take it in neither sense, but, as I have said, for the very knowledge itself and the firm assent, together with the effort to make ever greater progress in the truth once known. In this way all the trifles they put forward there collapse. The points I made about these matters in Part III, book 1, chapter 10, may also be consulted, where I answered the rest of their sophisms in three words, as they say.

units.la: 3. Conclusionis loco συλλογισμὸν instituunt ad populos plenam mendaciorum & calumniarum adversus doctrinam Ecclesiarum Reformatarum, & ne verbum quidem unicum verum dicunt paginis 59. 60. Calumnia enim est, nos divinam veritatem istâ contumelia afficere, quod CLARE proposita non sit in iis quæ ad æternam salutem animarum pertinent. Contrarium testantur ea quæ adversus Pontificios constanter disputamus, speciatim quæ cap. 8. hujus libri §. 1. à me dicta sunt secundùm receptam doctrinam in Ecclesiis nostris. Falsum est Reformationis caput in eo consistere, quòd dogmata omnia Necessaria ita clarè in Scripturâ proposita sint, ut sine CONTROVERSIA sint. Perspicuitas enim Scripturæ in alio consistit, ut supra ostendi. Calumnia est, nos homines inter incerta controversiarum fluctuare sinere sine spe exitus, aut indubitato remedii solatio. Verbum enim Dei nullam controversiam incertam esse finit, sed decidit & indicat quid verum quid falsum sit. Calumnia est nos opiniones nostras & conclusiones Magistrales nullâ sæpè ratione aut evidente consequentiâ nixas populo imprudenter obtrudere : Proponimus enim doctrinam verbi divini, & longe valere jubemus doctrinas quascunque & traditiones humanas. Calumnia est nos homines pios & Scripturarum reverentes suæ salutis ac pacis publicæ publicę studiosos damnare, persequi, gaudere tormentis eorum : Etenim, quantum ad nos attinet, verbum Dei sequimur, quod Hæreticis, speciatim Antitrinitariis apertis & simulatoribus anathema dicit, & docet iis non permittendum à Magistratu & Ecclesiâ ut venena sua in populos spargant. Calumnia est nos Theologiam totam Practicam in Speculativam transformare : Omnia Scripta nostra & omnia pulpita contra ipsos testantur.Calumnia est nos asserere Deum electos irresistibili vi trahere & tractos in immania scelera ac propudiosa quaelibet flagitia subinde ruentes revocare. Nam vocem Irresistibilis ipsis relinquimus, & docemus eos qui Christo per veram fidem insiti sunt, non posse non pie vivere, peccata abominari & odisse: Deum sanctificare sibi Ecclesiam, & jubere ut caveat sibi serio sedulo à peccato quocunque etiam ; quòd si autem infirmitate labantur filii Dei, & seriâ resipiscentiâ ad Deum redeant, Deum illos non æternùm perdere, sed veniam eis largiri ob meritum Iesu Christi, interim tamen castigare eos in hac vitâ gravissimè & sæpè exemplariter ; ac jubere ut flagitia ac scelera ab Ecclesia & Magistratu severè vindicentur ac puniantur. In eum finem etiam ministerium verbi in Ecclesiis nostris sonat, quod iram Dei & æternam condemnationem denunciat peccatoribus. Magistratum rogamus & per Deum exhortamur, ut puniat flagitia sine acceptione personarum. Scholas etiam habemus, in quibus juventus in pietate vera instituitur, & à vitiis ac flagitiis deterretur. Per consequens calumnia etiam est impudentissima, nos pulvillos axillis subdere, quibus homines securè indormiant cum salutis æternæ periculo. Non enim primò hominibus gratiam Dei proponimus, deinde justitiam : sed legem, justitiam & iram ipsius ob oculos illis ponimus, quò à peccatis caveant sub poenâ æternæ damnationis, & iræ Dei, quam etiam in hoc mundo contra peccatores in tertiam & quartam progeniem exserit. Inculcamus etiam beneficia praecepta à Deo, qua Spiritualia qua temporalia, quorum perpetua recordatio & sensus homines retinere debet in amore Dei & obedientiâ ipsis debitâ. Misericordiam autem & Electionis solatium non adhibemus nisi erga peccatores verè resipiscentes; nec dicimus eos qui impiè, flagitiosè, aut hypocriticè vivunt electos esse. Notam enim ac characterem Electionis esse bona opera ex verâ fide profecta, adeoque homines verè pios Electos esse dicimus. Calumnia adeóque etiam est, nos homines suspensos relinquere inter præcipitia desperationis aut securitatis. Nam adversus desperationem hominibus proponimus agnum Dei qui tollit peccata mundi; adversus securitatem Legislatorem & judicem Deum qui est ignis consumens; nec non Magistratus timorem, qui minister Dei est, vindex ad iram ei qui quod malum est fecerit. Calumnia etiam est, nos docere vel fingere Deum aut tàm prodigæ bonitatis, aut tàm rigidæ immanitatis esse, ut quenquam salvare velit sine sedulâ officii sui curâ, aut quenquam, nedum maximam hominum partem, perire velle sine propriâ suâ culpâ. Etenim hortamur omnes ut salutem suam procurent cum tremore, & Deum justum judicem esse qui neminem innocentem puniat. Calumnia est, nos velle haberi pro divinis oraculis ea quæ non sic revelata sint, ut sine manifestâ culpa ignorari aut in dubium vocari possint. Nam, ut verbum Dei in se & per se dogmata fidei perspicuè continet; ita qui ea non videt propriâ adeòque manifestâ sua culpa, cæcitate, negligentiâ, socordiâ, malitiâ non videt. Calumnia per consequens est, Reformatos Doctores jugum imponere hominibus, quod Deus sublatum esse vult, ac eos videri velle salutis hominum studiosos, interim famæ suæ tantùm velificari aut zelo suo abuti cum salutis populorum damno aut periculo, & totam laudabilis Reformationis gloriam imprudentia sua prostituere. Nam proponimus populis veritatem divinam, quæ humanum jugum non est, atque ex officii ratione hæresibus, erroribus, præsertim autem artibus & diabolicis conatibus Arminianorum; quò ita gloriam Dei & veritatis ipsius vindicemus, honorem æterni Filii Dei asseramus, laudabilem reformationem à labe hæreseum Socinianarum immunem præstemus; ab Ecclesiæ septis lupos & vulpeculas abarceamus; ne in perditionem à via salutis abducant per blasphemias suas populum quem Christus sanguine suo redemit; à Republica iram Dei avertamus; pacem in ea & Ecclesia conservemus; turbatam à simulatoribus Antitrinitariis rursus tranquillam, quantum in nobis est, reddamus; salutem denique nostram propriam procuremus. Postremò salsissimum est, Arminianorum scopum esse, ut ab hoc tàm ingenti periculo immunes præstent populos; ut Reformationi pristinum suum decus afferant, ut humeris hominū jugum istud eximant; & nullam aliam causamesse, inquiunt, quaRemonstrantes movet, & propter quam tot acerba odia & criminationes sustinent, huncque ipsum Doctorem tàm parùm sibi habent propitium. Nam per Dei gratiam extra periculum & jugum sunt populi, qui sibi ab Arminianis ministris cavent. Hi enim, non dicam Reformatà, sed totam Religione Christianam funditùs evertere laborant; prout non solùm ex eo patet, quòd nullum articulum fidei inconcussum & intemeratum reliquerunt; sed etiam ex detestandis dogmatis eorum quæ à me in Arcanis ipsorum prolata sunt. Quod dicunt, suæ doctrinæ scopum esse, ut populos ab æternâ perditione præservent; etiam salsissimum est. Nam scopus ipsorum est introducere blasphemias illas Turcicas Socinianorum contra S. S. Trinitatem, (quibus introductis seu admissis actum est de totâ Religione, & perinde est sive Christianus, sive Turca sive Iudæus sis) & omnia sursum deorsum vertere in Republicâ: ut ostendi parte secundâ Arcanorum. Ex quo etiam apparet, quæ sit illa Reformatio de quâ subinde hi Theologi gloriantur, cujus honorem se vindicatum & assertum cupere dicunt; nimirùm eadem Reformatio quam Socliniani profitentur & ubique præ se ferunt h. e. introductio idoli Antitrinitarii colendi loco unius veri & æterni Dei adorandi in tribus personis, qui non patietur sibi semper illudi ab his hominibus: Ex altera parte Reformatio Reipublicæ h. e. oppressio Reformatorum omnium cujuscunque status & conditionis sint: Hæc est duplex illa Reformatio quam hi homines moliuntur. Deus evertat molimina ipsorum. Atque hæc quidem etiam de isto decimo capite vindiciarum; ex quibus omnibus jam patet me etiam capite decimo Par. I. Arcan. injuriam nullam fecisse Arminianis, nec quicquam iis per calumniam improperâsse, quandoquidem ipsi fatentur se docere ea quæ illis in eo capite objeci.
units.tr: 3. As the conclusion of their argument they construct a syllogism [συλλογισμὸν], full of lies and calumnies against the doctrine of the Reformed Churches, and they do not say a single true word on pages 59 and 60. For it is a calumny to charge the divine truth with this insult, namely that it is not CLEARLY set forth in those matters that pertain to the eternal salvation of souls. The contrary is attested by what we constantly argue against the Papists, and especially by what I said in chapter 8, §1 of this book, in accordance with the doctrine received in our Churches. It is false that the chief point of the Reformation consists in this, that all necessary doctrines are set forth so clearly in Scripture that they are free from CONTROVERSY. For the perspicuity of Scripture consists in something else, as I showed above. It is a calumny to say that we allow people to be tossed about among uncertain controversies without hope of an outcome or the consolation of a sure remedy. For the Word of God does not allow any controversy to remain uncertain, but decides and shows what is true and what is false. It is a calumny that we impose on the people, often without any reason or evident consequence, our own opinions and magisterial conclusions. For we set forth the doctrine of the divine Word, and we bid all other doctrines and human traditions farewell. It is a calumny that we condemn, persecute, and take delight in the torments of pious men who respect the Scriptures and who are concerned for their own salvation and public peace. For, as far as we are concerned, we follow the Word of God, which pronounces anathema on heretics, especially on open and dissembling Antitrinitarians, and teaches that such people must not be permitted by the magistrate and the Church to spread their poisons among the people. It is a calumny that we transform the whole of practical theology into speculative theology. All our writings and all our pulpits bear witness against them. It is a calumny that we assert that God drags the elect with an irresistible force, and that, once dragged into monstrous crimes and shameful wickedness of any kind, they are called back again and again. For we leave the word irresistible to them, and we teach that those who have been grafted into Christ by true faith cannot but live piously, and abhor and hate sin; that God sanctifies the Church for himself and commands it to take earnest and diligent heed to itself against every sin; but if the children of God stumble through weakness and return to God by earnest repentance, God does not destroy them eternally, but grants them pardon for the merit of Jesus Christ, while nevertheless chastising them most severely and often exemplarily in this life; and that crimes and wickedness are to be severely avenged and punished by the Church and the magistrate. The ministry of the Word in our Churches also sounds to this end, for it denounces God's wrath and eternal condemnation upon sinners. We ask the magistrate and exhort him in God's name to punish crimes without respect of persons. We also have schools in which youth is trained in true piety and is deterred from vices and crimes. Consequently it is also a most shameless calumny that we place pillows under men's armpits on which they sleep soundly to the peril of eternal salvation. For we do not first set before men the grace of God and then righteousness; rather, we place before their eyes the law, righteousness, and God's wrath, so that they may beware of sins under the penalty of eternal damnation and of the wrath of God, which he also pours out in this world against sinners to the third and fourth generation. We also inculcate the benefits commanded by God, both spiritual and temporal, the perpetual remembrance and sense of which ought to keep men in the love of God and in the obedience owed to him. We do not, however, apply mercy and the comfort of election except to sinners who truly repent; nor do we say that those who live impiously, shamefully, or hypocritically are elect. For we say that the mark and character of election is good works proceeding from true faith, and so we say that men who are truly pious are elect. It is therefore also a calumny that we leave men hanging between the precipices of despair and security. For against despair we set before men the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world; against security we set God, the Lawgiver and Judge, who is a consuming fire; and likewise the fear of the magistrate, who is God's minister, an avenger for wrath upon him who does evil. It is a calumny also that we teach, or pretend, that God is either of such prodigal goodness or of such rigid cruelty that he wishes to save anyone without the diligent care of his duty, or wishes anyone, much less the greater part of mankind, to perish without their own fault. For we exhort everyone to work out their salvation with fear and trembling, and we teach that God is a just judge who punishes no innocent person. It is a calumny that we want to be regarded as divine oracles those things which have not been so revealed that they can be ignored or called in doubt without manifest fault. For just as the Word of God clearly contains in itself and by itself the doctrines of faith, so he who does not see them does not see them through his own, and therefore manifest, blindness, negligence, sloth, or malice. It is consequently a calumny that the Reformed teachers impose a yoke on men, which God wishes to be removed, and that they appear to wish to be zealous for men's salvation while in fact they only seek to advance their own reputation or abuse their zeal to the loss or danger of the people's salvation, and by their imprudence prostitute the whole glory of the praiseworthy Reformation. For we set before the people the divine truth, which is not a human yoke, and from a sense of duty we oppose heresies, errors, and especially the arts and diabolical endeavours of the Arminians; so that we may thereby vindicate the glory of God and of his truth, assert the honour of the eternal Son of God, provide a praiseworthy Reformation free from the stain of Socinian heresies; that we may keep wolves and foxes away from the fold of the Church, lest by their blasphemies they lead astray from the way of salvation the people whom Christ redeemed with his blood; that we may turn away God's wrath from the Commonwealth; that we may preserve peace in it and in the Church; that we may restore tranquillity, so far as lies in us, to what has been disturbed by dissembling Antitrinitarians; and finally that we may secure our own salvation. Lastly, it is most absurd to say that the aim of the Arminians is to keep the people free from so great a danger; to restore to the Reformation its former glory, and to lift this yoke from men's shoulders; and that there is no other cause, they say, which moves the Remonstrants, and on account of which they bear so many bitter hatreds and accusations, and hold this very Teacher in such little favour. For by the grace of God the people who beware of the Arminian ministers are outside the danger and the yoke. For these men, I will not say strive to overthrow the Reformed religion, but strive to overthrow the whole Christian religion from its foundations; and this is clear not only from the fact that they have left no article of faith unshaken and untouched, but also from the detestable doctrines of theirs which I have brought forward from their own Arcana. What they say, that the aim of their doctrine is to preserve the people from eternal perdition, is also most absurd. For their aim is to introduce those Turkish blasphemies of the Socinians against the most holy Trinity (once these are introduced or admitted, the whole of religion is at an end, and it makes no difference whether you are a Christian, a Turk, or a Jew), and to turn everything upside down in the Commonwealth, as I showed in the second part of the Arcana. From this it also appears what that Reformation is, of which these theologians from time to time boast, and whose honour they say they wish to be vindicated and asserted: namely, the very Reformation which the Socinians profess and openly display everywhere, that is, the introduction of an Antitrinitarian idol to be worshipped in place of the one true and eternal God who is to be adored in three persons, who will not allow himself to be always mocked by these men. On the other side, there is the Reformation of the Commonwealth, that is, the oppression of all Reformed people of whatever rank or condition they may be. This is that twofold Reformation which these men are striving for. May God overturn their schemes. And these things indeed concerning this tenth chapter of the defence; from all of which it is now clear that I did no injury to the Arminians even in chapter 10 of Part I of the Arcana, nor did I charge them with anything by calumny, since they themselves admit that they teach the things which I objected to them in that chapter.

units.la: FINIS LIBRI PRIMI.
units.tr: END OF THE FIRST BOOK.

units.la: ARCANORVM ARMINIANISMI Partis Quartæ LIBER SECUNDVS.
units.tr: THE FOURTH PART OF THE ARCANA OF ARMINIANISM: BOOK TWO

units.la: CAP. I. Examen Capitis primi lib. 2. Vindic.
units.tr: CHAPTER I. An Examination of Chapter 1 of Book 2 of the Vindiciae.

units.la: 1. ARMINIANI contra conscientiam suam negant, se in Apologia docere: Omnes cætus qui necessaria seu non controversa dogmata tenent, esse veram Ecclesiam. Item, Nullum cætum Christianum errare in Necessariis, sed eos cætus qui errant esse tantùm cætus impuros errantes in non Necessariis. 2. Arminiani contra conscientiam suam negant rursus, se docuisse in Apologia; Nulla dogmata controversa esse necessaria ad salutem; adeòque professionem doctrinæ non controversæ inter Christianos esse notam verè Ecclesiæ, quæ saltem indicet eam, non autem distinguat à falsâ. 3. An'ne Arminiani agnoscant aliquam Ecclesiam falsam; speciatim an'ne & quâ conscientiâ Reformatos habeant pro Ecclesiâ falsâ. 4. Arminiani fatentur se docere puram prædicationem verbi non esse notam veræ Ecclesiæ. Item: nullam esse notam propriè sic dictam veræ Ecclesiæ. inane effugium eorum circa scopum negativæ istius utriusque.
units.tr: 1. The Arminians deny, against their own conscience, that they teach in the Apology: all assemblies which hold the necessary or uncontroversial doctrines are the true Church. Likewise, that no Christian assembly errs in necessary matters, but that those assemblies which err are only impure assemblies erring in non-necessary matters. 2. The Arminians again deny, against their own conscience, that they taught in the Apology that no controversial doctrines are necessary to salvation, and so that the profession of uncontroversial doctrine among Christians is a mark of the true Church, which at least indicates it, but does not distinguish it from a false one. 3. Do the Arminians acknowledge any false Church; in particular, do they, and with what conscience, hold the Reformed to be a false Church? 4. The Arminians confess that they teach that the pure preaching of the Word is not a mark of the true Church. Likewise: that there is no mark properly so called of the true Church. A empty evasion of theirs concerning the aim of both these negative statements.

units.la: Apite primo libri secundi ostenderam Arminianos docere: Eos omnes cœtus Christianos esse veram Ecclesiam, qui non controversa inter Christianos dogmata tenent. Item: Nullum cœtum Christianum errare in Necessariis; sed eos cœtus qui errant, esse tantùm cœtus impuros errantes in non Necessariis. Ita Arminianos nos docere ostendi ex ipsorum doctrina de vera Ecclesia, collata cum dogmate, quo statuunt: Nulla dogmata controversa inter cœtus Christianos esse Necessaria ad salutem. Quid ad ista Arminiani? Negant p. 62. se ita docuisse: & quidem negant ex eo fundamento, quòd falsum sit Arminianos asseruisse; ea tantùm quæ extra controversiam sunt esse necessaria ad salutem. Et addunt: se credere multos cœtus Christianos errare in Necessariis.
units.tr: In the first part of the second book I had shown that the Arminians teach this: that all Christian assemblies which hold the doctrines not controverted among Christians are the true Church. Likewise: that no Christian assembly errs in necessary matters, but that those assemblies which err are only impure assemblies erring in non-necessary matters. I showed that the Arminians teach this from their own doctrine of the true Church, compared with the dogma by which they state: no controversial doctrines among Christian assemblies are necessary to salvation. What do the Arminians say to this? They deny, on p. 62, that they taught it. And indeed they deny it on the ground that it is false that the Arminians have asserted that only those things which are beyond controversy are necessary to salvation. And they add that they believe many Christian assemblies err in necessary matters.

units.la: 2. Verùm enim verò Arminiani negant illud contra propriam conscientiam, à qua convicti sunt se ita docere in Apologia & Responf. ad Excerp. ut ostendimus ampl่è, solidè, & perspicuè lib. 1. cap. 8. partis hujus Quartæ, Imò quod magis est, in Vindiciis suis eandem doctrinam reponunt, ut palàm fecimus Par. III. lib. 2. capit. 1.
