Nam obsequium subditorum Majestatem non facit, sed Majestatis jus &c. Alioquin Rex non esset Rex nisi subditi velint. Respondeo uno verbo, (nam tempus in his nugis terere nolo) non magis absurde dici Ecclesiam esse propter Christum, quàm Ecclesiam & omnes creaturas esse propter Deum, seu Deum omnia fecisse propter se ipsum Prov. 16. 4.
units.tr: 3. The second doctrine I had objected to them is this: "The kingdom of Christ can subsist even if all His subjects were seduced by His enemies, such as the heretics." They admit this, at p. 88, with their usual jeering, and at the start they harass what I said, that the Church was gathered by God not only for her own salvation but also for the sake of Christ's kingdom. By these words I indicated that God, who from eternity had decreed the kingdom for Christ the Mediator, had also decreed a people or subjects for Him, whom He Himself gathers. Nothing is truer than this. They attack it sophistically, first, on the ground that it is absurd to say "the Church gathers a kingdom for Christ." But I did not say this, nor do my words tend that way; rather I expressly said the contrary, namely that the Church is gathered by God; and so I ascribe the reign of Christ not to the Church but to God the Father. Second, they say, it will have to be said that the Church also exists on account of Christ, and not Christ only on account of the Church; and they call this absurd, (1) because in that case Christ and the Church would repay each other in turn, and each would owe the other reciprocal gratitude; (2) because subjects do not make a king: royal right does not depend on the will of the subjects; (3) because the people is not for the king, but the king for the people; (4) because royal majesty stands even if all the subjects rebel. They prove this: for the obedience of subjects does not make the majesty, but the right of majesty, etc. Otherwise a king would not be king unless the subjects wished it. I answer in one word (for I do not want to waste time on these trifles) that it is no more absurd to say the Church is for Christ than to say the Church and all creatures are for God, or that God made all things for Himself (Prov. 16:4).

units.la: Probationes ab ipsis allatae (ut jam de aliis ineptiis & falsitatibus quae in illis sunt nihil dicam) locum haberent, siquidem Ecclesiam statueremus causam efficientem Regni Christi, & siquidem Deus regnum tantum titulare & umbratile decrevisset Christo. Absurditas illa, quòd sic Regnum Christi à subditorum voluntate pendere dicatur, ipsorum Pelagianae sententiae competit, quâ statuunt gratiam efficacem determinari à voluntate humanâ, quòd profecto est Regnum Christi & ipsam voluntatem Dei voluntati humanae subjicere seu ab eâ suspendere.
units.tr: The arguments they have brought forward (not to mention the other silliness and falsehoods in their work) would hold, provided we held the Church to be the efficient cause of Christ's kingdom, and provided God had decreed for Christ only a titular and shadowy kingdom. That absurdity, that the kingdom of Christ is thus said to depend on the will of the subjects, belongs to their own Pelagian opinion, by which they hold that efficacious grace is determined by the human will; which indeed is to make the kingdom of Christ, and the very will of God, subject to the human will, or to hang upon it.

units.la: Post haec pag. 89. sophisticantur adversus id quod dixeram, respiciens ad verba Apostoli Ecclesiam esse columnam & firmamentum veritatis: dicuntque locum illum aliter legi & exponi posse, & in eâ re multas lineas inutiliter & nugatorie prodigunt. Nā ipsi statim subjiciunt: Esto tamen, Ecclesia tribuatur quod sit columna ac stabilimentum veritatis, dubium enim non est quin id sano sensu & recte accipi possit. Et sic approbant quod dixi. Quid igitur litigant? Sed ita volunt videri Vedelium refutasse.
units.tr: After this, at p. 89, they quibble against what I had said, looking to the words of the Apostle that the Church is the pillar and ground of the truth; and they say that this passage can be read and explained otherwise, and on this point they waste many lines to no purpose and in a trifling manner. For they immediately add: "Grant, however, that the Church is ascribed to be the pillar and stay of the truth; for there is no doubt it can be taken in a sound sense and rightly." And so they approve what I said. Why then do they quarrel? But they wish to appear to have refuted Vedel.

units.la: Inde relabuntur ad exagitandum quod dixeram Ecclesiam à Deo colligi etiam propter Regnum Christi. Et inquiunt: 1. nullum apicem esse in Scriptura sacra unde hoc vel verisimiliter concludi possit. 2. Scripturam docere; propter nos Iesum esse, non nos propter Iesum ut ille Rex sit. 3. Communis sententia est Regem propter populum esse, non populum propter Regem. 4. Concludunt: Sed prava & absurda ista opinio ex praedestinatione ista Calviniana oritur, quam ubique mordicus se tueri velle demonstrat Vedelius.
units.tr: Then they fall back to attacking what I had said, that the Church is gathered by God also for the sake of Christ's kingdom. And they say: (1) there is not a single trace in holy Scripture from which this could even probably be concluded; (2) Scripture teaches that Jesus is for us, not that we are for Jesus, so that He may be King; (3) the common opinion is that the king is for the people, not the people for the king; (4) they conclude: but this false and absurd opinion arises from that Calvinistic predestination, which Vedel demonstrates he wishes to defend everywhere with teeth and nails.

units.la: Respondeo ad. 1. Falsum illud esse. Nam quaero an nullus apex in Scriptura sit, qui Christum Mediatorem Regem vocet? Si hoc, quaero, an'non Deus decreverit ut Christus Rex esset ? Si hoc, quæro an'non etiam ei subditos decreverit colligere, adeoque decretum istud suum de Regno Christi effectui dare ? Hoc enim est quod volo, dum dico Ecclesiam esse propter Regnum Christi. Unde etiam secundum sophisma corruit. Tertium quod attinet; certè M. Episcopius si solidæ Philosophiæ aliquid haberet, nôsset illud dictum secundùm quid non autem simpliciter accipiendum esse. Nôrunt enim vel pueri logici, Relatorum unum esse propter alterum, seu ea se mutuò ponere & tollere. Ad quartum dico, doctrinam nostram illam ex verbo Dei fluere, quæ nos de Decretis Dei & eorum executione rectè sentire docet. Contraria autem Arminianorum sententia ex Pelagianismo ipsorum fluit, quo Dei decretum & gratiam à voluntate humanâ determinari cum veteribus Pelagianis statuunt.
units.tr: I answer to (1) that this is false. For I ask whether there is no trace in Scripture which calls Christ Mediator and King? If so, I ask, has not God decreed that Christ should be King? If so, I ask, has He not also decreed to gather subjects for Him, and so given effect to that decree of His concerning Christ's kingdom? For this is what I mean when I say the Church is for the sake of Christ's kingdom. Hence the second sophism also falls. As for the third point: certainly, if Master Episcopius had any solid grounding in philosophy, he would know that the saying is to be taken in a qualified sense and not absolutely. For even schoolboys of logic know that of relatives one is for the other, or that they mutually posit and remove each other. To the fourth I say that our doctrine, which teaches us to think rightly of God's decrees and their execution, flows from the Word of God; but the contrary opinion of the Arminians flows from their Pelagianism, by which, with the old Pelagians, they hold that God's decree and grace are determined by the human will.

units.la: Postea arrodunt argumentum quo ex Ephes. 1. 22. 23. ostenderam Regnum Christi non posse esse absque Ecclesiâ seu subditis. Nam Apostolus quemadmodum Ecclesiam corpus Christi, ita etiam πληρωμα illius complementum seu perfectionem vocat &c. Dicunt Ecclesiam ibi πληρωμα vocari non activa significatione, quia FACIT ut Christus Rex sive caput sit, sed contra passiva significatione, quia Christus Ecclesiam implet, h. e. cumulat omnibus necessariis bonis &c. Et probant ex eo quia Christus ibi simul vocatur is qui omnia implet in omnibus. Respondeo. 1. non dixi unquam Ecclesiam FACERE ut Christus Rex sit. Hoc illorum cavillum est. 2. prodit jam M. Episcopius, quàm parùm etiam in linguæ Græcæ cognitione profecerit. Nam ubi didicit vocem πληρωμα quando complementum seu perfectionem significat passivè sumi ? sumitur enim non pro eo quod impletur, sed pro eo quod implet sive perficit, seu quo aliud impletur vel perficitur. Adeoque probatio & causa propter quam πληρωμα passivè dicunt significare, nulla est. Restat igitur ut vera causa propter quam Apostolus addit τὰ πάντα ἐν πᾶσι πληρουμένῳ sit ea, quam D. Beza (ad cujus auctoritatem hi homines contra me Vindic. lib. 1. cap. 3. p. 22. aliâ occasione provocant) in Notis ad illum locum rectissimè observat; ut sciamus Christum per se non indigere hoc supplemento, ut qui efficit omnia in omnibus revera, nedum ut indigeat cujuspiam supplemento, quamvis pro immensâ bonitate Ecclesiam dignatur sibi corporis instar adjungere.
units.tr: Afterwards they gnaw at the argument by which, from Ephesians 1:22, 23, I had shown that the kingdom of Christ cannot exist without the Church or subjects. For the Apostle, just as he calls the Church the body of Christ, so also calls it His <bl>πληρωμα</bl> [pleroma], that is, His complement or perfection, etc. They say that the Church is called <bl>πληρωμα</bl> there not in an active sense, because it MAKES Christ to be King or head, but on the contrary in a passive sense, because Christ fills the Church, that is, heaps upon it all necessary good things, etc. And they prove it from the fact that Christ is there at the same time called He who fills all in all. I answer: (1) I never said that the Church MAKES Christ to be King; this is their quibble. (2) Master Episcopius already shows how little he has advanced even in the knowledge of the Greek tongue. For when did he learn that the word <bl>πληρωμα</bl> [pleroma], when it means complement or perfection, is taken in a passive sense? For it is taken not for that which is filled, but for that which fills or perfects, or by which something else is filled or perfected. So the proof, and the reason on account of which they say <bl>πληρωμα</bl> signifies passively, is nothing. It remains, then, that the true reason why the Apostle adds <bl>τὰ πάντα ἐν πᾶσι πληρουμένῳ</bl> [ta panta en pasi pleroumenō] is that which Dr. Beza (to whose authority these men, in another connection, appeal against me in Vindiciae, book 1, chap. 3, p. 22) rightly observes in his Notes on that passage: "so that we may know that Christ does not in Himself need this supplement, since He effects all things in all really, much less that He needs anyone's supplement, although by His immense goodness He deigns to join the Church to Himself as a kind of body."

units.la: Tandem Conclusionis loco inferunt, ex istâ receptâ interpretatione loci illius quam ego sequutus sum, fluere hæc absurda: 1. Christi Majestatem Regiam dependere à subditorum obsequio. 2. Sic sequi, subditos fore non qui qui sponte Christo se volunt submittere, sed qui non poterunt non se submittere, & Christus erit Rex non voluntarii populi, sed qui fatali necessitate pareant. Quibus opponunt suam sententiam circa hanc rem: nimirùm quòd Deus volens Christum Regem & subditos ei facere, fecerit id suppositâ praescientia, ut prius futuros aliquos libera voluntate subditos praesciret, quàm Christum Regem ordinaret. Et me vocant acerrimum Liberi arbitrii osorem. Respondeo ad 1. Hoc non sequitur ex nostrâ doctrinâ aut interpretatione; sed ex eorum opinione quâstatuunt gratiam efficacem Dei determinari à Libero arbitrio hominis. Hanc opinionem Pelagianam si haberemus; utique illud sequeretur. Ad 2. Nulla est consequentia: Subsistit enim spontaneitas & voluntarium etiamsi Pelagiani errores Arminianorum circa Gratiam Dei & Liberum arbitrium rejiciantur; speciatim quòd Liberum arbitrium determinet gratiam efficacem Dei, ipsum autem à gratiâ Dei non determinetur. Liberi arbitrii osor non sum, sed defensor; tribuo enim ei quod tribuendum esse ipsi Sacra Scriptura docet; quod profectò defendere est. Et adspiro cum omnibus filiis Dei ad plenam restaurationem Liberi arbitrii, eamque ex animo desidero. Quare non odi sed amo Liberum arbitrium. Hi homines autem osores sunt Liberi arbitrii, quia osores sunt doctrinæ orthodoxæ de Libero arbitrio. Et dum non rectè amant Liberum arbitrium, revera illud oderunt, ac loco illius Pelagianæ superbiæ idolum amant & amplectuntur. Fatalis necessitas, Pelagianorum etiam veterum calumnia est, Catholicis objecta ab ipsis, sed ab Augustino dudum diluta, & à nostris millies refutata. Atque hæc etiam ad caput istud vindiciarum. Ex quibus rursus apparet me ipsis calumniosè nihil imputasse; quandoquidem fatentur in eo dogmata sibi à me objecta, & tueri conantur.
units.tr: Finally, by way of conclusion, they infer that from this accepted interpretation of that passage, which I have followed, there flow these absurdities: (1) that Christ's royal majesty depends on the obedience of subjects; (2) that it follows that the subjects will be not those who willingly wish to submit themselves to Christ, but those who will be unable not to submit, and Christ will be King not of a willing people, but of those who obey by fatal necessity. Against these they set their own opinion on this matter, namely that God, wishing to make Christ King and subjects for Him, did so with foreknowledge supposed, so that He foreknew some subjects who would be future by free will before He ordained Christ King. And they call me "the most bitter hater of free will." I answer to (1): this does not follow from our doctrine or interpretation, but from their opinion, by which they hold that God's efficacious grace is determined by man's free will. If we held this Pelagian opinion, that would indeed follow. To (2): there is no consequence: spontaneity and the voluntary subsist even if the Pelagian errors of the Arminians about God's grace and free will are rejected; specifically, that free will determines God's efficacious grace, while it is not itself determined by God's grace. I am not a hater of free will but its defender; for I ascribe to it what holy Scripture teaches must be ascribed to it, which is indeed to defend it. And I aspire, with all the sons of God, to the full restoration of free will, and I desire it from my heart. Therefore I do not hate but love free will. These men, however, are haters of free will, because they are haters of the orthodox doctrine of free will. And while they do not love free will rightly, they in fact hate it, and in place of it they love and embrace the idol of Pelagian pride. Fatal necessity is also a calumny of the old Pelagians, thrown by them at Catholics, but long since refuted by Augustine, and by our men a thousand times. And these things are also said concerning this chapter of the Vindiciae. From which again it appears that I have imputed nothing calumniously to them, since they admit that the doctrines I objected to them are theirs, and try to defend them.

units.la: CAP. IV. Examen Capitis IV. Vindic. lib. 2.
units.tr: Chapter IV. Examination of Chapter IV of the Vindication, Book 2

units.la: 1. Arminiani negant contra conscientiam suam, se non habere pro Hæreticis eos quos tota Ecclesia Christiana habet pro Hæreticis. 2. Fatentur se Antitrinitarios non habere pro Hæreticis. 3. Negant contra conscientiam suam se docere Hodie sciri non posse quis sit Hæreticus. 4. Non negant se docere Hæreticos luposvè graves ves non esse nisi odiosa nomina. 5. Non negant se habere pro Hæreticis eos qui tenent dogmata orthodoxa de Trinitate opposita Antitrinitariis & eos coërcent. Αὐτοκατάκριτος quis secundùm veterem & Apostolicam doctrinam ex Eusebio? 6. Fatentur se docere, Hæresin de quâ quæstio est, non esse peccatum, & quomodo Hæresin quam Paulus vocat opus carnis, peccatum vocent. 7. 8. 9. Non negant se docere eandem esse planè involuntariam ; non esse opus carnis, imò ne scandalum quidem. 10. Contra conscientiam suam negant se docere: Ignorantiam omnem etiamsi ea culpabilis sit, excusare à peccato Hæreseos. 11. 12. Non negant se docere ; non solùm simplices Hæreticos seu ab aliis seductos non peccare, sed etiam seductores ipsos sine culpâ esse. Et ideò seductores eos odio dignos non esse. 13. Non negant se docere : Hæreticos non esse impios. 14. Fatentur se docere : Nullum Hæreticum esse blasphemum proprie sic dictum. 15. 16. 17. 18. 19. 20. 21. Fatentur item non negant alia multa horrenda dogmata in hac re sibi objecta. 22. Non negant se docere : Hæresibus & Schismatis januam optimè claudi, quando liberum exercitium Hæreticis permittitur & Schismaticis. Contrarium ostenditur experientiâ veteris Ecclesiæ secundùm Scripturam sacram. 23. Non negant se docere: Gravissima pericula imminere Ecclesiæ, speciatim Lutheranæ, quando liberum exercitium Hereticis non permittitur. 24. Contra conscientiam suam negant se docere Hæreticorum tolerantiam esse salutarem Reipublicæ. 25. Non negant se docere noxium & periculosum esse Reip. non tolerare Hæreticos : item se metum populorum incutere Magistratibus, ut tolerantiam Hæreticorum ab iis impetrent. 26. Fatentur se docere : Si Resp. turbetur ab Hæreticis, id illis crimini dandum non esse. An Hæretici rectè ab Arminianis comparentur cum Medicis, testimonium antiquitatis Ecclesiasticæ secundùm Scripturam Sacram. 27. Fatentur se docere : Hæreticos veniam errorum merereri pietate suâ; item, Eos salvos fieri æternùm.
units.tr: 1. The Arminians deny, against their own conscience, that they do not regard as heretics those whom the whole Christian Church regards as heretics. 2. They confess that they do not regard Antitrinitarians as heretics. 3. They deny, against their own conscience, that they teach that today it cannot be known who is a heretic. 4. They do not deny that they teach that heretics are not grave or serious sinners, but only odious names. 5. They do not deny that they regard as heretics those who hold orthodox doctrines of the Trinity opposed to the Antitrinitarians, and that they restrain them. Who is "self-condemned" [αὐτοκατάκριτος] according to the ancient and apostolic doctrine, from Eusebius? 6. They confess that they teach that the heresy in question is not a sin, and ask how they can call heresy, which Paul calls a work of the flesh, a sin. 7, 8, 9. They do not deny that they teach that it is entirely involuntary, that it is not a work of the flesh, and not even a scandal. 10. Against their own conscience they deny that they teach that ignorance of every kind, even if it is culpable, excuses from the sin of heresy. 11, 12. They do not deny that they teach not only that simple heretics, or those led astray by others, do not sin, but that even the seducers themselves are without fault, and therefore that those seducers are not worthy of hatred. 13. They do not deny that they teach that heretics are not impious. 14. They confess that they teach that no heretic is blasphemous in the proper sense of the word. 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21. They likewise confess, or do not deny, many other horrible doctrines on this matter that are charged against them. 22. They do not deny that they teach that the door to heresies and schisms is best closed when free exercise is granted to heretics and schismatics. The contrary is shown by the experience of the ancient Church, according to holy Scripture. 23. They do not deny that they teach that the gravest dangers threaten the Church, especially the Lutheran, when free exercise is not granted to heretics. 24. Against their own conscience they deny that they teach that the toleration of heretics is salutary for the commonwealth. 25. They do not deny that they teach that it is harmful and dangerous for the commonwealth not to tolerate heretics; likewise that they instil fear of the people into the magistrates, so that they may obtain toleration of heretics from them. 26. They confess that they teach that if the commonwealth is disturbed by heretics, this should not be imputed as a crime to them. Whether heretics are rightly compared by the Arminians with physicians: the testimony of ecclesiastical antiquity according to holy Scripture. 27. They confess that they teach that heretics merit pardon for their errors by their piety; likewise that they are saved eternally.

units.la: 1. PRimum dogma quod his hominibus cap.4. objeceram : est : Arminianos non habere pro Haereticis aut Haeresibus, quas Christiana Ecclesia tota qua Deum in tribus personis adorat habet pro Haeresibus aut Haereticis. Respondent, hoc falsum esse. At hoc negant rursus contra conscientiam suam. Nam ego solide illud probaveram pag. 124. 125. 126. Par. I. lib. 2. c. 4. ex eo, quod, etiamsi interdum eos, quos Ecclesia, ut dixi, tota habet pro Haereticis, interdum vocent Haereticos, non tamen id faciunt ex sua sententia, sed ex nostra hypothesi, h.e. omnium eorum qui unum Deum in tribus personis adorare Necessarium ad salutem credut, ut ostendi SEX locis ex Apologia ipsorum. Ad probationem criminis istius a me allatam illi nec verbo quidem respondent : sed contenti sunt crimen negare. Iudica, quisquis es, Candide Lector, quid sentiendum sit de reo, cui quando objicitur crimen aliquod, ille id negat audacter se commisisse. Quando autem accusator probationes affert, quibus ostendit reum crimen id commisisse; ad eas ne verbum quidem respondet, eas nec affirmat nec negat. Iudica an non talis reus in conscientia sua convictus sit, & pro convicto habendus.
units.tr: 1. The first doctrine that I had charged against these men in chapter 4 is this: that the Arminians do not regard as heretics or heresies what the whole Christian Church, which worships God in three persons, regards as heresies or heretics. They answer that this is false. But again they deny this against their own conscience. For I had solidly proved it at pages 124, 125, 126 of Part I, book 2, chapter 4, from the fact that, although they sometimes call heretics those whom the Church, as I said, regards entirely as heretics, they do not do so from their own opinion, but from our hypothesis, that is, of all those who believe that it is necessary for salvation to worship one God in three persons, as I showed from six passages of their own Apology. To the proof of this charge brought forward by me they do not respond even a word, but are content to deny the crime. Judge, whoever you are, kind reader, what should be thought of a defendant who, when some crime is charged against him, boldly denies that he committed it; but when the accuser brings forward proofs showing that the defendant committed the crime, does not answer a single word to them, neither affirming nor denying them. Judge whether such a defendant is not convicted in his own conscience and should not be regarded as convicted.

units.la: 2. Speciatim objeceram ipsis ; eos non habere Antitrinitarios seu Socinianos pro Haereticis. Hoc non negant, sed postulant argumenta quae demonstrent eos Haereticos esse. Et provocant ad rationes quib. Resp. ad Excerpta Cll. D.D. Proff. Leyd. utuntur : & invitant me ad eas refutandas, si possim. Verum enimvero, inquam ego, eas ratiunculas ipsorum non opus habere refutatione; quandoquidem jam ab ipsismet Arminianis in nihilum redactae sunt, dum in conscientia sua convicti, fatentur eas non esse prorsus apodicticas ut supra vidimus. Observa igitur, pie Lector, quod nolint habere pro Haereticis eos qui omnium Haereticorum, qui usque ad hoc seculum decimum sextum exstiterunt, teterrimi perpetuo a tota Ecclesia quae Deum in tribus personis adorat, fuerunt judicati. In qua aestimatione Socinianos esse ipsi Arminiani fatentur, in Resp. ad Excerp. p. 18. Fortasse dicetis, inquiunt, nihil gratius vobis esse, quam ut pax confici possit, sed ea lege, ut Remonstrantes opinionibus suis renuncient, & judicio vestro Synodico se submittant. Ita profecto credimus vos sentire : sed eadem lege pacem feceritis cum Judaeo, Turca &, Quos CHRISTIANORUM TETERRIMOS judicatis Socinianis. Qui Socinianos qui omnium teterrimi & maxime execrandi sunt Haeretici, non habent pro Haereticis; illi primo nunquam se a'sumino crimine purgabunt, sive jam dicant Pontificios, sive Reformatos, sive Lutheranos Hereticos Hæreticos esse: Secundò nunquam possunt dicere verè, se eos habere pro Hæreticis, quos tota Ecclesia, quæ Deum in tribus personis adorat, pro Hæreticis habet. Quòd hic p. 91. suggillant, quod observaveram de insidioso & invidioso modo loquendi ipsorum: perperàm faciunt. Nam nemo sibi nimium cavere potest à fraudibus eorum, quibus in rebus nec non in modis loquendi utuntur: qualis hoc loco est, quòd dicunt CII. Theol. Proff. vocare Hæreticos eos qui CIRCA fundamentalem articulum Religionis Christianæ errant. Nam alioquin τὸ CIRCA pro vocula IN sumi his monitoribus opus non habebam, qui scio eam à patribus in hoc negocio interdum ita sumi.
units.tr: 2. Specifically I had charged them that they do not regard the Antitrinitarians or Socinians as heretics. They do not deny this, but demand arguments that demonstrate that they are heretics. And they challenge me to the reasoning which the professors of Leiden, in the Response to the Excerpts, use, and they invite me to refute it, if I can. But truly, I say, those little arguments of theirs need no refutation, since they have already been reduced to nothing by the Arminians themselves, who, convicted in their own conscience, confess that they are not "altogether apodictic," as we saw above. Observe, therefore, pious reader, that they are unwilling to regard as heretics those who, of all the heretics who have existed down to this sixteenth century, have been judged by the whole Church that worships God in three persons to be the most abominable. In this estimation the Arminians themselves confess that the Socinians stand, in their Response to the Excerpts, p. 18: Perhaps you will say, they say, that nothing is more welcome to you than that peace could be made, but on the condition that the Remonstrants renounce their opinions and submit themselves to your synodical judgment. We indeed believe that you think this way; but on the same condition you would make peace with the Jew, the Turk, and those whom you judge to be the most abominable of Christians, the Socinians. Those who do not regard as heretics the Socinians, who are the most abominable and most execrable of all heretics, will, first, never clear themselves of this most serious charge, whether they now say that Papists, or Reformed, or Lutherans are heretics. Secondly, they can never truly say that they regard as heretics those whom the whole Church, which worships God in three persons, regards as heretics. What they here at p. 91 mock, namely my observation about their insidious and envious manner of speaking, they do wrongly. For no one can be too careful against their tricks, which they use in matters and also in their manners of speaking; such as here, where they say that the most illustrious theology professors call heretics those who err CIRCA the fundamental article of the Christian religion. For otherwise I would have no need, as I know these critics do, to take the little word CIRCA in the sense of IN, which I know the Fathers sometimes do in this matter.

units.la: 3. Tertium dogma est; Hodie sciri non posse quis sit Hæreticus: quod docent primùm eo prætextu, quia negant hodie dari judicium infallibile de Hæresi: Nulli homini aut Ecclesiæ iudicium infallibile de erroribus alioribus delatum est. Apol. c. 24. f. 259. a. ite, iudicium peremtorium de errore nulli mortalium competit, nisi quod pro se & suo animo quisque facit. ibid. f. 259. b. item: aliud est Hæresibus & Schismatibus omnibus ianuam aperire, aliud is aperire ianuam qui nullo infallibili iudicio convinci possunt, quod placita eorum hæreses sint. c. 25. f. 298. Deinde docent id eo prætextu, quia ad faciendum judicium de Hæresi requiratur, ut constet non solùm de errore, sed etiam tùm de malitia tùm de pertinacia Hæreticorum. Iam autem quemadmodum de errore modò dixerunt, ita etiam dicunt non posse fieri judicium de malitiâ & pertinaciâ, nec à Pontificiis, nec à Lutheranis, nec à Reformatis. Tertium prætextus est, quod tales homines non habeant requisita Hæreseos, quæ secundùm eos sunt tùm advertentia (adeòq; malitia) quâ homo sciat se errare, tamen studio seu de industriâ errare velit, tùm pertinacia: quæ omnia ab ipsis doceri ostensum est à nobis loco allegato p. 126. 127. 128. 129. Videamus, quid respondeant? Hoc falsum esse, inquiunt lib. 1. cap. 1. demonstravimus. Deinde ratiunculam afferunt, quâ ostendere conantur, me mihi in eâ accusatione contradicere; quia dico eodem cap. 4. eos habere pro Hæreticis illos qui αὐτοκατάκριτοι sunt. Hæc, inquiunt, si conciliare possit Vedelius, ne rem magnam præstuerit. Respondeo ad 1. Quod remittunt nos ad lib. 1. cap. 1. Vindic. id verò dilutum est à nobis lib. 1. cap. 1. hujus Partis Quartæ & prolegom. Par. III. cap. 4. ubi ita respondi ut protervia insignis horum rabularum manifestissima sit, & simul pateat eos contra propriam conscientiam me falsitatis arguere. Etenim cùm negassent initio se id docere: fatentur statim tertiâ aut quartâ lineâ post; se ita docere, ut ibi ostensum est. Unde jam facilis est responsio ad 2.
units.tr: 3. The third doctrine is this: that today it cannot be known who is a heretic. They teach this, first, on the pretext that they deny that today any infallible judgment about heresy is given: No infallible judgment on errors, of whatever sort, has been committed to any man or to the Church. Apology, ch. 24, f. 259a; a peremptory judgment about error belongs to no mortal, except what each man makes for himself and his own mind, ibid. f. 259b. Likewise: it is one thing to open the door to all heresies and schisms, another to open the door to those who cannot be convicted by any infallible judgment that their opinions are heresies, ch. 25, f. 298. Secondly, they teach this on the pretext that to make a judgment about heresy it is required that it be established not only concerning error, but also concerning the malice and the obstinacy of the heretics. Now, just as they have said about error, so they also say that a judgment about malice and obstinacy cannot be made, neither by the Papists, nor by the Lutherans, nor by the Reformed. Thirdly, the pretext is that such men do not have the requisites of heresy, which according to them are, on the one hand, awareness (and thus malice), by which a man knows that he is in error, yet wishes to err by design or deliberately, and, on the other hand, obstinacy. All these things, as shown by us in the passage cited at pp. 126, 127, 128, 129, have been taught by them. Let us see how they respond. This is false, they say, we demonstrated in book 1, chapter 1. Then they bring forward a little argument by which they try to show that I contradict myself in that accusation, because I say in the same chapter 4 that they regard as heretics those who are self-condemned [αὐτοκατάκριτοι]. If Vedelius can reconcile these things, they say, he will not have achieved a great thing. I answer, first, that they refer us to book 1, chapter 1 of the Vindication; but that has indeed been refuted by us in book 1, chapter 1 of this Part Four and in the Prolegomena of Part III, chapter 4, where I so answered that the impudence of these ranters is clearly evident, and at the same time it is plain that they, against their own conscience, accuse me of falsehood. For although at first they had denied that they teach this, they confess a line or four lines later that they teach it in the way that was shown there. Hence the answer to the second point is now easy.

units.la: Nam ex dictis patet, me non mihi, sed eos sibi contradicere ; quandoquidem fatentur se docere sciri hodie non posse quis sit Hereticus; & tamen dicunt esse quosdam Haereticos,& id sciri posse, ac rursus e contrario, statuunt Deum solum de animo hominis iudicare posse : item fas non esse alicui invito tribuere malitiam, ut ostendi Par.I.lib.2.c.4.p.133. Ita turpiter se hi homines implicant. Ex quo patet eos ( dum hic de αὐτοκαταχρίτως loquuntur ) vere αὐτοκαταχρίτως esse. Tales contradictiones ipsis novae non sunt, ut ex omnibus Quatuor Partibus Arcanorum unusquisque videre poterit. Ad incitas enim redacti sunt. Adeoque ineptum est, quod dicunt : Quomodo fieri potest ut Vedelius a Remonstrantibus, negari credat sciri posse quis sit Haereticus ; & nihilominus tamen eos culpet quod hos & illos habeant pro Haereticis &c. Nam ego haec duo facile credo, qui longe pejora de ipsis & credo & probavi. Purgent se illis si possunt.
units.tr: For it is plain from what has been said that I am not contradicting myself, but they are contradicting themselves. They admit that today it cannot be known who is a heretic, and yet they say that there are certain heretics and that this can be known. Conversely, they lay down that God alone can judge the mind of man; likewise it is not lawful to impute malice to anyone against his will, as I showed at Part I, book 2, chapter 4, p. 133. In this way these men shamefully entangle themselves. From this it is clear that they (while speaking here of being self-condemned [αὐτοκαταχρίτως]) are truly self-condemned [αὐτοκαταχρίτως]. Such contradictions are not new to them, as anyone may see from all four Parts of the Arcana. For they have been reduced to a dead end. So it is absurd of them to say: How can it be that Vedelius believes the Remonstrants deny that it can be known who is a heretic? and yet to blame him for regarding these and those as heretics, and so on. For I readily believe both of these things, since I believe and have proved far worse things about them. Let them clear themselves of those charges if they can.

units.la: Caeterum perspicue & solide, ut videre unicuique licet probaveram eos ita docere ; & quidem primo ex eo quod hoc praetextu utantur : quia nullum infallibile iudicium detur de errore alterius &c. Respondent Arminiani p.92. & non negant se ita docere; atque postquam rursus pari modo me contradictionis exinde arguere voluissent, quod ipsis contradictoria tribuam,(rem scilicet,ut alia nunc omittam, non novam hominibus pessimam causam defendentibus contra suam conscientiam ) id dogma defendere conantur,sed impertinentissime. Contendunt enim nullum dari infallibile judicium humanum;& non habent rationem infallibilis judicii divini h. e. quo Deus ipse in verbo suo controversiam decidit. Et de hac re h. e. an'ne detur infallibile judicium humanum supra a nobis, maxime autem & ex professo in Rationali Theologico actum est.
units.tr: Moreover, as anyone may see, I had proved clearly and soundly that they teach this. Indeed, first, from the fact that they use this pretext: that no infallible judgment is given concerning another's error, and so on. The Arminians reply at p. 92 and do not deny that they teach this. And when, after that, I wished to convict them in the same way of contradiction, by attributing to them contradictory positions (a thing, to omit other points for now, not new in men who defend a very bad cause against their own conscience), they try to defend that doctrine, but most impertinently. For they contend that there is no human infallible judgment, and they have no account of a divine infallible judgment, that is, one by which God himself decides the controversy in his Word. And concerning this matter, namely whether a human infallible judgment is given, the question has been treated by us above, and especially and expressly in the Rational Theology.

units.la: Secundum praetextum quo nixi negant in Apologia sciri hodie posse quis sit Haereticus, dixi in eo consistere, quod non possit fieri iudicium de malitia & pertinacia Haereticorum ; etiam non negant, sed postquam repetissent mendacium suum, quo dicunt Cl. Proff. Leydd. de formali haereseos statuere malitiam seu actum voluntatis malitiosum ( quod salsissimum esse ostendimus lib. 1. hujus Partis cap. 1. §. 1. ) negant saltem se docuisse non posse de pertinacia iudicium fieri a Pontificiis, atque eam negationem solita sua maledicentia & quidem petulantissime aspergunt homines hi & addunt : Contrarium enim verissimum est ; de ea Pontificios pronunciare posse diserte & in terminis adserunt. Verum enimvero ego solide ostendi eos statuere non posse fieri judicium a Pontificiis de pertinacia ; idque ex ipsorum Arminianorum verbis. Nam ajunt Apol. c. 24. f. 279. b. etsi Pontificii tribuant Ecclesiæ judicium infallibile de pertinacia adeòque eâtenus consequenter loquantur, tamen eos colorem tantum dare Hæreticidio quod tuentur: nec aliam viam esse quâ colorem ei dent aut speciem. Si Pontificii eâ ratione h. e. dum dicunt Ecclesiam habere judicium infallibile,colorem tantum dant & speciem Hæreticidio quod tuentur; certè non possunt infallibiliter judicare de Hæresi.Deinde Arminiani,& quidè merito, hinc inde carpunt Pontificios tàm in Apologia quàm in Vindiciis suis, speciatim istâ ipsâ p. 92. quòd tribuant Ecclesiæ judicium per se infallibile. Si igitur ex doctrinâ Arminianorum judicium infallibile non habent Pontificii etsi id venditent; certè secundùm Arminianos non possunt Pontificii,judicium infallibile de pertinacia habere. Et sic apparet M. Episcopium non flore meracioris vini aspersum (ut hic improbè calumniantes loquuntur) sed facibus Socinianarum blasphemiarum ebrium & diabolicâ petulantiâ plenum immeritò mihi convitium eo nomine dixisse.
units.tr: As for the second pretext on which they rest, when they deny in the Apology that it can be known today who is a heretic, I said that it consists in this: that no judgment can be made concerning the malice and obstinacy of heretics. They do not deny this, but after repeating their lie, by which they say that the most distinguished professors of Leiden lay down that malice, or a malicious act of the will, is the formal element of heresy (which we have shown to be most absurd in book 1, chapter 1, §1 of this Part), they at least deny that they taught that no judgment about obstinacy can be made by the Papists. And this denial these men, with their usual slander and with the most wanton petulance, besmirch and add: For the contrary is most true; they assert expressly and in so many words that the Papists can pronounce on it. But in truth I have soundly shown that they hold that no judgment about obstinacy can be made by the Papists, and I did so from the words of the Arminians themselves. For they say in the Apology, c. 24, f. 279 b, that although the Papists attribute to the Church an infallible judgment about obstinacy, and so far speak consistently, nevertheless they only give a colour to the persecution of heretics which they defend: nor is there any other way by which they give it colour or appearance. If the Papists, by that reasoning, that is, by saying that the Church has an infallible judgment, only give colour and appearance to the persecution of heretics which they defend, then certainly they cannot judge infallibly about heresy. Next, the Arminians, and rightly so, pick at the Papists here and there, both in their Apology and in their Vindiciae, and especially in this same passage at p. 92, because they attribute to the Church a judgment that is infallible in itself. If therefore, by the doctrine of the Arminians, the Papists do not have an infallible judgment, although they boast of it, then certainly according to the Arminians the Papists cannot have an infallible judgment about obstinacy. And so it appears that Episcopius, not sprinkled with the flower of purer wine (as these maliciously slandering men put it here), but drunk with the torches of Socinian blasphemies and full of diabolical petulance, rightly hurled reproach at me on that account.

units.la: Quod dixeram eos statuere, non posse judicium fieri de pertinaciâ à Reformatis & Lutheranis; non negant, sed fatentur, & tueri conantur. Ita tamen ut primò mihi invidiam conciliare conentur, quod Lutheranos & Reformatos cœtus distinguam: quasi, inquiunt p. 93. Lutherani Reformatis accenseri non merentur, & soli (Calvinista Reformati censeri debeant.)? Virus animi sui passim prodit Vedelius, cum statim post hæc verba ægrè ferre se ostendit, quod Remonstrantes Lutheranos etiam Reformatorum voce comprehendunt. Hic quis non videt hos calumniatores & Hypocritas Socinianos, quia talia dicunt, non habere quod dicant. Nostros cœtus Reformatos voco quia ipsi etiam Lutherani nos ita vocare scriptis suis adversùm nos editis solent. Ipsos autem Lutheranos voco, quia ipsi hoc nomine sese appellant. Voco igitur utramque partem eo nomine, quo utraque nominari gaudet. Quid in hac re criminis est à me admissum? Scio autem Lutheranos non habituros gratiam his assentatoribus (nolo enim dicere putidis assentatoribus, & iis convitium reddere, qui me Vindic. lib. 1. c. 5. p. 33. putidum Calvini assentatorem vocant) quod eos Reformatos hîc nominent; quandoquidem Arminiani adeò latè extendunt vocem Reformationis ut se & Socinianos apertos pro Reformatis habeant. Certè à talibus hominibus Reformatos se vocari Lutherani honorificum sibi non ducent. Quod dicunt me virus animi mei prodere adversum Lutheranos, faciunt contra conscientiam: nam ipsi infrà dicunt, me statuere Lutheranos non errare in fundamento salutis. Et multi ex ti ex Lutheranis Theologis (ut jam de aliis nihil dicam) nôrunt ex scriptis meis quo affectu erga ipsos sim. Calumniosum quoque est, quod dicunt me agrè tulisse Lutheranos vocari Reformatos à Remonstrantibus. Nam aliud nihil egi quàm iis (quia propositum mihi erat probare, Arminianos statuere non posse à Reformatis & Lutheranis judicium fieri de pertinaciâ) ostenderem, Arminianos in eo loco Apologiæ ex quo illud probavi, per vocem Reformatorum intelligere non nos tantùm sed Lutheranos etiam, de quâ re ut nemo dubitaret, probavi id ex eo quòd usitatum illis sit, sub hac voce etiam Lutheranos comprehendere. Itaque hic proterve faciunt hi homines dum me eo nomine calumniantur; qui certè Lutheranos longè in alio censu habeo, quàm ut eos damnè, quemadmodum ab his malè feriatis hominibus fit, qui Lutheranos unà cum Reformatis damnant & execrantur, quia tolerare nolunt Antitrinitarios, sed eos proscribunt ex Ecclesiâ & Republicâ, ut ostendi Part. I. lib. 2. cap.5. ad quod hi homines in Vindiciis suis ne verbum quidem respondent. Hoc obiter malitiæ horum hominum reponere necessum fuit; qui quia non habent quod mihi jure & verè respondere possint, hinc inde diverticula inepta quærunt in quæ excurrunt. Hoc unum est, quod circa Lutheranorum & Reformatorum judicium de pertinaciâ dicunt.
units.tr: As to my statement that they hold that no judgment about obstinacy can be made by the Reformed and the Lutherans, they do not deny it but admit it, and try to defend it. Yet they first try to win ill will for me because I distinguish the Lutheran and Reformed bodies: as if, they say at p. 93, the Lutherans did not deserve to be counted among the Reformed, and only the Calvinist Reformed ought to be counted? Vedelius everywhere betrays the venom of his mind, since he at once shows, after these words, that he is displeased that the Remonstrants include the Lutherans under the name of the Reformed. Here who does not see that these slanderers and hypocrites, the Socinians, have nothing to say because they say such things? I call our bodies Reformed because the Lutherans themselves are accustomed to call us so in the writings they publish against us. But I call the Lutherans Lutherans because they themselves use that name. So I call each party by the name by which each is pleased to be named. What fault have I committed in this matter? I know, however, that the Lutherans will not thank these flatterers (I do not wish to call them foul flatterers, and return reproach to those who in my Vindiciae, book 1, ch. 5, p. 33, call me a foul flatterer of Calvin) for naming them Reformed here; since the Arminians stretch the word Reformation so widely that they count themselves and open Socinians as Reformed. Certainly the Lutherans will not think it an honour to be called Reformed by such men. That they say I betray the venom of my mind against the Lutherans, they do against their own conscience: for they themselves say below that I lay down that the Lutherans do not err in the foundation of salvation. And many of the Lutheran theologians (to say nothing of others) know from my writings what my attitude towards them is. It is also a slander that they say I took it ill that the Lutherans were called Reformed by the Remonstrants. For I did nothing else than show them (since it was my purpose to prove that the Arminians hold that no judgment about obstinacy can be made by the Reformed and the Lutherans) that in that passage of their Apology from which I proved it, the Arminians by the word Reformed understand not only us but the Lutherans as well. Lest anyone doubt this, I proved it from the fact that it is customary for them to include the Lutherans under this term too. So these men act shamelessly here when they slander me on this score; I certainly hold the Lutherans in far too high esteem to condemn them, as these ill-behaved men do, who condemn and curse the Lutherans together with the Reformed because they are unwilling to tolerate Antitrinitarians but banish them from Church and Commonwealth, as I showed in Part I, book 2, ch. 5, to which these men in their Vindiciae do not reply even a word. I had to put this in passing against the malice of these men, who, since they have no proper and true answer to give me, seek silly detours here and there into which they run. This is the one thing they say about the judgment of the Lutherans and the Reformed concerning obstinacy.

units.la: Alterum sequitur: Dixeram p. 127. 128. Arminianos falsum dicere, dum inquiunt nos & Lutheranos non agnoscere normam infallibilem judicii nostri, aut ullum judicium infallibile: Etenim dixeram, Evangelicos omnes agnoscere normam infallibilem judicandi in terris, nimirum Scripturam: item, dixeram hominem tùm demum in judicando de hæresi aut de veritate falli non posse, quando ex verbo Dei unicè judicat, eique rationem suam omninò submittit, pænes quod verbum Dei norma judicii infallibilis est de rebus fidei. Hîc verò relabuntur in coccysmum suum de Vedelio & Ecclesiis Reformatis, ac vocant hoc validum argumentum & dicunt: Hic si Vedelius aquam sibi hærere non sentit, callum obductum menti suæ habet qui eum reddit ἀτναλγυνιότα. Item fingunt me sentire me presum eo argumento: Hoc argumento presum se sentit, inquiunt p.93. Rideo dum lego acutam subtilitatem horum hominum, quam retusam vide libro præcedente cap. 1. §. 4. Interim observet Lector, eos hoc solum carpere, quod dixi hominem falli non posse, quando unicè ex verbo Dei judicat & ei rationem suam submittit. Quòd autem eos falsitatis accusavi dum dicunt nos Evangelicos non agnoscere normam infallibile, ad idne γῷ quidem respondent. Hęc etiam de secundo eorum pretextu.
units.tr: The second point follows. I had said at pp. 127-128 that the Arminians speak falsely when they say that we and the Lutherans do not acknowledge an infallible rule of our judgment, or any infallible judgment. For I had said that all Evangelicals acknowledge an infallible rule of judging on earth, namely Scripture; likewise I had said that a man cannot then at last err in judging about heresy or about truth, when he judges solely from the Word of God and entirely submits his own reasoning to it, since the Word of God is the infallible rule of judgment in matters of faith. Here they fall back again into their own mockery of Vedelius and the Reformed Churches, and call this a strong argument, and say: Here, if Vedelius does not feel the water sticking to him, he has a callus over his mind, which makes him [ἀναλγυνιότα] insensitive. They also pretend that I feel myself pressed by this argument: He feels himself pressed by this argument, they say at p. 93. I laugh as I read the sharp subtlety of these men, which I showed to be blunt in the preceding book, ch. 1, §4. Meanwhile let the reader observe that they only pick at this, that I said a man cannot err when he judges solely from the Word of God and submits his reasoning to it. But as for my charge of falsehood against them, when they say that we Evangelicals do not acknowledge an infallible rule, they do not reply even a word to that. This is also said concerning their second pretext.

units.la: Tertium prætextum dixeram esse, quòd errantes qui communiter Hæretici vocantur non habeant requisita Hæreseos, advertentiam nimirum & pertinaciam. Respondent illi se tantùm ex hypothesi Cll. Proff. Leydd. ea dixisse qui supponant duo ista requisita necessaria &c. Verùm enimverò id falsum est. Nam primò falsum est Cll. Theoll. Leydd. statuere advertentiam esse de formali hæreseos aut illius requisitum. Secundo Arminiani ex propriâ suâ sententiâ sic loquuntur loco Apologiæ à me Par. I. lib. 2. cap.4. allegato: In Peccatis cæteris, inquiunt, sola ignorantia invincibilis excusat. Sufficit ut voluntaria sint contra Legem Dei sive quis advertat se contra Legem ipsam peccare, sive non advertat, dummodo advertere id possit & debeat. At in haresi voluntarium non sufficit, sed scientia insuper requiritur, quâ quis scit id quod sentit aut statuit repugnare Ecclesiæ, vel normæ secundum quam judicium faciendum esse creditur. Hinc in Hæretico quem illi sic vocant rejicientes sententiam totius Ecclesiæ de significatione vocis Hæreseos qui de levibus & nullius aut exigui usus quæstionibus altercatur, dicunt ejusmodi advertentiam esse: quippe, inquiunt, qui convictus est apud animum suum eas leves & nullius usus esse, & nihilominus tamen eas ubi potest avidè arripit & mordicus tenet. Apol. c. 24. f. 174. b.
units.tr: I had said that the third pretext is that the erring, whom they commonly call heretics, do not have the requisites of heresy, namely awareness and obstinacy. They reply that they said this only hypothetically, for those who assume these two requisites as necessary, referring to the most learned professors of Leiden. But that is false. First, it is false that the most learned theologians of Leiden hold awareness to belong to the formal nature of heresy or to be a requisite of it. Second, the Arminians themselves speak in their own voice in the passage from the Apology that I cited in Part I, book 2, chapter 4: In other sins, they say, only invincible ignorance excuses. It is enough that the sins be voluntary against the Law of God, whether a person realises that he sins against the Law itself or does not realise it, provided that he can and ought to realise it. But in heresy the voluntary is not enough; knowledge over and above it is also required, by which a person knows that what he thinks or decides is opposed to the Church, or to the rule according to which judgment is believed to be made. Hence in the heretic, as they call him, who rejects the judgment of the whole Church on the meaning of the word heresy, and who wrangles over trivial questions of no or little use, they say such awareness is present: for, they say, he is convinced in his own mind that these questions are trivial and of no use, and yet nonetheless he eagerly seizes them where he can and holds on to them tooth and nail. Apology, ch. 24, p. 174b.

units.la: Ita igitur ex propriâ suâ sententiâ advertentiam Hæretico tribuunt. Præterea etiam pertinaciam ex propriâ suâ mente dicunt esse de ratione Hæreseos. Ita enim in Vindiciis suis lib. 1. c. 1. p. 9. dicunt me in definitione, ut ibi loquuntur, Hæretici non ponere formale Hæretici aut Hæreseos, ubi inquiunt: De Hæreseos formali est pertinacia, ipsis Censoribus Leydensibus judicibus, qui insuper malitiam addunt. Item cap. 10. p. 56. Deinde cùm de formali Hæreseos sit pertinacia, quomodo Hæresis opponitur cognitioni ? Et in Resp. ad Excerp. D.D. Proff. Leydd. p. 41. ubi rationes afferunt, cur non agnoscant dogmata controversa oppositá Antitrinitariis pro Necessariis ad salutem, secundam rationem hanc ponunt: Quod causas errandi non leves habere videantur (Antitrinitarii) propter quas error eorum à pertinaciâ ac proinde ab hæreseos culpâ, quæ sine pertinaciâ nulla est à Doctoribus ipsis liber atque immunis censeri debeat. Vide jam candide Lector, quâ fronte hi homines audeant hoc loco dicere, me fœdum errorem errare, dum dico Arminianos ista duo requirere ad hæresin; item se tantùm ex hypothesi D.D. Proffesorum Leydensium ita dixisse. Ex his omnibus luce clarius meridianâ est, eos statuere hodie sciri non posse quis sit Hæreticus, sumtâ, tri dixi, voce illâ secundùm usum & sensum totius Ecclesiæ, quæ Deum in tribus personis necessariò esse adorandum statuit.
units.tr: So then, by their own opinion, they attribute awareness to the heretic. Moreover, they also say from their own mind that obstinacy belongs to the nature of heresy. For in their Vindications, book 1, ch. 1, p. 9, they say that I, in my definition, as they put it, do not set down the formal element of a heretic or of heresy, where they say: Obstinacy is of the formal element of heresy, according to the Leiden censors themselves, who moreover add malice. Likewise ch. 10, p. 56: Then, since obstinacy belongs to the formal element of heresy, how is heresy opposed to knowledge? And in the Reply to the Excerpts of the most learned Professors of Leiden, p. 41, where they give reasons why they do not acknowledge the disputed doctrines, opposed to the Antitrinitarians, as necessary to salvation, they put forward this second reason: Because the Antitrinitarians seem to have no slight causes of error, on account of which their error is to be judged free of obstinacy, and therefore free of the guilt of heresy, which, without obstinacy, is held to be no guilt at all, by the Doctors themselves. See now, candid reader, with what brazenness these men dare to say in this place that I err in a foul error when I say that the Arminians require these two things for heresy, and that they only said this hypothetically, on the supposition of the most learned Professors of Leiden. From all of this it is clearer than midday light that they hold that today it cannot be known who is a heretic, if we take that word, as I said, according to the usage and sense of the whole Church, which holds that God must necessarily be worshipped in three persons.

units.la: 4. Quartum dogma quod ipsis objeceram p. 129. 130. est: Haereticos luposve graves non esse nisi odiosa nomina. Hoc quàm falsum & impium dogma sit, ostenderam ibidem ex verbo Dei, & simul responderam exceptioni, quae in contrarium afferri poterat. Hoc vero boni hi viri non negant, sed tacent; & gravissimam hanc accusationem sicco pede transeunt; & ne verbulum quidem respondent, atque ad aliud transeunt.
units.tr: 4. The fourth dogma that I had objected to them, at pp. 129–130, is: That heretics and wolves are grave only as odious names. I had shown there, from the Word of God, how false and impious this dogma is, and at the same time I had answered the objection that could be brought against it. But these good men do not deny this; they keep silent. They pass over this most grave accusation with dry feet, and do not reply even a single word, but move on to something else.

units.la: 5. Porrò, cùm hi homines non habeant eos pro Haereticis, qui negant controversia inter Christianos dogmata; rursus, cùm non habeant pro Haereticis eos qui negant ea quae in confesso sunt, ut ostendi ibidem p. 130. 131. hinc quaestionem movi: Qui igitur tandem Arminiani Haeretici sint? Et ostendi p. 131. 132. eos cùm non habeant Antitrinitarios pro Haereticis, habere pro Haereticis eos qui vera dogmata de Trinitate adversus Antitrinitarios ita tuentur, ut eos tolerare nolint, sed coercean. Hanc accusationem non negant Arminiani, sed alia excurrunt, & multis nugis paginas 95. 96. 97. implent, quae ad rem non faciunt: cùm contrà (is enim scopus meus erat) debebant aut affirmando aut negando ad gravissimam hanc accusationem respondisse; nimirùm eos cùm non habeant Antitrinitarios pro Haereticis, habere tamen pro Haereticis eos coetus omnes, qui dogmata Orthodoxa de Trinitate tuentur & simul Antitrinitarios auctoritate publicà coercent. Quod cùm ita sit; mirum jam non est quòd sententiam de Haereticis Antitrinitariis & quidem blasphemis, perjuris, seditiosis (nam circa tales tantùm Antitrinitarios severior animadversio à quibusdam Magnis Theologis statuta est, ut rectissimè monent Cll. Proff. Leydd. Cens. Conf. c. 24. §. 9.) capitali supplicio afficiendis vocant Arminiani Resp. ad Excerp. p. 129. profanam & Barbaram Haeresin. Inter alia quae ibi nugantur p. 95. prolixè contra me disputant, ac si ibi loci contenderem Arminianos pro Haereticis habere TANTUM eos, qui quaestionibus levibus quae nullius aut exigui usus sunt &c. se & alios vexant. At ego non dixi eos TANTUM illos habere pro Haereticis; nam mihi propositum ibi non fuit ostendere hosne tantum an verò etiam alios pro Haereticis habeant: sed scopus, ut dixi, meus, fuit ostendere eos habere Ecclesias omnes quae Deum in tribus personis adorant, pro Haereticis, ex eo fundamento quòd statuunt eos Haereticos esse, qui levibus &c. quaestionibus & quae nullius usut sunt vexant alios; in quarum quaestionum levium & quae nullius usus sunt censu collocant Arminiani dogmata Orthodoxa de Trinitate, quemadmodum probavi.
units.tr: 5. Furthermore, since these men do not regard as heretics those who deny the doctrines disputed among Christians, and again, since they do not regard as heretics those who deny what is agreed upon, as I showed in the same place, pp. 130–131, I raised the question: Who, then, at last, are the Arminians who are heretics? And I showed at pp. 131–132 that, although they do not regard the Antitrinitarians as heretics, they do regard as heretics those who so defend the true doctrines about the Trinity against the Antitrinitarians that they will not tolerate them but want to coerce them. The Arminians do not deny this accusation, but they run off in other directions and fill pages 95, 96 and 97 with many trifles that have nothing to do with the matter; whereas, on the contrary (for this was my aim), they ought either to affirm or to deny, and reply to this most grave accusation: namely that, although they do not regard the Antitrinitarians as heretics, they do regard as heretics all those assemblies which defend the Orthodox doctrines about the Trinity and at the same time coerce the Antitrinitarians by public authority. Since this is so, it is no wonder that they call the sentence on the heretical Antitrinitarians, indeed the blasphemous, perjured and seditious ones (for only against such Antitrinitarians has a severer punishment been established by certain great theologians, as the most learned Professors of Leiden rightly remind us, Censure of the Confession, ch. 24, §9), who are to be punished by capital punishment, a profane and barbarous heresy, Reply to the Excerpts, p. 129. Among other things that they trifle over at p. 95, they dispute at length against me, as if I were there contending that the Arminians regard as heretics ONLY those who vex themselves and others with trivial questions that are of no or little use, and so on. But I did not say that they regard ONLY those as heretics; for it was not my purpose there to show whether they regard only these, or also others, as heretics. My aim, as I said, was to show that they regard as heretics all the churches which worship God in three persons, on the ground that they hold that those are heretics who vex others with trivial questions and questions of no use; and the Arminians count the Orthodox doctrines about the Trinity among such trivial questions of no use, as I have proved.

units.la: Porrò ostenderam p. 133. eos in doctrinâ suâ circa istos Hæreticos, qui quæstionibus levibus &c. se & alios vexant, sibi ipsis contradicere ut etiàm paulò ante §. 3. monui. Hïc respondent p. 96. hoc non esse Remonstrantes urgere, sed Paulo in os obloqui, qui tales vocat αὐτοκατακρίτως. Verùm enim verò primò Apostolus Tit. 3. v. 11. loquitur de homine Hæretico ut ex presse dicit v. 10. non autem de eo qui movet quæstiones quas scit leves esse. Fecerat quidem versu 9. mentionem quæstionum vanarum, sed non dixerat eum qui eas movet nôsse eas leves esse. Deinde salsissimum est & sine ullâ probatione dicitur ab Arminianis, neminem esse posse αὐτοκατάκριτον quàm qui convictus est apud animum suum quæstiones istas leves esse &c. Longè aliud significat ibi vox αὐτοκατάκειτ@ ut recte Eusebius indicat, qui locum illum Pauli refert ad Hæreticos eos, qui, ut hodiè Sociniani, non credunt Christum habere naturam divinam; ut ad Marcionem, Cerinthum & in genere ad omnes qui doctrinam veritatis adulterant Hæreticis dogmatibus. Ita enim lib. 4. hist. Ecclef. c. 13. postquam narrâsset factum S. Iohannis Evangelistæ fugientis Cerinthum & nolentis in eodem balneo cum eo versari ac vocantis eum hostem veritatis; postquam itidem narrâsset generosum factum S. Polycarpi nolentis sermonem miscere cum Marcione; (nam cùm Marcio in eum incidisset ac loqui cum eo volens quæsivisset, an'non ipsum nosset? Novi te, respondet S. Vir, primogenitum Satanæ) nec non cæterorum discipulorum qui Apostolos audierant simile zelum & aversationem Hæreticorum, dicit eos fecisse ὡς ἡ Παῦλος εἶπεν αἱρετικὸν ἄνθρωπον μετὰ μίαν ἡ δευτέραν νουθεσίαν παραιτοῦ εἰδὼς ὅτι ἐξέστραπται ὁ τοιοῦτος ἡ ἁμαρτάνει ὢν αὐτοκατάκριτος sicut & Paulus dixit: Hæreticum hominem post unam & alteram monitionem aversare, sciens quod talis eversus est & peccat proprio judicio condemnatus. Obiter addam ex loco illo Eusebii unumquemq; judicare posse, quo jure Arminiani dicant vetustissimos Christianos communionem coluisse cum iis qui docebat Christum habere tantùm naturam humanam non autem divinam. Ait enim Eusebius ibi; τοσαύτην οἱ Ἀπόστολοι καὶ οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτῶν ἔσχον εὐλάβειαν τὴν μὴ μίγνυσθαι λόγῳ κοινωνίαν τῷ παραχαράττοντι τὴν ἀλήθειαν tantam cautionem adhibebant Apostoli & discipuli eorum, ut ne sermonem quidem miscerent cum ullo eorum qui veritatem falsâ suâ doctrinâ adulterabant. Itaq; falsum etiam est, quod Arminiani dicunt p. 95. Hæreticos eos quos censor (imò tota Ecclesia,) vocat, non esse αὐτοκατάκριτος. Cæterùm quid diceret Polycarpus, si Episcopiû videret, hominê totum perfusum fæcibus Antitrinitariis & qui nulli veterum Hæreticorum protervia, malitiâ & turpitudine opinionum cedit?
units.tr: Furthermore, I had shown at p. 133 that in their teaching about these heretics, who vex themselves and others with trivial questions, they contradict themselves, as I also pointed out a little earlier, §3. Here they reply at p. 96: This is not the Remonstrants' argument, but to speak back to Paul to his face, who calls such men self-condemned [αὐτοκατακρίτως]. But first, the Apostle, Titus 3:11, speaks of a heretical man, as he expressly says in verse 10, and not of one who raises questions which he knows to be trivial. It is true that in verse 9 he mentions vain questions, but he does not say that the one who raises them knows them to be trivial. Next, it is most absurd, and asserted by the Arminians without any proof, that no one can be self-condemned [αὐτοκατάκριτος] except one who is convinced in his own mind that these questions are trivial, and so on. The word self-condemned [αὐτοκατάκριτος] there means something quite different, as Eusebius rightly indicates, who refers that passage of Paul to heretics who, like the Socinians today, do not believe that Christ has a divine nature; such as Marcion, Cerinthus, and in general all who corrupt the doctrine of truth with heretical opinions. For in book 4 of the Ecclesiastical History, ch. 13, after relating the deed of St John the Evangelist, who fled from Cerinthus and would not stay in the same bath with him, calling him an enemy of the truth, and after likewise relating the noble deed of St Polycarp, who would not hold conversation with Marcion (for when Marcion met him and, wishing to speak with him, asked whether he did not recognise him, the holy man replied: "I recognise you, the firstborn of Satan"), and also the similar zeal and aversion to heretics of the other disciples who had heard the Apostles, he says that they did this as Paul said: "Avoid a heretical man after one or two warnings, knowing that such a man is perverted and sins, being self-condemned" [ὡς ἡ Παῦλος εἶπεν αἱρετικὸν ἄνθρωπον μετὰ μίαν ἡ δευτέραν νουθεσίαν παραιτοῦ εἰδὼς ὅτι ἐξέστραπται ὁ τοιοῦτος ἡ ἁμαρτάνει ὢν αὐτοκατάκριτος]. Incidentally, from that passage of Eusebius each reader can judge by what right the Arminians say that the most ancient Christians maintained fellowship with those who taught that Christ had only a human nature and not a divine one. For Eusebius there says: the Apostles and their disciples had such great care not to mix even in conversation with those who corrupted the truth by their false doctrine [τοσαύτην οἱ Ἀπόστολοι καὶ οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτῶν ἔσχον εὐλάβειαν τὴν μὴ μίγνυσθαι λόγῳ κοινωνίαν τῷ παραχαράττοντι τὴν ἀλήθειαν]. So it is also false what the Arminians say at p. 95, that the heretics whom the censor (indeed the whole Church) calls heretics are not self-condemned. Besides, what would Polycarp say if he saw Episcopius, a man thoroughly steeped in the dregs of the Antitrinitarians, who yields to none of the old heretics in insolence, malice and the foulness of his opinions?

units.la: 6. Sextum dogma est, Hæresin de quâ quæstio est, v. g. Antitrinitariorum non esse peccatum, crimen, culpam. Fatentur p.97.98. ut & lib 1.c.1. p. 12.13. & alibi. & defendere conantur ex eo quòd non possimus judicare quod errantes tales studio errare velint & ex malitiâ in errore perseverant. Quod quàm ineptum sit, antè vidimus. Addunt quidem Hæresin eam de quâ Paulus loquitur esse peccatum: interim tamen non volunt Hæresin istam de quâ inter nos agitur, esse istam Hæresin, quam Paulus vocat opus carnis. Ita enim Apol.c.24. f.273. a. interim non volunt Remonstrantes hæresin istam de quâ inter nos agitur esse istam Hæresin quam Paulus opus carnis vocat. Nihil minus. Hæresis quæ carnis opus est, manifestum opus carnis est. At hæc de quâ quæritur, non est manifestum opus carnis &c. Similiter in Vindic. lib.2.c.9.p.172. Nec Hæresis prout eam describit Vedelius inter ista opera carnis censeri meretur, quæ is qui ea patrat, opera carnis esse novit, quaque ita sunt voluntaria uti odium, invidia, ebrietas aliaque opera carnis sunt. Deinde dicunt quidem eam Hæresin de quâ Paulus ibi loquitur, esse opus carnis & peccatum; sed non esse peccatum quâ error est, verum in quantum cum affectu pravo seu carnali conjunctus est, qui peccatum est, & qui in causâ est & facit ut error Hæresis sit. Interim quis affectus ille sit an cupiditas gloriæ, an malitia, an studium contradicendi &c. dicunt hoc nobis constare non posse; sed peccatum istud soli Deo notum esse credunt, ut loquuntur p. 98. Igitur uno verbo hæresis non est peccatum in se seu quâ error est, sed in quantum à peccato aliquo proficiscitur, quod soli Deo notum est. Hinc dicunt cap. 8. p. 157. etiam in Hæreticis talibus esse causam aliquam in voluntate aut affectibus, quæ eos culpâ reos facit. An non hoc est mundo illudere? Sed de hac re egimus Par. III. lib. 2. cap. 4. ut & de aliis novis Arcanis quæ capite 4. Vindic. produnt. Eò igitur Lectori recurrere libebit.
units.tr: 6. The sixth dogma is that the heresy under discussion, for example that the Antitrinitarians' error is no sin, crime, or fault. They confess this at pp. 97–98, as also at book 1, ch. 1, pp. 12–13, and elsewhere, and they try to defend it on the ground that we cannot judge that such erring people wish to err deliberately and persist in error out of malice. How absurd that is, we saw earlier. They do indeed add that the heresy of which Paul speaks is a sin, yet they will not grant that the heresy in our dispute is that heresy which Paul calls a work of the flesh. For thus at Apol. ch. 24, f. 273a: Meanwhile the Remonstrants do not want the heresy under discussion among us to be that heresy which Paul calls a work of the flesh. Not at all. A heresy which is a work of the flesh is a manifest work of the flesh. But the heresy in question is not a manifest work of the flesh, etc. Similarly in Vindic. book 2, ch. 9, p. 172: Nor does heresy, as Vedelius describes it, deserve to be counted among those works of the flesh which the one who commits them knows to be works of the flesh, and which are as voluntary as hatred, envy, drunkenness and the other works of the flesh are. Next, they indeed say that the heresy of which Paul speaks there is a work of the flesh and a sin, but that it is not a sin as error, only insofar as it is joined with a wicked or carnal affection, which is the sin and which is the cause that the error becomes heresy. Yet what that affection is, whether a desire for glory, malice, a zeal for contradiction, etc., they say cannot be known to us; they believe that this sin is known to God alone, as they speak at p. 98. So in a word, heresy is not a sin in itself, or as error, but insofar as it proceeds from some sin, which is known to God alone. Hence they say at ch. 8, p. 157 that even in such heretics there is some cause in the will or affections which makes them guilty of fault. Is this not mocking the world? But we dealt with this matter in Par. III, book 2, ch. 4, and also with the other new secrets which they bring forth in ch. 4 of the Vindicia. The reader may therefore be pleased to return there.

units.la: 7. Septimum est: Hæresin eam de quâ quæstio est, esse plane involuntariam, ut ostenderam Par. I. lib. 2. cap. 4. Quibus accedit quod in Apol. c.24. f.277. dicunt; Aliud est Hæresis, aliud crimen &c. Illam qui punit aut puniri curat, criminis culpam coram Dei tribunali gravissimam committit, quia crimen voluntaria culpa est. Hæresis plane involuntaria, & proprie sic dicta innocentia est. Non negant & nihil respondent.
units.tr: 7. The seventh is: that the heresy in question is altogether involuntary, as I showed in Par. I, book 2, ch. 4. To this is added what they say in Apol. ch. 24, f. 277: Heresy is one thing, crime another, etc. Whoever punishes it, or takes care that it is punished, commits the gravest fault of crime before the tribunal of God, because a crime is a voluntary fault. Heresy is altogether involuntary, and is properly called innocence. They neither deny this nor answer it.

units.la: 8. 9. Adeóque, docent, non esse opus carnis. Hoc etiam fatentur, ut vidimus §. 6. Imo ne scandalum quidem esse. Hoc etiam non negant sed sicco pede transeunt & ne γε quidem respondent.
units.tr: 8–9. And so, they teach, it is not a work of the flesh. They also confess this, as we saw in §6. Indeed, it is not even a scandal. This too they do not deny, but pass over with dry feet, and do not even answer with a "γε" [indeed].

units.la: 10. Decimum dogma est: Ignorantiam omnem etiamsi ea culpabilis sit, excusare excusare a peccato Hareseos. Hic cum convitiis solitis stuporis & inscitia su-pina, negant haec verba sua esse, sed esse citata ex Becano, & continere sententiam Pontificiorum, non autem Remonstrantium: qui si ita sentirent, tum me duplicem contradictionem iis tribuere necessum habere. Verum enim vero hic, optime Lector, rursus vide insignem proterviam & summam impudentiam horum hominum. Etenim primo Arminiani ne verbulo quidem aut ullo indicio in Apologia ostenderunt, se ea verba ex Becano citare, aut tanquam aliena ex aliena mente, non autem ex sua citare: Sed continuata serie cum verbis propriis suis antecedentibus & consequentibus connectunt. Verum est eos sol. 279. b. citare Becanum, ut ostendant quae sit Pontificiorum sententia de causis Pertinaciae. Sed postquam eum citassent his verbis: Pertinacia oriri potest vel ex obstinata maluti a vel ex infirmitate judicii vel aliunde, ut Martinus Becanus in tractatu suo de Haresi & Apostasia cap. 3. pluribus differt. Postquam, inquam, ita eum verbis illis citassent, ad se ipsos redeunt & ex propria sua sententia loqui pergunt. Nam immediate nulla alia voculā interposita dicunt: Atque hi sane (Pontificii) consequenter loquuntur, & colorem dant Haereticidio, quod tuentur. Nec alia via est, qua colorem ei dent aut speciem. Poena enim, capitalis praesertim, certo fundamento atque irrefragabili judicio niti debet. Haec dicunt f. 279. b. usque ad lineam ultimam inclusive. Pergunt sol. 280. a. linea prima: Quae res Reformatos merito movere debuisset, ut ab Haereticidio prorsus atque omnino abstinerent. Nam cum Ecclesia sua istam infallibilem judicandi auctoritatem non tribuant, ut in eo, quod verum esse statuit, errare non possit, qua via, quo jure eos qui contra Ecclesiam suam sentiunt, & in sententia sua perseverant, culpa aut criminis ullius postulabunt? Pertinacia enim pertinacia esse desinit, cum quis in eo quod credit aut sentit, errare se non advertit, adeoque se non errare firmiter persuasum sibi habet. Pertinacia creditur a multis fiducia. Omnis ignorantia sive ea inculpabilis sive culpabilis sit, excusat a peccato haeresis. In caeteris peccatis sola ignorantia invincibilis excusat. Sufficit ut voluntaria sint contra legem Dei, sive quis advertat se contra legem istam peccare, sive non advertat, dummodo advertere id possit & debeat. At in haeresi voluntarium non sufficit, sed scientia insuper atque advertentia requiritur, qua quis scit id quod sentit aut statuit repugnare Ecclesiae, vel norma secundum quam judicium faciendum esse creditur. Quia vero Ecclesiam vel normam talem infallibilem hic in terris non agnoscunt Reformati, hinc pertinacia nemo ab iis postulari potest. Et statim addunt objectionem quae ipsis moveri potest adversus praecedentia ista: At rationes sunt, inquies, luce meridiana clariores, quibus non ad sentire pertinacia est. Atque ad eam objectionem respondent: At, inquam, aliud est &c. Ex his luce clarius meridianâ est eos hoc dogma ex suâ propriâ mente proferre. Sed ut eò minus de hac re dubitari possit: addo secundo loco eos alibi etiam id dogma ex suâ propriâ mente proponere. Ita enim in Responsi ad Excerp. p. 58. ubi agunt de innocentiâ & pietate Hæreticorum: Attamen, inquies, hic error culpabilis est. Fatemur, sed culpam istam credimus idcirco in censum non venire apud Deum, quod is qui errorem istum errat, nsque adeò pietatem & obedientiam cordi habeat, ut ne quidem ab eâ per errorem istum, qui ad divertendum eum à pietatis studio comparatus est, avelli aut revocari se patiatur. Magnum hoc pii affectus ac studii argumentum est. Quod ajunt de contradictionibus rursus suis &c. id ad me non pertinet, cui propositum non est eorum contradictiones conciliare, in quas incidere tandem necessum est eos qui Spiritu erroris, non autem veritatis reguntur. Nec mirum est eos sibi contradicere qui fidem nullam in negocio Religionis, per consequens etiam in nullâ aliâ re amplius merentur.
units.tr: 10. The tenth dogma is: Every ignorance, even if it is culpable, excuses from the sin of heresy. Here, with their usual insults of stupor and supine ignorance, they deny that these words are theirs, and claim they are quoted from Becanus and express the opinion of the Papists, not of the Remonstrants; if they held this view, I would be obliged to attribute two contradictions to them. But truly, most excellent reader, see again the notable effrontery and the great impudence of these men. For first, the Arminians have not shown, by so much as a word or any sign in the Apology, that they cite those words from Becanus, or cite them as foreign words from a foreign mind rather than from their own. On the contrary, they join them in an unbroken sequence with their own preceding and following words. It is true that they cite Becanus at p. 279b, to show what the opinion of the Papists is about the causes of obstinacy. But after they had cited him in these words: Obstinacy may arise either from a stubborn will, or from weakness of judgment, or from elsewhere, as Martin Becanus discusses at length in his treatise on Heresy and Apostasy, ch. 3, after, I say, they had cited him in those words, they return to themselves and go on speaking from their own opinion. For immediately, with no other little word interposed, they say: And these Papists, to be sure, speak consistently, and give colour to the killing of heretics, which they defend. Nor is there any other way by which they could give it colour or appearance. For punishment, especially capital punishment, ought to rest on a sure foundation and an irrefutable judgment. They say these things at p. 279b, down to and including the last line. They go on at p. 280a, first line: This matter ought rightly to have moved the Reformed to abstain entirely and altogether from the killing of heretics. For since they do not grant their own Church that infallible authority of judging, so that it cannot err in what it declares to be true, by what way, by what right, will they demand guilt or any crime from those who think against their Church and persist in their opinion? For obstinacy ceases to be obstinacy when someone does not notice that he is in error in what he believes or thinks, and so is firmly persuaded that he is not in error. By many, obstinacy is taken to be confidence. Every ignorance, whether it is blameless or culpable, excuses from the sin of heresy. In other sins only invincible ignorance excuses. It is enough that the acts are voluntary against the law of God, whether someone notices that he sins against that law or does not notice, provided he can and ought to notice it. But in heresy the voluntary is not enough; knowledge and awareness are further required, by which someone knows that what he thinks or decides conflicts with the Church, or with the rule according to which judgment is believed to be made. But since the Reformed do not acknowledge such an infallible Church or rule here on earth, therefore no one can demand obstinacy from them. And immediately they add an objection which could be raised against them on the preceding points: But, you will say, there are reasons clearer than the noonday sun, to which not to assent is obstinacy. And to this objection they reply: But, I say, it is other, etc. From these things it is clearer than the noonday light that they put forward this dogma from their own mind. But so that there may be less room for doubt on this matter, I add, secondly, that they also put forward this dogma elsewhere from their own mind. For so in the Responsio ad Excerpta, p. 58, where they treat of the innocence and piety of heretics: Yet, you will say, this error is culpable. We admit it, but we believe that this fault does not come into account before God, because the one who errs in this error so holds piety and obedience in his heart that he does not even allow himself to be drawn away or recalled from it by the error, which is designed to turn him from the pursuit of piety. This is a great proof of a pious affection and zeal. As to what they say about their contradictions again, etc., that does not concern me, since it is not my purpose to reconcile their contradictions, into which those must at last necessarily fall who are ruled by the spirit of error and not of truth. Nor is it surprising that they contradict themselves, who no longer deserve any trust in the matter of religion, and consequently in no other matter either.

units.la: 11. 12. Undecimum dogma est; non solum simplices Hæreticos seu ab aliis seductos non peccare, sed etiam seductores ipsos sine culpâ esse. Duodecimum: Et ideò seductores eos odio dignos non esse.
