Hoc est quod ibidem dixeram ; quæ mea verba quia legerant hi homines ; hinc regerunt & dicunt ; Iudicare in Synodo non esse publicè docere. Probant exinde : 1. quia sic Presbyteri qui in verbo non laborant, tunc in Synodo publicè in verbo laborant & docent. 2. Cum iudicia in Synodo sæpenumero non diversa tantum sint, sed & contraria ; non diversa tantum sed & contraria publicè docebuntur in Ecclesia. 3. Dicunt in Synodo Dordracenâ sedisse Presbyteros ignaros prorsus lingua Latinæ ; qui per consequens non potuerint publicè docere. Resp. ad 1. & 3. Meræ nugæ sunt. Nam ego non memini presbyterorum sed indefinitè loquutus sum. Presbyteros quod attinet illi proprie & per se non veniunt ad Synodum docendi causâ, utpote qui repræsentant populum seu eos qui docentur, & nomine populi approbant aut rejiciunt ea quæ à Doctoribus proponuntur. Quando tamen Ecclesia presbyteros tales deligit (quod faciendum est quantum fieri potest) qui docti sint, aut alios eruditos & rerum Theologicarum bene peritos eò mittit ; illi ubi docent extraordinariè ad id à Deo per Ecclesiam vocati sunt. Et hoc est quod dicebam p. 179 quosdam præter Doctores ordinarios Ecclesiæ ad judicandum in Synodo à Deo per Ecclesiam legitimè vocatos esse. Unde etiam patet, hos homines prodere ignorantiam suam ; ac nescire quo fine presbyteri ad Synodum mittantur. Per consequens etiam patet eos absque causâ suggillare Synodum Dordracenam, eo prætextu quòd ille unus aut forte alter presbyterorum (viri profecto nobilitate, dignitate Magistratuum, pietate insignes, quos hi maledicentissimi homines stupidos & rusticos p. 126 appellant) non potuerint docere publicè. Ineptum etiam esse, quod pro pugnantibus ponunt, eos qui ordinariè non docent extraordinariè docere, unusquisque videt. Ad 2. Absurdum non est suffragia quæ decisionem Synodi antecedunt diversa aut contraria esse : nam tandem non contraria docentur sed una eademque doctrina proponitur à Synodo ex verbo Dei, cujus decisioni se submittunt caeteri melius ex verbo edocti. Nisi velint hi homines calumniari ipsam Synodum Apostolicam Hierosolymitanam Act. 15. in quâ initiò diversa imò contraria proponebantur & πολλὴ συζήτησις ἐγένετο v. 5. 6. 7.
units.tr: These men know that I spoke of such a judgment and called it public for this reason: because I had said that the Word of God does not grant public judgment on matters of faith to all and each of men, but to those whose office or calling it is. They say this is false, for the Word of God nowhere grants judgment to the Pastors alone, etc. I answer: does not the Word of God grant to the teachers and Pastors of the Church alone the office of teaching publicly, and also to those who have been called by God through the Church to perform this kind of act in a Synod? This is what I had said in that place. These men, since they had read my words, turn them back and say: To judge in a Synod is not to teach publicly. From this they argue: 1. because in this way the elders, who do not labour in the Word, would then in a Synod labour and teach publicly in the Word. 2. Since judgments in a Synod are often not merely different but even contrary, things that are not merely different but contrary would be taught publicly in the Church. 3. They say that in the Synod of Dort there sat elders wholly ignorant of the Latin language, who consequently could not have taught publicly. I reply to 1 and 3: these are mere trifles. For I do not remember having spoken of elders but of persons in general. As for the elders, they do not properly and of themselves come to a Synod for the sake of teaching, since they represent the people, or those who are taught, and in the name of the people they approve or reject what is proposed by the teachers. When, however, the Church chooses such elders (as must be done as far as possible) as are learned, or sends others who are erudite and well skilled in theological matters, these, when they teach, are called by God through the Church to do so in an extraordinary way. And this is what I was saying on p. 179: that certain persons, besides the ordinary teachers of the Church, are lawfully called by God through the Church to judge in the Synod. From this it is also plain that these men betray their own ignorance and do not know for what purpose elders are sent to a Synod. Consequently it is also plain that they slander the Synod of Dort without cause, on the pretext that this or that one of the elders (men truly distinguished by nobility, by the dignity of their magistracies and by piety, whom these most slanderous men call stupid and rustic, p. 126) could not teach publicly. Anyone can see that it is also absurd, when they set up as opposites, that those who do not teach in the ordinary way may teach in an extraordinary way. As for 2: it is not absurd that the votes which come before the decision of a Synod are different or contrary; for in the end nothing contrary is taught, but one and the same doctrine is set forth by the Synod from the Word of God, to whose decision the others, better instructed from the Word, submit. Unless these men want to slander the Apostolic Synod of Jerusalem itself, Acts 15, in which at first different and even contrary views were put forward, and there was much debate [πολλὴ συζήτησις ἐγένετο], vv. 5, 6, 7.

units.la: Pergunt,& addunt 4. Doctores in Synodo non comparere quâ Doctores sed quatenus repraesentantes Ecclesiam totam. Iam autem repraesentare Ecclesiam non possunt docendo ea quae Ecclesia ignorat, aut saltem consensione suâ non comprobavit. &c. Respondeo, Profectò hi Sociniani simulatores vel etiam in hac parte monstrant, praesertim a. M. Episcopius, quàm imperiti sint rerum Theologicarum. Dicunt Doctores comparere in Synodo quatenus repraesentant Ecclesiam totam. Hoc salsissimum est. Repraesentant enim seu exhibent partem Ecclesiae nimirum partem docentem; quemadmodum Presbyteri repraesentant alteram partem, nimirum eam quae docetur, quae tota in Synodo comparere non potest. Constat enim Ecclesia ex duabus illis partibus integrantibus. Itaque falsum etiam est, Doctores in Synodo non comparere ut Doctores. Falsum per consequens etiam est Ecclesiam non nòsse quae docentur in Synodo, aut consensione suâ non approbare illa. Nam novit Ecclesia illa quae domi remansit ea quae ibi docentur, tùm in persona eorum qui ipsam repraesentant, tùm in propria persona quando doctrina ab eâ antea recepta confirmatur à Synodo, prout in Dordracenâ contigit, tùm quando Synodus eos de gestis edocet ut Actorum 15. 22. 23. factum est.
units.tr: They go on and add a fourth point: the Doctors do not appear in the Synod as Doctors, but insofar as they represent the whole Church. Now they cannot represent the Church by teaching things the Church does not know, or at least has not approved by its consent, and so on. I reply that these Socinian pretenders, and especially Episcopius, show in this part too how inexperienced they are in theological matters. They say that the Doctors appear in the Synod insofar as they represent the whole Church. This is most absurd. They represent or exhibit only a part of the Church, namely the teaching part, just as the Elders represent the other part, namely the part that is taught, which cannot all appear in the Synod. The Church is made up of these two integral parts. So it is also false that the Doctors do not appear in the Synod as Doctors. And it is false, consequently, that the Church does not know what is taught in the Synod or does not approve it by its consent. For the Church that stayed at home knows what is taught there, both through the persons who represent it and in its own person, when a doctrine it had previously received is confirmed by the Synod, as happened at Dort; and when the Synod informs them of what was done, as happened in Acts 15:22, 23.

units.la: Addunt quintò: Doctor quâ Doctor non credit; Doctor quâ ovis est credit. Iudicium itaque eius de rebus fidei non est iudicium publicum sed privatum, quod cum singulis ovibus commune habet. Par & aequalis iudicandi potestas competit ovibus omnibus ac singulis. Nec magis iudicio Doctoris in rebus fidei obstringuntur oves, quam ovium iudicio Doctores. Et tandem concludunt scommatis & maledicentiâ suâ illâ cujus antea memini adversus Synodum Dordracenam & eos Presbyteros illius. Respondeo uno verbo: Doctor quâ Doctor docet quae credit. Et sic judicium ejus est publicum, quando in Synodo ex verbo Dei docet quid sit credendum. De pari potestate ovium & Doctorum &c. quod dicunt egimus Par. III. lib. 2. c. 5. §. 1. quò Lectorem remittimus. Atque haec quidem est praeclara illa Theologia horum hominum, quantum ad praesentem rem attinet. Quae quidem Theologia ipsorum ut fluit ex eo principio quòd Synodus non sit conventus tantùm delegatorum Doctorum & Presbyterorum, sed quòd Synodus sint illi etiam qui domi manent; prout initio statim suarum turrum turbarum ausi fuerunt dicere, contra usum voris illius receptum à tota Christianitate usque ad hæc tempora; (faciebant autem id eo fine ut eluderent judicium futuræ tunc Synodi) ita eò tendit, ut evincant Synodum non debere decidere ex verbo Dei quid aliis credendum sit, sed tantùm debere indicare quid ipsa credat, & aliis libertatem & optionem relinquere docendi quicquid velint. Hinc hoc loco adversus me contendunt; Doctores in Synodo non docere; judicium Synodicum etiam non esse judicium quod doceat. Quod si verum est, concidit profectò totum Ministerium. Si enim Pastores simul sumti & congregati in unum non possunt docere quid populis credendum sit, multò minus seorsim sumti poterunt aut debent docere; sed saltem tenentur indicare quid ipsi credant; non secus ac populi eorum non tenentur docere, sed interrogati indicare saltem quid credant. Aliter nos verbum Dei instruit; quod officium docendi instituit, cui, ubi docentur ea quæ Dominus præcepit ac revelavit, obedientia & fides deferenda est à populis Heb. 13. 27. & distinguit inter τὸ docere & reddere rationem fidei suæ. Pudeat hos homines, qui profectò de rebus sacris nugantur non aliter quàm Tyrones & novitii modò ad Religionem Christianam accedentes; quod mirum non est in iis qui Turcismi fundamenta in Belgio per blasphemias suas Socinianas nunc jaciunt. Deus eos confundat.
units.tr: They add, fifthly: The Doctor as Doctor does not believe; the Doctor as a sheep believes. His judgment on matters of faith is therefore not a public judgment but a private one, which he shares with individual sheep. Equal and like power of judging belongs to all the sheep, each and every one. Nor are the sheep bound by the judgment of the Doctor in matters of faith any more than the Doctors are bound by the judgment of the sheep. And at last they conclude with their jeers and slander, which I mentioned earlier, against the Synod of Dort and its Elders. I reply in one word: the Doctor as Doctor teaches what he believes. So his judgment is public when, in the Synod, he teaches from the Word of God what is to be believed. As for the equal power of the sheep and the Doctors, and so on, which they mention, we have dealt with it in Part III, book 2, chapter 5, §1, to which we refer the reader. This, indeed, is the splendid theology of these men, so far as the present question is concerned. Their theology flows from the principle that the Synod is not merely a gathering of delegated Doctors and Elders, but that those who remain at home also constitute the Synod. They dared to say this at the very start of their turbulent troubles, against the custom received by the whole Christian world up to these times. (They did so, indeed, with the aim of evading the judgment of the Synod that was then to come.) Their aim is to prove that the Synod ought not to decide from the Word of God what others must believe, but only indicate what it itself believes, leaving others free and at liberty to teach whatever they wish. Hence they argue against me here that the Doctors do not teach in the Synod, and that the judgment of the Synod is not a judgment that teaches. If this is true, the whole ministry certainly collapses. For if Pastors taken together and gathered into one body cannot teach the people what they are to believe, much less can they or ought they to teach when taken separately. They would be bound only to indicate what they themselves believe, just as their people are not bound to teach but, when asked, only to say what they believe. Scripture teaches otherwise: it establishes the office of teaching, to which obedience and faith are owed by the people when the things the Lord has commanded and revealed are taught (Heb. 13:17), and it distinguishes between teaching and giving an account of one's faith. These men should be ashamed, for they trifle about sacred matters no differently from novices and recruits only now coming to the Christian religion. This is no wonder in men who now lay the foundations of Turkism in Belgium by their Socinian blasphemies. May God confound them.

units.la: Denique volunt conciliare contradictionem quam ipsis p. 179. objeceram. Dixerant enim: in Synodis non admittantur nisi viri apti & idonei h. e. rerum divinarum periti, & qui in Scripturis potentes sunt, sensusque habent ad discretionem veri & falsi exercitatos Confess. c. 25. §. 2. In Apologia autem, ut vidimus dicunt Omnes æquo & pari iure admittendos esse, quia salutis æternæ negocium ad omnes æque pertinet. Et ostenderam eos contradictionem hanc in æternum conciliare non posse, quia scilicet maxima pars hominum ad quos salutis æterna negocium non minus pertinet, quàm ad doctissimum quemque, rudes seu infantes sunt in rebus fidei &c. Conciliare igitur p. 127. conantur hoc modo: In Synodis admittendos non esse nisi viros aptos & idoneos &c. quod interim dicunt admittendos omnes ad Synodum esse; se hoc velle, quòd etiamsi omnes ac singuli non admittantur nimia confusionis vitanda causa, tamen nulla decisio fieri debeat in Synodo, nisi prius relatione facta ad Ecclesias omnes ac singulas, earumque super omnibus sententia audita ac cognita. Hoc enim tantundem est atque omnes ac singulos admittere &c. Verum frustra conantur elabi. Nam dicunt in Apologia, non solum ad Ecclesias relationem faciendam esse, sed etiam omnes ac singulos comparendi jus habere ibere in IPSA SYNODO imò cujuslibet esse non expectare missionem Ecclesiæ, sed ACCURRERE ad Synodum ipsam: Cuiuslibet est, inquiunt, sine ulla missione ACCURRERE EO' UBI de salutis æterna negocio IN COMITIA ITUR.
units.tr: Finally they want to reconcile the contradiction that I had charged against them at p. 179. For they had said: In Synods only men who are fit and suitable are to be admitted, that is, skilled in divine matters, who are powerful in the Scriptures and have senses trained to distinguish true from false (Confession, ch. 25, §2). But in their Apology, as we have seen, they say that all are to be admitted with equal and like right, because the business of eternal salvation pertains equally to all. And I had shown that they could never reconcile this contradiction, because the greater part of men, to whom the business of eternal salvation pertains no less than to the most learned of all, are untaught and like infants in matters of faith, and so on. So at p. 127 they try to reconcile it in this way: Only men who are fit and suitable are to be admitted to Synods, and so on, while in the meantime they say that all are to be admitted to the Synod; they mean that even if not all and each are admitted, for the sake of avoiding excessive confusion, nevertheless no decision should be made in the Synod unless first a report has been made to all and each of the Churches, and their opinion on every matter has been heard and known. For this amounts to the same thing as admitting all and each, and so on. But they try in vain to slip away. For in the Apology they say that not only is a report to be made to the Churches, but that each and every one has the right to appear in the Synod itself; indeed, it is for anyone to come, not waiting for the Church's dispatch, but to RUSH to the Synod itself. It belongs to anyone, they say, without any commission, to RUSH TO THE PLACE WHERE the business of eternal salvation is conducted IN ASSEMBLY.

units.la: 2. Secundum dogma est: Eos qui ad Synodum admittuntur seu veniunt, debere nulli Ecclesiæ vel Confessioni obstrictos esse. Fatentur hoc p. 127. 128. Sed quia simul ostendi manifestissimè, eos hoc velle ut nimirùm Synodicæ personæ nulli veritati quæ in controversiam vocatur aut vocari potest obstrictæ sint, sed ea saltem indubitatè teneant, quæ extra controversiam sunt inter Christianos; negant hanc suam mentem esse; nam me recurrere inquiunt ad meum πρῶτον ψεῦδος quod ita nominant, de Necessariis & non Necessariis: & calumniantur me per illud πρῶτον ψεῦδος Libertatem prophetandi excisam velle, & Ecclesiæ auctoritate Pontificiorum in morem pugnare. Sed eos contra conscientiam suam negare propriam suam doctrinam ostensum est libro priore cap. 8. Et ex abundanti patet verissimam esse hanc accusationem, quia illud quod in verbo Dei totidem literis & syllabis expressum non est, etiamsi per consequentiam evidentissimam exinde deducatur, dicunt in verbo Dei non extare, ne hilum quidem de eo in Scriptura esse. v. g. Etiamsi de eo quod Spiritus S. Deus sit evidentissima & summè necessaria consequentia inferatur Ergò Spiritus S. est adorandus; dicunt tamen ne hilum quidem in Scriptura de adorando Spiritu S. esse, ut suprà vidimus. Quod addunt, me Libertatem prophetandi eâ ratione è medio tollere velle; item me Ecclesiæ auctoritate ubivis Pontificium in morem pugnare, ut ostendam aliquod dogma Hæreticum esse; calumniosum est, ut alibi ostendimus. Et quod dicunt me cataplasmata & malagmata hæc addere subinde Ex verbo Dei, item Epitheta Orthodoxa, pura, vera Ecclesiæ aut Synodi; de eo vidimus Par. III. lib. 1. c. 1.
units.tr: 2. The second doctrine is this: Those who are admitted to the Synod, or come to it, ought not to be bound to any Church or Confession. They confess this at pp. 127–128. But since I had shown very clearly at the same time that they mean by this that the members of the Synod are not bound to any truth that is, or can be, called into controversy, but only to those things that are beyond doubt and beyond dispute among Christians, they deny that this is their meaning. For they say that I recur to my first falsehood [πρῶτον ψεῦδος], as they call it, concerning Necessary and Non-necessary things, and they slander me through that first falsehood, claiming that I want to cut off the liberty of prophesying and to fight, in the manner of the Papists, with the authority of the Church. But it was shown in the first book, chapter 8, that they deny their own doctrine against their conscience. And, more than enough, it is clear that this accusation is most true. For they say that what is not expressed in the Word of God in so many letters and syllables does not exist in the Word of God, and that there is not even a jot of it in Scripture, even if it is deduced from it by a most evident consequence. For example, even if it is inferred from the fact that God is the Holy Spirit by a most evident and most necessary consequence that the Holy Spirit is to be worshipped, they nevertheless say that there is not even a jot in Scripture about worshipping the Holy Spirit, as we saw above. What they add, that I want to remove the liberty of prophesying by this method, and likewise that I fight everywhere in the manner of the Papists with the authority of the Church, in order to show that some doctrine is heretical, is slanderous, as we have shown elsewhere. And as to their saying that I subinately add these plasters and poultices, From the Word of God, and likewise the Orthodox, pure, true epithets of the Church or Synod, we have seen about this in Part III, book 1, chapter 1.

units.la: 3. Tertium est: Libertatem plenariam concedendam esse unicuique sine scrupulo & periculi metu in dubium vocandi, examinandi, proponendi quicquid in controversiam vocatur aut vocari potest. Fatentur; & dicunt hanc esse veram libertatem Deo summè gratam & divinæ veritati maximè gloriosam: contrariam verò sententiam meam esse meram Tyrannidem & servitutem Pontificiam, quam merito culparunt in Synodo Tridentinâ Protestantes, & quam ut experiar aliquando ego, dicunt me dignum esse &c. p. 130. 131. Excipiant saltem ea quæ in Religione Christiana certa ac firma sunt. Quasi scilicet vera controversa omnia dogmata certa ac firma non sint. Et quæ dogmata controversa item dogmata non certa, non firma, quæ liceat in dubium vocare intelligant hi homines vel ex eo patet, quod inter ea referunt etiam dogmata Orthodoxa de Trinitate oppositæ blasphemiis Antitrinitariorum. Hæc est egregia libertas illa, Deo summè grata & divinæ veritati maximè gloriosa, ut hi homines volunt. Contraria vero sententia h. e. quâ Hæreticis non permittitur in dubium vocare ea dogmata & liberè blasphemias suas evomere est Tyrannis scilicet. Protestantibus in Synodo Tridentina nunquam in mentem venit hæc impietas; nimirùm licere in dubium vocare, aut velle in dubium vocare omnia ea quæ in Religione Christiana controversa sunt aut controverti possunt. Porro, quia dixeram esse illam atrocissimam licentiam in veritatem divinam seu verbum Dei atque ipsum Deum: postulant illi ut rationem dent. Verùm enim vero, annondum didicerunt hi homines esse peccatum, contradicere veritati divinæ, utut in Controversiam ea vocetur, & verbum Dei prætexatur, (quod hic p. 130. vocant ex verbo Dei examen instituere,) illam, adeoque Deum ipsum mendacii arguere, ac dicere Dominus dixit cùm tamen Dominus non dixerit; nomen Dei temerè usurpare &c? Quæstio enim est hoc loco, & Arminiani (ut lib. 1. cap. 8. ostendimus) loquuntur, de dogmatis controversis quæ revera seu secundùm esse, non autem secundùm dici tantùm vera sunt. Calumnias quas p. 131. addunt contra Reformatas Eccle-sias prætereo.
units.tr: 3. Third: Full freedom must be granted to everyone, without scruple and without fear of danger, to call in question, examine and propose whatever is or can be brought into controversy. They admit this, and they say that this is true liberty, most pleasing to God and most glorious to divine truth. My opposing view, they say, is sheer tyranny and Papist servitude, which the Protestants rightly blamed at the Council of Trent, and which they say I deserve to suffer one day themselves, etc., p. 130, 131. At the very least, they should make an exception for what is certain and firm in the Christian religion. As if all the disputed doctrines were not certain and firm! That these men understand the disputed doctrines to be uncertain and unsettled, and so open to question, is clear from the fact that among them they include even the orthodox doctrine of the Trinity, set against the blasphemies of the Antitrinitarians. This is that outstanding liberty, most pleasing to God and most glorious to divine truth, as these men want it. But the opposing view, namely that heretics are not permitted to call those doctrines in question and to vomit forth their blasphemies freely, is, of course, tyranny. It never came into the minds of the Protestants at the Council of Trent that it is allowed, or that one may wish, to call in question everything that is controverted in the Christian religion or can be controverted. Further, because I had said that this is that most atrocious license against divine truth, or the Word of God, and God himself, they demand that I give a reason. But indeed, these men have not yet learned that it is a sin to contradict divine truth, however much it is put in controversy and whatever pretext is taken from the Word of God (what they here, p. 130, call "instituting an examination from the Word of God"), and so to accuse God himself of lying, saying "The Lord has said" when the Lord has not said it, and to use the name of God rashly, etc.? The question here is, and the Arminians speak (as we showed in book 1, chapter 8) of disputed doctrines that are truly true, that is, true in reality and in being, not merely in what is said. I pass over the calumnies they add against the Reformed Churches on p. 131.

units.la: 4. Quartum: Synodo non licere formare decreta, quibus certi aliquid & quod alii credere teneantur de Controversiis fidei decidatur.
units.tr: 4. Fourth: that a synod may not frame decrees by which something certain is settled, and which others are bound to believe, on controversies of faith.

units.la: Fatentur, postquam prius aliquantulum tergiversati essent; & defendunt ex eo, quòd ista sententia contineat præcipuum fundamentum Reformationis contra Pontificios, & me ut Pontificium traducunt. Repetunt etiam rationem quâ id probaverant, desumtam à fallibilitate judicii humani. Et quia ego ad id responderam, fallibilitatem istam non semper in actum educi, quandoquidem homo non errat, quando verbo Dei unicè nititur eique rationem suam submittit, adeòque in eo actu quo rectè ex verbo Dei judicat, errare non potest: ideò instant illi: Quasi verò hoc ratio illa inferat! Nihil minus. Rationis vis in eo posita est, quòd nulla Ecclesia quacunque tandem illa sit ita jus decidendi habeat, ut, quod in Synodo congregata semel statuit ac iudicavit verum esse & verbo divino consentaneum, id alii omnes ut rectè ex verbo Dei decisum approbare, eique in conscientiâ acquiescere teneantur. Et addunt ineptum esse & ἀπροσδιόνυσον quod dixi hominem non errare, quando verbo Dei unicè nititur, eique rationem suam submittit &c. Ineptum; nam, nam, aiunt, illa ratio tantundem valet, ac si Vedelius diceret: Homo quando errare non potest, tum errare non potest. Recte enim ex verbo Dei, quod errare non potest, iudicare, est non posse in iudicando errare. A'παραδιόντος: nam hoc non quaeritur, an homo cum recte iudicat in iudicio suo errare possit. Quis enim id affirmet? Sed an homo sive Ecclesia quae ex verbo Dei iudicat, etiamsi fiat ut recte iudicet, ius habeat statuendi ac iubendi ut istud quod iudicavit, ab omnibus sine controversia recipiatur atque admittatur. &c. Et addunt: nemo admittere aut credere tenetur aliquid verum esse, etiamsi forte verum sit, quia Ecclesia in Synodo congregata vel unanimiter vel maiori ex parte verum id esse & verbo divino consentaneum iudicavit &c.
units.tr: They admit this, after first hedging a little; and they defend it on the ground that this view contains the chief foundation of the Reformation against the Papists, and they drag me over to the Papists. They also repeat the argument by which they had proved it, taken from the fallibility of human judgment. And since I had answered that this fallibility is not always brought into act, since a man does not err when he rests solely on the Word of God and submits his reasoning to it, and so cannot err in that act by which he judges rightly from the Word of God, they press on: As if that argument drew this conclusion! Nothing of the sort. The force of the argument lies in this: no church, whatever it may be, has such a right to decide that what a synod, once gathered, has determined and judged to be true and consistent with the divine Word, all others are bound to approve as a decision rightly drawn from the Word of God and to acquiesce in it in conscience. And they add that what I said, that a man does not err when he rests solely on the Word of God and submits his reasoning to it, etc., is irrelevant [ἀπροσδιόνυσον]. Irrelevant; for, they say, that reasoning amounts to no more than if Vedelius said: "When a man cannot err, then he cannot err." For to judge rightly from the Word of God, which cannot err, is to be unable to err in judging. Beside the point [ἀπαραδιόντος]: for the question is not whether a man who judges rightly can err in his judgment. Who would affirm that? The question is whether a man or a church that judges from the Word of God, even when it comes about that it judges rightly, has the right to decree and command that what it has judged be received and admitted by all without controversy, etc. And they add: no one is bound to admit or believe something to be true, even if it happens to be true, simply because the church, gathered in synod, has judged it, either unanimously or by the greater part, to be true and consistent with the divine Word, etc.

units.la: Respondeo: Omnia ista impertinentia & nugatoria sunt, nixa eâ calumniâ ac si nos æquè ac Pontifi tribueremus ipsi Ecclesiæ ut summo judici & per se jus decidendi controversias, & diceremus eo ipso aliquid credendum esse quia, ut hic loquuntur, Ecclesia in Synodo congregata id verum esse & verbo divino consentaneum iudicavit. Id quod nunquam nobis in mentem venit; nec etiam ex nostrâ sententiâ sequitur; qui dicimus ideo decreto alicui acquiescendum esse, non quia ita Ecclesia judicavit, sed quia verbum Dei ita decidit controversiam. Responsum quod ratiunculæ ipsorum opposui firmum manet: nam si fallibilitas judicii humani non semper in actum educitur, seu, si homo non errat quando ex verbo Dei rectè judicat; certè fallibilitas judicii humani perperàm prætexitur ab Arminianis, ut evincant nihil unquam certi ab Ecclesiâ ex verbo Dei statui posse ad decidendas & finiendas controversias. Adeoque ineptum non est, quod dixi hominem quando unicè nititur verbo Dei & ex eo rectè iudicat errare non posse. Nec enim ista oratio identica, nedum nugatoria est ut fingunt hi homines, sed procedit à causâ ad effectum. Causa enim hujus effecti, quod homo non errat, est conformitas cum verbo Dei, seu quia homo in judicando unicè & verè sequitur normam verbi divini. Nec etiam ἀπροσδιόνυσ est; tùm, quia iis verbis aliud nihil intuli, quam perperam fallibilitatem Ecclesiæ prætexi ab Arminianis dogmati isti suo; tùm, quia status quæstionis non est is quem hîc Arminiani fingunt: sed an Synodo non liceat formare decreta quibus certi aliquid decidatur ex verbo Dei quod alii admittere & recipere teneantur, non ideo quia Synodus decidit, sed quia Deus controversiam in verbo suo ita decidit.
units.tr: I reply: all of this is beside the point and trifling, resting on the calumny that we, like the Papists, grant to the Church itself, as supreme judge, the right to decide controversies in its own right, and that we would thereby say that something must be believed simply because, as they put it here, the church gathered in synod has judged it to be true and consistent with the divine Word. This never entered our minds, nor does it follow from our view, since we say that assent must be given to a decree not because the church has so judged, but because the Word of God so decides the controversy. The answer I gave to their little argument stands firm. For if the fallibility of human judgment is not always brought into act, or, if a man does not err when he judges rightly from the Word of God, then certainly the fallibility of human judgment is wrongly pretended by the Arminians, in order to prove that nothing certain can ever be laid down by the Church from the Word of God for deciding and ending controversies. So it is not irrelevant that I said a man who rests solely on the Word of God and judges rightly from it cannot err. For this statement is not an empty tautology, much less trifling, as these men pretend, but proceeds from cause to effect. The cause of this effect, that a man does not err, is conformity with the Word of God, that is, because in judging he follows the rule of the divine Word alone and truly. Nor is it irrelevant; first, because by these words I inferred nothing else than that the fallibility of the Church is wrongly pretended by the Arminians for their dogma; and second, because the state of the question is not what the Arminians here imagine it to be. The question is whether a synod may not frame decrees by which something certain is decided from the Word of God that others are bound to admit and receive, not because the synod decides it, but because God has so decided the controversy in his Word.

units.la: 5. Quintum dogma est: Synodum non debere convenire in eum finem, præcisè ut decidatur controversia, quod illi vocant quovis modo decidere. Fatentur, & postquàm repetiissent ineptam vitiligationem circa id quod dixeram Ecclesiam Orthodoxam non quovis modo decidere controversias, sed ex verbo Dei; de qua re ante egimus, defendere id conantur convitiis & calumniis contra Synodum Dordracenam, sed per illius latus contra omnes Synodos Orthodoxas, quae inde ab initio in eum finem praecise convenere ut controversia non indecisa maneret, sed ex verbo Dei decideretur, prout ex historia & inductione omnium Synodorum ostendi potest. Quem finem ubi assequuta fuerat Ecclesia vetus, etiamsi Haeretici refragarentur & se ei submittere nollent, judicabat haereses excisas esse, populos errore liberatos, & quicquid Diabolus per fraudem molitus erat funditus sublatum, ut videre est ex Epistola Synodica Concilii Nicaeni apud Socrat. lib. 1. c. 6. & Theodor. lib. 1. c. 11. & Epistola Synodica Ariminensi Patrum Orthodoxorum ad Constantium, Socrat. lib. 2. c. 29. Caeterum quia ostenderam qua ratione de Synodo aut Ecclesia dici possit vel non possit eam decidere; nimirum eam non per se decidere litem, sed Deum antea illam in verbo suo decidisse; Ecclesiam vero saltem testem & interpretem esse verbi Dei: contra hoc illi p. 134. sophisticantur ex eo fundamento, quod decisio Synodi nova sit & a Deo ipso non facta &c. de qua falsitate vide Par. III. lib. 2. c. 6. §. 3. 4. item quod Ecclesia non possit simul esse & testis & interpres, quod pariter falsum esse ex Scriptura constat, quae docet veros Doctores simul & testes & interpretes esse voluntatis & veritatis divinae. Et addunt eadem p. 134. quia verbum Dei interpretatione opus habeat, unicuique liberam debere esse interpretationem; quae qualis & quam inepta sit consequentia unusquisque videt qui novit ex eo quia verbum Dei interpretatione opus habeat sequi, illud secundum mentem auctoris interpretandam esse, prout etiam ex praxi Christi & Apostolorum agendum esse constat. Videte mihi qualis Theologia sit horum hominum, & quam profunda scilicet scientia Theologica.
units.tr: 5. Fifth dogma: that a synod ought not to convene for the sole purpose that a controversy be decided, which they call deciding it in any way at all. They admit this; and after repeating their foolish quibble about what I had said, that the orthodox Church does not decide controversies in any way at all but from the Word of God (a matter we dealt with before), they try to defend it with abuse and calumnies against the Synod of Dort, but in effect against all the orthodox synods, which from the beginning convened for the sole purpose that a controversy should not remain undecided, but be decided from the Word of God, as can be shown from history and from the review of all the synods. When the ancient Church had attained this end, even if the heretics objected and refused to submit to it, it judged the heresies to be cut off, the peoples freed from error, and whatever the Devil had craftily set in motion utterly removed, as may be seen from the Synodal Letter of the Council of Nicaea in Socrates, book 1, chapter 6, and Theodoret, book 1, chapter 11, and the Synodal Letter of the orthodox Fathers at Ariminum to Constantius, Socrates, book 2, chapter 29. Moreover, because I showed in what sense it can or cannot be said of a synod or church that it decides something, namely that it does not decide the suit of itself, but that God had decided it beforehand in his Word, and the Church is only the witness and interpreter of the Word of God, they sophisticate against this on p. 134, on the ground that a synod's decision is new and not made by God himself, etc. For the falsity of this, see part 3, book 2, chapter 6, sections 3 and 4. Likewise they argue that the Church cannot be both witness and interpreter at once; that this too is equally false is clear from Scripture, which teaches that true teachers are both witnesses and interpreters of the divine will and truth. And on the same page 134 they add that because the Word of God needs interpretation, every individual should have free interpretation. What sort of consequence this is, and how foolish, anyone can see who knows that because the Word of God needs interpretation, it follows that it must be interpreted according to the mind of its author, as is also clear from the practice of Christ and the Apostles. Look at what sort of theology these men have, and how profound, forsooth, their theological learning is.

units.la: 7. Septimo conquestus eram p. 186. de eo quod decisiones omnium Conciliorum & Synodorum totius Ecclesiae Orthodoxae etiam veteris ex verbo Dei facta pro Tyrannicis & noxiis habeant. Non negant, sed contra in genere rursus acerrime invehuntur & maledicentissime in Synodos quae ita deciderunt (deciderunt autem ita omnes Synodi veteres) ac dicunt verbum Dei tantum praetextum esse, sed alia mundana & carnalia in causa esse &c. Atque ut speciem videatur habere oratio, allegant Pseudoconcilia sive conciliabula Haereticorum, item testimonia veterum & recentiorum de istis coetibus malignantium, quales speciatim sub Imperatoribus Arianis Grenis Gregorius Nazianzenus se vidisse ait: quæ omnia ad rem non fa-ciunt. Quæstio enim est de ipsis Synodis Orthodoxis ex verbo Dei ritè rectéque pronuntiantibus.
units.tr: 7. Seventhly, I complained (p. 186) that they hold that the decisions of all the Councils and Synods of the whole Orthodox Church, even the ancient ones, made from the Word of God, are tyrannical and harmful. They do not deny this; on the contrary, they again attack in general, and most abusively, the synods that so decided (and all the ancient synods did so decide), and they say that the Word of God is only a pretext, while other worldly and carnal motives are the real cause, etc. And to give their argument an appearance of plausibility, they cite pseudo-councils or conventicles of heretics, and likewise the testimonies of ancient and recent writers about those gatherings of malefactors, such as those which Gregory Nazianzen says he saw under the Arian emperors among the Greeks. None of this bears on the matter. The question concerns the Orthodox synods themselves, which pronounced rightly and correctly from the Word of God.

units.la: 8. Objeceram etiam p. 186. ipsos in Confessione suâ falsò dixisse: Ecclesiam veterem ita decidisse ut illi volunt; & dixeram eos hodie negare non posse, se falsò id dixisse. Nam cùm Cl. DD. Proff. Leydd. eos in Censurâ falsi-tatis in eâ re convicissent; Arminianos illam responsionem in Apologiâ suâ dissi-mulare, & ne verbo quidem ad eam replicare: cùm tamen, si candidè agere voluis-sent, non debuissent errorem illum suum silentio praeterire, sed agnoscere, exemplis piorum Doctorum veterum. In hoc mendacio se deprehensos esse non ne-gant, & ne verbo quidem replicant.
units.tr: 8. I had also objected (p. 186) that they had falsely said in their Confession that the ancient Church decided as they wish; and I had said that today they cannot deny that they said this falsely. For when the most distinguished professors of Leiden had convicted them of this falsehood in the Censure of Falsehood, the Arminians dissembled that answer in their Apology and did not even reply to it in a word, although, if they had acted honestly, they ought not to have passed over that error of theirs in silence, but to have acknowledged it, by the examples of the pious ancient teachers. They do not deny that they were caught in this lie, and they do not even reply to it in a word.

units.la: 9. Ostenderam quoque p. 186. 187. ipsos decisionibus Ecclesiæ verâ ex verbo Dei factis calumniosè imputare bella & persecutiones; hoc enim per accidens fieri, non secus atque ex Evangelio bella &c. oriuntur culpâ non Evangelii sed vitio hominum, Haereticorum, & aliorum non memorum officii sui: & sic causam malorum decretis Synodicis Orthodoxis non magis adscribendam esse, quàm Christo & Evangelio ipsius. Ad hoc etiam nihil respondent, sed saltem, etiamsi convicti sint, & nihil reponere possint, persistunt in maledicentiâ & calumniis suis contra Synodos Orthodoxas, & dicunt quamdiu decisiones ita instituentur (ut semper ea ab Ecclesiâ Orthodoxâ factæ sunt) pacem esse non posse &c. Ut vidimus Par. III. lib. 2. c. 6. §. 5. 6.
units.tr: 9. I had also shown (pp. 186–187) that they calumniously impute wars and persecutions to the decisions of the Church made truly from the Word of God; for this happens only by accident, just as wars and the like arise from the Gospel, not through the fault of the Gospel but through the vice of men, of heretics and of others who are not mindful of their duty; and so the cause of evils is no more to be ascribed to the Orthodox synodical decrees than to Christ and his Gospel. They do not answer this either; but even if they are convicted and cannot reply, they persist in their abuse and calumnies against the Orthodox synods, and they say that as long as decisions are made in the way they always have been made by the Orthodox Church, there can be no peace, etc. As we saw in Part III, book 2, chapter 6, §§ 5–6.

units.la: 10. 11. 12. 13. 14. 15. 16. 17. Objeceram quoque ipsis; quod do-cent: Non solùm decreta Synodica, sed etiam alias formulas publicas, nimirùm Symbola, Confessiones Ecclesiarum, & Catecheses non debere decidere quid aliis constanter firmiterque credendum sit de Controversiis fidei. 11. Quod docent: Formulas omnes illas ne quidem pro certis indicibus, nedum judicibus verorum sensuum habendas esse. 12. Formulas esse debere tantùm indices sententiæ quam auctores earum pro verâ habent. Et, quia decisiones tales postulant, quibus saltem indicet aliquis quid ipse credat; ostenderam ego falsitatem sententiæ istius, ex eo p. 188. 189. quod is non decidat, qui profitetur se hoc aut illud credere; sed tantùm is qui ex verbo Dei decidit, & tùm quidem, dicebam, ipse proprie loquendo & per se non decidit, sed Deus in verbo suo. 13. Imò ipsius Symboli Apostolici meliorem rationem non esse docent, utpote de quo non expresse constet illud esse Apostolicum. Unde etiam non simpliciter vocant hoc Symbolum Apostolicum, sed dicunt; de Symbolo Apostolorum quod vocatur. Dixeram etiam Arminianos illud Symbolum non habere pro certo praescripto fidei, & normâ secundariâ, ad quam examinanda sit omnis doomnis doctrina, pro quâ norma tamen Ecclesia Orthodoxa illud semper habuit. 14. Conquestus etiam sum pag. 190. 191. de convitiis eorum atrocissimis & horrendis quibus debacchantur in omnes formulas quæ Controversias decide-runt. Et, ut videre posset Lector, non solùm eos loqui de formulis Reformatorum, ostendi eos harum formularum quibus tot convitia dicunt, duo exempla allegare, unum Lutheranorum in formulâ Bergensi, alterum Reformatorum. 15. Similiter conquestus eram p. 192. de immodestiâ & petulantiâ eorum quâ in Symbolum Athanasii irrunt, dum dicunt eum SUPERBAM præfationem Symbolo suo præscripsisse &c. 16. Item, quòd non solùm nolint decreta Synodica & alias formulas publicas fieri eâ ratione ut iis decidatur quid aliis credendum sit; sed etiam postquam edita sunt, & quidem eâ ratione quam ipsi præscribunt, iis omnem auctoritatem eripiunt. Speciatim quòd volunt: earum auctoritati nullum, imò ne infirmum quidem locum in Ecclesia competere. 17. Item: Decisiones Synodorum, etiamsi rectè & ex verbo Dei facta sint, eos tantùm obligare, qui eas veras esse credunt, qui autem id sibi persuadere non possunt, eos non obligari illis. Ad hæc omnia octo quid respondent? Fatentur cap. 135. & defensionis loco nihil dicunt, nisi me ea non refutâsse. Cùm tamen sciant mihi propositum id non fuisse, ut expresse monueram cap. 1. lib. 1. Par. I. Arcanorum: & ex altera parte refutatione opus non habeant, quia nullo argumento ea quæ dicunt probaverant.
units.tr: 10–17. I had also objected to them that they teach: Not only synodical decrees, but also other public formulas, namely creeds, confessions of the Churches and catechisms, ought not to decide what others must steadfastly and firmly believe concerning the controversies of faith. 11. They teach that all those formulas ought not even to be held as sure indicators, much less as judges, of the true senses. 12. Formulas ought to be only indicators of the opinion which their authors hold to be true. And since such decisions demand something by which at least someone may indicate what he himself believes, I showed (pp. 188–189) the falsity of this opinion, because he does not decide who professes that he believes this or that, but only he who decides from the Word of God; and then, I said, he himself, properly speaking and of himself, does not decide, but God does, in his Word. 13. They teach that the Apostles' Creed is not of better authority, since it is not expressly established that it is Apostolic. For this reason they do not simply call it the Apostles' Creed, but say concerning the Creed of the Apostles which is called so. I had also said that the Arminians do not hold that Creed to be a sure prescribed rule of faith and a secondary norm by which every doctrine is to be tested, though the Orthodox Church has always held it as such a norm. 14. I also complained (pp. 190–191) of their most atrocious and horrible abuse, with which they rage against all the formulas which have decided controversies. And so that the reader might see that they speak not only of the formulas of the Reformed, I showed that to illustrate the formulas against which they hurl so many insults, they cite two examples, one of the Lutherans in the Formula of Berg, the other of the Reformed. 15. Similarly I complained (p. 192) of their immodesty and petulance in attacking the Athanasian Creed, while they say that he PROUDLY prefixed a preface to his creed, etc. 16. Likewise, that they not only refuse that synodical decrees and other public formulas be made in such a way as to decide what others must believe, but also, once they have been published, and indeed in the manner they themselves prescribe, they take away all authority from them. Specifically they want: no place, not even a weak one, in the Church to belong to their authority. 17. Likewise: The decisions of synods, even if they are made rightly and from the Word of God, bind only those who believe them to be true, while those who cannot persuade themselves of this are not bound by them. To all these eight points what do they reply? They confess it in chapter 135 and, by way of defence, say nothing except that I have not refuted these points. Yet they know that I did not intend this, as I had expressly warned in chapter 1 of book 1 of Part I of the Arcana; and on the other side they have no need of refutation, because they have proved nothing of what they say by any argument.

units.la: 18. Aliud ipsorum dogma est: Neminem, postquam acceptavit decretum, teneri illo diutius, quàm eâ lege, quatenus & quamdiu ipse in conscientiâ suâ judicat illud verum esse. Fatentur, & conantur id tueri contra argumenta mea, quibus ostenderam eos pessimam legem figere. Quem in finem multa impertinenter nugantur p. 135. 136. de necessitate judicii ac notitiæ ad fidem generandam; cùm tamen ipse notitiam eam & judicium urserim p. 193. & perpetuò urgeam. Deinde vocem Legis mutant in vocem conditionis, & dicunt se per legem intellexisse tantùm conditionem; atque ex eo posito fundamento plurima contra ea, quæ dixeram de falsitate dogmatis istius, deblatterant p. 136. 137. 138. 139. 140. Verùm enim verò illa mera impostura est. Sumunt enim revera vocem illam proprie; prout ex eo patet, quod non solùm verbum Dei, sed etiam, cum Socino suo, rationem humanam sumunt pro normâ credendorum seu interpretationis verbi divini. quemadmodum ostenderam Par. I. lib. 1. c. 4. quâ in doctrinâ suâ persistunt Vindic. lib. 1. c. 4. ut patet ex libro præcedente huius Partis cap. 4. Et nihil admittunt in rebus fidei quod non per omnia rationi conveniat. Et sic concidunt omnes illorum nugæ quibus tot paginas replent, ex hypothesi & fundamento istius impostura: Ita enim judicium humanum pro lege ponunt, ut simul rationem normam credendorum seu interpretationis verbi divini constituant. Quare nihil aliud addo; quàm quod in iis, quæ contra quartum meum argumentum nugantur p. 138. 139. 140. in patrocinium Hæreticorum, non tàm me quam Scripturam sacram oppugnant, quæ docet Hæreticos & quosvis falsos Doctores verbis quidem nomen Domini præscribere, & dicere Dominus dixit, adeoque ore profiteri se solum verbum Dei pro normâ ac regulâ doctrinæ suæ habere, re ipsâ autem rationem suam cœcam tanquam normam & ducem sequi. Calumniam, quâ dicunt p. 137. me multas Orthodoxorum formulas credere cum verbo Dei non convenire, abjicere, conculcare, damnare, transeo cum tota reliquâ calumniarum farragine.
units.tr: 18. Another of their doctrines is this: No one, once he has accepted a decree, is bound by it any longer than on this condition, insofar as and as long as he himself judges in his conscience that it is true. They confess this and try to defend it against my arguments, by which I had shown that they establish a most pernicious law. To this end they trifle at length, irrelevantly (pp. 135–136), about the necessity of judgment and knowledge for generating faith, though I myself had insisted on that knowledge and judgment (p. 193) and constantly urge it. Then they change the word law into the word condition, and say that by law they had understood only a condition; and on this foundation they babble a great deal against what I had said about the falsity of this doctrine (pp. 136–140). But this is pure imposture. For they take that word in its proper sense, as is clear from the fact that they take not only the Word of God but also, with their Socinus, human reason as the norm of what is to be believed, or of the interpretation of the divine Word, as I had shown in Part I, book 1, chapter 4. They persist in this doctrine (Vindication, book 1, chapter 4), as is clear from the preceding book of this Part, chapter 4. And they admit nothing in matters of faith which does not in every respect agree with reason. And so all their trifling, with which they fill so many pages, collapses, resting on the hypothesis and foundation of this imposture: for they set up human judgment as the law, so that at the same time they make reason the norm of what is to be believed, or of the interpretation of the divine Word. Therefore I add nothing else, except that in what they trifle against my fourth argument (pp. 138–140), in defence of the heretics, they attack not so much me as the holy Scripture, which teaches that heretics and all false teachers prescribe with their words the name of the Lord, and say the Lord has said, and thus profess with their mouths that they hold the Word of God alone as the norm and rule of their teaching, while in fact they follow their own blind reason as norm and guide. The calumny by which they say (p. 137) that I reject, trample on, and condemn many formulas of the Orthodox as not agreeing with the Word of God, I pass over, together with the whole remaining farrago of calumnies.

units.la: 19. Conquestus etiam eram Arminianos permittere unicuique à phrasibus formularum publicarum recedere pro lubitu, citra quàm ἑτεροδοξίας accusari debeat, aut in suspicionem venire Hæresios. Per phrases autem ostendi eos intelligere dogmata controversa, qualia sunt Orthodoxa dogmata de Trinitate p. 196. 197. Hoc etiam non negant sed fatentur p. 140. ac contemnunt accusationem hanc gravissimi momenti; dicunt ea vix triobolaria esse; esse minuta, levia & pene nihili. De quâ re judicium penes unumquemque Lectorem esto, qui Deum in tribus personis adorat.
units.tr: 19. I had also complained that the Arminians allow each person to depart from the wording of public formularies at will, without being accused of heterodoxy [ἑτεροδοξίας] or falling under suspicion of heresy. By their wording, I showed, they understand the controverted doctrines, such as the orthodox doctrines of the Trinity (pp. 196, 197). They do not deny this but admit it (p. 140), and they scorn this very serious charge, saying that these doctrines are scarcely worth three obols; they are trifling, slight and almost nothing. On this matter let every reader judge who worships God in three persons.

units.la: 20. Objeci etiam ipsis, eos in Apologiâ illos tantum habere pro ἑτεροδόξους qui negant ea quæ puris putis Scripturæ verbis expressa sunt. Hoc etiam non negant, sed uno fasciculo inter triobolaria, levia, & minuta ista comprehendunt. Imò persistunt in eâ re p. 141. ubi aiunt: ne λογομαχίαι & altercationes oriantur, tutissimum esse, stare, & se continere intra Scripturæ S. locutiones & Spiritus Sancti formulas, neque cuiquam molestiam creari debere qui intra eas continere se paratum esse ostendit, eosque qui aliter agunt, & ista locutione non sunt contenti, Schismatum ac dissidiorum omnium in Ecclesiâ auctores esse. Ubi auctoritates Theologorum Reformatorum quas afferunt ad rem non faciunt: illi enim non rejiciunt omnes phrases, sed eas tantùm quæ verbo Dei non nituntur, seu quarum res in eo non continentur; item phrases volunt non debere esse normam controversiarum fidei, sed tantùm ipsum verbum Dei, prout jacet, h. e. in Scripturis expressum est. Hæc mens summorum virorum Zanchii & Sturmii est, ut & reliquorum Reformatorum Theologorum.
units.tr: 20. I also charged them that in their Apology they regard only those as heterodox [ἑτεροδόξους] who deny what is expressed in the plain words of Scripture. They do not deny this either, but lump it together in one bundle with those trifles, slight matters and minutiae. Indeed they persist in the point (p. 141), where they say: to avoid word-battles [λογομαχίαι] and quarrels, it is safest to stand and keep ourselves within the expressions of Holy Scripture and the formulas of the Holy Spirit, and no one should be troubled who shows himself ready to keep within them; those who act otherwise and are not content with this form of speech are the authors of all schisms and dissensions in the Church. The authorities of the Reformed theologians which they cite do not bear on the matter. For those theologians reject not all phrases but only those that do not rest on the Word of God, or whose substance is not contained in it. They also want phrases not to be the norm of controversies of faith, but the Word of God itself, as it lies, that is, as it is expressed in the Scriptures. This is the view of the great men Zanchius and Sturmius, and of the other Reformed theologians.

units.la: 21. Objeci etiam p.198. ipsos id eo fine facere, ut non habeantur pro Schismaticis aut proHaereticis, adeoque non tolerandis in Ecclesia, qui phrases, ut loquuntur, formularum oppugnant, sed in Ecclesia sinu tolerentur; quia secundum ipsos Religio adeoque Θεοσέβεια non consistit in phrasibus formularum, & quia phrasibus & verbis uti, qua non sunt ipsius Spiritus S. est pedem ultra limitem Scripturae proferre, ut loquuntur Apol. c. 3. §. 4. Adeoque ostendi eos non pie nec sincere agere, dum sub nomine phrasium dogmata controversa vera negare & oppugnare docent, & in Ecclesiam Antitrinitarios introducere laborant. Haec etiam non negant, sed inter levia, minuta, & triobolaria ista comprehendunt; imo ut patet ex praecedentibus expresse idem repetunt, quemadmodum verba eorum exhibuimus sectione praecedente.
units.tr: 21. I also charged that they do this for the purpose that those who attack the phrases, as they put it, of the formularies should not be considered schismatics or heretics, and so should not be disowned by the Church but tolerated in the bosom of the Church; because, according to them, religion and therefore godliness does not consist in the phrases of the formularies, and because to use phrases and words which are not those of the Holy Spirit himself is to step beyond the limit of Scripture, as they put it in the Apology, chap. 3, §4. I therefore showed that they do not act piously or sincerely while, under the name of phrases, they teach that true controverted doctrines are to be denied and attacked, and labour to introduce Antitrinitarians into the Church. They do not deny this either, but lump it together with those slight matters, minutiae and trifles; indeed, as is clear from what precedes, they expressly repeat the same thing, as we set out their words in the preceding section.

units.la: 22. Libertatem integram docent debere unicuique inquirendi in formulas publicas, iisque sine scrupulo contradicendi. Ubi reprehenderam quod p. 199. Arminiani, cum libertatem istam limitent hac conditione; salvis semper modestia, charitatis, & prudentia Christiana legibus, omittunt primariam legem, nimirum salva ante omnia veritate divina quae in controversis dogmatis est. Hoc etiam non negant, sed sicco pede transeunt.
units.tr: 22. They teach that complete liberty must be granted to everyone to inquire into public formularies and to contradict them without scruple. Here I had reproved them (p. 199) because the Arminians, while limiting that liberty by this condition, always saving the laws of modesty, charity and Christian prudence, omit the chief law, namely above all saving the divine truth which is at stake in the controverted doctrines. They do not deny this either, but pass over it with dry feet.

units.la: Postea ostenderam inanitatem antidoti quod in tanta scilicet libertate adversus effrenem licentiam in speciem proferunt, nimirum prudentiam & charitatem; & probaveram eos non tradere verum antidotum, quia omittunt primarium remedium, absque quo prudentia nihil aliud quam versutia ac nequitia, & charitas pestis Ecclesiae, Reipublicae, & animorum est, adeoque vera prudentia & charitas non est. Illud autem primarium remedium ostendi esse scientiam secundum Deum, quam qui non habet, & tamen in formulas inquirit easque oppugnat, dicebam vae tali homini! Id quod probavi ex verbo Dei. Ostendi etiam, tunc conscientiae praetextum non juvare, & simul verum modum exhibui quo uti debeant qui in formulam aliquam inquirere volunt. Haec p. 199. 200. 201. 202. differunt. Haec etiam non negant, sed sicco pede transeunt & ne verbulo quidem respondent.
units.tr: Afterwards I showed the emptiness of the antidote which they put forward, in appearance, against unbridled licence within such liberty, namely prudence and charity; and I proved that they do not offer a true antidote, because they omit the primary remedy, without which prudence is nothing but cunning and wickedness, and charity is a plague to the Church, the commonwealth and souls; so true prudence and charity are not present. I showed that this primary remedy is knowledge according to God, and that whoever lacks it, yet inquires into the formularies and attacks them, I said, woe to such a man! This I proved from the Word of God. I also showed that the plea of conscience does not help them, and at the same time set out the true way in which those who wish to inquire into any formulary ought to proceed. These points are discussed on pp. 199, 200, 201, 202. They do not deny them either, but pass over them with dry feet and do not answer even a word.

units.la: Denique objeci quod decreta Synodica, Symbola, Confessiones, Catechesis, seu formulas Orthodoxas omnes ita extenuant ut tantum formulas humanas & auctoritatem humanam vocent. Et probavi eos perperam facere in eo, atque contra eorum cavillationem asserui distinctionem a Ill. DD. Profess. Leydd. allatam; quod nimirum etsi formulae tales formaliter h. e. respectu formae externae quae in compositione verborum & stylo consistit, consideratae humanum opus sint, tamen respectu materiae non sunt opus humanum, sed habent rem divinam, hoc est sensus divinos seu veritatem ipsam Dei. Hanc distinctionem, quam illi in Apologia ridcontent, ego solidam esse ostendi & cavilla ipsorum refutavi p. 203. 204. 205. Hæc etiam non negant, sed sicco pede transeunt; & ne verbulo quidem respondent. Quibus jam nihil aliud adjicio, quàm distinctionem illam, quâ aliquid, etsi formaliter non sit verbum Dei, materialiter tamen verbũ Dei est, non esse novam sed vetustissimam. Ita enim Origenes qui statuebat Epistolam ad Hæbreos non esse Pauli, ait τὰ νοήματα εἶναι τῆς Ἀποστόλης, ἡ δὲ φράσις inquit ἡ ἡ σωθήσεις ἀτομυσμονευόσαντος τινος τὰ Ἀποστολικὰ sensus esse Apostoli, phrasin autem & stylum seu compositionem esse cuiusdam qui Apostolica illa dogmata literis tradiderit, ut videre est apud Eusebium lib. 6. c. 19. Ex his omnibus jam apparet Arminianos ad maximam partem hujus capitis nihil respondere, adeoque me ipsis in eo nihil per calumniam attribuisse, quandoquidem omnia fatentur, aut non negant, exceptis duobus quæ contra propriam conscientiam negant.
units.tr: Finally I charged that they so belittle all the synodical decrees, creeds, confessions, catechisms, or orthodox formularies, that they call them merely human formulas and human authority. I showed that they do this wrongly, and against their cavil I asserted the distinction brought forward by the illustrious professors of Leiden: namely, that although such formularies, considered formally, that is with respect to the outward form which consists in the composition of words and style, are a human work, yet with respect to matter they are not a human work but have a divine content, that is, the divine meanings or the very truth of God. I showed that this distinction, which they mock in the Apology, is sound, and I refuted their quibbles (pp. 203, 204, 205). They do not deny these points either, but pass over them with dry feet, and do not answer even a word. To these things I now add nothing except that the distinction by which something, though formally not the Word of God, is nevertheless materially the Word of God, is not new but very ancient. For Origen, who held that the Epistle to the Hebrews was not Paul's, says: the thoughts are of the Apostle [τὰ μὲν νοήματα εἶναι τοῦ Ἀποστόλου], but the phrasing [ἡ δὲ φράσις] and style, or composition, belongs to someone who committed those apostolic doctrines to writing, as may be seen in Eusebius, book 6, chap. 19. From all this it now appears that the Arminians answer almost nothing in the greater part of this chapter, and so I have attributed nothing to them in it by calumny, since they confess or do not deny all of it, except for two points which they deny against their own conscience.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CAP. VII.

units.la: Examen Capitis VII. Vindic. lib. 2.
units.tr: Examination of Chapter VII of the Vindication, Book 2.

units.la: 1. Arminiani fatentur se docere officium ministrorum esse docere quod rectum ipsis videtur. 2. Fatentur se docere officium ministrorum esse recusare obedientiam Magistratui, quando ipsis videtur contraria verbo Dei præcipere. 3. Fatentur se concedere libertatem prophetandi omnibus à se dissentientibus &c. 4. Fatentur se ad ministerium verbi admittere eos qui negant Pædobaptismum præceptum esse à Deo, & eum usurpare nolunt. Convicti mendacii de Francisci Junii sententia circa Pædobaptismum nihil respondent. 5. Fatentur se docere ministerium verbi non esse à Deo simpliciter præceptum seu non esse necessarium simpliciter necessitate præcepti. 6. Ad id quod ostendi eos ministerium verbi evertere doctrinâ suâ de Controversiis dogmatis; non id negant, nec fatentur, sed Lectori illudunt versiculo.
units.tr: 1. The Arminians confess that they teach the office of ministers to be to teach what seems right to them. 2. They confess that they teach the office of ministers to be to refuse obedience to the magistrate whenever it seems to them that he commands what is contrary to the Word of God. 3. They confess that they grant freedom of prophesying to all who dissent from them, etc. 4. They confess that they admit to the ministry of the Word those who deny that infant baptism is commanded by God, and who will not practise it. Convicted of falsehood concerning Francis Junius's opinion on infant baptism, they make no reply. 5. They confess that they teach that the ministry of the Word is not simply commanded by God, or that it is not necessary by the simple necessity of a precept. 6. To my showing that by their doctrine of controversies in doctrine they overthrow the ministry of the Word, they neither deny this nor confess it, but mock the reader with a little verse.

units.la: 1. PRimum quod ipsis objeceram est hoc dogma: Officium ministrorum esse docere quod rectum ipsis videtur. Hic post sophisticam puerilem rilem & ineptam vitilitigatione circa id quod praedicationem verbi vocaveram,& quidem recte,materiam seu objectum ministerii, quia nimirum illud versatur circa verbum Dei praedicandum (unde ipsorum puerilis sophisticatio concidit) fatentur se ita docere, sed adduntse non negare,officium ministri requirere ut doceat quod revera verum est. Verum enimvero hoc non liberat ipsos crimine Libertinismi. Etenim itaque extendendum non est officium nimirum ut non solum doceant, quod revera verum est simul & videtur; sed etiam ut doceant, quod etiamsi revera non sit veritas divina, tamen videtur rectum ipsis esse. Verum officium eorum est tantum docere id quod ita videtur rectum esse ipsis, ut simul revera rectum sit; seu potius, secundum stylum Spiritus Sancti & praeceptum Dei, non debent docere quod rectum videtur, sed quod revera rectum est. Hinc Deus non vult permittere populo suo, ut faciat quod sibi rectum videtur: Ne facitote quisque quicquid rectum videtur in oculis ejus Deuter. 12. 8. Per consequens,si non vult ut quis faciat quicquid rectum videtur in oculis ejus; certe etiam non vult, ut quis doceat quicquid rectum videtur. Et Paulus. 1. Tim. 3. 9. docet ministrum debere retinere secretum fidei in pura conscientia, adeoque non vult ut separentur unquam veritas & conscientia bona. Et cap. 4. v. 6. docet eum esse bonum ministrum Christi,qui veritatem profitetur,non autem errores, v.7. qui profecto saepe homini veritas esse videntur. Et Tit. 1. 9. ait officium eorum esse docere sanam doctrinam, & ut tenaces sint fidelis illius sermonis, c.2. 1. ut sint in corrupti in doctrina Tit.2. 7. ut in doctrina habeant sanum sermonem & qui non possit condemnari v. 8. His & similibus modis enunciat Spiritus S. officium ministrorum,non autem periculosissimo modo illo quem sermo veritatis non patitur, sed rejicit & damnat, cum Deut. 12. 8. Deus ait: Ne facitote quisque quicquid rectum videtur in oculis ejus. Contra haec omnia quam late extendant officium ministrorum Arminiani, patet ex eo quod ibidem p. 142. dicunt, se agnoscere ministrum peccare, si docet quod rectum ipsi videtur, si scilicet per suam propriam culpam erret. Sub quibus verbis quale Arcanum lateat patet ex Par. III. Arcan. lib. 1., cap. 2. nimirum Antitrinitariorum blasphemias illas Turcicas contra Filium Dei non esse peccata: imo Haeresin omnem quae communiter sic vocatur peccatum non esse,ut supra vidimus.
units.tr: 1. First, I had objected to them this doctrine: The office of ministers is to teach what seems right to them. Here, after a childish and foolish quibble about what I had called the preaching of the Word, and rightly so, namely the matter or object of the ministry (because it is concerned with the Word of God to be preached, whence their childish sophistry collapses), they confess that they teach this way, but add that they do not deny that the office of the minister requires him to teach what is truly true. But this does not in fact free them from the charge of Libertinism. For the office must not be extended so that ministers teach only what is truly true and at the same time seems so; it must also be extended to their teaching what, even if it is not really the divine truth, nevertheless seems right to them. Rather, the office of ministers is only to teach what so seems right to them that it is at the same time really right; or rather, according to the manner of speaking of the Holy Spirit and the precept of God, they ought not to teach what seems right, but what is really right. Hence God does not wish to permit his people to do what seems right in their own eyes: You shall not do every man whatever seems right in his own eyes, Deut. 12. 8. Consequently, if he does not wish that anyone do whatever seems right in his eyes, he certainly does not wish that anyone teach whatever seems right. And Paul, 1 Tim. 3. 9, teaches that the minister must hold the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience, and so he does not wish truth and a good conscience ever to be separated. And in chapter 4, verse 6, he teaches that he is a good minister of Christ who professes the truth, not errors, verse 7, which indeed often seem to man to be the truth. And Titus 1. 9 says that their office is to teach sound doctrine, and to be firm in that faithful word; chapter 2, verse 1, that they be sound in doctrine; Titus 2. 7, that in doctrine they have sound speech which cannot be condemned, verse 8. In these and similar ways the Holy Spirit states the office of ministers, and not in that most dangerous way which the word of truth does not admit, but rejects and condemns, since at Deut. 12. 8 God says: You shall not do every man whatever seems right in his own eyes. How far the Arminians extend the office of ministers, in contrast to all these things, is clear from the fact that on the same page, 142, they say that they acknowledge that a minister sins if he teaches what seems right to him, that is, if he errs through his own fault. What secret lies hidden under these words is clear from Par. III, Arcanum book 1, chapter 2: namely that those Turkish blasphemies of the Antitrinitarians against the Son of God are not sins; indeed, that all heresy, which is commonly called sin, is not sin, as we saw above.

units.la: Observetur quod hoc loco p. 142. dicunt: Neque enim adeo male quisquam nisi malignus sentire potest de Remonstrantibus, quasi credant ministros obligari ad docendum quicquid ipsis pro arbitrio ipsorum absque, ulla Dominici praescripti reveti reverentiâ & religione rectum videtur. Pulchrè in speciem. Qualis autem sit illa reverentia & religio quam Arminiani agnoscunt & docent, patet ex Vindic. lib. 1. c. 3. p. 23. ubi eos qui Scripturæ falsum sensum affingunt, dicunt Scripturam Sacram maximè revereri: Absque eâ enim esset, inquiunt, contemtim haberent omnia & de sensu eorum manum non verterint. Egregiam verò reverentiam & religionem erga Scripturam sacram seu præscriptum Dei!
units.tr: Let it be noted that in this passage, page 142, they say: For no one can think so badly of the Remonstrants, unless he is malicious, as to believe that ministers are bound to teach whatever seems right to them at their own discretion, without any reverence and religion towards the Lord's prescribed rule. Beautifully put, in appearance. But what kind of reverence and religion the Arminians acknowledge and teach is clear from Vindication book 1, chapter 3, page 23, where they say that those who attribute a false sense to Scripture most of all revere Holy Scripture: For without it, they say, they would hold everything in contempt, and would not have turned their hand to its sense. What an excellent reverence and religion towards Holy Scripture, or the prescribed will of God!

units.la: 2. Porrò illâ occasione ostenderam eos docere : Causam propter quam ministri teneantur non obedire Magistratui, esse quando judicant in conscientiâ suâ præscriptum Magistratus non esse Dei præscriptum : item, si contrario verbo Dei jubere aut vetare NOBIS.VIDEATUR. Cùm tamen debebant dixisse, non parendum esse Magistratui jubenti exercere ministerium non nisi ex præscripto suo, seu quando contrarium verbo Dei cultum mandat: item quando contraria verbo Dei jubet aut vetat, ut probaveram p. 207. Fatentur se ita docere, & respondent eodem modo quoad præcedens membrum : nimirum se non excludere etiam alterum illud, & se agnoscere peccare hominem quando facit aliquid secundùm judicium suum falsum & CULPABILITER erroneum. Quâ ratione quàm lata porta aperiatur Hæreticis sic ab Ecclesiâ Orthodoxâ vetere & modernâ appellatis, speciatim Antitrinitariis, unusquisque videt. Hi enim secundùm hanc hypothesin Arminianorum non peccant, quando Magistratus mandatis de non seminandis blasphemiis suis non obediunt, quia nimirùm Hæreticis, speciatim Antitrinitariis, VIDETUR vetare contraria verbo Dei, & quamvis errent, tamen secundùm Arminianos non errant CULPABILITER. Ecce obedientiam illam præclaram Arminianorum erga Magistratû, de quâ tantopere verbis inanissimis gloriantur.
units.tr: 2. Moreover, on that occasion I had shown that they teach: That the cause on account of which ministers are bound not to obey the magistrate is when they judge in their conscience that the magistrate's prescript is not the prescript of God; likewise, if he commands or forbids what is contrary to the Word of God, as it SEEMS TO US. Whereas they ought to have said that one must not obey a magistrate who orders the exercise of the ministry except in accordance with its own prescript, or when he commands worship contrary to the Word of God; likewise when he commands or forbids what is contrary to the Word of God, as I had proved on page 207. They confess that they teach this, and reply in the same way regarding the preceding clause: namely, that they do not exclude that other alternative either, and they acknowledge that a man sins when he does something according to his false judgment, and erroneous in a culpable way. By what reasoning a wide door is opened to heretics, so called by the Orthodox Church, ancient and modern, especially to the Antitrinitarians, everyone can see. For according to this hypothesis of the Arminians, these men do not sin when they do not obey the magistrate's commands about not sowing their blasphemies, because clearly it SEEMS to heretics, especially the Antitrinitarians, that what is contrary to the Word of God is forbidden; and although they err, nevertheless, according to the Arminians, they do not err CULPABLY. Behold that splendid obedience of the Arminians towards the magistrate, of which they boast so much in most empty words.

units.la: 3. Secundum modum, quo ministerium verbi evertunt, dixi esse doctrinam eorum de Libertate prophetandi. Statuunt enim libertatem prophetandi seu docendi in Ecclesiâ permittendam esse talem, quâ liceat Scripturam sacram interpretari & Deum colere pro suo proprio judicio in omnibus iis quæ sunt controversa inter Christianos. Et hanc concedendam esse omnibus sectis, in specie Hæreticis, nec non iis qui sibi persuadent se extraordinarias revelationes Spiritus S. habere; talesque interpretationes esse conjunctas cum summâ Dei reverentiâ, & nequaquam periculosas seu noxias veritati.
units.tr: 3. The second way in which they overthrow the ministry of the Word, I said, was their doctrine of the Freedom of prophesying. For they lay down that freedom of prophesying, or of teaching, must be permitted in the Church of such a kind that it is lawful to interpret Holy Scripture and to worship God according to one's own private judgment in all those matters which are disputed among Christians. And this must be granted to all sects, specially to heretics, and also to those who persuade themselves that they have extraordinary revelations of the Holy Spirit; and such interpretations are said to be joined with the highest reverence towards God, and by no means dangerous or harmful to the truth.

units.la: Respondent 1. se concedere libertatem prophetandi OMNIBUS à se dissentientibus h.e. nolle ut ipsis per vim eripiatur: sed exinde negant sequi, se evertere ministerium. Deinde ad coccysmum suum contra Vedelium delium relabuntur,cum calumniis & maledicentiâ adversus eum atque omnes eos qui ipsorum impiam doctrinam de libertate prophetandi non admittunt, & dicunt nullâ re magis everti ministerium quàm per tales. Denique remittunt Lectorem ad cap.tertium libri primi Vindic. ubi dicunt se demonstrâsse quàm absurda sint quæ Remonstrantibus isto paragrapho tribuo.
units.tr: They reply, first, that they grant freedom of prophesying to ALL who dissent from them, that is, that they are unwilling that it be snatched from them by force; but from this they deny that it follows that they overthrow the ministry. Then they fall back into their own outcry against Vedelius, with calumnies and abuse against him and against all those who do not admit their impious doctrine of freedom of prophesying, and they say that the ministry is overthrown by nothing more than by such people. Finally, they refer the reader to chapter 3 of book 1 of the Vindication, where they say they have demonstrated how absurd are the things which I attribute to the Remonstrants in this paragraph.

units.la: Verùm enimverò consequentia est evidentissima; nam natura ministerii & interpretationis Scripturæ Sacræ, non consistit in effreni illâ licentiâ, in quâ illi libertatem prophetandi constituunt. Quod dicunt se nolle ut per vim eripiatur libertas prophetandi omnibus à se dissentientibus: respondeo 1. eos sibi ipsis contradicere, volunt enim in Vindiciis,non permittendam esse eam Reformatis,sed eos durioribus remediis coercendos, ut ostendi Par. II. Arcan. lib. 1. 2. dico eos non solùm hoc velle ut per vim non eripiatur ista libertas dissentientibus,sed etiam ut illi in Ecclesiam Dei introducantur. Verum me dicere patet tùm ex eo quòd cum Antitrinitariis blasphematoribus communionem colere se profitentur, nec non cùm Anabaptistis; tùm etiam ex eo, quod libertas prophetandi ad Ecclesiam pertinet, in quâ prophetiam volunt esse liberam, ut patet ex Par. I. lib. 1. c. 3. & libro præcedente huius Partis Quartæ; & quidem inter alia ex eo, quod dicunt: Spiritum h. e. interpretationes, quas quis se habere suggestione Spiritus Dei credit, profectò omnino liberum esse vult Apostolus in Ecclesiâ. Apol. c. 4. f. 275.b. Patet etiam ex doctrinâ Apologiæ de Tolerantiâ, quam in Par. I. lib. 2. cap. 5. & lib. 2. cap. 5. huius partis expositimus. Per vim quid intelligant, manifestum est, nimirùm omnem, quæcunque etiam illa sit, corporalem resistentiam, quâ Hæreticorum conatibus obviam itur, speciatim prohibitionem conventiculorum privatorum. Convitia & calumnias Deo, & coccysmum suo loco relinquo. Quod autem inter alia dicunt p. 144. Videat Vedelius ne aliquando in caput suum eandem sibam cudi malo & damno suo sentiat. iis verbis quid sibi velint, nôrunt sapientes quibus actiones & res gestæ horum hominum notæ sunt, & qui meminerunt eorum quæ suprà Vindic. lib. 2. c. 6. p. 130. 131. dixêre: nimirùm, me dignum esse qui Tyrannidem experiar non solùm Pontificiorum, Lutheranorum, Anabaptistarum, sed etiam alius cuiusvis sectæ, quando mihi aliquando coràm eâ in Synodo comparendum erit. Hoc mihi sufficit; nam intelligenti dixerunt. Sed Deus me & alios fidos servos suos præservabit à Synodo Arminianorum h. e. Socinianorum simulatorum. Quod ad caput 3. lib. 2. Vindic. Lectorem remittunt, bene habet & ex animi mei sententia; nam ibi Lector turpitudinem huius sectae & vidit & videbit.
units.tr: But in truth the consequence is most evident; for the nature of the ministry and of the interpretation of Holy Scripture does not consist in that unbridled licence in which they establish freedom of prophesying. As to their saying that they are unwilling that freedom of prophesying be snatched by force from all who dissent from them, I answer: first, that they contradict themselves, for in the Vindications they wish that this freedom be not permitted to the Reformed, but that they be restrained by harsher remedies, as I showed in Par. II, Arcanum book 1. Second, I say that they not only wish that this freedom not be snatched from dissenters by force, but also that they be introduced into the Church of God. That I am right is clear both from the fact that they profess to cultivate communion with the Antitrinitarian blasphemers, and likewise with the Anabaptists; and also from the fact that the freedom of prophesying pertains to the Church, in which they want prophecy to be free, as is clear from Par.
