Hic meminerit Lector, quòd §. 6. docent Excommunicationem esse voluntariam tantum modo secessionem ab aliquo. Ex quo etiam patet id quod hoc loco dicimus, nimirum eos docere : Hæreticis anathema dicendum non esse. Et tamen hi homines anathema, imò anathema Maranatha denunciant vivis & mortuis, qui docent Hæreticos insigniter blasphemos & perjuros capitali supplicio affici posse ; imò expresse damnant eos qui Hæreticorum corporalem coercitionem etiam sine supplicio capitali licitam esse dicunt, ut tum ex superioribus patet, tum ex capite sequenti patebit, tum denique ex Resp. ad Excerp. p. 129. &c. Ubi dicunt eos qui ullâ corporali coercitione Hæreticis resistendum esse docent, non posse communionem habere cum Deo & filio ejus Jesu Christo. An non hoc est anathema dicere omnibus coetibus quiDeum in tribus personis adorant?
units.tr: 8. The sixth dogma is: heretics ought not to be anathematized. They teach this on the pretext that "Christ does not condemn them expressly, nor is it obvious by consequence to all." In particular, it was shown that they "are unwilling to say anathema to those Antitrinitarians." They confess all this on p. 153 and persist in it; on the contrary, they say that heretics exist and are perhaps worthy of anathema, and likewise that those who think otherwise are tyrants, as we saw in Part III, book 2, chapter 8, §5. To that end they abuse the words of Bucer and Francis Junius, who certainly do not speak of heretics. Here the reader should remember that in §6 they teach that excommunication is merely a voluntary secession from someone. From this too it is clear what we are saying here, namely that they teach: heretics ought not to be anathematized. And yet these men denounce anathema, indeed anathema Maranatha, on the living and the dead, namely on those who teach that heretics who are notoriously blasphemous and perjured can be subjected to capital punishment. Indeed they expressly condemn those who say that bodily restraint of heretics is lawful even without capital punishment, as is clear both from what has gone before, from the following chapter, and finally from the Response to the Excerpts, p. 129 and following. There they say that those who teach that heretics must be resisted by any bodily coercion "cannot have communion with God and with his Son Jesus Christ." Is this not to pronounce anathema on all the assemblies that worship God in three persons?

units.la: 9. Septimum dogma est : Hæreticis silentium imponendum non esse. Fatentur, post aliquot nugas, quibus nova quædam Arcana nobis produnt, ut vidimus Par. III. lib. 2. c. 8. & persistunt, eo prætextu, quòd nemo unquam Hæreticum sic definierit, quemadmodum à me definitum esse dicunt lib. 1. Par. I. cap. 1. Ad quod respondimus libro præcedente cap. 1. ubi ostendimus Arminianos nodum in scirpo quærere, & fingere me definitionem dedisse Hæretici, cùm tamen non nisi descriptionem, ut loco de quo quæstio est, nimirùm p. 210. Par. I. lib. 2. c. 8. expresse eam voco, & quidem verissimam dederim illius. Mendaciis, conviciis, calumniis, suis, (qualis est me ex familiâ eorum esse qui cum vetera omnia refixerint & nova sua in eorum locum substituerint, in capita eorum Magistratus auxilium implorem quos Haereticos exisitimem ) quibus etiam hoc loco me petunt, fruantur per me licet. Addideram p. 218. 219. patere jam ex dogmatis istis allegatis, quomodo intelligendum sit primum placitum eorum, quo volunt disciplinam Ecclesiasticam debere exerceri sine noxa ; nimirum mentem eorum hanc esse, ne repellatur excommunicatus, si ritibus sacris ante reconciliationem se immisceat; ne Magistratus ab Ecclesia moneatur ut coerceat Haereticos ; ne Anathema iis dicatur ; ne denique iis silentium imponatur. Haec hi homines non negant, & ne verbo quidem respondent, adeoque in conscientia sua convicti sunt, se falsum dixisse quando hic loci p. 148. dicunt, se tantum de noxa corporali loqui.
units.tr: 9. The seventh dogma is: Heretics are not to be silenced. After some trifles, by which they present to us certain new mysteries, as we saw in Part III, book 2, chapter 8, they admit this and persist, on the pretext that no one has ever defined a heretic as they say I have defined him in book 1, Part I, chapter 1. To this we replied in the preceding book, chapter 1, where we showed that the Arminians seek a knot in a bulrush, and pretend that I gave a definition of a heretic, when in fact I expressly call it only a description, as in the place in question, namely p. 210, Part I, book 2, chapter 8, and indeed I gave the most accurate one of him. As for their lies, reproaches, and calumnies (such as that I belong to the family of those who, having overturned all the old things, have set up their new ones in their place, and that I implore the aid of the magistrate against the heads of those whom I consider heretics), with which they assail me here too, let them enjoy them so far as I am concerned. I had added at pp. 218–219 that it is already clear from the dogmas cited what must be understood by their first tenet, by which they hold that church discipline must be exercised without harm: namely, that their meaning is this, that an excommunicated person is not to be repelled if he mixes himself into the sacred rites before reconciliation; that the magistrate is not to be urged by the Church to restrain heretics; that they are not to be anathematized; and finally that they are not to be silenced. These men do not deny this, nor do they answer even a word, and so they are convicted in their own conscience of having spoken falsely when here, at p. 148, they say that they speak only of bodily harm.

units.la: 10. Octavum & nonum talia sunt, ut in iis, postquam multis circumlocutionibus in praecedentibus dogmatis usi essent, jam aperto ore quid in pectore gerant, proloquantur. Octavum igitur dogma est. Non esse exercendam disciplinam Ecclesiasticam in eos qui errant in fundamento, nisi constet eos voluntaria culpa in errorem incidisse. Iam autem statuunt, ut supra vidimus, Haeresin plane esse involuntariam & propie dictam innocentiam. Unde jam sequitur, eos nolle permittere ut disciplina Ecclesiastica exerceatur adversus Haereticos. Hic quia constricti tenentur, dici non potest in quos gyros hinc inde sese contorqueant ut evadere possint, sed frustra. Itaq; magnum acervum nugarum congerunt p. 155. 156. 157. 158. quas data opera usq; adeo involvunt ut nihil supra, quo scilicet oculorum aciem fallant atque effugiant. Huc autem omnia uno verbo redeunt: Haeresin quae communiter sic a tota Ecclesia vocatur ( qualis Haeresis est Antitrinitariorum ) esse involuntariam, adeoque disciplina Ecclesiastica non coercendam. Esse autem aliam Haeresin quae sit voluntaria, adeoque per disciplinam Ecclesiasticam corrigenda. Si quaeras optime Lector, quae sit illa Haeresis; scias eos fingere Haeresin quae in rerum natura non est, & quam serpentinis suis verborum involucris & tegmentis per calumniam impudentissimam & plane Satanicam inhonestissime imputant Reformatis Ecclesiis, contra has exercendam disciplinam Ecclesiasticam contendunt, ut vidimus Par. III. lib. 2. c. 8. §. 9. O Deus bone, patierisne diutius ut pestilentissimi hi homines Tibi, Ecclesiae tuae, & toti orbi adeo nefarie ac improbe illudant! Claudunt tandem praeclaram istam dissertationem suam dicto gemino Salviani & Augustini, quae ad rem non faciunt. Nam Salvianus (cujus illud dictum hi homines quavis quâvis occasione suis libris infercire quærunt, & subinde apud populum venditant, adeò ut qui ex plebibus eorum literati sunt illud ad unguē recitare nôrint) comparativè loquitur de Hæreticis, h. e. comparat eorum impietátem cum impietate Catholicorum, & docet hos longè graviùs peccare quàm illi, quia veram Dei cognitionem habent, quam illi non habent. Nec negat Hæreticos punitum iri à Deo, sed dicit se nescire gradum supplicii: QVALITER in die judicii puniendi sint, nemo potest scire nisi judex. Et addit, Deum PATIENTIAM eis commodare, quo ipso notat Hæreticos Deum offendere errore suo, utpote cui patientiâ Deus commodat. Augustinus autem negat se velle auctorem esse ut saviatur in Manichaeos, tùm ob alias causas, tùm quia ipse olim Manichaeus fuerit. Et tamen Manichaei perpetuò coërciti ab Orthodoxis Imperatoribus fuêre, & hi eo nomine laudati ac defensi ab Augustino.
units.tr: 10. The eighth and ninth are of such a kind that, after using many circumlocutions in the preceding dogmas, they now speak out openly what they carry in their breast. The eighth dogma, therefore, is: Church discipline is not to be exercised against those who err in the foundation, unless it is established that they fell into error through voluntary fault. Now they maintain, as we saw above, that heresy is altogether involuntary and properly speaking innocence. From this it follows at once that they are unwilling to permit church discipline to be exercised against heretics. Here, since they are held fast, it cannot be said in what circles they twist this way and that in order to escape, but in vain. So they heap up a great mass of trifles at pp. 155, 156, 157, 158, which they deliberately involve so intricately that nothing is above them by which, namely, they might deceive and escape the sight of the eyes. But all of this comes back to one thing: that the heresy which is commonly called such by the whole Church (such as the heresy of the Antitrinitarians) is involuntary, and therefore church discipline is not to be exercised against it; and that there is another heresy which is voluntary, and therefore to be corrected by church discipline. If you ask, most excellent reader, what that heresy is, know that they invent a heresy which does not exist in the nature of things, and which, with their serpentine wrappings and coverings of words, by the most shameless and utterly Satanic calumny they most dishonourably impute to the Reformed Churches, and against these they contend that church discipline is to be exercised, as we saw in Part III, book 2, chapter 8, §9. O good God, will you suffer any longer that these most pestilential men mock you, your Church, and the whole world so wickedly and wrongly! At last they close this splendid dissertation of theirs with a double saying of Salvian and Augustine, which do not bear on the matter. For Salvian (whose saying these men seek to stuff into their books on every possible occasion, and keep peddling among the people, so that those among their common folk who are literate know it by heart) speaks comparatively about heretics, that is, he compares their impiety with the impiety of Catholics, and teaches that these sin far more gravely than those, because they have a true knowledge of God which the others lack. Nor does he deny that heretics will be punished by God, but says that he does not know the degree of punishment: HOW they are to be punished on the day of judgment, no one can know except the judge. And he adds that God lends them PATIENCE, by which very phrase he indicates that heretics offend God by their error, since God lends them patience. Augustine, however, denies that he wishes to be the author of its being raged against the Manichaeans, both for other reasons and because he himself was once a Manichaean. And yet the Manichaeans were constantly restrained by the orthodox emperors, and these were praised and defended by Augustine on that account.

units.la: 11. Nonum dogma est: Non esse mandatum à Deo separare à se errantes, aut se ab illis segregare. Fatentur, & provocant ad Responsionem suam ad octavum dogma modò consideratum; & tamen adeò protervi sunt ut dicant se in eâ responsione vanitatis me redarguere. Tu candide Lector judica.
units.tr: 11. The ninth dogma is: It is not commanded by God to separate from themselves those who err, or to keep themselves apart from them. They admit it, and appeal to their reply to the eighth dogma just considered; and yet they are so shameless as to say that in that reply they refute my vanity. Judge for yourself, candid reader.

units.la: 12. Decimum quod ipsis objeci est, eos tollere disciplinam Ecclesiasticam exercendam adversus Hæreticos doctrinâ suâ de Tolerantiâ, de Hæresi, item de libertate prophetandi. Si enim Hæretici (quales sunt Antitrinitarii) in Ecclesiæ communionem per Tolerantiam illam recipiendi sunt; si, an Hæreticus quis sit, sciri non potest; Si Hæresis non est peccatum, sed innocentia, & quidem summa; si Hæretici sunt homines piissimi; si æternùm salvi fiunt &c. certè ex Ecclesiâ per disciplinam ejici non debent. Idem etiam sequitur ex doctrinâ eorum de Libertate prophetandi: Si enim Hæreticis licet docere in Ecclesiâ, Ergò ex eâ ejiciendi non sunt &c. Respondent pari modo quoad præcedens, & simul quoque remittunt Lectorem ad capita Vindic. de libertate prophetandi, tolerantiâ mutuâ, & Hæresi: in quibus non negant, sed fatentur ea quæ modò commemoravi.
units.tr: 12. The tenth thing I objected to them is that by their doctrine of Toleration, of Heresy, and likewise of the liberty of prophesying, they abolish church discipline to be exercised against heretics. For if heretics (such as the Antitrinitarians) are to be received into the communion of the Church through that Toleration; if it cannot be known whether someone is a heretic; if heresy is not a sin but innocence, and indeed the highest innocence; if heretics are the most pious men; if they are saved eternally, etc., then certainly they ought not to be cast out of the Church by discipline. The same follows from their doctrine of the Liberty of prophesying: for if heretics are allowed to teach in the Church, therefore they are not to be cast out of it, etc. They reply in the same way as to the preceding, and at the same time they also refer the reader to the chapters of the Vindication on the liberty of prophesying, mutual toleration, and heresy: in which they do not deny, but confess, the things I have just mentioned.

units.la: Porrò ad hæc duo dogmata, quibus pleno ore eloquuntur sententiam suam de non exercendâ disciplinâ Ecclesiasticâ contra Hæreticos, quos tota Ecclesia quæ Deum in tribus personis adorat, sic vocat, refer quod in isto ipso capite 8. Vindiciarum quod nunc examinamus p. 146. dicunt; contra Hæreticos minimè oportere exercere disciplinam Ecclesiasticam: At videmus, proh dolor! inquiunt, plerasque Ecclesias totas esse in exercendâ disciplinâ sciplina contra eos quos minime oportet; & cum in manifestos peccatores rigide ex præscripto Christi & Apostolorum exercenda sit, istis posthabitis ac plane praeteritis exerceri in solos fere errantes. Et ne quis putet eos loqui tantum de eorum iniquitate aut Tyrannide qui in orthodoxos quos pro Hæreticis habent exercent disciplinam Ecclesiasticam; addunt: Vedelium tantum hic videamus, totius disciplinæ exercitium, cujus defectum in Remonstrantibus hic culpat, in solos Hæreticos dirigit. Nunc igitur judica, candide Lector, annon verè & jure de iis conquestus fuerim, quod disciplinam Ecclesiasticam contra Hæreticos exercendam evertant.
units.tr: Moreover, concerning these two dogmas, in which they speak out fully their opinion about not exercising church discipline against heretics (whom the whole Church that worships God in three persons calls so), compare what they say in this same eighth chapter of the Vindications which we are now examining, at p. 146: against heretics it is by no means right to exercise church discipline: But we see, alas! they say, that most churches are entirely engaged in exercising discipline against those whom they ought by no means to discipline; and whereas it is to be exercised rigorously against manifest sinners according to the prescription of Christ and the Apostles, these men, neglected and wholly passed over, are to be disciplined almost only in the case of erring persons. And lest anyone think that they speak only of the iniquity or tyranny of those who exercise church discipline against the orthodox whom they regard as heretics, they add: Let us see only Vedel here, who directs the whole exercise of discipline, whose lack among the Remonstrants he blames here, solely against heretics. Now judge, candid reader, whether I have not complained of them truly and rightly, that they subvert church discipline which ought to be exercised against heretics.

units.la: Conclusionis loco dixeram p.221. eos in æternum conciliare non posse hæc duo effata: nimirùm disciplinam exercendam esse adversus Hæreticos, de quibus quæstio est, ut ipsi loqui solent, & quidem sine noxâ: item disciplinam exercendam non esse adversus eos ipsos Hæreticos. Ad hoc etiam ne verbo quidem respondent, & sic in hac quoque parte se non solum falsitatis sed & improbitatis atque impostura quâ orbis oculis illudere volunt; convictos esse ostendunt.
units.tr: By way of conclusion I had said at p. 221 that they cannot reconcile these two assertions for ever: namely, that discipline is to be exercised against the heretics in question, as they are wont to say, and indeed without harm; and likewise that discipline is not to be exercised against those very heretics. To this they do not even answer a word, and so in this part too they show themselves convicted not only of falsehood but also of wickedness and of an imposture by which they want to mock the eyes of the world.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: Examen Capitis IX. Vindic. lib. 2.
units.tr: Examination of Chapter IX of the Vindication, Book 2.

units.la: I. Arminiani fatentur se docere Ministros debere Magistratui obedientiam recusare, quando in conscientia sua judicant præscriptum Magistratus repugnare verbo Dei. 2. Fatentur se docere Magistratum non debere impedire quò minus ministri doceant, quod rectum ipsis videtur. 3. Fatentur se docere Magistratus posse tantum prohibere ne minister doceat in locis publicis non autem privatis. 4. Fatentur se docere: Magistratum nullum jus habere prohibendi conventicula privata Hæreticorum. 5. Levitas turpissima & detestanda Arminianorum, dogmata sua mutantium prout statui externo rerum suarum putant illud nocere aut expedire, speciatim circa dogma præcedens. 6. Vindicantur argumenta Auctoris contra istud dogma à fraudibus & sophismatis eorum. 7. Fatentur se Reges, Principes, Magistratus qui conventicula privata Hæreticorum prohibent Tyrannidis & injustitiæ justitiæ condemnare, & in eâ maledicentiâ perseverant. Eos contra conscientiam suam, auctoris doctrinam orthodoxam calumniatos esse ostenditur. Contumeliosa doctrina eorum in arma Illustrissimorum Ordinum fœderatorum & aliorum quorundam Tyrannis resistentium. 8. Fatentur se docere Magistratum nullam habere potestatem prohibendi subditis liberam professionem Religionis suæ; & eum debere unicuique suam Religionem liberam facere & unicuique concedere exercitium suæ Religionis. 9. Fatentur se docere Hæreticos nullo plane corporali modo coercendos à Magistratu. 10. Eos contra conscientiam suam negare Hæreticos jure posse coercere Magistratum, qui ipsos coercere vult. 11. Fatentur atrocissima & horrenda convitia, quæ in Reges, Principes, Magistratus Orthodoxos exspuunt qui Hæreticos coercent, & in iis perseverant. Auctoris doctrina à calumniâ impudentissimâ Arminianorum vindicata. Quæstio decisa, an'ne Illustrissimi Ordines fœderati Belgii coerceant Hæreticos? 12. Eos contra conscientiam suam negare duplicem potestatem, quam Magistratui in hac re illusoriè & contumeliosè permittunt, ostenditur. 13. Fatentur se docere Hæreticos contumaciter blasphemos non afficiendos esse blasphemiæ pœnâ à Magistratu. 14. Non negant se docere: Hæreticos puniendos non esse etsi Rempublicam turbent. 15. Fatentur se docere Apostatas ad Iudæos non esse capitali pœnâ afficiendos.
units.tr: 1. The Arminians confess that they teach that ministers ought to refuse obedience to the Magistrate when in their own conscience they judge that the Magistrate's command conflicts with the Word of God. 2. They confess that they teach that the Magistrate ought not to hinder ministers from teaching what seems right to them. 3. They confess that they teach that the Magistrate can forbid a minister to teach only in public places, not in private ones. 4. They confess that they teach that the Magistrate has no right to forbid the private conventicles of heretics. 5. The most shameful and detestable levity of the Arminians, who change their doctrines as they think the outward state of their affairs is harmed or helped by them, especially concerning the preceding doctrine. 6. The arguments of the author against that doctrine are defended from their frauds and sophisms. 7. They confess that kings, princes and magistrates who forbid the private conventicles of heretics condemn as tyranny and injustice what is justice, and they persist in that slander. It is shown that they have, against their own conscience, slandered the author's orthodox doctrine. Their insulting doctrine is aimed at the arms of the Illustrious Confederated Orders and of certain others who resist tyranny. 8. They confess that they teach that the Magistrate has no power to forbid subjects the free profession of their religion, and that he ought to leave each person his religion free and grant each the exercise of his own religion. 9. They confess that they teach that heretics are not at all to be restrained by the Magistrate by any bodily means. 10. Against their own conscience they deny that the Magistrate, who wishes to restrain heretics, can rightly restrain them. 11. They confess that they spit out the most atrocious and horrible insults against kings, princes and orthodox magistrates who restrain heretics and persist in doing so. The author's doctrine is vindicated from the most shameless slander of the Arminians. The question is settled: whether the Illustrious Confederated Orders of Belgium restrain heretics? 12. It is shown that they, against their own conscience, deny the twofold power which they grant the Magistrate in this matter, mockingly and insultingly. 13. They confess that they teach that heretics who are obstinately blasphemous are not to be punished by the Magistrate with the penalty for blasphemy. 14. They do not deny that they teach that heretics are not to be punished even if they disturb the commonwealth. 15. They confess that they teach that apostates to Judaism are not to be punished with capital punishment.

units.la: I. CApite nono antequam ad dogmata objecta respondeant, scoptice imitantur verba mea quibus Magistratus non quosvis sed eos compellaveram qui Hæreticos verè sic dictos coërcent, & longam præfationem vicissim præmittunt p. 158. 159. 160 161. ad Reges & Principes, speciatim ad Illustrissimos Ordines Belgii, quæ tota consistit in calumniis non solùm contra me sed etiam contra Ecclesias omnes Reformatas, speciatim Belgicas, quibus pro more suo salsissimè imputant causam dissidiorum & malorum Belgii, quibus putidis calumniis ut & cavillationibus diluendis horum Socinianorū simulatorum tempus terere nolo. Ad rem ipsam h. e. ad dogmata venio, quibus dixi eos quintum metum medium confervandæ fidei & Religionis Christianæ, quod est Magistratus potestas circa res sacras inutile plane reddere adversum Hæreticos. Id dixi ab iis fieri quinque modis quorum primus consistit in dogmate de potestate Magistratus in ministros Ecclesiæ. Hanc potestatem dixi Arminianos eripere Magistratui duplici ratione. Una est, dum statuunt: Ministros debere Magistratui ordinanti aliquid circa cultum Dei seu functiones Ecclesiasticas obedientiam recusare, quando judicant in conscientia sua præscriptum Magistratus repugnare verbo Dei. Cùm debebant dixisse ministros tunc debere recusare Magistratui obedientiam quando revera verbo Dei contraria præcipit, non autem quando ipsis videtur contraria illi præcipere. Fatentur illud dogma suum p. 162. & contendunt adversum me, judicium proprium hominis esse NORMAM faciendorum, ac me qui id nego arguunt supinæ stultitiæ,& dicunt me ingentem insanire insaniam. Atque ut id probent, relabuntur ad coccysmum suum de Vedelio, quem protrahunt ad tribunal Regis seu Principis Evangelici, coram quo mentiuntur me judicium meum normam facturum facti mei, non autem unicè solum verbum Dei. Cæterùm quia suam sententiam probare conati erant ex Actor. c. 4. v. 19. Oportet enim Deo plus obedire quàm hominibus: ostenderam ego eos abuti loco illo & perperàm ad institutum suum detorquere. Ad hoc nihil respondent.
units.tr: I. In chapter nine, before they answer the doctrines objected to them, they mimic in a mocking way my words, in which I had addressed magistrates not in general but those who restrain heretics truly so called. In turn they prefix a long preface, pp. 158, 159, 160, 161, addressed to kings and princes, and especially to the Illustrious Orders of Belgium. This whole preface consists of slanders not only against me but also against all the Reformed Churches, especially the Belgian ones, which they wrongly and in their usual way blame for the causes of the dissensions and evils of Belgium. I do not want to waste time refuting these foul slanders and cavils of these pretended Socinians. I come to the matter itself, that is, to the doctrines, by which I said they make the fifth means of preserving the faith and the Christian religion, namely the power of the Magistrate in sacred matters, wholly useless against heretics. I said they do this in five ways, the first of which consists in the doctrine concerning the power of the Magistrate over the ministers of the Church. I said that the Arminians take this power away from the Magistrate in a twofold way. One is when they lay down: "Ministers ought to refuse obedience to a Magistrate who orders something concerning the worship of God or ecclesiastical functions, when they judge in their conscience that the Magistrate's command conflicts with the Word of God." They should have said that ministers ought then to refuse obedience to the Magistrate when he really commands what is contrary to the Word of God, and not when it merely seems to them that he commands what is contrary. They confess this doctrine of theirs at p. 162, and they contend against me that a man's own judgment is the rule of what is to be done. They accuse me, who deny this, of supine folly, and say that I rave with great madness. To prove this, they fall back on their clamour about Vedel, whom they drag before the tribunal of the king or the evangelical prince, before which they falsely claim that I would make my judgment the rule of my deed, and not solely the Word of God. Moreover, since they tried to prove their view from Acts 4:19, "For we ought to obey God rather than men," I had shown that they abuse that passage and wrongly twist it to their purpose. They answer nothing to this.

units.la: 2. Simile est quod objeci,eos docere: Magistratum non debere impedire quo minus ministri doceant quod rectum ipsis videtur. Quâ ratione ostenderam p. 224. 225. eos portam patentissimam omnis generis Hæreticis aperire: Magistratum quippe sic cogi cedere Hæreticis qui docent utique quod rectum ipsis videtur &c. Hoc etiam non negant, & ne verbo quidem respondent.
units.tr: 2. Similar is what I objected, that they teach: "The Magistrate ought not to hinder ministers from teaching what seems right to them." On this ground I had shown at pp. 224, 225 that they open a very wide gate to heretics of every kind, since the Magistrate would thus be forced to yield to heretics who teach whatever seems right to them, and so on. They do not deny this either, and they do not even answer it in words.

units.la: 3. Altera ratio quâ Magistratui eripiunt potestatem in Pastores, in eo posita est, quòd statuunt Magistratum posse tantùm prohibere, ne minister doceat in templis seu locis publicis, non autem in privatis. Fatentur p. 163. & persistunt, sine ullâ ratione aut confirmatione illius dogmatis.
units.tr: 3. The other way in which they take away the Magistrate's power over ministers lies in their claim that "the Magistrate can only forbid a minister to teach in churches or public places, not in private ones." They confess this at p. 163, and they persist in it without any reason or confirmation of that doctrine.

units.la: 4. Cum hoc dixi cohærere secundum modum quo Magistratus potestatem plane inutilem reddunt adversum Hæreticos. Docent enim: Magistratum nullum jus habere prohibendi & impediendi conventicula privata Hæreticorum religionis gratiâ convenientium. Imò eum ne quidè habere potestatem ut edistis ea impediat. Item non licere sese per seditionem opponere Magistratui in eum finem ut templa seu loca publica retineantur invito eo; licere autem docere in locis privatis ubi Magistratus jubendi ac prohibendi jus non habeat. Item: Magistratus stratui hoc solum circa conventicula permittunt, ut interesse eis possit, turbas impedire & ordinem in iis tueri ac conservare; adeoque conventicula praesentia sua & auctoritate confirmare, tutorem ac curatorem eorum esse debere. Fatentur & persistunt; saltem dicunt non debere nominari conventicula: Ut isto odiosō, inquiunt, nomine censeantur coetus eorum qui Religionis & conscientiae causa congregantur non permittit aequitas vestra. Compellant autem Illustrissimos Ordines, qui longe pientiores sunt, quam ut iniquum existiment conventus Haereticorum privatos conventicula appellari.
units.tr: 4. I said that this coheres with the way in which they make the power of the Magistrate wholly useless against heretics. For they teach: "The Magistrate has no right to forbid and hinder the private conventicles of heretics who gather for the sake of religion. Indeed, he does not even have the power to hinder them by an edict." Likewise: "It is not lawful to oppose the Magistrate by sedition in order to keep churches or public places against his will; but it is lawful to teach in private places where the Magistrate has no right to command or forbid." Likewise: "The Magistrates may permit only this regarding conventicles: that he may be present at them, check disturbances, and preserve and maintain order in them; and so, by his presence and authority, he should confirm the conventicles, and be their guardian and curator." They confess and persist in this; at least they say that conventicles ought not to be so named: "Your equity does not permit that the gatherings of those who assemble for the sake of religion and conscience be judged by that hateful name." They address the Illustrious Orders, who are far too pious to think it unjust that the private meetings of heretics be called conventicles.

units.la: 5. Fatentur igitur se docere, Magistratum nullum jus habere prohibendi conventicula, seu, si ita volunt, conventus privatos Religionis causa institutos; in eo persistunt, & ad argumenta, quae pestilentissimae isti sententiae oppositi, multas nugas regerunt p. 163. 164. 165. 166. 167. 168. 169. & acerrime tuentur hanc suam sententiam; idque cum summis convitiis & maledicentia sibi solita, non adversus me solum, sed etiam adversus Principes & Magistratus qui Haereticorum conventicula impediunt. Hic mihi vide quisquis es, candide Lector, seu Reformatae Religioni nostrae, seu Arminianae, seu cuivis alii coetui qui Deum in tribus personis adorandum esse profitetur addictus sis, insignem & detestandam levitatem horum hominum in negocio Religionis. Ante paucos annos enim contrariam sententiam docebant & tuebantur; tunc scilicet cum Magistratus qui ipsorum causae favebant edictis severissimis prohiberent & multis gravissimis aliisque punitionibus corrigerent; & dissiparent de facto conventus privatos Reformatorum. De ea re quando conquerebantur nostri; regerebant Arminiani non solum in hypothesi Magistratum conventus eos Reformatorum dissipantem recte facere, sed etiam in thesi doctrinam eam professi sunt. In quam rem argumento utebantur eo, quod meum primum est, ut mox videbimus, nec non exemplis Imperatorum Christianorum, auctoritate Augustini, item Legibus Justinianeis. Ut dubium multum animo Lectoris pii & candidi superfit, verba eorum adscribere non pigebit, propter exteros praesertim, quibus res ignota esse potest. Antequam Synodus Nationalis Dordracena celebraretur, Pastores Ecclesiarum Reformatarum Zelandicarum in eo distritu qui Walachria vocatur Epistolam suam quandam publici juris fecerunt anno 1617. qua exteros Theologos statum Ecclesiarum Belgii edocent. Huic Epistolae eodem tempore Arminiani prolixum scriptum opposuerunt Latino quoque sermone editum, impressum Lugduni Batavorum a Johanne Patio jurato & ordinario Typographo grapho Academiæ, ut titulus ipse seu frontispicium libri indicat. In illo scripto ad illam partem Epistolæ quâ Walachrianæ Ecclesiæ conquerebantur, conventus Reformatorum privatos prohibitos & dissipatos esse instinctu Arminianorum ministrorum qui causæ Arminianorum favebant: Respondent illi pag. 105. Alterum est, quod scribunt Pastores Walachrienses, Magistratus eos conventus tum indictis multis gravissimis prohibere, tum illatis alicubi dissipasse. Non diffitemur. Quanta enim ex hoc schismate tum Rempublicam, tum Ecclesias nostras maneant incommoda, provide vident, ET CUM ECCLESIÆ SE NUTRICIOS AC TABULÆ UTRIUSQUE CUSTODES A DEO CONSTITUTOS ESSE EX SACRIS LITERIS DIDICERINT, Muneris sui, esse putant, non permittere, ut paucorum studiis post Lutheranum schisma in Germania, post Puritanorum in Anglia, Reformatorum coetus propter has de prædestinatione controversias novo & deplorando schismate in alias partes dispescantur. Atque hic Constantini, Valentiniani, Gratiani, Theodosii Christianorum Imperatorum vestigiis insistunt, qui severissimis legibus contra Donati partem sanxerunt, ut videre est apud Augustinum Epistola 196 contra Donatistas, etiam multas subinde indicendo schismatis auctoribus. Sic enim idem Augustinus contra Epistol. Parmen. lib. 1. c. 7. Imperatorum autem justitiam legesque quæ vehementes adversus eos latæ sunt, quis ignorat? In quibus una generalis adversus omnes qui se Christianos dici volunt, & Ecclesiæ Catholicæ non communicant, sed in suis separatim conventiculis congregantur, id continet, ut vel ordinator Clerici vel ipse ordinatus denis libris auri multetur: Locus vero ipse quo impia separatio congregatur, redigatur in fiscum. Nota quoque sunt ea quæ adversus privatos conventus legibus sancita sunt. L. Conventicula C. de Episcopis & Clericis: (conventicula illicita extra Ecclesiam in privatis ædibus celebrari prohibemus: proscriptionis domus periculo imminente, si Dominus eius in ea clericos nova ac tumultuosa conventicula extra Ecclesiam celebrantes suscepe-rit. vide Nov. 131. c. 8. & 58. Ita Arminiani in illo suo scripto omnium nomine edito. Similiter Episcopius in Thesibus privatis disp. 17. p. 14. (actus, collegia, conventicula sine summarum potestatum venia & indulgentia nedum invitis & nolentibus illis habere nulli Christiano fas est. Unde manifestum est. 1. levitas horum hominum in negocio Religionis, & dogmatibus etiam maximi momenti, qualis est doctrina orthodoxa de potestate Magistratus circa coercitionem Hæreticorum. 2. Patet exinde eos levitate illâ uti prout vident rebus suis consultum atque utile. Si hodie affirmatio dogmatis alicujus ipsorum rebus & conatibus idonea est, affirmant. Si autem cras negatio ipsorum sectæ promovendæ utilis videtur, negant: prout ex hoc exemplo patet. Nam cùm illi templa possiderent, & nostri privatim convenirent, ac Magistratus ipsis addicti conventus privatos nostros prohiberent: jus illud plenâ manu Magistratui tribuerunt. Hodie autem quo templa publica & loca ordinaria cultui divino destinata non possident, ac in privatis ædibus conveniunt, & Pastores Reformati Illustrissimos Ordines rogant, ut eorum conventicula impediant: jus illud Magistratui plane eripiunt. Unde 3. patet, verum esse quod supra etiam dixi aliâ occasione, nimirùm hos homines propter levitatem suam in tanto negocio, nullam amplius fidem nec in negocio Religionis, nec in alio quovis negocio quod Religionis causâ profectò longè minus est, mereri, quando dicunt se hoc vel illud credere aut docere. Hodie enim aliquid affirmant, cras obliti omnis pudoris & honestatis illud negabunt, non vi veratis victi (ut errantes interdum solent, imò ut magni Ecclesiæ Doctores fecêre, sed qui liberè simul confessi sunt, se sententiam falsam olim tenuisse & ei renunciare quia ex verbo Dei veritatem jam didicerint) sed prout rebus suis expedire & statum earum flagitare judicant. Ex quo etiam apparet jam 4. quæ sit vera norma Religionis Arminianæ, adeóque quæ & qualis illa sit Religio. Nimirùm præterquàm quòd Socianismum in Ecclesiam introducere conantur, esse factionem Politicam, cui hoc vel contrarium dogma adaptant, prout è re factionis illius est; prout ipsi vel rerum potiuntur vel non potiuntur, & vel incrementum aut detrimentum sectæ suæ metuunt; quemadmodum ex hoc exemplo luce clarius meridianâ patet, nec nò ex eo quòd jam videri volunt agnoscere dogmata quædam controversa necessaria ad salutem, quia viderunt doctrinam contrariam quam in Apologiâ profitentur invidiam ipsis oppidò magnam conciliare, adeóque vehementer rebus suis nocere posse.
units.tr: 5. They therefore admit that they teach that the magistrate has no right to forbid conventicles, or, if they prefer, private assemblies instituted for the sake of religion. They persist in this, and in answer to the arguments opposed to that most pestilential opinion they heap up many trifles (pp. 163, 164, 165, 166, 167, 168, 169), and they defend their view most fiercely. They do so with the greatest abuse and slander, as is their habit, not only against me but also against princes and magistrates who hinder the conventicles of heretics. Here, whoever you are, candid reader, whether you are attached to our Reformed religion, or to the Arminian, or to any other assembly which professes that God is to be worshipped in three persons, see the remarkable and detestable levity of these men in matters of religion. For a few years ago they taught and defended the contrary opinion, namely at the time when magistrates who favoured their cause issued most severe edicts forbidding the assemblies of the Reformed, punished them with many grievous penalties, and in fact dispersed their private gatherings. When our people complained about this, the Arminians replied that the magistrate who dispersed the Reformed assemblies did right, not only in hypothesis but also in thesis, and they professed that doctrine. For this they used an argument which is my first, as we shall soon see, as well as the examples of Christian emperors, the authority of Augustine, and the Justinianic laws. Lest much doubt remain in the mind of the pious and candid reader, I will not hesitate to quote their words, especially for foreigners, to whom the matter may be unknown. Before the National Synod of Dort was held, the pastors of the Reformed Churches of Zeeland in the district called Walcheren published a letter of theirs in 1617, by which they informed foreign theologians of the state of the Churches of Belgium. At the same time the Arminians opposed to this letter a lengthy writing, also published in Latin, printed at Leiden by John Patius, sworn and ordinary printer to the University, as the title or frontispiece of the book indicates. In that writing, in reply to that part of the letter in which the Walcheren Church complained that the assemblies of the Reformed had been forbidden and dispersed at the instigation of the Arminian ministers who favoured the Arminian cause, they answer (p. 105): The other point is that the Walcheren pastors write that the magistrates have forbidden those assemblies by imposing many most grievous penalties, and in some places have dispersed them. We do not deny it. For they clearly foresee how many inconveniences from this schism threaten both the commonwealth and our Churches; and since they have learned from holy letters that the Churches have been constituted by God as nurses and as guardians of both tables, they think it is their duty not to permit that the Reformed assemblies, through the zeal of a few, be split into other parts by a new and lamentable schism over these controversies about predestination, as happened after the Lutheran schism in Germany and after the Puritan schism in England. And in this they follow the footsteps of the Christian emperors Constantine, Valentinian, Gratian and Theodosius, who by most severe laws sanctioned against the party of Donatus, as may be seen in Augustine, Epistle 196 against the Donatists, also imposing many fines on the authors of schism. For so the same Augustine, against the Epistle of Parmenian, book 1, chapter 7. Who does not know the justice of the emperors and the vehement laws enacted against these men? In them there is one general law against all who wish to be called Christians, and do not communicate with the Catholic Church but gather separately in their own conventicles, providing that either the ordainer of a cleric or the ordained man himself be fined ten pounds of gold, and that the place where the impious separation gathers be confiscated to the treasury. Also well known are the things sanctioned by law against private assemblies. L. Conventicula, C. de Episcopis et Clericis: We forbid illicit conventicles to be held outside the Church in private houses, under the threat of the proscription of the house if its owner has received clerics celebrating new and tumultuous conventicles outside the Church. See Nov. 131, c. 8, and 58. Thus the Arminians in that writing of theirs, published in the name of them all. Similarly Episcopius in his private Theses, disp. 17, p. 14: It is not lawful for any Christian to hold acts, colleges, or conventicles without the leave and indulgence of the supreme powers, much less against their will and wishes. Hence it is clear: 1. the levity of these men in a matter of religion, and in doctrines of the greatest moment, such as the orthodox doctrine about the power of the magistrate to coerce heretics. 2. It appears from this that they use that levity as they see it is expedient and useful for their affairs. If today the affirmation of some doctrine suits their affairs and endeavours, they affirm it; if tomorrow the denial seems useful for promoting their sect, they deny it, as is clear from this example. For when they possessed the churches, and our people met privately, and magistrates favourable to them forbade our private assemblies, they granted that right to the magistrate in full measure. But today, when they do not possess the public churches and the places set apart for divine worship, and meet in private houses, and the Reformed pastors ask the most illustrious Orders to hinder their conventicles, they wholly snatch that right from the magistrate. Whence 3. it is evident that what I said above on another occasion is true, namely that these men, on account of their levity in so great a matter, deserve no further trust either in matters of religion or in any other matter, which is certainly far less a matter of religion, when they say that they believe or teach this or that. For today they affirm something, and tomorrow, forgetting all shame and honesty, they will deny it, not conquered by the force of truth (as erring men sometimes are, as indeed great doctors of the Church have done, who freely confessed that they had formerly held a false opinion and renounced it because they had now learned the truth from the word of God), but as they judge it expedient for their affairs and demanded by their condition. From this also now appears 4. what is the true rule of the Arminian religion, and so what and of what kind that religion is. Namely, besides the fact that they are trying to introduce Socinianism into the Church, it is a political faction, which adapts this or the contrary dogma as is convenient for that faction: as they either hold power or do not, and fear either the growth or the loss of their sect. This is clearer than the midday light from this example, and also from the fact that they now wish to appear to acknowledge certain controverted dogmas as necessary to salvation, because they have seen that the contrary doctrine which they profess in their Apology has brought them very great odium, and so could greatly harm their affairs.

units.la: 6. Porrò ostenderam ego p. 228. doctrinam Arminianorum quâ eripiunt Magistratui jus prohibendi conventicula Hæreticorum esse pessimam & salsissimam, tribus argumentis, quæ sophisticè convellere multis nugis, calumniis & impostu-ris conantur. Primum meum argumentum erat ex eo petitu, quòd doctrina ista eorum nititur fundamento falso; nimirùm Magistratum ideò habere potestatem coactivam in locis publicis, quia eorum Dominus sit; & sic contra non habere potestatem coactivam in locis privatis quia eorum Dominus non sit. Et ostendi hanc veram causam non esse potestatis illius coactivæ. Vera enim causa est, dicebam, quia ei cura Religionis demandata à Deo est, & sic tenetur eam sar-tam tectam præstare ac defendere adversus corruptelas humanas h. e. Hæreses, schismata, idololatriam, superstitionem, impietatem, profanitatem. Hoc officium Magistratus non dependet à loco hoc vel illo, sed à perpetua ordinatione sive instituto Dei. Et sic quia hæc causa perpetua est, effectus etiam perpetuus est. Quare te-netur non minus in locis privatis, quam publicis verum ac purum Dei cultum conservare, utpote qui non minus in illis quam in his locis corrumpi potest.
units.tr: 6. Moreover, I had shown on p. 228 that the doctrine of the Arminians, by which they snatch from the magistrate the right to forbid the conventicles of heretics, is most pernicious and utterly false, by three arguments, which they try to overthrow sophistically with many trifles, calumnies and deceptions. My first argument was drawn from this, that their doctrine rests on a false foundation, namely that the magistrate has coercive power in public places because they belong to his lord, and so conversely has no coercive power in private places because they do not belong to his lord. And I showed that this is not the true cause of that coercive power. For the true cause, I said, is that the care of religion has been entrusted to him by God, and so he is bound to preserve and defend it safe and sound against human corruptions, that is, heresies, schisms, idolatry, superstition, impiety and profanity. This office of the magistrate does not depend on this or that place, but on the perpetual ordinance or institution of God. And so, since this cause is perpetual, the effect too is perpetual. Wherefore he is bound to preserve the true and pure worship of God no less in private places than in public, since it can be corrupted no less in the former than in the latter.

units.la: Hic ita respondent hi homines, ut manifestum rursus faciant, se fraudulentia & impudentia singulari orbi illudere velle. Et quidem respondent quatuor modis. Primo, inquiunt, hoc esse petere principium. Hoc enim est quod quaeritur, an cura Religionis eo usque vobis ab Altissimo Cœli Domino demandata sit, ut vi coactiva in locis privatis coetus prohibeatis ac disturbetis qui solius Religionis causa conveniunt. Et, ut probent hoc ipsum in quaestione esse, redeunt ad Coccysmum suum de Vedelio si ei interdicerentur Daventriæ coetus privati. Sed quis hic non videt hos homines omnem honestatis curam deposuisse, & saltem hoc agere ut aliquid dicant, ac eo-sucum faciant hominibus? Dicunt me principium petere, seu id quod in quaestione est. Qua conscientia hoc dicere possunt? Dixi eorum doctrinam, quod scilicet Magistratus non habeat jus in conventicula privata, prohibenda, falso fundamento niti hoc, nimirum quod ideo Magistratus habeat potestatem coactivam in locis publicis; non autem in privatis, quia horum Dominus non sit. Hoc fundamento se niti negare non possunt nec negant; verba enim Apologiæ c. 25. f. 297. a nobis in eum finem allegata, expressissima sunt. Est'ne hoc principium petere? Deinde probavi istud fundamentum falsum esse, afferendo veram causam: quæ est, ideo Magistratum habere potestatem coactivam in locis publicis, quia ei cura Religionis a Deo demandata sit, & sic tenetur eam conservare ac defendere contra corruptelas humanas, hæreses &c. Est'ne hoc principium petere? Unde intuli per consequens, eum habere etiam potestativam in locis privatis, & consequentiam probavi, quia hoc officium Magistratus non dependet a loco hoc vel illo, sed a perpetua ordinatione Dei, item quia verus Dei cultus non minus potest corrumpi in locis privatis, quam publicis. Est'ne hoc principium petere? Pudeat hos homines, si vel mica pudoris & reverentiæ erga Deum & homines iis superest! Quid? existimant ne Christianos fatuos esse, quibus adeo illudendum sit? Quod eo gravius est quia hic audent in eam rem nomen Dei temerè usurpare, dum non sine singulari hypocrisi, Altissi-mum cœli Dominum appellant.
units.tr: Here these men respond in such a way as to show once again that they wish to deceive the whole world with their fraud and shamelessness. They respond in four ways. First, they say, this is begging the question. For the point in dispute is whether the care of religion has been committed to you by the Most High, the Lord of heaven, so that you may by coercive force prohibit and disturb in private places those assemblies that meet for religion alone. To prove that this is the very question at issue, they return to their absurd charge against Vedelius, namely that if private assemblies were forbidden at Deventer. But who does not see here that these men have cast off all concern for honesty, and at least aim only to say something and make people laugh? They say that I beg the question, that is, that I assume what is in dispute. With what conscience can they say this? I stated their doctrine, that the magistrate has no right to forbid private conventicles, and that this rests on a false foundation, namely that the magistrate has coercive power in public places because he is their lord, but not in private places, because they are not his. They cannot deny that this is their foundation, and they do not deny it; the words of the Apology, chapter 25, page 297, which we quoted for this purpose, are most explicit. Is this begging the question? Then I showed that this foundation is false, by setting out the true cause: the magistrate has coercive power in public places because the care of religion has been committed to him by God, and so he is bound to preserve and defend it against human corruptions, heresies, and so on. Is this begging the question? From this I inferred by consequence that he also has power in private places, and I proved the consequence, because this office of the magistrate does not depend on this place or that, but on the perpetual ordinance of God, and also because the true worship of God can be corrupted in private places no less than in public. Is this begging the question? Let these men be ashamed, if any crumb of shame and reverence toward God and men remains in them! What, do they think Christians are such fools that they may be mocked so easily? This is all the more grievous because they dare here to use the name of God rashly, calling him, not without a remarkable hypocrisy, the Most High, the Lord of heaven.

units.la: Quod negant, ex eo, quòd cura Religionis à Deo Magistratibus demandata sit, sequi eum habere jus in conventicula privata, mirandum est, cùm eo ipso argumento usi fuerint anno 1617 ad defendendam sententiam hanc quam nos defendimus, & quam jam ita veteratorie oppugnant, atque ex cura illa demandatâ Magistratibus intulerint, eum habere jus in conventicula privata, ut patet ex verbis eorum, quæ paulò antè allegavimus ex responso ad Epistolam Walachrianam. Unde rursus jam videre est levitatem horum hominum, qui, cùm ipsi in allegato responso doceant ex eâ cura &c. id sequi, jam tamen negant id exinde sequi. Hæc prima est eorum responsio ad istud meum argumentum.
units.tr: That they deny that it follows from the fact that the care of religion has been committed to magistrates by God that he has a right over private conventicles is astonishing, since in 1617 they used this very argument to defend the opinion that we defend, and which they now attack so craftily. From that committed care they inferred that the magistrate has a right over private conventicles, as is clear from their own words, which we quoted a little above from their reply to the Walachrian Letter. Hence one can again see the levity of these men, who, while they teach in the cited reply that this follows from that care, now deny that it follows. This is their first answer to my argument.

units.la: Secundò respondent p.464. se Magistratui nolle adimere potestatem ut Religionem defendat adversus corruptelas humanas; sed hoc fieri debere non ulla à corporali coercitione sed tantum armis & mediis spiritualibus, seu argumentis & rationibus, atque hanc suam responsionem calumniis & maledicentiâ suâ caninâ contra me exornant. Probant autem suam responsionem 1. ex eo quia spiritualium morborum spiritualia sunt remedia. 2. quia vim adhibere sit errores stabilire, animos alienare, corruptelas augere, Antistites Ecclesiarum segnes ac socordes reddere ad defensionem veritatis. Respondeo, hos homines expressè & directè verbo Dei repugnare, quod commendat eos Reges, ut Asam, Josiam, Ezechiâ &c. qui religione non solum armis spiritualibus, sed etiâ mediis corporalibus adversus corruptelas humanas, idololatriam, superstitionem &c. defenderunt. Primam ratiunculam quod attinet, si ea vera est, certè ne quidem in locis publicis Magistratus ullam habet potestatem coactivam, quam tamen Arminiani ei tribuunt. Falsum etiam est, spiritualibus morbis esse opponenda remedia tantum spiritualia. Id enim verum est de iis morbis quamdiu in actus externos quibus corpus inservit non erumpunt, in detrimentum, offensam & noxam publicam. Alias nullum peccatum esset coercendum corporaliter, quia omne peccatum est morbus spiritualis. Alterum quod attinet, falsum est coercitione conveniente civili errores stabiliri, & corruptelas augeri. Contrarium testatur experientia veteris Ecclesiæ, cuius experientiæ hi omnes ignari sunt ut manifestum faciunt. Animos alienari Hæreticorum & male feriatorum hominum multorum eâ ratione non dubito; sed de hoc Magistratui orthodoxo non est laborandum, cui sufficere debet amor Dei & bonorum subditorum. Et sunt infiniti ex errantibus, qui quando convenienconvenienti modo Magistratus actibus externis eorum resistit, cogitare incipiunt de errore suo, & ei renunciant, ac veritatem amplectuntur, ut testatur experientia veteris Ecclesiæ, nec non Augustinus Epist. 48. ad Vincentium, adeoque tunc Magistratum verè amare incipiunt. Nam qui verè Hæretici sunt Magistratum suum verè non amant, ut & res & experientia testatur. Simulant enim tantùm affectum bonum, sed quamdiu Magistratus officio suo adversum eos non fungitur: quo ubi fungi incipit, erumpit morbus in odia manifesta, maledicentiam, molitionem parricidiorum, prout hoc Illustrissimus Heros Mauritius memoriæ gloriosæ expertus est à grege Arminiano, quem tamen Principem Deus clementer & mirabiliter protexit, ut solet sæpissimè defendere assertores gloriæ, veritatis, Ecclesiæ suæ.
units.tr: Second, they answer on page 464 that they are unwilling to take away from the magistrate the power to defend religion against human corruptions; but this must be done not by any bodily coercion, only by arms and spiritual means, that is, by arguments and reasons; and they adorn this answer with their calumnies and their dog-like slander against me. They prove their answer, first, because the remedies for spiritual diseases are spiritual. Second, because to apply force is to establish errors, alienate minds, increase corruptions, and make the ministers of the Churches slothful and careless in defending the truth. I reply that these men directly and expressly contradict the Word of God, which commends kings such as Asa, Josiah, and Hezekiah, who defended religion not only with spiritual arms but also with bodily means against human corruptions, idolatry, superstition, and so on. As for their first little argument, if it were true, then certainly the magistrate would have no coercive power even in public places, which the Arminians nevertheless grant him. It is also false that spiritual diseases must be opposed only by spiritual remedies. That is true of those diseases only so long as they do not break out into external acts, which the body serves, to the public detriment, offence, and harm. Otherwise no sin would be to be restrained bodily, since every sin is a spiritual disease. As for the second point, it is false that by fitting civil coercion errors are established and corruptions increased. Experience of the ancient Church bears witness to the contrary, and all these men are ignorant of that experience, as they show. That the minds of many heretics and ill-disposed men are alienated by this means I do not doubt; but the orthodox magistrate need not trouble himself about this, for the love of God and of good subjects ought to be enough for him. And there are countless erring persons who, when the magistrate resists their external acts in a fitting manner, begin to reflect on their error, renounce it, and embrace the truth, as the experience of the ancient Church testifies, and as Augustine in Epistle 48 to Vincentius also witnesses, and so then they begin to truly love the magistrate. For those who are truly heretics do not truly love their magistrate, as both the facts and experience show. They only feign a good disposition, but so long as the magistrate does not discharge his duty against them; when he begins to do so, the disease breaks out into open hatred, slander, and plotting of murders, as the most illustrious hero Maurice of glorious memory experienced from the Arminian flock, though God mercifully and wonderfully protected that prince, as he is wont very often to defend the champions of his glory, truth, and Church.

units.la: Quod dicunt, segnes eo modo fieri in defensione veritatis Pastores, id primò non nisi per accidens fit; deinde hypocriticè ab ipsis dicitur. Si enim Arminianos tanta cura veritatis tangit, & metus ne segnes Antistites fiant, cur non potius curam habent salutis animarum pereuntium per seductionem Hæreticorum, speciatim Antitrinitariorum, quos in Ecclesiam introducunt, & nullo modo corporali resisti iis à Magistratu volunt? Rursus, si eos tanta cura veritatis defendendæ tangit, cur eam Hæreticorum speciatim Antitrinitariorum pedibus conculcandam objiciunt? Denique si eos tanta cura veritatis tangit, cur inter conditiones tolerantiæ mutuæ, libertatis prophetandi &c. nunquam referunt conservationem veritatis divinæ; sed tantùm aliarum meminerunt quæ absque istâ conditione illusoriæ & perniciosissimæ sunt? Hæc ad secundam eorum responsionem.
units.tr: As for their saying that ministers become slothful in this way in defending the truth, first, this happens only incidentally; second, it is said by them hypocritically. For if the Arminians are so concerned for the truth, and fear lest ministers become slothful, why do they not rather care for the salvation of souls that perish through the seduction of heretics, especially the Antitrinitarians, whom they introduce into the Church and whom they wish to be resisted by the magistrate in no bodily way at all? Again, if they are so concerned to defend the truth, why do they object that the truth is to be trampled underfoot by heretics, especially Antitrinitarians? Finally, if they are so concerned for the truth, why among the conditions of mutual toleration, liberty of prophesying, and so on, do they never mention the preservation of divine truth, but only mention other things which without that condition are illusory and most pernicious? These are my remarks on their second answer.

units.la: Tertia eorum responsio: Negant hanc quam attuli esse veram causam potestatis coactivæ Magistratus, ex eo, quod alioquin exinde sequatur Magistratum non debere etiam permittere Hæreticis ut privatim apud se sentiant & credant quod verum esse putant; sic sequi silentium iis imponendum esse; item ne quidem permittendum ut domi quisque sua cum familia sua exercitia sua obeat; item non licere iis scriptis & libris editis disseminare Hæreses suas & errores; item eos cogi debere ad audiendum verbum Dei. p. 164. 165. Respondeo: non sequitur ex eo debere actibus internis Hæreticorum aliâ ratione quàm docendo vim fieri. Ad actus solum externos extendit se potestas coactiva illius, & quidem eos quibus alios inficere volunt, quibus Ecclesiam turbant, quibus jus suum ei eripere ac vendicare Synagogæ suæ volunt. Sed de hac re, & ad quos speciatim actus externos & quomodo se extendat illa potestas coactiva, agemus cum Deo suo loco in opere nostro de prudentia veteris Ecclesiae.
units.tr: Their third answer: they deny that the cause I have stated is the true cause of the magistrate's coercive power, because otherwise it would follow that the magistrate ought not even to permit heretics to think and believe privately among themselves what they hold to be true; so silence would have to be imposed on them; likewise it would follow that no one may even be permitted to carry on his own exercises at home with his family; likewise that it would not be lawful for them to spread their heresies and errors by writing and publishing books; likewise that they ought to be compelled to hear the Word of God. Page 164, 165. I reply: it does not follow from this that violence must be done to the internal acts of heretics in any other way than by teaching. The coercive power of the magistrate extends only to external acts, and indeed to those by which they wish to infect others, by which they disturb the Church, and by which they wish to seize and claim for their own synagogue a right that belongs to the Church. But we shall treat of this matter, and of which external acts in particular that coercive power extends to and how, in its own place, with God's help, in our work on the prudence of the ancient Church.

units.la: Quarto respondent p.165. me mihi contradicere, dum hic curam Religionis quae Magistratui demandata est, & quâ tenetur impedire conventicula Haereticorum privata, voco perpetuam ordinationem & institutionem Dei, & tamen lib. 1. cap. 3. Par. I. dixi, Magistratus debere impedire actus externos Haereticorum nisi fides publica seu leges fundamentales Regnorum ac Rerump. obstent. Respondeo haec nequaquam pugnare. Nam Deus requirit a Magistratu, ut impediat actus illos externos Haereticorum, quando & in quantum id facere in eius est arbitrio ac potestate; quae quidem est conditio sub qua Deus actus externos tales & alios similes a Magistratu & quovis homine flagitat. Quando autem id revera penes eum non est, innocens est, si tolerat quod mutare in eius potestate non est. Atque hoc est verum fundamentum fidei publicae & Legum fundamentalium quibus Haeretici tolerari a quibusdam Regnis & Rebuspublicis solent. Quando autem id in potestate Principis sit aut non sit, indicabo volente Domino ex experientia veteris Ecclesiae secundum scripturam sacram in eodem tractatu.
units.tr: Fourthly, they reply (p. 165) that I contradict myself, since here I call the care of religion, which is entrusted to the magistrate and by which he is bound to hinder the private conventicles of heretics, a perpetual ordinance and institution of God, and yet in book 1, chapter 3, Part I I said that the magistrate ought to hinder the external acts of heretics unless public faith or the fundamental laws of kingdoms and commonwealths stand in the way. I answer that these statements by no means conflict. For God requires of the magistrate that he hinder those external acts of heretics when and to the extent that it lies within his will and power; and this is the condition under which God demands such external acts, and others like them, of the magistrate and of any person whatever. When, however, it is not in his power, he is innocent if he tolerates what is not in his power to change. And this is the true foundation of public faith and of the fundamental laws by which heretics are commonly tolerated in certain kingdoms and commonwealths. Whether it lies within the power of the prince or not, I will show, the Lord willing, from the experience of the early Church in accordance with Holy Scripture, in the same treatise.

units.la: Nec enim hic pro arbitrio fingenda est possibilitas aut impossibilitas, quomodo v. g. Tyranni & persecutores quando orthodoxos opprimere volunt id in potestate sua esse putant tunc cum bello, incendiis, caedibus, exactionibus & aliis violentiae generibus subditos suos copellere possunt ad Apostasiam; sed sunt certi & veri casus quidam, qui in Ecclesia Dei contigere ex cuius experientia secundum Scripturam sacram de ea re judicium est faciendum, quos ibidem exponam, aut quando id illi quorum jussis ac potestati obtemperare debeo, illud a me postularint. Ad quos casus qui non attendit Princeps, suo ingenti damno aut Reip. atque Ecclesiae discit, quod alieno malo discere poterat. Quare manifestum est suo more Arminianos calumnia me petere dum p. 166. evincere volunt ex contradictione illa imaginaria me conscientiae meae rationem non habere aut Illustrissimos Ordines omnesque adeo Reges ac Magistratus qui sectas aliquas tolerant reos agere pastorum injuste & contra Deum initorum. Sed hoc mirum non est, eos ita calumniose in hac re me traducere; quia hi homines, cum omnia scire se putent, nihil nec solidae eruditionis nec pietatis habent, sed tantum ex Plauto, Martiali, Petronio & similibus in promtu habent verborum phaleras, quibus fucum faciant simplicioribus aut incautioribus. Sic itaq; adversarii Ecclesiae quae Deum in tribus personis adorandum esse credit, circa primum argumentum meum sophisticati sunt.
units.tr: For here the possibility or impossibility is not to be invented at will. For example, when tyrants and persecutors wish to oppress the orthodox, they think it is in their power when, by war, arson, slaughter, exactions and other kinds of violence, they can compel their subjects to apostasy. But there are certain definite and true cases which have occurred in the Church of God, and from their experience a judgement is to be made concerning this matter according to Holy Scripture; I shall set these out in the same place, or when those to whose commands and power I am obliged to submit have demanded it of me. A prince who does not heed these cases learns at his own great cost, or at the cost of the commonwealth and the Church, what he could have learned from another's harm. Therefore it is plain that, true to their custom, the Arminians attack me with calumny, when they wish to prove from that imaginary contradiction that I have no regard for my conscience, or that all the most illustrious Lords and all kings and magistrates who tolerate certain sects act wrongly and are guilty of breaking the covenants made with God by the ministers. But this is no wonder, that they slander me so maliciously in this matter; for these men, since they think they know everything, have neither solid learning nor piety, but only have ready to hand, from Plautus, Martial, Petronius and similar writers, the trappings of words with which to deceive the simpler or more incautious. Thus the adversaries of the Church, which believes that God is to be worshipped in three persons, have been sophistical in regard to my first argument.

units.la: Secundum meum argumentum erat : Quia per eam Arminianorum doctrinam Magistratus potestas subjicitur libidini & arbitrio uniuscuiusque nebulonis, Haeretici, fanatici &c. statim enim ut ipsi videbitur, seu ut judicabit in conscienti a sua a doctrinam Ecclesia falsam, suam autem veram esse opinionem, conventicula instituet eo pretextu quod Magistratui juris nihil sit in loca privata. Non negant hoc sequi, nec dicunt injuria aut perperam facturos Haereticos & fanaticos si privata conventicula instituant; saltem contendunt nullos fanaticos aut alios qui conventicula instituunt privata nebulones dici debere, & illud nomen in orthodoxos Pastores qui privatos conventus instituerunt, & in me retorquent: Videat, inquiunt, an non eadem nomenclatura DIGNOS sic faciat omnes fratres ac fymmyftas suos qui &c. item, si Vedelio cum suis exercitium Religionis interdictum iretis, proceres, an non repente inter ipsos etiam nebulones conspiceretur & forte dux gregis ? item dicunt id nomen non minus facile in me retorqueri posse &c. Observetur haec modestia horum hominum, qui idco, si ea hypothesis vera sit quam ego posui, nimirum quosdam homines qui turbare Ecclesiam & Rempublicam volunt, ac contra Magistratus vere orthodoxi dicta venena sua ac blasphemias spargere, Nebulones esse (id quod profecto nemo seu Reformatus seu Lutheranus seu Pontificius sit negare potest) exinde dicunt sequi Reformatos Doctores & populos qui privatim Deum colere cogun-tur dignos esse qui Nebulones vocentur. Increpet te Deus Satan! Calumnias quas contra Reformatos coetus ab ipsis ante Synodum Nationalem oppressos evomunt pretereo. Ubi in eo etiam falsum loquuntur, quod dicunt Reformatos coetus, cum in templa Arminiani introducerentur & orthodoxi privatim convenire mallent, quam ab his hominibus seduci, clamasse hoc solo nomine segreges suos coetus licitos esse, quod Religionis exercitium adimere etiam in locis privatis esset conscientiarum Tyrannis & servitus intolerabilis. Falsissimum enim est orthodoxos unquam istam thesin sive generalem enunciationem tuitos esse; saltem in hypothesi & de se loquentes dicebant sibi injuriam fieri dum obtrude-rentur ipsis tales ministri; & punirentur quod mallent alio excurrere aut segreges coetus facere quam istos audire qui quales sint res loquitur.
units.tr: My second argument was this: Because by this doctrine of the Arminians the power of the magistrate is made subject to the lust and will of every scoundrel, heretic, fanatic, etc.; for as soon as it seems fit to them, or as they judge in their own conscience that the Church's doctrine is false and their own opinion true, they will set up conventicles on the pretext that the magistrate has no right over private places. They do not deny that this follows, nor do they say that heretics and fanatics act wrongly or unjustly if they set up private conventicles. They merely contend that no fanatics or others who set up private conventicles ought to be called scoundrels, and they turn that name back upon the orthodox ministers who set up private assemblies, and upon me: Let him see, they say, whether the same name does not fittingly apply to all his brothers and fellow-initiates who etc. Likewise: If you were to forbid Vedel and his people the exercise of religion, would not, lords, scoundrels and perhaps the leader of the flock suddenly be seen among them? Likewise they say that this name can be turned back upon me no less easily, etc. Observe the modesty of these men, who therefore say that, if the hypothesis I have put forward is true, namely that certain men wish to disturb the Church and the commonwealth and, against the truly orthodox magistrates, scatter their poisons and blasphemies, these are scoundrels (which certainly no one, whether Reformed, Lutheran or Papist, can deny), it follows, they say, that the Reformed teachers and peoples who are compelled to worship God in private deserve to be called scoundrels. May the Lord rebuke you, Satan! I pass over the calumnies which they pour out against the Reformed congregations, which were oppressed by them before the National Synod. They also speak falsely where they say that when Arminians were introduced into the churches and the orthodox preferred to meet privately rather than be seduced by these men, the Reformed congregations shouted that their separate assemblies were lawful on this ground alone, that to take away the exercise of religion even in private places would be a tyranny over consciences and an intolerable slavery. For it is most false that the orthodox ever upheld that thesis or general statement; at least, speaking hypothetically and of themselves, they said that a wrong was done to them when such ministers were forced upon them, and that they were punished because they preferred to go elsewhere or form separate assemblies rather than hear those who speak of matters as they are.

units.la: Argumentum meum tertium erat: Quia per istam doctrinam Arminianam injustitia & Tyrannidis condemnatur omnis Magistratus Christianus, qui Haereticis non permittit conventicula; quia scilicet id sibi arrogant quod de ejus jure non est. An eum doctrina ista summo periculo non exponat ipse viderit. Certe secundum hanc doctrinam non possunt non juste facere populi si Magistratui sese oppose opponant, prohibenti conventicula in iis locis, in quibus ipsi juris nihil est. Hic fatentur Arminiani, & profitentur se Reges, Principes, Magistratus, qui conventicula privata Haereticorum prohibent injustitiae ac Tyrannidis condemnare p. 267. 168. & dicunt nihil criminis in eo esse : Quid criminis, inquiunt, in eo esse potest? Et addunt : se Regimen Provinciarum confoederatarum Belgii libertatis omnis azylum laudare non posse, nisi culpent eos qui contrario animo sunt, & facto suo Regimen harum provinciarum & aliorum Principum ac Regum qui variis sectis conventus permittunt damnant. Haec maledicentia in Reges & Principes qui sibi jus tribuunt in Haereticorum conventicula; &, quod gravius est, persistentia & contumacia in isto scelere observetur diligenter. Hoc primum est, quod respondent. Deinde untuntur retorsione contra me qua Illustrissimos Ordines compellant; & me ex eo quia dico hac Remonstrantium doctrina Tyrannidis & injustitiae damnari omnes Reges, Principes, Magistratus, qui conventicula privata Haereticis non permittunt; ex eo, inquam, inferunt, me alios Reges ac Principes, speciatim illustrissimos Ordines, condemnare, quod permittant varios segreges coetus in sua Republica, me ideo ingratum hominem vocant, imo ingratissimum hospitem in Republica hac, me per latera aliorum Regum ac Principum Regimen illustrissimorum Ordinum traductum esse velle. Et ironice inquiunt : Nempe Regimen vestrum damnandum est ne illi (Reges & Principes) injustitia & Tyrannidis damnentur. Item dicunt, me, dum Regibus ac Principibus in quorum ditione non vivo, patrocinari velle videor, Regimen illustrissimorum Ordinum sub quibus vivo, infamare. In summa me Dominos, Patronos, & Rectores meos postulare irreligiositatis in Deum & Legem ipsius.
units.tr: My third argument was this: Because by this Arminian doctrine every Christian magistrate who does not permit heretics conventicles is condemned as unjust and tyrannical; because, clearly, he claims for himself what is not within his right. Whether this doctrine does not expose him to the greatest danger, let him see for himself. Certainly, according to this doctrine, the peoples cannot but act justly if they oppose the magistrate who forbids conventicles in those places over which they have no right. Here the Arminians admit, and profess, that they condemn as unjust and tyrannical those kings, princes and magistrates who forbid the private conventicles of heretics, and they say there is no crime in this: What crime, they say, can there be in this? And they add that they cannot praise the government of the United Provinces of the Netherlands as a refuge of all liberty, unless they blame those of contrary mind, and by their conduct condemn the government of these provinces and of other princes and kings who permit assemblies of various sects. This slander against the kings and princes who claim for themselves the right over the conventicles of heretics is carefully observed, and, what is more serious, their persistence and obstinacy in this wickedness. This is the first thing they reply. Next they use a counter-charge against me, by which they address the most illustrious Lords. From my saying that by this Remonstrant doctrine all kings, princes and magistrates who do not permit private conventicles to heretics are condemned as unjust and tyrannical, they infer, I say, that I condemn other kings and princes, and especially the most illustrious Lords, because they allow various separate assemblies in their commonwealth; they therefore call me an ungrateful man, indeed the most ungrateful guest in this commonwealth, and say that I wish the government of the most illustrious Lords to be dragged through the sides of other kings and princes. And ironically they say: Surely your government must be condemned, lest those (kings and princes) be condemned for injustice and tyranny. Likewise they say that while I seem to plead for kings and princes in whose dominion I do not live, I defame the government of the most illustrious Lords under whom I live. In short, they charge me with demanding irreligion towards God and his Law against my lords, patrons and rulers.

units.la: Verum enimvero Arminianos hic malitiose & contra conscientiam suam me calumniari, mera rabie incitatos, quia vident se constrictos teneri vi veritatis a me propositae, manifestum est ex iis verbis meis quae modo p. 165. 166. ipsi allegarunt ex Par. I. lib. 1. c. 3. ubi dixi Haereticis non permittendos esse conventus suos nisi fides publica obstet, & leges fundamentales Regnorum aut Rerumpublicarum. Et videantur quae paulo ante dixi, ubi calumniam eorum dilui qua mihi contradictionem affingunt. Deinde quis non videt, hos homines hypocritice saltem me perstringere ac si Magistratus meos postularem irreligiositatis in Deum & Legem ipsius: cum ipsi traducant eos & omnes Reformatae nostrae Religioni ex animo addictos tanquam Haereticos, imo tales qui voluntaria Haeresi laborent, item tali cum qua forte nulla haeresis est comparanda? Estne hoc pietatis & religionis nomine commendare Magistratus suos, an vero an verò irreligiositatis in Deum & Legem ipsius? Hæc est gratia quam proceribus referunt hi homines pro conniventiâ ipsorum. Non prætereundum est, quòd exemplo Illustrissimorum Ordinum proterve se & doctrinam suam impiam palliare volunt. Fatentur ipsi hic illustrissimos Ordines tolerare non omnis generis sectas & Hæreses, sed varias tantùm. Quod verum est: nam Ordines Illustrissimi nunquam voluerunt tolerare Socinianos, sed quando intellexerunt eos sese provinciis his ingerere velle, ejecerunt illos, & libros eorum igni adjudicârunt. At Arminiani volunt in Vindiciis suis omnibus omninò sectis Christiani nominis (exceptis Reformatis) permitti conventus suos; præsertim autem Antitrinitariis seu Socinianis, imò has habent pro verâ Ecclesiâ. Quare impudenter faciunt dum se palliare volunt exemplo Ordinum Illustrissimorum.
units.tr: But that the Arminians here slander me maliciously and against their own conscience, goaded by sheer rage because they see themselves held fast by the force of the truth I have set forth, is plain from those words of mine which they have just cited from pp. 165-166, from Par. I, lib. 1, c. 3, where I said that heretics are not to be allowed their assemblies unless public faith and the fundamental laws of kingdoms or commonwealths stand in the way. See also what I said a little earlier, where I refuted their calumny by which they impute contradiction to me. Next, who does not see that these men, at least hypocritically, berate me as if I were accusing my magistrates of irreligion against God and his Law, when they themselves brand them, and all who are heartily devoted to our Reformed religion, as heretics, indeed as men who labour under voluntary heresy, and with whom perhaps no heresy can be compared? Is this commending one's magistrates in the name of piety and religion, or rather of irreligion against God and his Law? This is the thanks these men render to the nobles for their connivance. It must not be passed over that they wish, by the example of the Most Illustrious Orders, to cloak themselves and their impious doctrine shamelessly.
