They themselves admit here that the Most Illustrious Orders tolerate not every kind of sect and heresy, but only certain ones. That is true: for the Most Illustrious Orders never wished to tolerate the Socinians, but when they understood that the Socinians wished to thrust themselves into these provinces, they expelled them and condemned their books to the fire. But the Arminians want, in their Vindications, that all sects of the Christian name whatsoever (except the Reformed) be permitted their assemblies, especially the Antitrinitarians or Socinians; indeed they regard these as the true Church. Wherefore they act impudently when they wish to cloak themselves with the example of the Most Illustrious Orders.

units.la: Post istam calumniam adversum me, in quâ valdè sibi placent & prolixè immorantur, relabuntur p. 166. ad coccysmum suum contra Ecclesias Reformatas ac Vedelium, & ad calumnias & convitia contra eum & Reformatas Ecclesias earumque doctrinam, denique contra Ecclesiam Genevensem cuius civitatis latte me totum imbutum esse dicunt &c.
units.tr: After this calumny against me, in which they take great pleasure and dwell at length, they relapse, at p. 166, into their outcry against the Reformed Churches and Vedelius, and into calumnies and abuse against him, the Reformed Churches and their doctrine, and finally against the Church of Geneva, of which city they say I am wholly imbued with the milk, etc.

units.la: Denique ea verba aggrediuntur quibus dixi doctrinam Arminianam quâ injustitia & Tyrannidis damnant Magistratus eos qui conventicula Haereticorum prohibent, Magistratum summo periculo exponere, & secundùm hanc doctrinam non posse non juste facere populos si Magistratui se opponunt prohibenti conventicula &c. Hæc verba quæ verissima sunt etiam calumniosissimè traducunt, postquam præmisissent rursus coccysmum suum de Ecclesiis Reformatis, & eas in locum Hereticorum constituissent, unà cum calumniis planè diabolicis contra eas, ideò quòd se adversus vim injustam aliorum defenderint, prout in Galliâ, Belgio, Germaniâ & alibi factum, atque in Germaniâ etiamnum fit. Et dicunt me hic populos ad rebellionem concitare, & jus iis tribuere ut Magistratui se PERVIM opponant; ac contrà contendunt omnes eos subditos qui Tyrannis sese armis opponunt pessimè facere in quocunque loco sint. Hoc enim non licere; & addunt: Neque unquam licet, quod simpliciter non licet. Atqui hanc etiam esse impudentissimam calumniam manifestum est. Dixi enim Arminianos hac suâ doctrinâ, Reges, Principes & Magistratus illos summo periculo exponere: quod profectò verissimum est. Nam qui populis Hæreticis persuadere conantur, Reges & Principes eorum Tyrannos esse, an'non eos Principes summo periculo exponunt? Dixi etiam, ex etiâ, ex hypothesi & doctrinâ Arminianâ necessariò sequi, populos juste facere si Magistratui se opponant, & sic non ex meâ sed horum hominum hypothesi argumentatus sum: & quidem non dixi, si Magistratui se per vim opponant; sed simpliciter voce generali usus sum, ac dixi si Magistratui se opponant: quod fieri posse variis modis certum est. Nam potest fieri verbis, proscindendo Magistratum convitiis, Tyrannidis eum accusando, ut hoc loco Arminiani faciunt, qui dicunt se in eo recte facere, & persistunt in petulantiâ illâ suâ; ac prout post habitam Synodum Nationalem illustrissimum Heroem Mauritium & Ordines illustrissimos horrendis convitiis proscíderunt Tyrannidis eos subinde accusantes. Potest fieri etiam facto nimirum continuando conventicula sua contra voluntatem & jussa Magistratus. Quod adeò verum est, ut calumniatores hi ipsi, convicti in conscientiâ suâ calumniæ istius, agnoscant me generali modo loquendi usum esse, & dicant: Nunquam se ab hoc tam turpi ac foedo crimine expediet, nisi opponere sese Magistratui exponat per non desistere à coetibus faciendis, etiamsi id Magistratus vetet. Ubi negant hoc esse se Magistratui opponere, dicentes: At an hoc sit se Magistratui opponere &c. vos videritis. Quod profectò non negabant tunc cum Reformati privatim conveniebant: tunc enim ipsos seditionis & factionis ob eam causam accusabant. Sed ego Lectori dijudicandum relinquo, annon Hæretici tunc se Magistratui etiam in hac parte opponant, quando invitis ac repugnantibus, prohibentibus, reclamantibus, minitantibus Regibus ac Principibus conveniunt. Verùm mirandum non est, quòd Arminiani hîc negant, Hæreticos eâ ratione se Magistratui opponere; quandoquidem ne ferre quidem possunt, ut audacia eo nomine accusentur Hæretici, prout fit ab ipsis in Responf. ad Exc. Cll. DD. Proff. Leydd. ubi quia Clarissimi Viri dixerant Synodos atq; Ecclesias Reformatas in Belgio Magistratus suos interdum rogâsse, ut audaciam quarundam sectarum refrenarent; illi hoc nomen audacia ferre non possunt, & acriter ac calumniosissimè illud perstringunt ibidem p. 131.
units.tr: Finally, they attack the words in which I said that the Arminian doctrine, by which they condemn as unjust and tyrannical those magistrates who forbid the conventicles of heretics, exposes the magistrate to the greatest danger, and according to this doctrine the people cannot but act justly if they oppose a magistrate who forbids their conventicles, etc. These words, which are most true, they also traduce most calumniously, after first repeating their outcry against the Reformed Churches, placing them in the place of heretics, together with frankly diabolical calumnies against them, on the ground that they defended themselves against the unjust violence of others, as has been done in France, the Netherlands, Germany and elsewhere, and as is still done in Germany. They say that I here stir up the people to rebellion and grant them a right to oppose the magistrate by force; and on the contrary they contend that all subjects who resist tyrants by arms do very wrongly, wherever they may be. For this, they say, is not lawful, and they add: Nor is it ever lawful, what is simply not lawful. But that this too is a most impudent calumny is plain. For I said that the Arminians, by this their doctrine, expose their kings, princes and magistrates to the greatest danger, which is most truly the case. For those who try to persuade heretical peoples that their kings and princes are tyrants, do they not expose those princes to the greatest danger? I also said that it necessarily follows from the hypothesis and doctrine of the Arminians that the people act justly if they oppose the magistrate; so I argued not from my own hypothesis but from theirs. And indeed I did not say, if they oppose the magistrate by force; I used a general term simply and said if they oppose the magistrate, which is certainly possible in various ways. It can be done by words, by tearing the magistrate apart with abuse and accusing him of tyranny, as the Arminians do here, who say they do right in this and persist in that wantonness of theirs; and as, after the National Synod, they tore apart the most illustrious hero Maurice and the Most Illustrious Orders with horrible abuse, accusing them from time to time of tyranny. It can also be done by deed, namely by continuing their conventicles against the will and commands of the magistrate. This is so true that these calumniators themselves, convicted in their own conscience of this calumny, acknowledge that I used a general mode of speech, and say: He will never be freed from this so base and foul a crime unless he exposes himself to opposing the magistrate by not ceasing to hold assemblies, even if the magistrate forbids it. Where they deny that this is opposing the magistrate, saying: But whether this is to oppose the magistrate, etc., you will see. They certainly did not deny this at the time when the Reformed used to meet privately; for then they accused them of sedition and faction on that very ground. But I leave it to the reader to judge whether heretics do not then oppose the magistrate also in this respect, when they meet against the will, in resistance to, forbidding, protesting against and threatening kings and princes. Yet it is not to be wondered at that the Arminians here deny that heretics oppose the magistrate in that way, since they cannot even bear that heretics be accused of audacity on that account, as they do in their Response to the Excerpts of the most distinguished professors of Leiden. There, because those distinguished men had said that the synods and Reformed Churches in Belgium had sometimes asked their magistrates to restrain the audacity of certain sects, the Arminians cannot bear the name audacity, and bitterly and most calumniously assail it in the same place, p. 131.

units.la: Porrò quòd hîc ut & p. 173. (ubi inter alia dicunt Nullam unquam satis gravem ac justam causam esse posse, qua subditos armet in Rectores suos &c.) contendunt, nullis subditis licere armis sese defendere adversus Tyrannos, speciatim Reformatis nullis omninò subditis in nullo plane loco terrarum licere libertatem conscientiarum defendere armis adversùs Tyrannum, sine exceptione resistentiæ quâ Tyranno resistitur persequenti subditos contra privilegia sua, Edicta fundamentalia & pacta reciproca ciproca quæ æquè principem ac populum obligant; de eâ re egimus Par. II. lib. 1. cap. 10. ubi ostendimus quàm contumeliosum hoc sit & injurium in illustrissimos Ordines fœderati Belgii,& omnes ac singulas illius provincias, nec non in alios qui se justis titulis contra vim injustam defendunt,prout hodiè in Germaniâ fit, approbantibus illa arma Serenissimis Regibus M. Britanniæ, Galliæ &c. Addo saltem Arminianos etiam in hac re fidem nullam mereri quando dicunt hanc suam mentem esse & doctrinam in istâ re de quâ quæstio est. Nam primò cùm iis conventicula severè interdicta essent, & factiosiores in exilium ejecti post Synodum Nationalem deliberârunt Theologi hi an'ne viâ facti, ut loquebantur, liceret illustrissimorum Ordinum jussis se opponere; & pluralitate suffragiorum, concluserunt, sibi faciendum illud esse, prout ostendimus Par. II. cap. 6. lib. 1. Quam deliberationem insequuta est conspiratio contra vitam Principis Mauritii benedictę memorię & contra Rempublicam, ut patet ex sententiis Ordinum quæ contra conjuratos latæ & executioni mandatæ fuerunt. Deinde in Apologiâ & Responsione ad Excerpta DD. Proff. Leydd. expressè conceptis verbis tradunt populos Hæreticos quosvis habere jus ut Magistratum coërceant vi corporali qui ipsos vi corporali coërcere vult, prout mox videbimus. Unde manifestum est quid de horum hominum assertionibus, negationibus, fide, pietate, candore, Religione sit sentiendum. Atque hæc de secundo modo quo Magistratus curam ac potestatem inutilem reddunt Ecclesiæ tuendę adversus Hæreticorum fraudem ac rabiem.
units.tr: Moreover, that here, as also at p. 173 (where among other things they say that no cause, however grave and just, can ever be such as to arm subjects against their rulers, etc.), they contend that no subjects are allowed to defend themselves by arms against tyrants; and specifically that the Reformed, no subjects anywhere on earth, are allowed to defend liberty of conscience by arms against a tyrant. This is without the exception of resistance by which a tyrant is resisted when he persecutes subjects against their privileges, fundamental edicts and reciprocal pacts, which bind prince and people alike. We treated this matter in Par. II, lib. 1, cap. 10, where we showed how insulting and injurious this is to the Most Illustrious Orders of the united Netherlands, and to all and each of its provinces, and also to others who defend themselves by just titles against unjust violence, as is done today in Germany, with the Most Serene Kings of Great Britain, France, etc., approving those arms. I add only that the Arminians deserve no trust even in this matter when they say that this is their mind and doctrine on the question at issue. For first, when conventicles had been strictly forbidden them, and the more factious had been expelled after the National Synod, these theologians deliberated whether it were lawful, as they put it, "via facti," to oppose the commands of the Most Illustrious Orders; and by plurality of votes they concluded that this had to be done, as we showed in Par. II, cap. 6, lib. 1. This deliberation was followed by the conspiracy against the life of Prince Maurice of blessed memory and against the commonwealth, as appears from the sentences of the Orders which were passed against the conspirators and carried into execution. Then, in their Apology and Response to the Excerpts of the professors of Leiden, they expressly and in so many words hand down that heretical peoples have any right to restrain by physical force the magistrate who wishes to restrain them by physical force, as we shall presently see. Whence it is plain what is to be thought of these men's assertions, denials, faith, piety, candour and religion. And so much on the second way in which magistrates render the care and power of protecting the Church against the deceit and rage of heretics useless.

units.la: 8. Tertius modus est, quo docent Magistratum nullam habere potestatem inhibendi subditos ut ne palàm profiteantur quod sentiunt, imò contrà contendunt, eum debere unicuique suam Religionem liberam facere, & unicuique concedere exercitium Religionis suæ. Fatentur, & persistunt in eo, cum coccysmo contra Vedelium, cui ut eripiant libertatem conscientiæ hortantur Arminiani Proceres Patriæ: Si dubitat Vedelius, ab illo incipite Proceres &c. Cæterùm præterquàm quòd ostenderam eos in Apologiâ Cyri exemplum perperàm adducere ad probandam doctrinam hanc suam,etiam ostenderam ex doctrinâ ipsorum sequi non solùm conventicula privata,sed etiam templa publica permittenda de jure esse Hæreticis à Magistratu, & sic eum jus quoque non habere iis eripienda loca publica. Ad hæc Arminiani nihil respondent, sed ea sicco pede transeunt.
units.tr: 8. The third way is that they teach the magistrate has no power to forbid subjects from openly professing what they believe. On the contrary, they contend that he ought to leave each person's religion free and grant each the exercise of his own religion. They admit this and persist in it, mocking Vedelius, whom the Arminian leaders of the country urge to take away freedom of conscience: "If Vedelius hesitates, begin with him, gentlemen," and so on. Besides this, I had already shown that in their Apology they wrongly cite the example of Cyrus to prove this doctrine of theirs. I had also shown that, on their doctrine, the magistrate may rightly permit heretics not only private conventicles but also public churches, and so he has no right to take public places away from them either. To this the Arminians say nothing; they pass over these points without getting their feet wet.

units.la: 9. Quartus modus est, dum contendunt Hæreticos nullo planè modo corporali coërcendos à Magistratu aut ullâ etiam minimâ ratione ladendos esse aut vexandos. Fatentur, p. 170. 171 172. & in eo perfistunt atque defendere conantur mendaciis iisdem, quibus supra h. e. speciatim testimonio Antiquitatis, & excurrunt in Hæreticidia simplicium Hæreticorum, aut eorum qui Hæretici esse videntur cùm non sint ; id quod in quæstione non est, nec à me aut aliis orthodoxis unquam dictum. Et claudunt calumniis contra Rempublicam & Ecclesiam Genevensem ac Doctores illius, vocantes me alumnum civitatis & Ecclesiæ ipsius qua etiamnum rubet à cruore innoxio, & à sanguinariis Præceptorum suorum consiliis ac judiciis p. 172. Ita illi habent Serveti supplicium pro cruore innoxio, qui perjuriis Magistratui, blasphemiis Deo illuserat vocans Trinitatem, monstrum triceps, Cerberum tricipitem, spectrum Diabolicum. Quo nomine placidissimi ingenii vir Philippus Melanchton Theologus nunquam satis laudandus Genevensem Rempublicam commendavit, miratus reperiri quosdam qui judicium illud improbarent. Ita enim in Epistolâ ad Bullingerum : Legi etiam qua de Serveti blasphemiis respondistis, & pietatem & judicia vestra probo. Iudico etiam Senatum Genevensem recte fecisse, quod hominem pertinacem & non omissurum blasphemias sustulit. Et miratus sum esse qui severitatem illam improbet. Eadem sententia est aliorum quoque Evangelicorum, eorum etiam ex ipsis qui Reformatis iniquiores esse solent, e quorum numero est Balthasar Meisnerus, qui addit de eâ re loquens, Servetum merito punitum neminem ex Lutheranis facile negaturum Sect. Sec. quæst. Practic. p. 625. 626.
units.tr: 9. The fourth way is when they contend that heretics must in no way be restrained by the magistrate by bodily force, nor be harmed or harassed in any way, however slight. They admit this (pp. 170, 171, 172) and persist in it, trying to defend it with the same lies as above, namely by appealing to the testimony of antiquity. They then rush off into slaughters of simple heretics, or of those who seem to be heretics though they are not, which is not the question at issue and was never said by me or any other orthodox writer. They close with calumnies against the Republic and Church of Geneva and its teachers, calling me "a nursling of that city and of that Church, which still blushes from innocent blood and from the bloody counsels and judgments of its own teachers" (p. 172). So they regard the execution of Servetus as the shedding of innocent blood, though he had mocked the magistrate with perjuries and God with blasphemies, calling the Trinity a three-headed monster, a three-headed Cerberus, a diabolical specter. For this reason Philip Melanchthon, a theologian of the most gentle temper and never sufficiently praised, commended the Republic of Geneva, marvelling that some people were found who disapproved of that judgment. For he writes in his letter to Bullinger: I have read also what you replied concerning Servetus' blasphemies, and I approve both your piety and your judgments. I also judge that the Senate of Geneva did right in removing a man who was obstinate and would not cease from blasphemies. And I marvelled that there are those who disapprove of that severity. The same opinion is held by other Evangelicals, including some of those who are usually more unfair to the Reformed, among them Balthasar Meisner, who, speaking of this matter, adds that no one among the Lutherans would easily deny that Servetus was rightly punished (Sect. 2, Quaest. Pract., pp. 625, 626).

units.la: 10. Hùc pertinere dixi p. 231. quòd docent formaliter & expressè, Hæreticos JURE posse coërcere Magistratum, qui ipsos coërcere vult, & jus hoc illis NECESSARIO competere. Idque ex hoc fundamento, quod hîc ponunt, nimirum : Par omnium in omnes jus esse. Quod fundamentum absurdissimè ab ipsis poni ostendi p: 232. Hic vero negant se ita docuisse, cùm prius p. 173 dixissent (ut solent facere in Vindiciis suis quando constricti tenentur ita ut elabi non possint, & aut nihil aut vix aliquam fraudem inveniunt, quâ Lectori imponant) Catera quæ sequuntur, nec oleum nec lucernam olent, vultis ne, proceres, ut ad ea respondeam? Vix possum, adeò sunt putida & vernilia. Percurram, ne in minutiis cum Vedelio immorari videar, & fingunt me ipsis convitia ibi dicere, quod probant ex eo, quia dixi, eos formaliter & expressè seditiones docere. Postquam ita præfati essent; negant se hoc docuisse, & ut speciem habeat negatio eorum, fingunt se recitare locum Apologiæ, quem in hunc finem allegavi, sed ita ut taceant verba ea in quibus propositio eorum seditiosa continetur, & recitant tantùm fundamentum quod dixi sententiæ suæ : Par omnium in omnes omnes jus est, Ac dicunt in his verbis ne quidem umbram ejusmodi doctrinae esse: se enim primo non loqui de Haereticis qui Dei aut Ecclesiae alicujus divina judicio aliquo infallibili damnati sint Haereseos, sed de Haereticis quos haec aut illa Ecclesia censuit Haereticos, h.e. uno verbo se loqui de Haereticis qui sic in significatione recepta dicuntur. Deinde se non tribuere jus hoc subditis Magistratus alicujus in suum proprium Magistratum: & probant exinde, quia ubivis docent ac contendant nullam unquam satis gravem ac justam causam esse posse, quae subditos armet in Rectores suos. Sed id tantum volunt inquiunt, verba ista, Par omnium in omnes jus est, Nulli Magistratui soli aut prae caeteris jus istud coercendi datum esse. Eodem jure vicissim uti posse, si velit, Magistratum quemlibet in subditos suos a se dissentientes, e.g. Magistratum Lutheranum in Calvinistas ditionis suae subditos, quo Magistratus Calvinista in Lutheranos utitur: Cur enim non minus liceat Lipsiae, Jenae & alibi (Calvinistis civitate interdicere quam Genevae? &c. Eandem rationem esse omnium aliorum dicunt. Ita Respondent Arminiani. Verum rursus contra propriam conscientiam negant se hoc docuisse, & in ea convicti sunt se contra eam palliare velle improbitatem suam. Non multis agam de hac re, sed perspicue & vere. Tibi, quisquis es optime Lector, qui Deum times, candorem ac honestatem amas, mendacium & impostturam aversaris, ac cupis provincias has paci ac tranquillitati domesticae restitui, judicium rei permitto. Dicunt illi se hoc tantum dicere verbis a me citatis: nimirum si Magistratus subditos suos addictos Religioni quam pro falsa habet persequatur, tunc Magistratum vel Principem alium aliquem jus habere subditos suos proprios qui Religioni alterius illius Magistratus addicti sunt persequi. Ego vero dixi Arminianos docere si Magistratus Haereticos persequatur, eos jus habere Ipsum Magistratum suum coercendi. Hic est status quaestionis. Nunc expende, candide Lector, egone verum dixerim an illi? ut judicare possis de hac re, en verba Apologiae a me citata in eum finem, integra & bona fide. Ita igitur dicunt cap. 24. f. 259. a. Nulla carnalis coercitio, nulla poena errantibus constituta a Deo est. Nulla ratio recta constituti permittit: OMNES IN SE IPSUM ARMAT, qui in alios quos errare credit, armatur: Par omnium in omnes jus est. Qui sibi jus tribuit coercendi ALIOS, idem ALIIS IN SE IPSUM IDEM IUS ut concedat NECESSE est. Nulli homini aut Ecclesiae judicium infallibile de erroribus aliorum delatum est, &c. Vides Arminianos hic nequaquam dicere in alios vel in subditos alterius Magistratus &c. Sed expresse & quidem bis diccre: IN SE IPSUM &c. Omnes in se ipsum armat, qui in alios quos errare credit, armatur &c.
units.tr: 10. I have said that this belongs to the point (p. 231) because they teach formally and expressly that heretics may by right restrain the magistrate who wishes to restrain them, and that this right belongs to them necessarily. And they base this on the foundation they lay down here, namely: There is an equal right of all against all. I showed on p. 232 how absurdly they lay down this foundation. But here they deny that they taught this, although earlier (p. 173) they had said (as they usually do in their Vindiciae when they are hemmed in so that they cannot escape and find little or no trick by which to deceive the reader): The rest that follows smells neither of oil nor of lamp. Do you wish, gentlemen, that I answer it? I can hardly, so rotten and servile is it. I will run through it, lest I seem to linger over trifles with Vedelius. And they pretend that I there charge them with insults, which they prove from the fact that I said they formally and expressly teach sedition. After this preamble they deny that they taught it, and to give their denial some appearance they pretend to recite the passage of the Apology which I cited for this purpose, but so as to omit the words in which their seditious proposition is contained, and they quote only the foundation I mentioned for their opinion: There is an equal right of all against all. And they say that in these words there is not even a shadow of such a doctrine. For they say, first, that they do not speak of heretics who have been condemned by some infallible divine judgment of God or of some Church as heretics, but of heretics whom this or that Church has judged to be heretics, that is, in a word, they speak of heretics who are so called in the accepted sense. Next, they do not grant this right to the subjects of any magistrate against their own magistrate. And they prove this from the fact that everywhere they teach and maintain that no cause, however grave and just, can ever arise which arms subjects against their rulers. But they wish only, they say, these words, "There is an equal right of all against all," to mean that no magistrate alone, or above others, has been given the right to restrain others, and that each may in turn use that right, if he wishes, against any magistrate who dissents from him in his subjects, for example a Lutheran magistrate against the Calvinist subjects of his dominion, as a Calvinist magistrate uses it against Lutherans. For why should it be less lawful at Leipzig, Jena and elsewhere to exclude Calvinists from a city than at Geneva? and so on. They say that the reasoning is the same for all others. So the Arminians reply. But again they deny against their own conscience that they taught this, and, being convicted on this point, they wish to cover their wickedness with that denial. I shall not spend many words on this matter, but speak clearly and truthfully. To you, best of readers, whoever you are, who fear God, love candor and honesty, abhor lies and imposture, and desire that these provinces be restored to domestic peace and tranquility, I leave the judgment of the matter. They say that they meant only what the words I cited express: namely, that if a magistrate persecutes his subjects who adhere to the religion he considers false, then the magistrate or some other prince has the right to persecute his own subjects who adhere to the religion of that other magistrate. But I said that the Arminians teach that if a magistrate persecutes heretics, they have the right to restrain that very magistrate of theirs. This is the state of the question. Now weigh it, candid reader: have I spoken the truth, or they? So that you may judge the matter, here are the words of the Apology I cited for this purpose, complete and in good faith. In chapter 24, page 259a, they say: No carnal coercion and no punishment for those in error is established by God. No sound reasoning permits it: THE ONE WHO ARMS AGAINST OTHERS WHOM HE BELIEVES TO BE IN ERROR ARMS AGAINST HIMSELF: there is an equal right of all against all. He who grants himself the right to coerce OTHERS must NECESSARILY grant OTHERS the same right against himself. No infallible judgment about the errors of others has been committed to any man or Church, and so on. You see that the Arminians here do not say against others or against the subjects of another magistrate, but say expressly, and indeed twice: AGAINST HIMSELF, etc. The one who arms against others whom he believes to be in error arms against himself, etc.

units.la: Item: Qui sibi jus tribuit coërcendi alios, idé aliis in ipsum idem jus ut concedat ne-cesse est. Hæc verba honesti hi viri fraudulenter omittunt in citatione loci à me allegati, quia nimis evidentia sunt. De hac fraude egimus etiam in Prolegom. Part. III. Ut tamen adhuc melius videas genium & indolé horum hominum, scito eos non ita tantum docere in Apologia, sed etiam in Responsi. ad Excerp. D.D. Proff. Leydd. editâ post Apologiam a. 1631. in quibus non minus expresse loquūtur & docent positâ hac hypothesi & doctrinâ ipsorum, quòd subditis Hæreticis privatim conveniendi libertas debeatur, & ea libertas ipsis à Magistratu negetur, tunc per se viam sterni subditis ad rebellionem, & illud pené necessarium esse, & vocant hoc dolorem quo nullus justior sit. Ut res tota facilè & rectè percipi possit, nota Cll. D.D. Proff. Leydd. in Appendice Excerptorum suorum p. 39. reprehendisse illos, quod loca & conventicula privata excipiant à curâ & potestate Magistratus, ac dixisse: Quòd autem illi curam illam atque inspectionem Magistratus nunc limitant, atque ad templa publica restringunt, id valde ridiculum est, cùm ita non sint loquuti, quando Utenbogardus librum de officio Magistratus conscripsit, editaque Ultrajectensia ac Schielandica pro ipsis adversus Contra-Remonstrantes fuerunt publicata. Adde quòd hac ipsorum exceptio turbulentis ingeniis viam sternat, quâ se ex Magistratus potestate subducere satagunt. Respondent ad hæc posteriora verba Arminiani p. 137. 138. inter alia hoc modo: Deinde qua verisimilis ratio dari potest, quòd exceptio ista turbulentis ingeniis viam sternat, quâ se ex Magistratus potestate subducant? Nam aut libertas ista debetur iis aut non debetur. Si debetur iis, justa est exceptio sive viam iis sternat ad rebellionem sive non sternat ad rebellionem. Quanquam ut usus libertatis qui iis jure debetur per se viam sternat ad rebellione ratio non sinti. Quid sentis, candide Lector, est'ne ista exceptio quæ viam sternit ad rebellionē justa dicenda, non secus ac ea quæ viam ad eam non sternit? Hactenus tergiversati ibi sunt Arminiani, jam confitentem reum audi. Pergunt enim: Imò si debetur iis & nihilominus tamen negatur, UT VIAM IIS PER SE STER-NAT AD REBELLIONEM PENE NECESSARIUM EST. Nullus enim dolor Justior, quàm is quem gignit libertatis quæ debetur ereptio aut negatio. Si non debetur & nihilominus indulgetur ac conceditur à Magistratibus, beneficio isto flectuntur potius ad liberale obsequium quàm ad rebellionem. Judica jam pie Lector, de ingenio & indole horum Thelogorum. Habes enim hic rursus exemplum insigne, ex quo appa-ret eos nullam conscientiam amplius habere, quandoquidem contra eam adeò impudenter negare audent se docere, quod revera docent. Vides etiam insigne exemplum fraudulentiæ eorum, quâ veritatis lucem effugere conantur, & latebras improbitatis quærunt, quando in conscientia suâ deprehenduntse convictos esse. Vides per consequens, quàm parùm agant causam conscientiæ; sed eos hoc agere potius ut imponant orbi toti, & provincias has impune turbent. Vides eos seditionum & rebellionum professos Magistros esse, & quando convicti illius criminis atrocissimi & turbulentiæ sunt, contentos esse negare illud, & dicere se contrarium sentire ac statuere. Vides denique verissimum esse, quod dixi antehac jam aliquoties, eos nullam ampliùs fidem in negocio Religionis mereri, nedum in aliis minoribus negotiis, speciatim iis fidendum non esse, quando dicunt se contrarium sentire & ubivis docere. Bone Deus respice tandem Provincias has, & libera eas ab his impostoribus; aperi oculos omnium, ut videant quàm turpiter Magistratibus & omnibus aliis illudant homines isti, ut intelligant & deprehendant fraudes, audaciam, & impudentiam Satanæ, ac rectè dijudicent an'ne isti ministri Spiritu Dei an verò Spiritu mendacii agantur & gubernentur?
units.tr: Likewise: Whoever claims for himself the right to restrain others must necessarily grant the same right to others against himself. These honest men dishonestly leave out these words in their citation of the passage I quoted, because they are too plainly against them. I dealt with this trick also in the Prolegomena, Part III. But so that you may see even better the character and disposition of these men, know that they teach this not only in their Apology but also in their Reply to the Excerpts of the most learned doctors and professors of Leiden, published after the Apology in 1631. There they speak no less plainly and teach, on the basis of this hypothesis and doctrine of theirs, that subjects who are heretics ought to have liberty to meet privately, and that when the magistrate denies them this liberty, a way is thereby laid open for subjects to rebellion, and that this is almost necessary, and they call this a pain than which none is more just. So that the whole matter may be easily and rightly understood, note that the learned doctors and professors of Leiden, in the Appendix to their Excerpts (p. 39), rebuked them for excepting private places and conventicles from the care and power of the magistrate, and said: That they now limit that care and oversight of the magistrate and restrict it to public churches is very ridiculous, since they did not speak so when Uytenbogaert wrote his book on the office of the magistrate, and the Ultrecht and Schieland edicts were published in their favour against the Counter-Remonstrants. Add that this exception of theirs lays open a way for turbulent minds, by which they strive to withdraw themselves from the power of the magistrate. The Arminians answer these last words on pages 137 and 138, among other things, in this way: Next, what plausible reason can be given that this exception lays open a way for turbulent minds by which they may withdraw themselves from the power of the magistrate? For either that liberty is owed to them or it is not owed. If it is owed to them, the exception is just, whether or not it lays open a way to rebellion. Although the use of the liberty which is owed to them by right does not, in itself, lay open a way to rebellion, there is no reason for this. What do you think, candid reader? Is that exception, which lays open a way to rebellion, to be called just, no differently than one which does not lay open a way to it? Up to this point the Arminians have dodged the question there; now hear the accused confessing. For they go on: Indeed, if it is owed to them and nevertheless it is denied, IT IS ALMOST NECESSARY THAT IT LAYS OPEN A WAY TO REBELLION IN ITSELF. For no pain is more just than that which is produced by the taking away or denial of a liberty that is owed. If it is not owed, and yet is granted and conceded by the magistrates, they are moved by this favour rather to free obedience than to rebellion. Now judge, pious reader, of the character and disposition of these theologians. For here again you have a remarkable example from which it appears that they no longer have any conscience, since they so shamelessly dare to deny that they teach what in fact they do teach. You also see a remarkable example of their deceitfulness, by which they try to escape the light of truth and seek hiding places for their wickedness when they find themselves convicted in their own conscience. You see, consequently, how little they serve the cause of conscience, but rather how they aim to deceive the whole world and to disturb these provinces with impunity. You see that they are professed masters of sedition and rebellion, and when they are convicted of that most atrocious crime and of turbulence, they are content to deny it and to say that they think and hold the opposite. Finally, you see that what I have said several times before is most true: they deserve no further trust in matters of religion, let alone in other, lesser matters, and especially that they are not to be trusted when they say they think otherwise and teach otherwise everywhere. Good God, look at last upon these provinces and free them from these impostors; open the eyes of all, that they may see how shamefully these men mock magistrates and all others, that they may understand and detect the frauds, boldness and impudence of Satan, and rightly judge whether these ministers are moved and governed by the Spirit of God or rather by the spirit of lying.

units.la: Quod dicunt p. 174. Geneva Lutheranis civitate interdici mera calumnia est. Nam contrà, Lutherani omni officiorum, honoris & benevolentiæ genere ibi afficiuntur, quemadmodum Principes, Comites, Barones, Nobiles, ignobiles, Theologi, Politici, divites, pauperes, exules, viatores Lutherani testari possunt: cujus rei infinita exempla ibi occurrerunt, tùm ante me, tùm tredecim illis annis quos in eâ Academiâ docui. Et tantum abest, ut Lutherani eâ civitate ejiciantur, ut potius illa Lutheranorum multorum cujuscunque status & conditionis, etiam Magnatum refugium fuerit temporibus gravissimis Germaniæ nostræ, atque etiamnum fit. Sed mirum esset, si semel hi homines veritatem de Reformatis Ecclesiis & Magistratibus dicerent, speciatim de sanctâ atque innocentissimâ Ecclesiâ & Republicâ Genevensi; quod Epitheton scio ægre laturos illos qui Hæreticos speciatim Antitrinitarios innocentissimos, pios, piissimos san-ctissimos appellant, Genevæ autem quam præ cæteris oderunt, subinde convitia dicunt, prout hic rursus Tyrannidis matricem vocant, & quidem eo titulo quòd Lutheranis civitate interdicat.
units.tr: What they say on page 174, that Geneva forbids the Lutherans the city, is pure calumny. For on the contrary, the Lutherans are there received with every kind of duty, honour and goodwill, as Princes, Counts, Barons, nobles, commoners, theologians, politicians, rich men, poor men, exiles and travellers who are Lutherans can testify; infinite examples of this have occurred there, both before my time and in the thirteen years I taught in that Academy. And so far is it from the case that Lutherans are cast out of that city, that it has rather been, and still is, a refuge for many Lutherans of every rank and condition, even magnates, in the most troubled times of our Germany. But it would be a marvel if these men for once told the truth about the Reformed Churches and magistrates, especially about the holy and most innocent Church and Commonwealth of Geneva. I know that those who call heretics, especially Antitrinitarians, most innocent, pious, most pious, most holy, will be displeased by this title, and that they often hurl abuse at Geneva, which they hate above all others; so here again they call it the mother of tyranny, and indeed under that title because it forbids the Lutherans the city.

units.la: 11. Hùc dixi etiam pertinere atrocissima convitia & horrenda quæ in Magistratus orthodoxos exspuunt qui Hæreticos quocunque etiam corporali modo coercent, vocant Magistratum talem carnalem, dicunt eam Ismaelis vestigiis insistere; non esse spiritualis aut veri Christiani titulo dignum; esse a Spiritu Christi alienum, scelus admittere quando eos ladit aut vexat. Eatentur.
units.tr: 11. I have said that the most atrocious abuse and the horrible insults which they spew against orthodox magistrates also belong here: those who restrain heretics by any means, even bodily, they call such a magistrate carnal, and say that he treads in the footsteps of Ishmael; that he is not worthy of the title of spiritual or true Christian; that he is alien to the Spirit of Christ; that he commits a crime when he harms or vexes them. They admit it.

units.la: Fatentur Arminiani p. 174. & dicunt se ita tantum de exteris Principibus, Regibus & Magistratibus loqui, me autem ( praeclara scilicet excusatio ! ) convitiari Ordinibus Illustrissimis, quia Haereticis liberos atque inoffensos coetus indulgeant ; & suadent ob eam causam Ordinibus ut me his Provinciis ejiciant : vivere eum jubete ubi ista coercitiones locum habent, ut discat non convitiari potestatibus, quarum subditus est, & officio subditi digna loqui ac scribere. Et tandem pollicentur, se perpetuo benedictionem a Domino rogaturos Illustrissimis Ordinibus, & OMNIBUS STUDIIS votisque contendere velle ut Deus inspiret omnibus Regibus ac Pricipibus hunc animum ut tolerent omnis generis Haereticos in suis Regnis ac Provinciis. Cujus precationis (ut hoc obiter dicam) membrum prius quantum valeat apud Deum, conjici potest ex posteriore. Interim observent Magistratus & Principes exteri, si qui de his audient ; quae sint STUDIA Arminianorum, & caveant suis Provinciis, civitatibus & Ecclesiis ab horum hominum praeclaro illo conatu.
units.tr: The Arminians admit on page 174 and say that they speak thus only of foreign Princes, Kings and magistrates, but that I (a splendid excuse, to be sure!) rail at the Most Illustrious Orders, because they allow heretics free and unhindered assemblies; and for this reason they urge the Orders to expel me from these provinces: Order him to live where those restraints have their place, so that he may learn not to rail at the powers of which he is a subject, and to speak and write what befits a subject. And at last they promise that they will ever ask a blessing from the Lord for the Most Illustrious Orders, and that they will strive with ALL their ZEAL and prayers that God may inspire all Kings and Princes with this disposition, to tolerate every kind of heretic in their kingdoms and provinces. Of this prayer (to say this in passing) the first part's worth before God may be conjectured from the latter. Meanwhile let the magistrates and foreign Princes, if any of them hear of these things, observe what the aims of the Arminians are, and let them guard their provinces, cities and churches against this splendid undertaking of these men.

units.la: Dicunt igitur me convitiari Illustrissimis Ordinibus, ideo quod non coerceant varias sectas quae in his provinciis sunt. In quo eos contra conscientiam facere suam paulo ante a nobis est ostensum. Cui accedit, quod ego quidem, etsi tolerentur Haeretici quidam in his provinciis, tamen videam eos non absque omni coercitione corporali esse, quam omnem Arminiani ac simpliciter abesse volunt. Nam primo qui haereticam Religionem profitentur non ad honores & Reip. administrationem cum orthodoxis admittuntur, aut saltem non facile nec ordinarie. Deinde scio conventicula privata Haereticorum etiam Edictis sublata esse. Tertio scio ea edicta, in quibusdam praesertim locis, executioni dari. Quarto scio Illustrissimos Ordines nunquam voluisse ante hac tolerare, ne in Republica quidem sua, Socinianos, sed eos ejecisse ex his provinciis, ut antea dixi. Quinto scio Illustrissimos Ordines antehac coercuisse Arminianos : Unde ipsi infra cap. XI. p. 216. queruntur veritatem ( ita vocant impia & execranda dogmata sua & factiosam suam inobedientiam, qua Magistratus Edictis obedire nolebant ) per vim oppressam fuisse. Et addunt, sibi non licuisse contra hiscere. Argumenta, inquiunt, omnia erant ferrea, & Syllogismi numella ac compedes. Prator Maiorem propositionem, Lictor minorem, & conclusionem faciebat carcer. Scio etiam eorum edicta contra eos nondum esse abrogata, & quamvis jam M. Episcopius cum suis capita insolenter extollat contra ea abusi bonitate Procerum quibus imponunt ; tamen scio eos adhuc coerceri saltem in quibusdam provinciis,&c ciis, & ne quidem privata conventicula iis, nedum publica permitti templa. Scio etiam eos coërceri aliis quoque modis ab Illustrissimis Ordinibus & aliis Magistratibus. Unde ipsi in hoc capite nono p. 161. dicunt Religionem suam jam quidé latiore paululum vultu sed tamé adhuc depresso vultu, & inter spem ac metum dubiam esse. Haec omnia adeo vera sunt, nimirum coërceri aliquo modo corporali. Haereticos in his provinciis ut hi homines sui obliti (ut solent illi facere qui non studio veritatis sed contentionis & mendacii aguntur) ipsi illud fateantur, dum p. 167. cupiunt, ut Illustrissimi Ordines omnibus subditis suis parem libertatem in negocio Religionis concedant: Quid criminis in eo esse potest, si Remonstrantes in ista libertate patria nati atque educati omnibus subditis vestris parem libertatem optantes, profiteantur &c. Ut adeo falsa sit Hypothesis quam Arminiani hic ponunt, nimirum Illustrissimos Ordines non coercere ulla coercitione corporali Haereticos; item me habere Illustrissimos Ordines in eo censu; ac si nulla coercitione corporali Haereticos coercerent. Denique non despero (alioquin in hoc negocio laboris nihil impenderem) Deum miserturum harum provinciarum, & inspiraturum animos procerum, ut intelligant quales homines sint hi Theologi, & eos pro officii sui ratione magis etiam coërceant, ac ab iis seductos populos moneant, quam turpiter ipsis Pastores eorum hactenus illuserint. Hoc secundo loco respondsum esto ad calumniam istam. Tertio denique falsum est, convitia ista Arminianorum pertinere tantum ad Reges & Principes exteros. Nam dum ita in genere convitiantur omnibus Magistratibus, qui Haereticos ullo modo corporali coercent; certum est ista convitia pertinere non minus ad Illustrissimos Ordines, qui etiam Haereticos quosdam & Schismaticos coercent ac coercuerunt, quam ad exteros Reges ac Principes. Idque eo magis quòd antehac Illustrissimos Ordines ob edicta contra ipsos lata in suis scriptis acerrimè perstrinxerunt, imò etiamnum illis eo nomine convitiantur, ut vidimus Par. II. Arcan. lib. 1. Et quid facturos eos putamus, ubi insolentiam horum ministrorum denuò compescuerint Illustrissimi Ordines? an non haec convitia quae hoc loco dicunt, ad ipsos pertinebunt? Imò quae non convitia tunc dicturos esse Arminianos Proceribus putamus? Quibus omnibus convitiis addamus hoc ex quo unusquisque intelliget illa ad Illustrissimos etiam Ordines pertinere, quod dicunt in Resp. ad Excerpta p. 130. Quicumque aliis armis contra Haereses aut Haereticos, quá tales, cateroquin probos piosque, quàm spiritualibus pugnant aut pugnari consulant, EOS OMNES carnales homines, & conscientiarum Tyrannos rannos censendos esse aperte profitentur Remonstrantes, nec fieri posse ut communionem habeant cum Deo & Filio eius Iesu Christo. Obiter observetur, hos homines indignum iudicare Magistratum cum titulo Christiani, ut paulò ante vidimus, qui Haereticos coercet: cum scriptura sacra nos aliter longè iudicare doceat, nimirùm eos homines non esse dignos titulo Christiani qui Orthodoxos seu veram Ecclesiam persequuntur. Ita enim Paulus censet se ipsum indignum qui vocetur Apostolus quia persequutus sit Ecclesiam 1. Cor. 15. 9.
units.tr: They say, then, that I rail against the Illustrious Orders because they do not restrain the various sects that exist in these provinces. It was shown a little earlier that in doing so they act against their own conscience. To this I add that, even if some heretics are tolerated in these provinces, I see that they are not free from all bodily coercion, which the Arminians want to be entirely absent. First, those who profess a heretical religion are not admitted to honours and the administration of the commonwealth alongside the orthodox, or at least not easily or ordinarily. Second, I know that private conventicles of heretics have been abolished even by edicts. Third, I know those edicts are being put into execution, especially in certain places. Fourth, I know that the Illustrious Orders never wished before now to tolerate even the Socinians in their own commonwealth, but expelled them from these provinces, as I said before. Fifth, I know the Illustrious Orders have in the past restrained the Arminians. Hence they themselves complain, in chapter XI, p. 216, that the truth (so they call their impious and execrable dogmas and their factious disobedience, by which they refused to obey the magistrates' edicts) was oppressed by force. They add that it was not permitted them to kick back against it. The arguments, they say, were all iron, and the syllogisms little rings and shackles. The praetor made the major premise, the lictor the minor, and the prison made the conclusion. I know too that the edicts against them have not yet been repealed, and although M. Episcopius and his people now hold up their heads insolently against them, relying on the goodwill of the nobles whom they impose upon, I know they are still restrained, at least in certain provinces, etc., and not even private conventicles are allowed them, let alone public churches. I know too that they are restrained in other ways by the Illustrious Orders and by other magistrates. Hence they themselves, in this ninth chapter, p. 161, say that their religion is now indeed somewhat more cheerful in countenance, but still downcast, and doubtful between hope and fear. All these things are so true, namely that they are restrained in some bodily way. That these heretics in these provinces (as these men, forgetful of themselves, usually do when they are driven not by zeal for truth but by contention and lying) themselves confess it, while on p. 167 they desire that the Illustrious Orders grant equal liberty in matters of religion to all their subjects: What crime can there be in this, if Remonstrants, born and brought up in that liberty of the fatherland, wishing equal liberty for all your subjects, profess etc. So false is the hypothesis which the Arminians put forward here, namely that the Illustrious Orders restrain heretics by no bodily coercion, and likewise that I count the Illustrious Orders in that number, as if they restrained heretics by no bodily coercion. Finally, I do not despair (otherwise I would expend no labour on this business) that God will pity these provinces and inspire the minds of the nobles, so that they understand what sort of men these theologians are, and restrain them more, according to the duty of their office, and warn the peoples seduced by them, than their pastors have shamefully deluded them up to now. This is my answer to that calumny, as the second point. Thirdly and finally, it is false that these railings of the Arminians pertain only to foreign kings and princes. For while they rail in general against all magistrates who restrain heretics by any bodily means, it is certain these railings pertain no less to the Illustrious Orders, who also restrain, and have restrained, some heretics and schismatics, than to foreign kings and princes. All the more so since before now the Illustrious Orders, on account of edicts passed against them, have assailed the Arminians most bitterly in their writings, and even now rail at them on that account, as we saw in Part II, Arcanum, book 1. And what do we think they will do when the Illustrious Orders again curb the insolence of these ministers? Will these railings they utter in this place not pertain to them? Indeed, what railings do we think the Arminians will then not utter against the nobles? To all these railings add this, from which anyone will understand that they pertain also to the Illustrious Orders: in the reply to the Excerpta, p. 130, they openly profess that whoever fight, or advise others to fight, against heresies or heretics as such, with weapons other than spiritual ones, though otherwise upright and pious, ALL OF THEM the Remonstrants declare to be carnal men and tyrants of consciences, and say that they cannot have fellowship with God and his Son Jesus Christ. Let it be noted in passing that these men judge the magistrate who restrains heretics unworthy of the title of Christian, as we saw a little before; whereas holy Scripture teaches us to judge quite otherwise, namely that those are not worthy of the title of Christian who persecute the orthodox or the true Church. For Paul counts himself unworthy to be called an apostle because he persecuted the Church, 1 Cor. 15. 9.

units.la: 12. Huc insuper pertinere dixi p. 234. 235.236. quòd, ne nihil omninò concedere videantur Magistratui quo Haereticos coercere corporaliter possit, scurriliter & illusorie ei permittunt duplicem potestatem; quarum prior est ut Magistratus flagellum è funiculis faciat, & eo Haereticos Christi exemplo è templis ejiciat. Altera ut verbis seu ore ita eos objurget, ut ad eam increpationem sive objurgationem verbalem mortui concidant, idque exemplo Petri Ananiam & Sapphiram divinitus morte ferientis. Hic p. 174. 175. 176. negant se hanc duplicem potestatem Magistratui concessisse, & aiunt se saltem dixisse argumentum Cll. DD. Proff. Leydensium ex istis exemplis petitum non procedere. Verùm eos contra conscientiam suam etiam hac in parte agere manifestum fiet unicuique ex verbis Apologiae quae ibi loci de quo quaestio est citavi. Nam ibi non solùm dicunt argumentum orthodoxorum Theologorum non procedere, sed etiam dicunt, se Magistratui hoc jus plena manu tribuere ut ex templis publicis etiam flagello in eum finem facto ejiciat Haereticos: item dicunt: Si orthodoxi Theologi exemplo Petri recte uti velint, debere eos concludere Magistratui integrum esse, ut vi acris objurgationis suae ad mortem usque objurget Haereticos; si hoc concluserint Theologi orthodoxi, dicunt eos recte facturos, & se eis non contradicturos. Item vocant illud Consilium quod dent ipsi Arminiani. Ne Lectori scrupulus aut dubium ullum maneat, en verba ipsorum quae loco eo de quo quaestio est h. e. Par. I. lib. 2. c. 9. p. 234. 235. ex Apologia cap. 24. f. 269. a. b. citavi. Denique, inquiunt, pone ab ejectione vendentium & ementium e templo per flagellum facta recte colligi ejectionem Haereticorum Magistratui licitam esse, nihil tamen aliud colligetur, quam ejectionem ex publicis templis ad Magistratum pertinentibus, licite a Magistratu fieri posse, & quidem, si necesse sit, flagello e funiculis ei fini facto, ulterius aut plus concludere nemo potest. At hoc ius Magistratui plena manu tribunt Remonstrantes: Hac ergo in parte imitetur Magistratus Christum. Quod si vero etiam pergat eos ejicere Synagogis &c. Item: Si vero Censor etiam velut Petrum hos trum hos occidisse verbo, vel vi acris obiurgationis sua, idem posse facere Magistratum si velit, concludat, & recte fecerit, nec erit ullus mortalium qui refragabitur. Nam si obiurgationem illam Deus ratam habeat, & eum qui obiurgatur perimat, iustam eam fuisse & divinitus approbatam iudicabitur: Sin minus, liberum relinquetur obiurgatis, obiurgationi isti non parere, utpote ad exemplum Petri non facta. Sed hoc lene consilium non ferunt, qui nihil nisi scalpra, equuleos & carceres spirant. Ecce ibi quoad priorem potestatem exprese dicunt, se Magistratui hoc ius plenum manu tribuere ut Haereticos templis eiiciat, & quidem si necesse sit flagello ex funiculis ei rei facto. Quoad posteriorem dicunt, orthodoxos Theologos debere ita inferre seu concludere, & eos RECTE facturos ac se nequaquam refragaturos esse item hanc objurgationem vocant consilium lene, & conqueruntur quod illud spretum & rejectum iri videant. Atque in illis verbis eorum vis consistit querelae meae, ut p. 235. 236. expresse urseram, adversus exceptionem quam sola cum aliqua specie honestatis in sui excusationem afferre posse videbantur. Ad quam instantiam meam nihil respondent, nisi Apologiam non affirmare Magistratum secundum literam debere imitari factum Christi. Quod ipsum est, quod ego ibi ostendi, h. e. hanc esse ipsius Apologiae doctrinam, ad cujus rei probationem a me allatam ne verbulum quidem respondent, sed contenti crimen negare, probationem illius sicco pede transeunt. En igitur rursus fidem horum hominum, atque improbitatem, qui tamen denuo ita delicatas aures habent, ut, cum adeo impudenter in ora Regum, Principum ac Magistratuum illusoriae huius potestatis concessione spuere, & eos manifestissima contumelia afficere ausi fuerint, ferre non possint quod conquestus fuerim eos scurriliter & illusorie in ea re egisse; sed de ea re tanquam gravissimo convitio querantur homines hi, ut scilicet videantur non sine causa me, quid me dico? imo Reges, Principes, Magistratus, Ecclesias, populos diabolica sua maledicentia conspuisse. Convitia & calumnias eorum hic praetereo, nec non extravagationem, qua me fortassis excepturum hoc vel illud fingunt ut nugis multis chartas compleant, & simplicioribus imponant, dum videri voluntrefutasse ea quae in mentem mihi nunquam venerunt, nedum ut a me dicta sint, aut ut adeo ineptus fuerim qui talia ad ipsorum imposturas exciperem; & tamen cum dixissent inquiet fortasse Vedelius &c. adeo protervi sunt, ut formata exceptione quam finxerunt me fortassis afferre posse, exclament o vanum hominem! & sic mihi convitium dicant eo nomine, & postea multis nugis oppugnent umbram quam sibi finxerunt. Judica rursus Lector de &tor de Spiritu & indole horum hominum. Non prætereundum est eos, dum ita contra conscientiam suam agunt, & negant se docere quæ docent, adeò tamen impudentes esse, ut illustrissimos Proceres compellare ausint, & eos eorumque conscientiam in testem innocentiæ suæ vocare p. 175. Hoc responsum, Proceres, anscurrile & illusorium est? Testor vos & conscientiam vestram. Et tamen ibidem post multam tergiversationem fatentur contumeliam priorem ibidem his verbis: o vanum hominem! Cum flagello e funiculis facto Magistratum uti posse concedunt Remonstrantes, non id volunt quasi alia vi non possit uti, nec alia arma adhibere quàm flagellum e funiculis factum. Passim enim in Apologia suâ docent, Magistratum quâlibet vi uti posse contra eos qui loca publica, templa, atque oratoria eorum invadere aut usurpare sibi volunt. Sed ut sub unâ istâ specie corporalis coercitionis omnem aliam comprehensam esse iudicarent. Ecce profitentur hic SECONCEDERE Magistratü uti posse flagello e funiculis facto (quod tamen orthodoxi Theologi non dixerant) item habent hoc pro SPECIE unâ corporalis coercitionis quâ Magistratus uti possit, sub quâ alias omnes dicunt se comprehendere.
units.tr: 12. I have said that the following also belongs here (pp. 234, 235, 236): so that they may not seem to concede the magistrate no power at all to coerce heretics bodily, they grant him, in a buffoonish and mocking way, a twofold power. The first is that the magistrate may make a whip of cords and with it drive heretics out of the temples, as Christ did. The second is that he may rebuke them with words or speech so sharply that they fall dead at that verbal rebuke or reprimand, after the example of Peter, who by divine power struck Ananias and Sapphira dead. Here (pp. 174, 175, 176) they deny that they have granted the magistrate this twofold power, and they say that they only argued that the argument of the most learned professors of Leiden, drawn from those examples, does not hold. But it will be plain to anyone, from the words of their Apology which I cited in the place under discussion, that they act against their own conscience even on this point. For there they not only say that the argument of the orthodox theologians does not hold, but also say that they grant this right to the magistrate with full hands, namely that he may drive heretics out of public temples, even with a whip made for that purpose. Likewise they say: if the orthodox theologians wish to use the example of Peter rightly, they should conclude that it is lawful for the magistrate to rebuke heretics with the force of his sharp rebuke even unto death. If the orthodox theologians draw this conclusion, they say, they will be acting RIGHTLY, and we will not contradict them. They also call this a counsel which the Arminians themselves give. So that the reader may have no scruple or doubt, here are their own words, which I cited in the place under discussion, that is, Part I, book 2, chapter 9, pp. 234, 235, from the Apology, chapter 24, f. 269 a, b: Finally, they say, suppose it is rightly inferred from the expulsion of sellers and buyers from the temple by a whip that the expulsion of heretics is lawful for the magistrate, nothing more will be inferred than that expulsion from public temples, which belong to the magistrate, can lawfully be done by the magistrate, and indeed, if necessary, with a whip made of cords for that purpose; no one can conclude anything further or more. But the Remonstrants grant this right to the magistrate with full hands: in this respect, then, let the magistrate imitate Christ. But if he should go on to drive them out of the synagogues, etc. Again: But if the censor should also, like Peter, wish to kill these men by a word, or by the force of his sharp rebuke, let him conclude that the magistrate can do the same if he wishes, and he will have done rightly, and there will be no mortal who will object. For if God approves that rebuke and kills the one who is rebuked, it will be judged to have been just and divinely approved. But if not, the rebuked will be left free not to obey that rebuke, since it was not done after the example of Peter. But those who breathe nothing but scalpels, racks and prisons do not endure this gentle counsel. There, then, with regard to the first power, they expressly say that they grant this right to the magistrate with full hands, to drive heretics out of the temples, and indeed, if necessary, with a whip made of cords for that purpose. With regard to the second, they say that the orthodox theologians ought so to infer or conclude, and that they would be acting RIGHTLY and would by no means oppose them; this rebuke they call a gentle counsel, and they complain that they see it being despised and rejected. And in those words of theirs lies the force of my complaint, which I pressed on pp. 235, 236, against the objection which they alone seemed able to bring forward, with some show of honesty, in their own defence. To this challenge of mine they reply with nothing, except that the Apology does not affirm that the magistrate must imitate the deed of Christ according to the letter. That is precisely what I showed there, namely that this is the doctrine of the Apology itself; and to the proof I brought for it they do not reply even a word, but, content to deny the charge, they pass over the proof dry-shod. Behold again, then, the good faith and the wickedness of these men, who nonetheless have such delicate ears that, although they have dared so shamelessly to spit upon the faces of kings, princes and magistrates with this concession of an illusory power, and to load them with the plainest insult, they cannot bear that I complained that they acted in a buffoonish and mocking way in this matter. Instead these men complain of that as a most serious reproach, as if it were without cause that I (what am I saying? rather the kings, princes, magistrates, churches and peoples) had spat upon them with their diabolical slander. I pass over their abuse and calumnies here, and also the digression by which they pretend that I will perhaps take up this or that point, so that they may fill their pages with many trifles and impose on simpler readers, while they seem willing to refute things that never came into my mind, let alone things that I said, or as if I were so foolish as to take up such things for their impostures. And yet, when they had written Vedelius will perhaps say, etc., they are so impudent that, having framed an objection which they pretend I might perhaps bring forward, they cry out O vain man!, and so hurl abuse at me on that account, and afterwards they assail with many trifles the shadow they have invented for themselves. Judge again, reader, of the spirit and character of these men. It must not be passed over that, while they act so against their own conscience and deny that they teach what they teach, they are nonetheless so impudent as to address the most illustrious nobles and to call them and their conscience to witness of their innocence (p. 175): Is this answer, nobles, buffoonish and mocking? I call you and your conscience to witness. And yet in the same place, after much shifting, they confess the earlier insult in these words: O vain man! When the Remonstrants concede that the magistrate can use a whip made of cords, they do not mean that he cannot use any other force, or employ other arms than a whip made of cords. For throughout their Apology they teach that the magistrate can use any force whatever against those who wish to invade or usurp for themselves their public places, temples and oratories. But they judge that every other kind of coercion is included under this one kind of bodily coercion. Behold, here they profess that they CONCEDE that the magistrate can use a whip made of cords (which, however, the orthodox theologians had not said); likewise they hold this as ONE KIND of bodily coercion which the magistrate may use, and they say that all the others are included under it.

units.la: 13. Quintus modus est, quo statuunt Arminiani Hæreticos contumaciter blasphemos pœnâ blasphemiæ à Magistratu afficiendos non esse. Fatentur, & persistunt in eo p.277.178. posteaquam vafrè & fraudulenter statum controversiæ involvissent, imò mutâssent: Quinto, inquiunt, distinctionem inter Hæresin & blasphemiam quæ à Remonstrantibus facta est taxat Vedelius. Distinctio hæc fuit: Blasphemia &c. Sed ista mera fraus est. Non enim scopus meus fuit distinctionem exagitare illam, sed propositum mihi fuit dogma istud exponere seu recitare Arminianorum, & rationem quam afferunt ibidem diluere, ut à me factum. Quare nugæ ipsorum in quas ibi excurrunt impertinentes sunt; quibus oppugnant quod dixi omne scelus adeoque nullam non blasphemiam cum ignorantia & cæcitate conjunctam esse. Quâ in re non contra me sed contra Scripturam pugnant, quæ impios homines & qui dicunt in corde suo non esse Deus stultos appellat Psal. 14. 1. item: Jehova e cœlis prospectat super filios hominum, ut videat an sit ullus qui intelligat qui exquirat bonum. v. 2. Similiter Psal. 53. 2. 3. & alibi. Plura afferre nolo in re evidentissimâ. Ubi tamen nec Scriptura vult, nec mea mens est, omne scelus cum omni, seu simplice ignorantiâ sive puræ negationis esse conjunctum, sed cum aliquâ, seu pravæ dispositionis, quæ varia est, & vel major vel minor pro diversitate peccatorum. Speciatim autem de blasphemiis illud probavi loco eo Arcan. de quo quæstio est p.237. ex eo quia blasphemiæ Turcarum cum ignorantiâ conjunctę sunt, item quia Iudæorum blasphemia ex ignorantiâ est, teste Scripturâ, quam in hujus rei probationem ipsi Arminiani allegant 1. Cor. 2.8. Act. 3. 17. Luc: 23. 34. & fatentibus Arminianis dum Apolog. c. 24. f.264. dicunt eos qui à Christianismo ad Iudaismum deficiunt, ideò pœnâ blasphemiæ puniendos non esse, quia Iudæi inquiunt, urgebit ad eos Legis promissa pertinere tanquam ad veros Iudæos, verisimiliter atque unici Dei cultores. Quibus verbis an'non simul indicant Arminiani Iudæos nescire se blasphemare, imò putare se rectè facere? Et tamen audent hi homines negare p. 178. quod dixeram eos fateri Iudæos ex ignorantiâ Christum blasphemare. Quod eò turpius est; quia ibidem ipsi dicunt Iudæorum blasphemiam ex ignorantiâ proficisci dici posse: Sic enim Remonstrantes statuunt: Etsi Iudæorum blasphemia hactenus ex ignorantiâ proficisci dici possit &c. Sed quid opus est, ut multis de hac re laborem, cùm ipsi fateantur p. 177. 178. omne scelus cum aliqua ignorantiâ esse coniunctum, & in eum finem allegent Aristotelem Ethic. lib. 3. c. 1. & Proverb. 14. item loca illa de Iudæorum ignorantiâ, quæ omnia quomodo interpretentur Arminiani, ad me jam non pertinet, cui satis est eos fateri id quod in me reprehendunt. Sed placuit his omnibus, quò involutus maneret status quæstionis, & Lector non facile animadverteret cujus rei à me accusati essent, duas integras paginas istis suis nugis complere. Et profectò impossibile est ei qui ipsorum scriptum tantum legerit & non contulerit cum meo, conjicere hic & in multis aliis locis quisnam status quæstionis sit. Quod quo fine ab ipsis fiat, facilè unusquisque videt.
units.tr: 13. The fifth way is that in which the Arminians determine that obstinate blasphemous heretics are not to be punished by the magistrate with the penalty for blasphemy. They admit this, and they persist in it (pp. 177, 178), after they had craftily and fraudulently involved, indeed changed, the state of the controversy: Fifthly, they say, Vedelius criticises the distinction between heresy and blasphemy which the Remonstrants made. The distinction was this: blasphemy, etc. But this is sheer fraud. For my aim was not to attack that distinction, but my purpose was to set out or recite the Arminian doctrine on this point, and to refute the reasoning they offer there, as I did. Therefore their trifles into which they run there are beside the point; with them they attack what I said, that every crime, and so every blasphemy, is joined with ignorance and blindness. In this they fight not against me but against Scripture, which calls impious men, and those who say in their heart that there is no God, fools (Ps. 14:1). Likewise: Jehovah looks down from heaven upon the sons of men, to see whether there is anyone who understands, who seeks after good (v. 2). Similarly Ps. 53:2, 3, and elsewhere. I do not wish to bring forward more in a matter so evident. Yet neither Scripture nor my mind holds that every crime is joined with every ignorance, whether simple ignorance or pure negation, but with some kind of wrong disposition, which varies, and is greater or less according to the diversity of sins. Specifically, concerning blasphemies, I proved in that place of mine under discussion (p. 237) that the blasphemies of the Turks are joined with ignorance, and likewise that the blasphemy of the Jews arises from ignorance, as Scripture witnesses, which the Arminians themselves cite in proof of this (1 Cor. 2:8; Acts 3:17; Luke 23:34). And the Arminians themselves admit this when, in the Apology, chapter 24, f. 264, they say that those who fall from Christianity to Judaism are not to be punished with the penalty for blasphemy, because the Jews, they say, are urged to think that the promises of the Law pertain to them as to true Jews, probably and worshippers of the one God. Do the Arminians not by these words at the same time indicate that the Jews do not know that they blaspheme, indeed think that they do right? And yet these men dare to deny (p. 178) what I had said, that they admit the Jews blaspheme Christ out of ignorance. This is all the more shameful because in the same place they themselves say that the blasphemy of the Jews can be said to arise from ignorance: For thus the Remonstrants hold: although the blasphemy of the Jews up to now can be said to arise from ignorance, etc. But why should I labour at length on this matter, since they themselves admit (pp. 177, 178) that every crime is joined with some ignorance, and to that end they cite Aristotle, Ethics book 3, chapter 1, and Proverbs 14, as well as those passages about the ignorance of the Jews? How the Arminians interpret all these is no longer my concern; it is enough for me that they admit what they blame in me. But it pleased them to fill two whole pages with these trifles, so that the state of the question might remain involved, and so that the reader would not easily notice of what they accused me. And indeed it is impossible for anyone who has read only their writing, and has not compared it with mine, to guess here, and in many other places, what the state of the question is. For what purpose they do this is easily seen by everyone.

units.la: 14. Objeci etiam ipsis quod docent, non puniendos esse tales Hæreticos quamvis blasphemi contumaciter sint, & Regna & Respublicas turbent. Non negant, sed supra falsi sunt, cùm ipsorum verba à nobis alio fine allegata essent.
units.tr: 14. I also objected to them that they teach that heretics, even if they blaspheme stubbornly and disturb kingdoms and commonwealths, are not to be punished. They do not deny it, but they are wrong to complain, since their words were cited by us for a different purpose.

units.la: 15. Objeceram etiam p. 239. 240. quod docent: Apostatas eos qui à Christianismo ad Iudaismum deficiunt non esse capitali pœna afficiendos; quam pœnam capitalem Constantinus M. contra Apostatas ad Iudæos primus sed verbo Dei convenienter decrevit, ut videre est apud Sozomenum lib. 3. c. 16. Hic postquam dixissent, se id non AFFIRMASSE (quâ voce uti solent quando volunt dicere se aliquid non iisdem literis & syllabis dixisse) fatentur hanc suam mentem esse, & eam defendere conantur p. 179.180.181. ita ut nobis Arcanatalia nova sua revelent ad quæ omnes honesti viri exhorrescunt; quæ videre est Par. III. lib. 2. c. 9. Hoc igitur dogma audent tueri hi homines, cùm tamen fateantur Judæos non indirectè sed directè atque apertè Christum blasphemare. Atque ex his omnibus jam apparet me verissimè dixisse p. 241. Arminianos inter alia illudere Magistratui, dum Architectonicâ potestatè ei tribuere se in Ecclesiasticis dicunt; quandoquidem eam potestatem doctrinâ suâ de coërcendis Hæreticis ferè totâ ex professo evertūt, ut ex allegatis dogmatis corú patet
units.tr: 15. I had also objected, at pages 239 and 240, to their teaching that apostates who fall away from Christianity to Judaism are not to be punished with capital punishment. Constantine the Great was the first to decree this capital punishment against apostates to Judaism, and he did so in accordance with the Word of God, as can be seen in Sozomen, book 3, chapter 16. Here, after saying that they had not AFFIRMED this (a phrase they are accustomed to use when they wish to say that they have not said something in the same words and syllables), they admit that this is their own opinion and try to defend it at pages 179, 180 and 181, so that they reveal to us their new Arcana, at which all honest men shudder; these can be seen in Part III, book 2, chapter 9. These men therefore dare to defend this dogma, although they admit that the Jews blaspheme Christ not indirectly but directly and openly. And from all this it now appears that I spoke most truthfully at page 241 when I said that the Arminians, among other things, mock the magistrate, since they say that they grant him architectonic power in ecclesiastical matters, while by their doctrine on restraining heretics they almost wholly and deliberately overturn that power, as is clear from the dogmas cited.

units.la: Conclusio verbosissima huius capitis p. 181. 182. 183. 184. quâ rursus ad illustrissimos Ordines se convertunt, examen non meretur. Vix enim ulla sententia est, quæ non mendaciis & calumniis scateat, ut unicuique doctrinæ Reformatæ, adeòque meæ gnaro, necnon doctrinæ & ingenii Arminiani ex his quæ hactenus ab aliis & à nobis dicta sunt perito notum est. Uno verbo, tota illa oratio eò tendit ut Proceres non solùm ab Hæreticidio (cuius à me ne verbo quidem mentio facta erat) sed etiam, contrà quàm hactenus ab illustriss. Ordinibus factum, à quacumq; coërcitione Hæreticorum penitùs abstineant, & omnibus generis Hæreticis conventus ac liberum exercitium Religionis suæ indulgeant. Hic est scopus illorum, ex quo quantum sibi sumant licentiæ in reprehendendo & reformando Regimine illustrissimorum Ordinum homines hi, contra quorum famam & sortem lata edicta abrogata nondum sunt, quot etiam mendaciis & calumniis tàm abominandum propositum, quale est introductio præsertim Socinianarum blasphemiarum, opus habeat, unusquisque sapiens intelligit.
units.tr: The very wordy conclusion of this chapter, at pages 181, 182, 183 and 184, in which they again turn to the most illustrious Orders, does not deserve examination. For there is scarcely any sentence that does not teem with lies and calumnies, as is known to anyone acquainted with Reformed doctrine, and with the doctrine and character of the Arminians, as learned from what has hitherto been said by others and by us. In a word, the whole speech tends to this: that the nobles should abstain entirely not only from the slaughter of heretics (of which I had not made even a word of mention) but also, contrary to what the most illustrious Orders have hitherto done, from any restraint of heretics, and should grant to heretics of every kind assemblies and free exercise of their religion. This is their aim; and every wise man understands how much licence these men take in censuring and reforming the government of the most illustrious Orders, against whose reputation and fortune the edicts issued have not yet been repealed, and how much lying and calumny such an abominable proposal requires, the kind that introduces especially the Socinian blasphemies.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CAP. X.

units.la: Examen Capitis decimi Vindic. lib. 2.
units.tr: Examination of Chapter 10 of Book 2 of the Vindiciae

units.la: I. Argumenta auctoris quibus offensum fuerat Arminianos per ista dogmata suo Atheismo crasso fenestram aperire, vindicantur adversus jejuna effugia & fraudes illorum. Primi argumenti soliditas vindicatur. Arminiani fatentur se omnis generis Hæreses, prout ea vox communiter usurpatur ab orthodoxis, in Ecclesiam introducere velle. 2. Secundi argumenti soliditas vindicatur. 3. Tertii argumenti veritas ostenditur contra insignem impostu-ram Arminianorum. 4. Quartum argumentum vindicatur. 5. Nec non quintum. 6. Denique sextum.
units.tr: I. The author's arguments, by which he had shown that the Arminians open a window to crass atheism through these doctrines, are defended against their feeble evasions and frauds. The soundness of the first argument is defended. The Arminians admit that they wish to introduce into the Church every kind of heresy, in the sense in which the orthodox commonly use that word. 2. The soundness of the second argument is defended. 3. The truth of the third argument is shown against the notorious imposture of the Arminians. 4. The fourth argument is defended. 5. Likewise the fifth. 6. Finally, the sixth.

units.la: 1. HActenus ostendimus adversus effugia, fraudes & imposturas turpissimas Arminianorum veritatem & æquitatem querelæ nostræ, quæ in eo consistit, Arminianos Theologos Libertinismum in fide seu doctrinâ h. e. Atheismum subtilem in Ecclesiam Dei introducere, in eum præcipuè finem, quantum ad Religionis negotium attinet, ut Socinianarum blasphemiarum professionem publicam introducant. Nunc quæstio restat à me proposita cap. x. Par. I. lib. 2. An ne Arminiani eâdem doctrinâ suâ Atheismo crasso senestram aperiant. Capite igitur allegato attuleram sex argumenta quibus affirmativam probaveram. Ad hæc ita respondent capite suo undecimo ut, post plurimas impudentissimas calumnias, contumelias, & convitia contra totam Reformatam, Ecclesiamnon contra me solum, inter alia ac si sanguinem Hæreticorum & aliorum errantium sitirem &c. quibus calumniis & nugis replent paginas 184.185. 186. 187. partim directè negent, partim in doctrinam Reformatarum Ecclesiarum de Prædestinatione & annexis quatuor articulis retorquent. Retorsio illa & accusatio quâ nostræ doctrinæ illi Atheismum impingunt vetus & diabolica calumnia est, ut patet ex cap. 10. libri præcedentis, & quæ millies ab aliis refutata est. Quare eam prætereo, & Deo ultori relinquo, qui tandem hos homines contra cœlum (nam ipsius veritatem contumeliosè simul & blasphemè petunt dum orthodoxam doctrinam calumniantur) tantâ cum insolentiâ & malitiâ insurgentes confundet. Paucis saltem fraudes & imposturas eorum detegam quibus soliditatem argumentorum meorum sed frustrà, eludere, conantur.
units.tr: 1. So far we have shown, against the evasions, frauds and most shameful impostures of the Arminians, that our complaint is true and fair. It consists in this: the Arminian theologians introduce into the Church of God libertinism in faith or doctrine, that is, a subtle atheism, and this chiefly with the aim, so far as the business of religion is concerned, of introducing a public profession of the blasphemies of the Socinians. Now there remains the question I raised in chapter 10, part I, book 2: Whether the Arminians, by this same doctrine of theirs, do not open a window to crass atheism. In the chapter cited I had set out six arguments by which I proved the affirmative. In reply, in their eleventh chapter, after very many most shameless calumnies, insults and abuse against the whole Reformed Church, and not against me alone, and as if I thirsted for the blood of heretics and other erring persons, etc. (they fill pages 184, 185, 186 and 187 with such calumnies and trifles), they partly deny my points outright and partly turn them back upon the Reformed doctrine of predestination and the four articles annexed to it. That retorsion, by which they charge our doctrine with atheism, is an old and diabolical calumny, as is clear from chapter 10 of the preceding book, and it has been refuted a thousand times by others. I therefore pass it over and leave it to God, the avenger, who will at last confound these men, who rise up against heaven (for while they slander orthodox doctrine they attack its very truth, insultingly and blasphemously) with such insolence and malice. I will only briefly lay bare their frauds and impostures, by which they try, but in vain, to escape the force of my arguments.

units.la: Primum meum argumentum ex eo desumtum est; quòd Arminiani ex professo, ut ostensum Par. I. libris duob. nunc rursus his duobus libris Par. IV. omnis generis hæreses & sectas in Ecclesiam Dei introducere laborant. Jam autem Hæreses evertunt necessaria quæ inter Christianos controversa sunt &c.
