Respondent illi, se tunc reos fore Atheismi; si Hæreses introducerent quæ revera & judicio divino exitiales hæreses sunt. Jam autem se non introducere tales Hæreses & sectas in Ecclesiam; sed tales quæ non nisi judicio humano Hæreses sunt, quales introducere dicunt esse nihil aliud quàm pacem Ecclesiæ procurare p. 187. Respondeo: Nititur hoc effugium turpissimâ illâ hypothesi ipsorum, nimirum controversa vera dogmata non esse decisa à Deo ipso, & niti tantum certitudine humanâ non autem divinâ. Quod salsissimum est. Vera enim controversa omnia dogmata decisa sunt in verbo Dei, adeóque ab ipso Deo, quod ipsi, quemadmodum αὐτοκατάκειτοι in multis aliis sunt, fiis sunt, fatentur in Dedicatione Vindiciarum, ut libro præcedente vidimus. Itaque falsum est quod dicunt se non introducere in Ecclesiam Hæreses quæ judicio divino tales sunt, sed quæ tantùm judicio humano tales sunt. Introducunt enim Hæreses tales quæ evertunt necessaria dogmata controversa, seu Hæreses de quibus quæstio est, item quas Censor sic vocat, ut ipsi in Apologia loquuntur; quales sunt Hæreses Antitrinitariorum quas ipsi non negant sed fatentur se in Ecclesiam introducere velle, negant saltem eas Hæreses esse. Unde jam pius Lector de soliditate argumenti primi mei facile judicare potest. Videt enim eos effugere non posse, nisi explodendo significationem quæ omni tempore in Ecclesiâ receptâ fuit vocis Hæreseos, ac negando Hæreses tales quæ sic communiter ab orthodoxis vocantur, quales sunt Antitrinitariorum, hæreses esse.
units.tr: My first argument rests on this: that the Arminians, as I showed in part I, books 2, and now again in part IV, books 2, deliberately labour to introduce every kind of heresy and sect into the Church of God. Now heresies overthrow the necessary doctrines that are disputed among Christians, etc. They reply that they would then be guilty of atheism if they introduced heresies that are truly and by divine judgment pernicious heresies. But they do not introduce such heresies and sects into the Church; they introduce only those which are heresies by human judgment alone. Such heresies, they say, to introduce is nothing other than to procure the peace of the Church (p. 187). I answer: this evasion rests on their most shameful hypothesis, namely that the disputed true doctrines have not been decided by God himself, and rest only on human certainty and not on divine. This is utterly false. For all the disputed true doctrines have been decided in the word of God, and therefore by God himself. In many other matters they themselves are self-condemned [αὐτοκατάκριτοι], as they confess in the Dedication of the Vindiciae, as we saw in the preceding book. So it is false that they say they do not introduce into the Church heresies which are such by divine judgment, but only those which are such by human judgment. For they do introduce heresies which overthrow the necessary disputed doctrines, or heresies about which there is question, also what the Censor calls such, as they themselves say in their Apology. Such are the heresies of the Antitrinitarians, which they do not deny but confess they wish to introduce into the Church; they only deny that these are heresies. Hence the pious reader can easily judge of the strength of my first argument. He sees that they cannot escape it except by rejecting the meaning which the word heresy has always had in the received Church, and by denying that heresies which are commonly called such by the orthodox, such as those of the Antitrinitarians, are heresies.

units.la: Addunt præter retorsionem, quæ calumniâ solitâ illâ contra doctrinam de Electione & perseverantiâ nititur, etiam aliam p. 189. quę nititur hac falsitate; quòd nimirùm Hæretici quos orthodoxa Ecclesia sic vocat, quales sunt Antitrinitarii; nullo indubitato atque infallibili judicio evinci possint esse Hæretici. Quod falsum esse ex antedictis patet. Et ampliè in Rationali Theologico de hac re egimus, ubi ex professo hanc quæstionem tractavimus. Falsò etiam dicunt, nos omnes cœtus segreges vi oppressos cupere. Patet denique istam retorsionem non minùs Lutheranos quàm Reformatos concernere, adeóque si procedat illa, tùm Lutheranos ab Arminianis non minùs quàm nos Atheismi accusari.
units.tr: In addition to the retorsion, which rests on their usual calumny against the doctrine of election and perseverance, they also add another (p. 189), which rests on this falsehood: that heretics whom the orthodox Church so calls, such as the Antitrinitarians, cannot be proved to be heretics by any indubitable and infallible judgment. That this is false is clear from what has been said. We have treated this question at length, and professedly, in the Rational Theology. They also falsely say that we desire all separated congregations to be forcibly suppressed. Finally, it is clear that this retorsion concerns the Lutherans no less than the Reformed. Hence, if it held, the Lutherans would be accused of atheism by the Arminians no less than we are.

units.la: Secundò ostendi eos Atheismo crasso fenestram aperire per doctrinam suam de Trinitate, & quidem duplici modo: 1. dum docent Mysterium Trinitatis nullum usum per se habere. Hoc eludere conantur p. 190. impostura illâ quâ usi sunt in hac re lib. 1. c. 7. fingentes nos urgere usum Mysterii illius quatenus Pater Filius Spiritus S. tres personæ sunt absque ullâ (ut hic loquuntur) relatione aut conceptu essentiæ sive divinitatis quam communem habent; ac se hoc tantùm negare dicunt. Quo protervius & fraudulentius dici nihil potest; ut ostensum à nobis est libro præcedente c. 7. Deinde ostendi eos fenestram aperire Atheismo per doctrinam suam de Trinitate etiam aliâ ratione; dum scilicet dogmata orthodoxa illa notoria de Trinitate, quæ Antitrinitarii Hæretici oppugnant, non habent proNecessariis ad salutem &c. Respondent ita ut utantur illâ impostura solitâquâ, ut etiam suprà vidimus lib. 1. c. 7. dicunt se nec affirmare nec negare illorum necessitatem. Sed hoc est orbi illudere. Nobis sufficit, eos non habere illa pro Necessariis; & multis argumentis impiam suam illam do-ctrinam defendere conari. Et supra ostendimus, ἐποχὴν seu dubitatio-nem illam Arminianorum talem esse, ut simul simpliciter negent ea esse necessaria. Postea consequentiam argumenti mei impugnant, ita ut po-stulent sibi probari ea dogmata esse Necessaria. Et quia id probaveram exinde, quia si dogmata illa non sunt Necessaria, tunc corruat totum my-sterium illud, adeóque tota Religio Christiana; quod ipsum ostendi ex ex eo, quia si ista dogmata necessaria non sunt, tum secundùm alias hy-potheses Arminianorum licet negare & oppugnare sensum verum illius mysterii absque periculo salutis, absque notâ hæreseos, absque crimine impietatis; imò negantes illum sensum haberi debent pro membris ve-ræ Ecclesiæ. Hic regerunt illi in his nihil absurdi esse, sed ea vera esse omnia, & me qui ea pro absurdis habeo ineptire dicunt; & addunt, me principium petere. Tu judica, pie Lector, an non cum summâ impudentiâ dicant in meo argumento esse petitionem principii, ideò quia dixi istas hypotheses impias esse, hi homines autem istas hypotheses suas pro im-piis non habent.
units.tr: Secondly, I showed that they open a window to crass atheism through their doctrine of the Trinity, and indeed in two ways. 1. While they teach that the mystery of the Trinity has no use in itself. They try to evade this by the same imposture they used on this point in book 1, chapter 7, pretending that we urge the use of that mystery in so far as the Father, Son and Holy Spirit are three persons without any (as they put it here) relation or concept of the essence or divinity which they have in common; and they say they only deny this. Nothing can be said more brazenly and fraudulently, as we showed in the preceding book, chapter 7. Next, I showed that they open a window to atheism through their doctrine of the Trinity by another route, namely, that they do not hold those orthodox and well-known doctrines of the Trinity which the Antitrinitarian heretics attack to be necessary to salvation, etc. They reply in their usual imposture, as we saw above in book 1, chapter 7: they say they neither affirm nor deny their necessity. But this is mocking the world. It is enough for us that they do not hold these things to be necessary, and that they try to defend their impious doctrine by many arguments. And above we showed that the Arminians' suspension of judgment [ἐποχήν], or doubt, is of such a kind that they simply deny these things to be necessary at the same time. Next they attack the consequence of my argument, insisting that these doctrines be proved to be necessary. Since I had proved this by arguing that if those doctrines are not necessary, then the whole mystery falls, and therefore the whole Christian religion; which I showed from the fact that if these doctrines are not necessary, then according to the other hypotheses of the Arminians it is permitted to deny and attack the true sense of that mystery without danger to salvation, without the mark of heresy, without the crime of impiety; indeed, those who deny that sense ought to be held as members of the true Church. Here they retort that there is nothing absurd in these things, but that all of them are true, and they say that I, who hold them to be absurd, am talking nonsense; and they add that I am begging the question. Judge for yourself, pious reader, whether they do not with the greatest impudence say that there is a begging of the question in my argument, because I said that those impious hypotheses are impious, while these men do not hold their own hypotheses to be impious.

units.la: Et quia addideram ista dogmata orthodoxa seu istum sensum mysterii de Trinitate esse verum sensum, collapso autem vero sensu huius myste-rii ipsum mysterium perire; quia nullum verbum Dei, nullum myste-rium possit esse absque suo vero sensu. Illi respondent aliud esse verum sensum, aliud sensum necessarium. Quod primò ad rem non facit; sive e-nim sensus verus necessarius ad salutem sit sive non necessarius, collabi-tur utique illud ipsum cuius sensus est, modò verus sensus sit. Deinde falsum est hunc sensum non esse necessarium: nam si mysterium est ne-cessarium, certè etiam illius verus sensus est necessarius. Denique ad-dunt p. 192. nihil periculi esse etsi doctrina seu mysterium Trinitatis pereat, si sen-sus iste creditu necessarius non est. De quâ horrendâ impietate istorum ho-minum, quam etiam tradit in Thesibus suis privatis M. Episcopius, vidi-mus Par. II. lib. 1. c. 4.
units.tr: And because I had added that these orthodox doctrines, or this sense of the mystery of the Trinity, are the true sense, and that once the true sense of this mystery has collapsed, the mystery itself perishes, because no word of God and no mystery can exist without its true sense. They reply that the true sense is one thing, the necessary sense another. This is first of all beside the point. For whether the true sense is necessary to salvation or not, that of which it is the sense certainly falls, provided the sense is true. Next, it is false that this sense is not necessary; for if the mystery is necessary, certainly its true sense is also necessary. Finally, they add (p. 192) that there is no danger, even if the doctrine or mystery of the Trinity perishes, if that sense is not necessary to be believed. We saw in part II, book 1, chapter 4, the horrible impiety of these men, which M. Episcopius also sets out in his private Theses.

units.la: Utuntur postea p. 192. retorsione, quâ volunt evincere, eos Tyran-nidi & per Tyrannidem Atheismo latam portam aperire qui urgent ista dogmata ut necessaria ad salutem, & violatæ totius Religionis Christia-næ accusant eos qui ea non habent pro Necessariis. In quâ retorsione nobis pandunt nova quædam Arcana, quæ Par. III. lib. 2. c. 10. vidimus: præter falsitatem quâ dicunt me agnoscere mysterium illud prout con-troversum est inter nos & Antitrinitarios non esse ἀπρὸς in Scripturâ. id quod me dixisse in æternum non probabunt, etsi unum atque alterum terminum Antitrinitariis constringendis ab Ecclesiâ vetere primitùs adhibitum in câ ῥητῶς non inveniri haud negem. Quod aiunt me agnoscere id non reperiri in Scripturâ per consequentiam evidentem sensu Arminiano, verum est; sed nobis sufficit quòd illud in Scripturâ evidenter, clarè, & perspicuè reperitur evidentiâ tali quæ naturæ sacrarum literarum conveniens est, & ab omnibus credentibus sive orthodoxis, etiam ab ipsis hostibus convictis perspicuè deprehenditur.
units.tr: Afterwards, at p. 192, they use a counter-charge, by which they want to prove that those who press these doctrines as necessary to salvation open the door to tyranny, and through tyranny to atheism, and they accuse of violating the whole Christian religion those who do not hold them to be necessary. In this counter-charge they unfold some new secrets, which we saw in Part III, book 2, chapter 10. Besides the falsehood by which they say that I acknowledge that the mystery, as it is disputed between us and the Antitrinitarians, is not expressly stated in Scripture, they will never prove that I said this, although I do not deny that one or another term used by the ancient Church against the Antitrinitarians is not found expressly in Scripture. That they say I acknowledge it is not found in Scripture by an evident consequence in the Arminian sense is true; but it is enough for us that it is found in Scripture evidently, clearly and plainly, with an evidence suited to the nature of the sacred letters, and that it is plainly recognised by all believers, whether orthodox, and even by the enemies themselves when they are convinced.

units.la: 3. Tertium meum argumentum ex doctrinâ eorum de Evidentiâ petitum est, quam Evidentiam requirunt ad dogma aliquod necessarium constituendum. Postulant enim, dicebam, evidentiam talem, quæ omnibus obvia sit, quæ apud omnes in confesso sit, quam unusquisque, modo sanum sinciput habeat, agnoscat. Hinc dogmata quæ errantibus obvia non sunt ob affectum aliquem, quo præoccupati sunt, &c. negant evidentia simpliciter esse, sed dicunt, esse saltem tibi, mihi, evidentia. Hac ratione non solùm Hæreticis, sed etiam Atheis fenestram & portam patentissimam aperiri luce clarius meridianâ ostendi, non solùm rationibus claris & solidis, sed etiam ex ipsâ experientiâ p. 246. 247. 248. 249. 250. Ad quæ illi opponunt farraginem ingentem nugarum, quibus tredecim paginas replent, quæ omnes nituntur istâ insigni impostura, quâ supra lib. 1. cap. 8. Vindic. negârunt se docere dogmata Necessaria ita evidentia esse ut apud omnes in confesso sint. Unde hic dicunt p. 194. Certum est consequentias quasdam esse quæ per se evidentes & claræ sunt omnibus & singulis hominibus, quarum tamen evidentia in controversiam vocari potest ab iis quos præiudicio aut alio aliquo morbo animi laborare manifestum est, & allegant exemplum adorationis hostiæ. Verùm eos contra Apologiam suam disputare, quæ talia non habet pro evidentibus, nec non contra propriam suam conscientiam, patet ex iis quæ lib. 1. cap. 8. hujus Partis disseruimus. Unde jam prioribus imposturis aliam insignem addunt fraudulentiam. Etenim sciunt vim argumenti mei in his præcipuè verbis consistere, quibus dixi Arminianos evidentiam talem postulare quæ apud omnes in confesso sit; item, quam unusquisque, modo sanum sinciput habeat, agnoscat; item eos non habere pro simpliciter evidentibus ea quæ ob affectum aut præiudicium errantibus obvia non sunt, sed tantùm pro mihi, tibi evidentibus. Hic quia vident se iis verbis urgeri, ideo in recitatione argumenti mei omittunt ea, & suppriment per notulam quâ voces hæ duæ ET CÆTERA exprimi solent: atque ita formant argumentum meum p. 193. Qui ad constituendum necessarium aliquod dogma, docent docent necessariam esse evidentiam talem quæ omnibus obvia sit & illis verbis subjungunt notulam hanc, nimirum &c. eorum doctrina non solum quibuscunque Hæreticis, sed etiam Atheis senestram & portam bipatentem aperit. Ita formant argumentum. Deinde, ut eò tutius nugari & Lectori imponere possint, ne verbo quidem, in totâ istâ suâ futilissimâ & fusissimâ sophisticatione, meminerunt vocum illarum quas suppriment. Videat rursus honestus & candidus Lector, ex hac insigni fraude ac dolo, indolem atque ingenium horum hominum, & judicet an ne aliqua honestas & conscientia in iis reliqua sit. ô plene omni dolo, dicebat Paulus Act. 13.10. Pudeat eos atque iterum pudeat! Sic igitur concidunt omnes illæ operosissimæ nugæ, una cum calumniosa retorsione illorum, quâ inferre volunt & impingere nobis Atheismum ex nostrâ doctrinâ quam illorum impiæ doctrinæ de evidentiâ oppositimus.
units.tr: 3. My third argument is drawn from their doctrine of evidence, which they require in order to establish any doctrine as necessary. For, I said, they demand such evidence as is open to all, which is admitted by all, and which everyone recognises provided he has a sound head. Hence doctrines which are not open to those in error, because of some affection by which they are preoccupied, and so on, they deny to be evident simply, but say they are evident at least to you, or to me. I showed, in a manner clearer than midday light, that by this reasoning a very wide window and door are opened not only to heretics but even to atheists, not only by clear and solid arguments but also from experience itself, at pp. 246–250. To this they oppose a huge heap of trifles, with which they fill thirteen pages, all of which rest on that notable imposture by which, in book 1, chapter 8 of the Vindication, they denied that they teach that the necessary doctrines are so evident that they are admitted by all. Hence here they say at p. 194: It is certain that there are some consequences which are evident and clear in themselves to all and to each man, yet whose evidence may be called in question by those who are manifestly suffering from prejudice or some other disease of the mind, and they cite the example of the adoration of the host. But that they dispute against their own Apology, which does not count such things as evident, and also against their own conscience, is plain from what we discussed in book 1, chapter 8 of this Part. Hence they now add another notable fraud to their earlier impostures. For they know that the force of my argument lies especially in these words, in which I said that the Arminians demand such evidence as is admitted by all; likewise, which everyone recognises provided he has a sound head; likewise that they do not hold as simply evident those things which, because of affection or prejudice, are not open to those in error, but only as evident to me or to you. Since they see themselves pressed by these words, in reciting my argument they leave them out, and suppress them by the little mark with which the words ET CAETERA are usually indicated; and so they frame my argument at p. 193 thus: Those who, in order to establish some doctrine as necessary, teach that evidence is necessary such as is open to all, and to these words they add this little mark, namely &c.: their doctrine opens a window and a double-open door not only to any heretics but even to atheists. That is how they frame the argument. Then, so that they may trifle more safely and deceive the reader, in the whole of that most futile and most prolix sophistry they do not so much as mention, even by a word, the words they have suppressed. Let the honest and candid reader again see from this notable fraud and deceit the character and disposition of these men, and judge whether any honesty and conscience remain in them. O full of all deceit, Paul said (Acts 13:10). Let them be ashamed, and again ashamed! Thus all those laborious trifles collapse, together with their slanderous counter-charge, by which they wish to bring atheism upon us from our doctrine, which we set against their impious doctrine of evidence.

units.la: 4. Quartum argumentum meum est p. 151. desumtum ex eo quod non contenti Libertatem prophetandi extendere ad ea quæ controversa sunt, extendunt etiam ad ea quæ in futurum controverti possunt, & ex necessariorum dogmatum censu eximunt omnia ea. Hic, quia aliter evadere non possunt, recurrunt ad alteram illam consuetam sibi fraudem & impostorem, quâ negant se in Apologiâ suâ ita de Necessariis docere ut eorum censu omnia controversa eximant. Sed eos id contra conscientiam suam negare supra est ostensum. Et tamen hi homines audent dicere p. 206. 207. Videlius fatentur ex ipsis Remonstrantium verbis constare, controversa omnia ad quæ Remonstrantes libertatem prophetandi extendunt ea tantum esse, quæ non sunt scitu ac creditu necessaria. Quæ quidem summa impudentia est, ne quid gravius dicam. Nec enim vola nec vestigium illius rei est ibi loci, imò in totâ primâ parte Arcanorum. Sed contrà ubique hoc ago & urgeo, ac perpetuo de hoc conqueror, quòd docent nulla dogmata controversa esse necessaria scitu ac creditu ad salutem. Et quidem hoc non semel repeto in isto ipso capite de quo jam quæstio est. Unde rursus de candore & honestate horum hominum unusquisque judicet, qui tamen ita pravi sunt, ut me eo nomine audeant hic frontis perfrictæ arguere & aliis convitiis petere.
units.tr: 4. My fourth argument, at p. 151, is taken from the fact that they are not content to extend liberty of prophesying to those things which are controverted, but extend it also to those which may be controverted in the future, and exclude all such things from the list of necessary doctrines. Here, since they cannot otherwise escape, they have recourse to their usual other fraud and imposture, by which they deny that in their Apology they teach about the necessary things in such a way as to exclude from their number all the controverted matters. But that they deny this against their own conscience has been shown above. And yet these men dare to say at pp. 206–207: They more freely confess that it is clear from the very words of the Remonstrants that all the controverted matters to which the Remonstrants extend liberty of prophesying are only those which are not necessary to be known and believed. This is indeed great impudence, not to say anything harsher. For there is neither trace nor vestige of that thing in that place, indeed in the whole first part of the Arcana. On the contrary, everywhere I labour at this point and constantly complain of it, that they teach that no controverted doctrines are necessary to be known and believed for salvation. And indeed I repeat this not once in this very chapter which is now under discussion. Hence let each man again judge of the candour and honesty of these men, who are nevertheless so perverse that they dare here to accuse me, on that account, of brazen-faced impudence and to attack me with other insults.

units.la: Quod autem ad id probandum, nimirum se non extendere libertatem prophetandi ad controversa necessaria ad salutem, allegant Apolog. f. 283. ubi dicunt se à libertate prophetandi excipere ea quæ clarè ac perpicuè definita sunt in verbo Dei: id merus fucus est. Constat enim Apologiam per ea quæ clara ac perspicuè definita sunt in verbo Dei intelligere quæ apud omnes apud omnes in confesso sunt, ut ostendi Par. I. lib 1. cap. 6. & hac Par. IV. lib. 1. cap. 8.
units.tr: As for proving this point, namely that they do not extend liberty of prophesying to controverted matters necessary to salvation, they cite their Apology, f. 283, where they say that they exclude from liberty of prophesying those things which are clearly and plainly defined in the Word of God. This is mere pretence. For it is established that by the things clearly and plainly defined in the Word of God the Apology understands those which are admitted by all, as I showed in Part I, book 1, chapter 6, and in this Part IV, book 1, chapter 8.

units.la: Porrò, hoc non contenti isti homines, ut Lectori fucum magis faciant, abutuntur candore meo quo usus sum dum p. 252. dixi: Erfi Remonstrantes controversias quae hodie INTER CHRISTIANOS COETUS agitantur aut in futurum agitari possunt, non necessarias esse statuant; tamen fatentur fieri posse ut quis qui Christianus videri vult etiam Necessaria in dubium vocet, & allegavi verba eorum ex Apol. c. 1. sol. 32. a. Exinde volunt mihi homines pag. 207. impudentiae arguere, quod toties sibi objeeerim,'quod statuant nulla dogmata esse Necessaria quae inter Christianos controversa sunt aut controverti possunt. Sed in hac re profecto contra conscientiam suam faciunt. Etenim expresse dixi Arminianos ita docere de dogmatis illis veris quae controversa sunt aut controverti possunt inter COETUS CHRISTIANOS, non autem de iis quae hic aut ille Atheus aut nebulo negare potest, qui coetus publicos facere non possunt, quia ut Athei in coetus convenirent hactenus princeps aut Magistratus nullus permisit. Et ut magis videas, optime Lector, verum esse quod dico, nimirum eos contra conscientiam suam mihi injuriam facere, ipsi fatentur p. 208. me distinguere inter coetus Christianos, & unum aut alterum hominem: ut hic excipias, inquiunt, distinctione aliqua inter coetus Christianos, & Christianum quemlibet; quaecunque ab illis in controversiam vocantur aut vocari possunt ea non esse necessaria, at a particulari aliquo Christiano necessaria in dubium vocari posse &c. Ubi quod dicunt me excepturum distinctione ista inter coetus Christianos &c. id etiam summa protervia est: cum jam ibi expresse dixerim Arminianos distinguere ea ratione. Adeoque quod addunt stultam esse distinctionem istam, & me ideo Anticyras ablegant; in iis non mihi sed sibi convitia dicunt, quorum haec distinctio & doctrina est. Et, ut eo magis videant injustitiam suam; alibi etiam inter coetus Christianos & inter singulos Christianos distinguunt in materia de controversis: & profitentur aliquid in controversiam posse vocari a singulis Christianis, quod extra controversiam fuit semper in tota Ecclesia. Nam cum Cll. Theoll. Proff. Leyd. in Excerptis suis ipsis objecissent, quod inter fundamenta Christianismi hactenus in Ecclesia positum fuerit, Christum ex semine mulieris immediate, ex semine Davidis mediate natum esse secundum Scripturam: Respondent illi in Resp. ad Excep. p. 50. Ecclesiam semper credidisse Christum ex substantia matris sua conceptum ac natum esse, non modo non negant Remonstrantes, sed & firmiter credunt. An omnes id semper crediderint Christiani stiani quis dixerit? ut ostendant non omnes Christianos id credidisse, asse-runt ibidem exemplum, non coetus alicujus aut diversorum coetuū Christianorum, sed Hilarii quem dicunt VIDERI sentire Mariam praeter concipiendi, gestandi, pariendi ministerium nihil contulisse de suo ad corpus Christi.
units.tr: Furthermore, not content with this, these men, in order to make more of a show of deceit before the reader, abuse the candour with which I wrote at p. 252, where I said: Since the Remonstrants hold that the controversies which are today debated, or may be debated in the future, among CHRISTIAN ASSEMBLIES are not necessary; yet they confess that it can happen that someone who wishes to be regarded as a Christian may call even necessary things in doubt, and I cited their words from Apol. c. 1, sol. 32 a. From this, the men wish to accuse me at p. 207 of impudence, because I have so often objected to them that they hold that no doctrines are necessary which are controverted among Christians or may be controverted. But in this matter they surely act against their own conscience. For I expressly said that the Arminians teach this of those true doctrines which are controverted, or may be controverted, among CHRISTIAN ASSEMBLIES, and not of those which this or that atheist or scoundrel may deny, who cannot hold public assemblies, since hitherto no prince or magistrate has permitted atheists to meet. And that you may see more clearly, best reader, that what I say is true, namely that they do me wrong against their own conscience, they themselves confess at p. 208 that I distinguish between Christian assemblies and one or another man: you exempt, they say, by some distinction between Christian assemblies and any Christian whatever; whatever things are called in question or may be called in question by them, these are not necessary, but by some particular Christian they may be called in doubt as necessary, etc. Where they say that I shall except by that distinction between Christian assemblies, etc., this too is the height of shamelessness, since I had already said there expressly that the Arminians distinguish in that way. And so, when they add that this distinction is foolish, and therefore send me off to Anticyra, they are speaking insults not to me but to themselves, whose distinction and doctrine this is. And, to make their injustice the more evident, they also elsewhere distinguish, on controverted matters, between Christian assemblies and individual Christians, and they profess that something may be called in controversy by individual Christians which has always been outside controversy in the whole Church. For when the most learned Professors of Leiden in their Excerpts had objected to them that among the foundations of Christianity hitherto established in the Church is this: that Christ was born immediately of the seed of the woman and mediately of the seed of David, according to Scripture, they replied in their Answer to the Exceptions, p. 50: The Remonstrants not only do not deny but firmly believe that the Church has always believed that Christ was conceived and born of the substance of his mother. Who would say that all Christians have always believed this? To show that not all Christians believed it, they cite in the same place not an example from any assembly or from different assemblies of Christians, but that of Hilary, who, they say, SEEMS to hold that Mary contributed nothing of her own to the body of Christ beyond the ministry of conceiving, bearing and giving birth.

units.la: Praetereo quòd p. 207. rursus adeò protervi sunt, ut audeant conscientiam meam appellare, & plurimis convitiis in me debacchari, quòd dixerim eos fateri, fieri posse ut quis ea in dubium vocet quae necessaria sunt: cùm tamen ipsi ibidem conceptis verbis dicant, Remonstrantes fateri quidem necessaria in dubium vocari posse; & ego nullâ aliâ mente nec sensu id ipsis tribuerim, quàm eo quo fatentur se id dicere, ut unusquisque videre potest.
units.tr: I pass over the fact that on p. 207 they are so shameless as to appeal to my conscience and rage against me with many insults, because I said they admit that someone may call into doubt things that are necessary. Yet they themselves say there, in so many words, The Remonstrants admit that necessary things may indeed be called into doubt; and I could not have attributed this to them in any other mind or sense than the one they themselves profess, as anyone can see.

units.la: 5. Quintò dixeram p. 252. eos fenestram aperire Atheismo crasso, dum eos quos pro Haereticis tota Ecclesia Christiana habet, excusant ideò, quòd si ἀδίνατα moveant h. e. Necessaria oppugnent, id imprudenter faciant, Apolo. c. 24. f. 274. b. Unde inferebam, Atheum suppeditatam habere sibi excusationem, se scilicet per imprudentiam Necessaria ad salutem evertere. Hoc est meum argumentum. Respondent illi p. 208. 209. cum convitiis more solito, se per ἀδίνατα non intelligere necessaria, sed quae necessaria esse videntur, etiamsi non necessaria sint, imò plane falsa, & quę moveri ac in dubium vocari aut oppugnari universae Christianitatis interest. Et dicunt hoc esse manifestum ex antecedentibus & consequentibus, eoque uno manifestissimè, quod in eodem Apologiæ folio dicunt ἀδίνατα tàm clarè ac dilucidè definita esse à Deo vt à nemine sine divina veritatis contemtu negari possint aut in dubium vocari. Adeoque dicunt me falsò supponere ἀδίνατα movere & necessaria oppugnare Remonstrantibus unum idemque esse. Hic fidem tuam appello, candide Lector, & dijudicandum tibi relinquo, an non rursus hi homines contra conscientiam suam loquantur? verba quae citavi loco de quo quaestio est, clara sunt haec, capite allegato Apologiæ: Mirum est Censores hos usque adeò sollicitè coercitionem eorum (de Haereticis sermo est) urgere qui si ἀδίνατα κινῶσι non nisi imprudenter & per errorem purum id faciunt: cùm de coercendis per Magistratum iis qui praecepta Iesu Christi de industriâ & debit à liber à voluntate quotidie violant, &c. ne cogitent quidem. Notum est autem tibi, Lector optime, quod ἀδίνατα κινεῖ fit nimirum movere quae moveri non debent, quâ Phrasi Cll. D.D. Proff. Leydd. usi erant in Censurâ Confessionis, dicentes: Arminianos libertatem prophetandi extendere velle etiam ad eos qui ἀδίνατα κινοῦσι qui non movenda movent, i. e. qui in controversiam vocant ea quae in controversiam vocanda canda aut quæ oppugnanda non sunt. Quis non videt aliud esse ἀκίνητα & aliud quæ ἀκίνητα non sunt sed videntur, seu aliud esse, movere ea quæ movenda non sunt, & aliud movere ea quæ movenda esse non videntur? Quæ igitur audacia est, cum dixeris: Hæreticos movere ea ἀκίνητα, interpretari id per ea quæ ἀκίνητα videntur? Et ut res clarior etiam, seu potius certior fiat, consídera verba istorum hominum à me allegata, & ea compara cum responso eorum, & luce clarius meridiana videbis, malam fidem & conscientiam horum hominum. Dicunt verbis à me allegatis: Hæretici si ἀκίνητα κινῶσι imprudenter & per errorem purum putum id faciunt. Quod si hoc verum est, quâ igitur conscientiâ dicere possunt, se per ἀκίνητα intelligere ea quæ ἀκίνητα seu necessaria esse videntur, & tamen revera non sunt talia, sed sunt non necessaria, imò etiam plane falsa &c. Certè si Hæretici talia ἀκίνητα movent, quæ non sunt revera ἀκίνητα sed non necessaria imò falsa, non possunt dici imprudenter & per errorem ea movere, sed dicendi sunt prudenter, & rectè, sive veritate ita postulante atque ex præscripto verbi divini agere. Quod dicunt idem patere ex antecedentibus & consequentibus, illud quoque falsum est. Nam in iis semper per τὰ ἀκίνητα intelligunt ea quæ necessaria revera sunt, nisi quando expresse ibi addunt, interdum quædam ἀκίνητα videri, censeri, seu credi, ut à Pontificiis, quæ ἀκίνητα non sunt: prout patet ex iis ipsis verbis quæ contra me allegant: Qui ἀκίνητα κινῶσι &c. & omnibus sequentibus in eo sol. 275. a.
units.tr: 5. Fifthly, I had said on p. 252 that they open a window to gross atheism, since they excuse those whom the whole Christian Church holds to be heretics, on the ground that if they stir the unmovable things [ἀκίνητα], that is, attack necessary things, they do so imprudently, Apol. c. 24, f. 274 b. From this I inferred that the atheist has an excuse ready to hand, namely that through imprudence he overturns the necessary things of salvation. This is my argument. On pp. 208 and 209 they reply, with their usual insults, that by the unmovable things [ἀκίνητα] they do not mean necessary things, but things that seem necessary even if they are not, indeed things that are plainly false, and which it concerns the whole of Christianity to have moved, called into doubt or attacked. They say this is clear from what precedes and what follows, and most clearly from the same page of their Apology, where they say that the unmovable things [ἀκίνητα] have been defined by God so clearly and plainly that no one can deny or call them into doubt without contempt for the divine truth. Hence they say I falsely assume that moving the unmovable things [ἀκίνητα] and attacking necessary things are one and the same for the Remonstrants. Here I appeal to your good faith, kind reader, and leave it to you to judge whether these men are not again speaking against their own conscience. The words I quoted from the passage in question are clear, and they stand in the chapter of the Apology I cited: It is remarkable that these Censors press so eagerly for the restraint of those (the heretics are meant) who, if they stir the unmovable things [ἀκίνητα], do so only imprudently and through sheer error, when the question is of restraining by the magistrate those who deliberately and of their own free will violate the precepts of Jesus Christ every day, etc.; they do not even think of this. You know well, best reader, that stirring the unmovable things [ἀκίνητα] means, of course, moving what ought not to be moved. The learned Doctors and Professors of Leiden used this phrase in their Censure of the Confession, saying: The Arminians wish to extend the freedom of preaching even to those who stir the unmovable things [ἀκίνητα], who move what should not be moved, that is, who call into controversy what should not be called into controversy, or what should not be attacked. Who does not see that the unmovable things [ἀκίνητα] are one thing, and things which are not unmovable but seem so are another, or that moving what ought not to be moved is one thing, and moving what does not seem to be movable is another? What audacity is it, then, when you say that heretics move the unmovable things [ἀκίνητα], to interpret this as meaning things that seem unmovable? And to make the matter clearer, or rather more certain, consider the words of these men that I quoted, compare them with their reply, and you will see the bad faith and conscience of these men more clearly than daylight at noon. They say, in the words I quoted: If heretics stir the unmovable things [ἀκίνητα], they do so imprudently and through pure error. If this is true, with what conscience can they say that by the unmovable things [ἀκίνητα] they mean things that seem to be unmovable, but in fact are not such, being rather non-necessary or even plainly false, etc.? Certainly, if heretics move unmovable things that are not really unmovable but non-necessary or even false, they cannot be said to move them imprudently and through error; they must be said to act prudently and rightly, since the truth so requires and they act in accordance with the prescription of the divine Word. That they say this also appears from what precedes and what follows: that too is false. For in those passages they always understand by the unmovable things [τὰ ἀκίνητα] the things that really are necessary, except where they expressly add that certain things seem, or are judged or believed, to be unmovable, as by the Papists, when they are not unmovable; as is clear from the very words they cite against me: Those who stir the unmovable things [ἀκίνητα], etc., and from all that follows on p. 275 a.

units.la: At, inquiunt, se expresse in præcedentibus dicere Hæreticos non movere ἀκίνητα: quomodo igitur loco à me citato potest credi quòd voluerint dicere Hæreticos movere ἀκίνητα? Respondere possem, mihi non posse præjudicare si sibi contradicant homines malam causam tuentes, & nullius fidei. Sed id in præsentiarum dicere nolo: agam enim candidè perpetuò. Nec enim ibi ulla contradictio est: nam in loco à me allegato, non dicunt Hæreticos movere ἀκίνητα sed qui si ἀκίνητα movent, adeóque loquuntur ex posito sed non concesso, quasi dicant posito sed non concesso eos movere ἀκίνητα, cogitandum est eos imprudenter & per errorem purum putum id facere. Deinde falsum est, ut diximus, eos movere ἀκίνητα, nam qui ἀκίνητα movent pejores sunt Hæreticis &c. Hæc est genuina mens horum hominum.
units.tr: But, they say, they expressly stated in what precedes that heretics do not move the unmovable things [ἀκίνητα]; how then can it be believed from the passage I cited that they meant to say that heretics move the unmovable things [ἀκίνητα]? I could reply that I cannot be blamed if men who defend a bad cause and have no credibility contradict themselves. But I do not wish to say that at present, for I shall proceed with candour throughout. There is in fact no contradiction here. For in the passage I cited they do not say that heretics move the unmovable things [ἀκίνητα]; they say if they move the unmovable things [ἀκίνητα], and so they speak hypothetically, not concessively, as if they said: granting, but not conceding, that they move the unmovable things [ἀκίνητα], we must think that they do so imprudently and through pure error. Then it is false, as we have said, that they move the unmovable things [ἀκίνητα], for those who move the unmovable things [ἀκίνητα] are worse than heretics, etc. This is the true mind of these men.

units.la: Porrò quòd dicunt, me falsò sumere hanc hypothesin, quasi Remonstrantibus unum & idem sint ἀκίνητα & necessaria, in eo contra conscientiam suam me falsitatis arguunt. Id quod ex eâ insigni fraudulentiâ eorum proficiscitur, quâ negant se docere in Apologiâ: Nulla controversia inter inter Christianos esse necessaria ad salutem, & dicunt jam, se quaedam necessaria agnoscere quae controversa sunt. Itaque, secundum doctrinam Vindiciarum, Necessaria & ἀδιάφορα non sunt unum & idem, sed necessaria latius patent quam ἀδιάφορα: Nam sic omnia, ἀδιάφορα sunt necessaria, sed non omnia necessaria sunt ἀδιάφορα, ut patet speciatim ex cap.8. Vindic. lib. 1. p. 47. secundum doctrinam autem Apologiae ἀδιάφορα & necessaria sunt Synonyma, quia in ea illa tantum docent esse Necessaria ad salutem quae apud omnes in confesso sunt, seu extra Controversiam posita. Quod si igitur jam, ex quo primam Partem Arcanorum legerunt, ἀδιάφορα & necessaria ipsis amplius non sunt idem; id vero non me falsitatis, sed ipsos turpissimae levitatis & malae causae arguit, ac vi veritatis a me constrictos & convictos eo redactos esse docet, ut non solum sibi contradicere, sed etiam propriam doctrinam suam contra conscientiam suam negare coacti sint, ut possent malam causam tueri, in quae defendenda contra propriae conscientiae dictamen persistere volunt. Et tamen audent hi homines hoc loco p. 209. ut simplicioribus imponant, me stuporis & ineptiarum arguere ob hoc quintum argumentum meum. Pudeat ipsos.
units.tr: Furthermore, when they say that I falsely assume this hypothesis, as if for the Remonstrants the unmovable things [ἀκίνητα] and necessary things were one and the same, they accuse me of falsehood against their own conscience. This comes from that notable fraud of theirs, by which they deny that they teach in the Apology: No controversy among Christians concerns things necessary to salvation, and now they say that they acknowledge certain necessary things that are controverted. Accordingly, according to the teaching of the Vindiciae, necessary and adiaphora [ἀδιάφορα] are not one and the same; necessary things extend more widely than adiaphora [ἀδιάφορα]. For all adiaphora [ἀδιάφορα] are necessary, but not all necessary things are adiaphora [ἀδιάφορα], as is clear especially from ch. 8 of the first book of the Vindiciae, p. 47. But according to the teaching of the Apology, adiaphora [ἀδιάφορα] and necessary things are synonyms, because there they teach that only those things are necessary to salvation which are admitted by all, or placed beyond controversy. If, then, since they read the first part of the Arcana, adiaphora [ἀδιάφορα] and necessary things are no longer the same for them, this does not prove me false but proves them most shameful in their levity and in their bad cause; it shows that they have been forced by the power of truth, constrained and convicted by me, to the point where they are compelled not only to contradict themselves but also to deny their own doctrine against their own conscience, so that they may defend a bad cause, which they are determined to maintain against the dictate of their own conscience. And yet these men dare, on this point, p. 209, to charge me, to deceive simpler readers, with stupidity and folly for this fifth argument of mine. Let them be ashamed.

units.la: 6. Sextum meum argumentum nititur ea hypothesi Arminianorum, qua permittunt in dubium vocare omnes sensus qui obscuriores sunt, & varias aut abstrusiores interpretationes admittunt. Unde intuli non solum Haereticis, sed etiam Atheis fenestram aperiri oppugnandi omnia dogmata necessaria. Etenim nullus locus est adeo aut manifestus, qui non obscuritatis praetextu, aut quod sensus varios & abstrusiores admittat, depravari possit, prout experientia testatur vetus & moderna. Nec valet exceptio: locos illos claros esse, & non admittere aliam interpretationem. Responsionem enim jam sibi suppeditatam habet a Remonstrantibus TIBI NON MIHI. Hoc est argumentum meum. Hic responsionis loco Arminiani quinque paginas variis nugis replent, quae eo redeunt 1. se expresse distinguere loca clara sua luce & quae interpretatione non egent a locis obscuris p. 210. 2. me statuere nullum Scripturae locum esse adeo clarum ac manifestum, qui non sensus varios & abstrusiores admittat, & hic omnes Christianos testes contra me vocant: Hic iam ego, inquiunt, Christianos omnes testor p. 211. 3. probare me debuisse nullos locos Scripturae sua luce claros esse, non autem debuisse probare, praetexti illud posse ab Atheis, ibid. 4. falsum esse quod dixi Haereticos omnia loca Scripturae obscura credidisse, aut obscurare voluisse imo obscurasse. nam nullum unquam Haereticum repertum qui obscurum esse dixerit Fures, adulteros, homicidas &c. aliosque legirupas non ingressuros in regnum gnum cœlorum &c. sine fide impossibile esse ut placeamus Deo ; Fidem in Iesum Christum esse necessariam ad salutem, aliaque huiusmodi infinita. Et sic falsum est, inquiunt p. 212. quod Vedelius ait, omnes Scriptura locos ab Haereticis depravatos fuisse aut depravari posse sub praetextu obscuritatis, aut quod varios & retrusiores sensus admittant. Id enim de sensibus illis, quos verba immediate & quidem nulla figura aut tropo vestita prae se ferunt salsissimum est. Quin alia loca licet suâ luce clara depravaverint, dubitari non posse ; sed depravationis causam dicunt non esse defectum claritatis locorum ipsorum, sed vel affectum aliquem carnalem, vel hypothesin quandam falsam, & afferunt exemplum Pontificiorum p. 213. Denique p. 214. utuntur retorsione contra me, quâ inferunt me hoc argumento meo portam amplissimam aperire Atheismo crasso, quia dico nullum locum Scripturae adeo clarum ac manifestum esse, quam Atheus praetextu obscuritatis, aut quod varios aut abstrusiores sensus admittat, depravare non possit. Ratio consequentiae : quia sic Atheus nullam causam habet deserendi Atheismum suum. Probant : Quomodo enim, aut qua gravi ratione adductus, credet Scripturam istam a Deo profectam esse, tanquam indubitatam ac certam sensus omnis ac cultus divini sive fidei & vitae normam, cujus sensus omnes in universum obscuri sive non clari & manifesti sint &c. Repugnare hoc sapientiae, bonitati, justitiae Dei si Scriptura obscure iubeat, clare & manifeste non doceat, si sensus omnes Scriptura obscuri sint &c.
units.tr: 6. My sixth argument rests on the Arminian hypothesis by which they allow all senses that are more obscure to be called into doubt, and admit various or more abstruse interpretations. From this I inferred that a window is opened not only to heretics but also to atheists for attacking all necessary doctrines. For there is no passage so plain that it cannot be corrupted under the pretext of obscurity, or because it admits various and more abstruse senses, as ancient and modern experience attests. Nor does the exception hold: that those passages are clear and admit no other interpretation. For the atheist has such a reply already supplied by the Remonstrants TO YOU, NOT TO ME. This is my argument. Here, by way of reply, the Arminians fill five pages with various trifles, which come down to this: (1) they expressly distinguish passages clear in their own light and not needing interpretation from obscure passages, p. 210; (2) I maintain that there is no passage of Scripture so clear and manifest that it does not admit various and more abstruse senses, and here they call all Christians to witness against me: Here I now, they say, call all Christians to witness, p. 211; (3) I ought to have proved that no passages of Scripture are clear in their own light, not merely that the atheist could use this pretext, ibid.; (4) it is false that I said heretics believed, or wished to obscure, or indeed did obscure, all the obscure passages of Scripture; for no heretic has ever been found who said that thieves, adulterers, murderers, etc., and others of that kind will not enter the kingdom of heaven, etc., that without faith it is impossible to please God, that faith in Jesus Christ is necessary to salvation, and countless other things of this sort. And so, they say, p. 212, it is false what Vedelius asserts, that all passages of Scripture have been corrupted by heretics, or can be corrupted under the pretext of obscurity, or because they admit various and more abstruse senses. For this is utterly false of those senses which the words put forward immediately and clothed in no figure or trope. Indeed, though they have corrupted other passages that are clear in their own light, it cannot be doubted; but they say the cause of the corruption is not a lack of clarity in the passages themselves, but either some carnal affection or some false hypothesis, and they cite the example of the Papists, p. 213. Finally, on p. 214 they turn the argument back against me, inferring that by this argument of mine I open the widest door to gross atheism, because I say that no passage of Scripture is so clear and manifest that the atheist cannot corrupt it under the pretext of obscurity, or because it admits various or more abstruse senses. The reasoning is this: because thus the atheist has no reason to abandon his atheism. They prove it thus: For how, or moved by what serious reason, will he believe that this Scripture came from God, as an indubitable and certain norm of all sense and of all divine worship, or of faith and life, if all its senses are in general obscure, or not clear and manifest, etc.? It would be inconsistent with the wisdom, goodness and justice of God if Scripture commanded obscurely and did not teach clearly and manifestly, if all the senses of Scripture were obscure, etc.

units.la: Paucis respondeo. Ad primum quod attinet, quis non videt me praeoccupasse & praevenisse exceptionem istam his meis verbis p. 254. Nec valet exceptio : locos illos claros esse, & non admittere aliam interpretationem. Responsionem enim sibi suppeditatam habet Atheus à Remonstrantibus : TIBI NON MIHI. Viderunt hoc & legerunt Arminiani. Cur non respon-derunt ad hoc? Cur sicco pede praeterierunt? Causa est, quia ista sententia Arminianorum quâ responsum illud suppeditant (exstat autem Apolog. c. 24. f. 286) arguit malam fidem eorum & conscientiam, quâ audent negare se docere in Apologiâ de evidentiâ Necessariorum ea quae conceptis verbis ibi docent. Secundum calumniosum est. Non enim dixi Scripturae nullum locum esse, qui non sensus varios & abstrusiores admittat. Expressè enim dixi nullum Scripturae locum esse adeo clarum ac manifestum, qui non obscuritatis praetextu aut quod sensus varios & abstrusiores admittat, depravari possit. PRAETEXI dixi posse obscuritatem, aut quod sensus varios & abstrusiores admittat. Hanc calumniam ipsi vident; itaque, postquam refutassent doctrinam illam quam mihi calumniose affingunt, objiciunt sibi ipsis: De obscuritatis praetextu loquitur quitur Vedelius, inquies. Et respondent. Nihil minus, inquam. Addit enim; aut quòd varios & abstrusiores sensus admittat. Hic rursus quis non videt, eos fraudulenter agere, cùm vocem pratextus ab illis verbis(aut quod varios & abstrusiores sensus admittat) separant? Quis non videt me vocem pratextus æque ad posteriora illa verba quàm ad voce obscuritatis referre? Pudeat hos impostores: qui ipsi vident, quàm frivolum sit sophisma hoc. Itaque addunt: Deinde aliud est pratextus obscuritatis, aliud obscuritas. Probandum erat Vedelio &c. Vide jam, optime Lector, conscientiam horum hominum, qui apertæ & manifestæ suæ fraudis testes audent appellare omnes Christianos.
units.tr: I answer briefly. As for the first point, who does not see that I anticipated this objection in these words of mine on p. 254: Nor is the objection valid, that those passages are clear and do not admit any other interpretation. For the atheist has been supplied with an answer by the Remonstrants: TO YOU, NOT TO ME. The Arminians saw this and read it. Why did they not reply to it? Why did they pass over it without a word? The reason is that this Arminian opinion, by which they supply that answer (it stands in the Apology, ch. 24, f. 286), shows their bad faith and conscience, in that they dare to deny that they teach in the Apology on the evidence of the necessary truths what they there teach in so many words. The second point is slanderous. I did not say that there is no passage of Scripture which does not admit various and more obscure senses. What I said expressly is that there is no passage of Scripture so clear and manifest that it cannot be distorted on the pretext of obscurity, or because it admits various and more obscure senses. I wrote pretext, and said that obscurity, or the admitting of various and more obscure senses, could be the pretext. They themselves see this slander. So, after refuting the doctrine they falsely attribute to me, they object to themselves: Vedelius, you will say, speaks of a pretext of obscurity. And they reply: "Not at all, I say. For he adds: or because it admits various and more obscure senses." Here again, who does not see that they act fraudulently, when they separate the word pretext from those words (or because it admits various and more obscure senses)? Who does not see that I refer the word pretext equally to those latter words as to the word obscurity? Let these impostors be ashamed; they themselves see how frivolous this sophism is. So they add: Next, a pretext of obscurity is one thing, obscurity another. Vedelius had to prove, and so on. Now consider, excellent reader, the conscience of these men, who dare to appeal to all Christians as witnesses of their own plain and manifest fraud.

units.la: Ad tertium respondeo, me id probare non debuisse, quod ex meâ mente & scopo non est, & quod nunquam docui, nunquam sensi. Et ad id quod de prætextu dicunt eum nullâ ratione niti: respondi loco eo de quo quæstio est, præoccupando, eum niti doctrinâ Arminianorum docentium ea non esse simpliciter evidentia quæ tibi, non mihi evidentia sunt.
units.tr: As for the third point, I answer that I ought not to have proved what is not my meaning or purpose, and what I never taught and never held. As for their claim that the pretext has no basis at all, I answered it in advance at the passage in question, by showing that it rests on the Arminian doctrine that those things are not simply evident which are evident to you, but not to me.

units.la: Quartum impertinens est. Non enim dixi Hæreticos corrupisse omnia loca Scripturæ clarissima, prætextu obscuritatis (quamvis si hoc dixissem verum dixissem) sed posse illud contingere. Id quod ostendi experientiâ multorum clarissimorum Scripturæ locorum quæ corruperunt actu. Unde sequitur, id etiam aliis clarissimis Scripturæ locis contingere posse. Parium enim eadem est ratio. Exempla quod attinet, posset sufficere quoddixi modò, nimirum si corrupta nondum sunt illa dogmata, posse corrumpi in futurum. Sed nec experientia deest. Nam quod adulteros & fornicatores attinet, refert Alphonsus de Castro Martinum de Magistris docuisse, fornicationem non esse peccatum, quia testimonia Scripturæ non sint de eâ re expressa. Id quod testatur homo Pontificius de Pontificio. Et nôrunt qui rerum Gallicarum periti sunt Monachum Cahierium docuisse, non prohiberi præcepto septimo adulterium, sed vocem Hebraicam alio modo exponendam esse. Libertini, contra quos Magnus ille servus Dei Calvinus calamum fortissimè strinxit, docebant nullas actiones lege Dei prohibitas, ut furta, adulteria, esse peccata: nam peccatum esse tantùm opinionem. Unde etiam patet falsò dixisse supra Arminianos p. 198.199. nunquam Diabolum per quemquam studuisse detorquere sensum istum: infideles, impii quâ tales sine poenitentiâ salvari non possunt. Quis enim non videt Libertinos eum detorsisse, imò quantum in se erat, evertisse? Dogmata de fide quod attinet: ipsi Arminiani negare non possunt esse corrupta variè; sed hoc boni hi viri vocant; varie sentire de expositionibus terminorum. Et quæso an'non illi corrumpunt dogmata illa,imò evertunt funditùs, qui audent docere: Eos colere verum Deum qui colunt eum qui non est Pater Filius Spiritus Sanctus: Christum commendâsse Religionem modernam Iudæorum tanquam divinam: Deficientes à Christianismo ad Iudaismum persistere in cultu veri Dei? Quod dicunt alia loca luce suâ clara corrumpi posse ob affectum aut præjudicium aliquod id verum quidem est; sed re pugnat ipsorum doctrinæ: nam in Apologia docent talia non esse simpliciter evidentia.
units.tr: The fourth point is irrelevant. I did not say that the heretics have corrupted all the clearest passages of Scripture on the pretext of obscurity (although, if I had said it, I would have said truly), but that this could happen. I showed this from the experience of many of the clearest passages of Scripture which they have actually corrupted. From this it follows that the same could happen to other very clear passages of Scripture too, for the reason is the same for like cases. As for examples, what I have just said would be enough, namely that doctrines not yet corrupted can be corrupted in future. But experience is not lacking either. As for adulterers and fornicators, Alphonsus de Castro reports that Martin de Magistris taught that fornication is not a sin, because Scripture contains no express testimony on the matter. A Papist bears witness here to a Papist. And those who know French affairs know that the monk Cahier taught that adultery is not forbidden by the seventh commandment, but that the Hebrew word must be explained in another way. The Libertines, against whom that great servant of God, Calvin, wielded his pen most vigorously, taught that no actions forbidden by the law of God, such as theft and adultery, are sins, for sin is only an opinion. From this it is also plain that the Arminians, on pp. 198–199 above, were wrong to say: The devil has never tried to twist this sense through anyone: unbelievers and the impious, as such, cannot be saved without repentance. For who does not see that the Libertines twisted it, or indeed, as far as they could, overturned it? As for doctrines concerning faith, the Arminians themselves cannot deny that they have been corrupted in various ways; but these good men call this to hold varying views about the explanations of terms. And I ask: do not those men corrupt those doctrines, or rather utterly overthrow them, who dare to teach: That those worship the true God who worship him who is not the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit; that Christ commended the present religion of the Jews as divine; that those who fall away from Christianity to Judaism persist in the worship of the true God? That they say other passages which are clear in their own light can be corrupted through some affection or prejudice is indeed true; but this contradicts their own doctrine, for in the Apology they teach that such things are not simply evident.

units.la: Denique retorsionem quod attinet, quis non videt eam calumniâ niti ac si docerem Scripturæ sensus & quidem omnes in se obscuros, seu non claros,& non manifestos esse? In ea re se calumniari me & mihi injuriam facere ipsi nõrunt, qui suprà in hoc ipso capite sententiam meam exhibuerunt, qua dixi Scripturam sacram suâ naturâ evidentem esse; & praterea evidentem fidelibus h. e. credentibus & assentientibus veritati propositæ Scripturis, denique iis qui ex hostibus convicti sunt. Atque ex his omnibus jam clarum ac manifestum est, subsistere soliditatem argumentorum illorum meorum & frustrà Armianos fraudibus & imposituris suis ea aggressos esse; adeòque verissimum esse doctrinam eorum in Par.I. Arcanorum exhibitam portam patentissimam Atheismo crasso aperire.
units.tr: Finally, as for the counter-charge, who does not see that it rests on a slander, as if I taught that the senses of Scripture, indeed all of them, are obscure in themselves, that is, not clear and not manifest? The Arminians cannot fail to know that they slander me and do me wrong in this matter, since they themselves set out above, in this very chapter, my opinion, in which I said that Holy Scripture is evident by its own nature; and further, evident to the faithful, that is, to those who believe and assent to the truth proposed in the Scriptures, and finally to those who have been convinced by their enemies. And from all this it is now clear and manifest that the solidity of my arguments stands, and that the Arminians attacked them in vain with their frauds and deceits; and therefore it is most true that their doctrine, set out in Part I of the Arcana, opens a very wide gate to gross atheism.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CAP. XI.

units.la: Examen Capitis Ultimi Vindic. lib. 2.
units.tr: Examination of the Last Chapter of the Vindiciae, Book 2.

units.la: 1. Calumnia quadam & falsitates Arminianorum diluuntur. Quæstio an liceat fidem Patrum pro exemplo proponere, decisa breviter ex Scriptura & antiquitate Ecclesiastica. 2. Arminiani non negant ea quæ ipsis objecta erant, ut ostenderetur populos eorum deserere doctrinam eorum ipsosque debere; nec eis fidem amplius deferre debere, & denique causam eorum quinquarticulariam injustissimam esse.
units.tr: 1. Certain slanders and falsehoods of the Arminians are refuted. The question whether it is lawful to propose the faith of the Fathers as an example is briefly decided from Scripture and ecclesiastical antiquity. 2. The Arminians do not deny the things that were objected to them, namely that it was shown that their peoples desert their doctrine and ought to desert them, that they should no longer be trusted, and finally that their Five Articles cause is most unjust.

units.la: 1. CAput undecimum Vindiciarum nihil continet quàm calumnias contra Ecclesias Reformatas earumque doctrinam, nec non convitia quæ mihi dicunt, denique falsitates ac mendaaia quibus causam suam
units.tr: 1. The eleventh chapter of the Vindiciae contains nothing but calumnies against the Reformed Churches and their doctrine, together with the insults they heap on me, and finally the falsehoods and lies by which they commend their cause

units.la: ad eos quos in sententiam suam perduxerunt commendant. Possem igitur plane illud praeterire. Ne tamen habeant de quo conquerantur paucis examinabo ea quae cum specie aliqua dicere forte videntur, caeteris nugis, falsitatibus, calumniis omissis:
units.tr: to those whom they have brought over to their opinion. I could therefore pass it over altogether. Yet, so that they may have nothing to complain of, I will briefly examine those points which may perhaps seem to say something with some plausibility, and I will leave aside the rest of their trifles, falsehoods and calumnies.

units.la: Primo negant quod dixeram, populos qui his Theologis fidem habuerunt circa Quinque articulos, miserè circumventos & turpiter deceptos ab iis fuisse. Judica Lector ex Quatuor Partibus Arcanorum, speciatim ex Parte hac Quarta collata cum ipsorum responso, an non verissimum illud sit: h. e. an non praetextu quinque illorum Articulorum turpiter imposuerint Pastores Arminiani tum toti Orbi, tum speciatim gregibus suis, dum tam horenda monstra enixi illi tandem sunt, quibus gravidi diu erant. Unde patet quales sint magnificae gloriationes eorum, de suae causae bonitate & innocentia sua, quas p. 216. vibrant.
units.tr: First, they deny what I had said, that the peoples who put their trust in these theologians regarding the Five Articles were wretchedly deceived and shamefully misled by them. Let the reader judge from the Four Parts of the Arcana, and especially from this Fourth Part, compared with their reply, whether that statement is not most true: that is, whether the Arminian ministers did not shamefully deceive the whole world, and especially their own flocks, under the pretext of those five articles, while they at last brought forth those monstrous births with which they had long been pregnant. From this it is plain what magnificent boasts they make, on page 216, about the goodness and innocence of their cause.

units.la: Dixeram deinde populos quibus illi imposuerunt secessisse a doctrina quae in his Ecclesiis Belgii antehac communi consensu recepta erat. Hunc enim esse sensum verborum quibus dixi eos secessisse ab ea doctrina Ecclesiarum Reformatarum in qua Patres Belgarum sanctè in Christo vitam duxerunt ac finierunt, unusquisque videt. Negant illi hoc & pag. 217. probationis loco dicunt Melanchtonem in Germania, Bullingerum in Helvetia, Baronem in Anglia, Holmannum in Hollandia, aliosque alibi plures docuisse dogmata quinquarticularia Arminianorum. Egregia scilicet probatio! Addunt alteram probationem, Secessionem primitus a vobis factam non esse lippis & tonsoribus notum est. Ejecti fuistis nobiscum &c. At ego loquutus eram de secessione a doctrina, illi loquuntur de separatione a coetu. Subjungunt ibidem audacissimam falsitatem, dicentes, me dixisse Lutheranos cum Ecclesiarum Reformatarum doctrina in omnibus tam controversis quam non controversis dogmatis consentire. Quod nunquam dixi: Sed utinam mihi liceret dicere illud salva veritate! Dicunt etiam me facere fidem Patrum avorum ac proavorum normam aut exemplum fidei. Id quod falsum est. Saltem enim iis verbis descripsi doctrinam nostram ab adjuncta circumstantia temporis, quod nimirum sit pristina illa doctrina, quae inde ab initio, quo lux Evangelii his Provinciis affulserat, in iis publice annunciata fuerit, non autem ista Arminianorum. Quamvis, si fidem Orthodoxorum Patrum nostrorum exemplum fidei posterorum fecissem, non male fecissem. Nam commendat Scriptura eos qui Religionem veram Patrum ac pietatem eorum secuti sunt, & contra reprehendit eos qui eam non sunt sequuti, prout speciatim videre est in historia Posterorum Davidis. Hinc S. Ambrosius Valentinianum juniorem a matre Justina Ariana seductum τῆς [?] τε πατρὸς ἀντιμιμνῄσκειν εὐσεβείας, ᾗ τὸν κλῆρον παρελκάλει φυλάττειν ἢ παρέλαβεν ἀπλοῦ. revocabit ei in memoriam patris pietatem (Religionem orthodoxam intelligit oppositam blasphemiis Arianorum) & hortabatur ut hereditatem illam quam a Patre acceperat sibi eripi non pateretur ut apud Theodoritum videre est lib.5.c.13.
units.tr: I had then said that the peoples whom they deceived had seceded from the doctrine which had hitherto been commonly received in these Churches of the Netherlands. Everyone can see that this is the meaning of my words, namely that they seceded from that doctrine of the Reformed Churches in which our Dutch fathers lived and died holily in Christ. They deny this, and on page 217, as proof, they say that Melanchthon in Germany, Bullinger in Helvetia, Baron in England, Holmannus in Holland, and several others elsewhere taught the Arminian five-article doctrines. What an excellent proof! They add another proof: That the secession was not first made by you is known to the blear-eyed and to barbers. You were expelled from us, etc. But I was speaking of secession from a doctrine; they speak of separation from a congregation. In the same place they add a most audacious falsehood, saying that I wrote that the Lutherans agree with the doctrine of the Reformed Churches in all doctrines, both controverted and uncontroverted. I never said that; but would that I could say it without violating the truth! They also say that I make the faith of our grandfathers and great-grandfathers the norm or example of faith. This is false. At least I described our doctrine, by an added circumstance of time, as that ancient doctrine which, from the beginning when the light of the Gospel shone upon these Provinces, was publicly proclaimed among them, and not those Arminian doctrines. Yet if I had made the faith of our orthodox fathers an example of faith for their descendants, I would not have done wrongly. For Scripture commends those who followed the true religion and piety of their fathers, and on the contrary rebukes those who did not follow it, as may be seen especially in the history of David's descendants. Hence St. Ambrose, when Valentinian the Younger had been led astray by his mother Justina, an Arian, τῆς [?] τε πατρὸς ἀντιμιμνῄσκειν εὐσεβείας, ᾗ τὸν κλῆρον παρελκάλει φυλάττειν ἢ παρέλαβεν ἀπλοῦ (he means by the orthodox religion the piety of the father, set against the blasphemies of the Arians) — he will recall to his memory his father's piety, and exhorted him not to allow that inheritance which he had received from his father to be snatched away from him, as may be seen in Theodoret, book 5, chapter 13.

units.la: Hic observetur etiam insignis falsitas, qua audent ibidem dicere, plerosque Patrum, avorum, proavorum Belgarum qui Evangelii cognitionem habuerunt, a Calvino & ejus doctrina alienissimos fuisse, ex eo tempore quo Evangelium iis annunciatum fuit. Qua in re ipsi se mendacii arguunt in Responf. ad Excerp. Cll. D.D. Proff. Leydd. in qua Belgas qui sub Hispanico jugo & inquisitione fuerunt, coetus vocant non suos sed nostros; item dicunt expresse eos non suae sed nostrae sententiae addictos fuisse; item non suos sed nostros gemuisse sub illo jugo, vocant etiam eos non suam sed nostram sectam, & denique fatentur se defecisse a Religione Patrum suorum Belgarum. Ita enim p. 126. Videte ergo etiam atque etiam, inquiunt ad modo laudatos orthodoxos Theologos, an non hac ratione Hispanam sive Albanam savitiam olim contra segreges ac non raro armatos coetus VESTROS &c: Item p.125. Nec causam videre possunt Remonstrantes, cur hoc agre ferant Doctores, qui cum suis ὁμοιοῦσιοις hactenus, in primis cum sub jugo Pontificio gemerent, conscientiarum, & sine quibus conscientiis suis satisfieri non posse clamabant, exercitiorum coetuumque libertatem, sibi suaq; sacta postulare, atque ubi opus fuit vi atque armis afferre ac vindicare non dubitarunt. Et p.136. Non sufficiebat olim vobis vestrisque illa clementia, cum publicorum exercitiorum libertatem vobis concedi postulabatis, ne conscientiis vestris vis fieret, &c. Atque haec non tantum erat vestra oratio, cum adhuc sub persecutionum jugo gemebatis. Et p. 127. Hoc unum sufficeret, quod in Remonstrantes fidei quondam vestrae consortes &c. Atqui dicunt locis allegatis, eandem fidem nostram fuisse Patrum nostrorum in Belgio. Itaque defecisse se simul fatentur a fide Patrum suorum. Per consequens salsissimum est, quod dicunt Patres, avos, proavos plerosque fuisse ejusdem sententiae cum Arminianis.
units.tr: Here also one should note the remarkable falsehood by which they dare to say that most of the Dutch fathers and grandfathers who had knowledge of the Gospel were most alien to Calvin and his doctrine from the time the Gospel was preached to them. In this matter they convict themselves of lying in their Response to the Excerpts of the Honourable Professors of Leiden, in which they call the Belgians who lived under the Spanish yoke and the Inquisition not their but our congregations; again they say expressly that they were devoted not to their but to our opinion; again they say they groaned under that yoke not as their but as our sect; and finally they confess that they have fallen away from the religion of their Belgian fathers. For thus on page 126: See therefore again and again, they say to the orthodox theologians just quoted, whether it is not for this reason that the Spanish or Alban cruelty was once directed against the separate and not rarely armed congregations of YOURS, etc. Again, on page 125: The Remonstrants cannot see why the teachers, who with their homoousians have hitherto, especially while they groaned under the Papal yoke, crying out that liberty of conscience, and without which their consciences could not be satisfied, demanded for themselves and their own the liberty of worship and of assemblies, and where necessary did not hesitate to assert and defend it by force and arms, should now take this so hard. And on page 136: That clemency did not suffice for you and yours once, when you demanded that the liberty of public worship be granted to you, lest violence be done to your consciences, etc. And this was not merely your language while you were still groaning under the yoke of persecution. And on page 127: This one thing would suffice, that the Remonstrants were once companions of your faith, etc. Yet they say in the passages cited that our faith was the same as that of our fathers in Belgium. So they simultaneously confess that they have departed from the faith of their fathers. Consequently it is most false that they say the fathers and grandfathers were for the most part of the same opinion as the Arminians.

units.la: Porro, exhortatus eram populos horum Theologorum, ut disputationibus subtilibus illis exigere quod reliquum ipsis vitae est nolint, sed sancte, pie, tranquille pacate nobiscum vivere. Probant illi hoc.& p. 220. dicunt me sanum consilium illis dare. Sed inferciunt, me tantum tria dogmata ad salutem necessaria statuere p. 218. 219. 220. Sed ista summa falsitas ac calumnia est, quam in æternum probare non possunt. Et æque facile quis aquam ex pumice expresserit, ac eam mentem ex verbis meis, quibus dico populos eorum non debere contendere nobiscum Reformatis qui Jesum Christum æternum Deum verumque hominem verâ fide amplectimur, & per solum illius meritum nos justos esse coram Deo credimus, & conamur fidem nostram per bona opera Deo & hominibus probare. Nam posito, omnes eos qui ab his ministris decepti sunt non dissentire a nobis nisi in Quinque articulis; conveniunt utique nobiscum in aliis dogmatibus tam controversis quam non controversis præter illa de Deitate Christi &c. ad salutem necessariis. Et ipsi hic dicunt me in Par. I. Arcan. multa dogmata controversa dicere necessaria ad salutem esse.
units.tr: Further, I had exhorted the peoples of these theologians not to demand, by those subtle disputations, the rest of the life that is left to them, but to live with us holily, piously, quietly and peaceably. They prove this, and on page 220 they say that I give them sound counsel. But they add that I lay down only three doctrines as necessary to salvation, on pages 218, 219 and 220. This is a most gross falsehood and calumny, which they can never prove; and one could as easily squeeze water out of a pumice stone as draw that meaning from my words, in which I say that their peoples ought not to contend with us Reformed, who embrace Jesus Christ with true faith as the eternal God and true man, and who believe that through his merit alone we are righteous before God, and who strive to prove our faith by good works before God and men. For granted that all those who have been deceived by these ministers differ from us only in the Five Articles, they surely agree with us in other doctrines, both controverted and uncontroverted, except those concerning the Deity of Christ, etc., which are necessary to salvation. And they themselves here say that I, in the First Part of the Arcana, call many controverted doctrines necessary to salvation.

units.la: Hortantur postea p.221. suos ad pacem & tranquillitatem colendam nobiscum Reformatis, sed hortantur multo cum felle, & amarulentia, & calumniis, dum dicunt Reformatos gravissimis & summis malis atque injuriis affecisse populos Remonstrantium, & perdere voluisse, eos etiamnum odisse, eorum hostes esse, nullam benevolentiam, nullum amorem in Reformatis erga populos eorum esse. Imo p. 224. nos Magistratus etiamnum sollicitare in excidium populorum eorum qui doctrinæ Arminianæ de Quinque articulis adhærent. Estne hoc ad pacem hortari, eos præsertim quos dicunt virium satis habere ad turbas dandas in Republica? Ab intestinis, inquiunt, motibus & convulsionibus libera erit ( Respublica ) sivos QUANQUAM POTESTIS, turbare nolitis. Vides, Lector, indolem & animum horum hominum.
units.tr: Afterwards, on page 221, they urge their people to cultivate peace and tranquillity with us Reformed, but they urge it with much gall, bitterness and calumny, while they say that the Reformed have inflicted the gravest and greatest evils and injuries upon the peoples of the Remonstrants, have wished to destroy them, still hate them, are their enemies, and that among the Reformed there is no goodwill or love toward their peoples. Indeed, on page 224, they still incite us to stir up the magistrates to the ruin of those peoples who cling to the Arminian doctrine of the Five Articles. Is this to exhort to peace, especially those whom they say have strength enough to stir up disturbances in the Commonwealth? The Commonwealth, they say, will be free from internal movements and convulsions (the Commonwealth) if you do not wish to disturb it, although you CAN. You see, Reader, the disposition and mind of these men.

units.la: Dicunt p. 221. 222. sua dogmata non esse impia, blasphema; se non introducere Libertinismum, seu Atheismum. Iudicet Lector, ex consideratione dogmatum illorum quæ a nobis Partibus Quatuor Arcanorum sunt exhibita. Et quia dixeram Arcana ista horrenda ipsorum fluere ex doctrina eorum de prædestinatione, Libero arbitrio, & gratia Dei (quod ut vidimus Par. III. lib. 2. cap. 11. ipsi fatentur) adeo ut nemo renunciare possit horrendis istis dogmatis sive Arcanis, nisi doctrinæ isti tanquam fonti eorum renunciet: inferunt, exinde sequi me totam antiquitatem arguere ream istorum horrendorum quæ dixi dogmatum; item Libertinismi & Atheismi. Sed illud non sequitur, nam tota Antiquitas non fuit addicta doctrinæ ipsorum de Libero arbitrio, & qui ex Patribus Liberum arbitrium hominis irregeniti asseruerunt, nequaquam eò prolapsi sunt & excurrerunt quò Arminiani: verum hoc tantum sequitur, Patres illos errasse, & errare omnes eos qui doctrinam Arminianorum rum de Libero arbitrio, ampleƈtuntur, quandoquidé ex eâ doƈtrinâ illa Arcana Arminianismi necessario fluunt,ut luce clarius meridianâ & ipso- rum Arminianorum propris verbis ostendere possem. Cæteras calumnias & falsitates omnes, speciatim quas paginis duabus ultimis contra doƈtrinam nostram de præde stinatione evomunt, præteréo,ut initiò monui.
units.tr: They say (pp. 221, 222) that their doctrines are neither impious nor blasphemous, and that they do not introduce Libertinism or Atheism. Let the reader judge from the doctrines themselves, as we have set them out in the Four Parts of the Arcana. Because I had said that those horrible Arcana of theirs flow from their doctrine of predestination, free will, and the grace of God (which, as we saw in Part III, Book 2, chapter 11, they themselves confess), so that no one can renounce those horrible dogmas or Arcana unless he renounces that doctrine as their source, they infer that it follows that I accuse the whole of antiquity of being guilty of the horrible dogmas I mentioned, and likewise of Libertinism and Atheism. But that does not follow. The whole of antiquity was not committed to their doctrine of free will, and those among the Fathers who asserted the free will of unregenerate man by no means slid and ran as far as the Arminians did. What follows is only this: that those Fathers erred, and that all who embrace the Arminian doctrine of free will err, since those Arcana of Arminianism flow necessarily from that doctrine. I could show this clearer than the midday light, and from the very words of the Arminians themselves. All their other calumnies and falsehoods, especially those they vomit in the last two pages against our doctrine of predestination, I pass over, as I warned at the outset.

units.la: 2. Unum adhuc quod præcipuum est, observandum venit. Ostenderam p. 260. 261. 263. ex propriis hypothesibus horum Theologorum sequi, primò populos Remonstrantium debere eos deserere & ad nos nostramque doƈtrinam redire.
